noticias.titulo: Meta rethinks 2030 climate goals as AI data centres drive emissions up
noticias.resumen: Rising data centre energy needs force Meta to review sustainability targets amid growing corporate climate retreat.
noticias.texto:
Meta rethinks 2030 climate goals as AI data centres drive emissions up
Rising data center energy needs force Meta to adjust its sustainability targets amid growing corporate climate retreat.
Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, has said it is reconsidering its 2030 deadline for reaching net-zero emissions because of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, in the latest sign of a broad corporate retreat from climate pledges.
The company is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing and interim milestones, including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal”, Rachel Peterson, Meta’s vice president of data centres, and Blair Swedeen, its global head of net zero and sustainability, said in the company’s annual sustainability report on Thursday.
Meta reported that its net carbon-equivalent emissions rose 45 percent in 2025 to 11.8 million tonnes, a figure that is itself based on accounting methods that climate advocates view with scepticism.
“When we set our net zero emissions goal, we anticipated steady growth, falling clean energy costs, and changes in the broader system that would enable progress at the pace we envisioned. The reality has been far more complex,” the executives wrote in the report. They said delivering on Meta’s vision “requires building the infrastructure that powers AI”.
What was the pledge?
In 2020, Meta set a goal of net-zero emissions across its entire value chain by 2030, in line with the Paris Agreement, which aims to hold long-term warming to 1.5C (2.7F) above pre-industrial levels.
Net zero means eliminating emissions as far as possible and buying credits from carbon removal projects to offset those that cannot be eliminated. The value chain covers emissions from sources such as purchased goods and services, as well as capital goods such as equipment, buildings and vehicles.
Data centres’ growing footprint
A study published this week in the journal Nature Sustainability found that 403 of the most powerful data centres in the United States accounted for about 2 percent of the country’s electricity use and a carbon footprint comparable to Denmark’s, the AFP news agency reported.
About 1,200 such “hyperscale” data centres are online, and hundreds more are planned. Globally, data centres used about 415 terawatt hours of electricity in 2024, about 1.5 percent of supply, and that could nearly double by 2030, according to the International Energy Agency.
A wider retreat
During US President Donald Trump’s second term, major American businesses have stepped back from environmental commitments.
The trend is not confined to Big Tech. General Motors, which set a goal of selling only zero-emission vehicles by 2035, backed the Trump administration’s weakening of a fuel economy rule this year.
Walmart acknowledged in 2024 that it would miss its first emissions target. Google, which pledged in 2020 to run on carbon-free energy by 2030, said this year that its emissions were still rising.
Coca-Cola and Pepsi have changed the baseline years for their emissions targets and weakened their ambitions.

noticias.titulo: Democrats say law firm gave $11.8m in free services to Trump administration
noticias.resumen: Three top Democrats called Trump's dealings with law firms a case of 'official coercion' and pledged investigations.
noticias.texto:
Democrats say law firm gave $11.8m in free services to Trump administration
Three top Democrats called Trump’s dealings with law firms a case of ‘official coercion’ and pledged investigations.
Democrats in the United States say their investigation has revealed that the law firm Kirkland & Ellis provided at least $11.8m in free legal work to President Donald Trump’s administration.
On Thursday, Representative Jamie Raskin, Senator Richard Blumenthal and Senator Adam Schiff released a statement calling the sum evidence of Trump’s “unprecedented official coercion of major law firms”.
Since Trump returned to the White House for a second term, he has issued executive orders seeking to bar certain law firms from receiving security clearances and government contracts.
His administration has also threatened law firms with workplace discrimination investigations. Those orders and probes have led some of the firms to enter into settlements with the Trump administration, offering millions of dollars in free services.
“We have recently received substantial and profoundly troubling information that this corrupt bargain went much further than originally understood,” the three Democrats said in the statement, citing the $11.8m in services.
They proceeded to request records from nine other law firms, in an effort to determine if they too had done free work on behalf of the Trump administration.
“Since April 2025, the lawmakers have repeatedly demanded answers about the ten firms’ dubious multimillion-dollar deals with President Trump,” the statement said.
“However, to date, the vast majority of the firms still have yet to provide any substantive answers or turn over a single responsive document.”
Midterm shift
The three Democrats involved in Thursday’s statement include lawmakers poised to take leadership roles in investigations during the upcoming 120th Congress.
The Democratic Party won control of both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections.
That will give the party power over Congress’s ability to oversee investigations and issue subpoenas. The new Congress is slated to be sworn in on January 3.
Raskin is currently the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee. Blumenthal, meanwhile, is the ranking member of the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.
Schiff, for his part, gained fame for leading Trump’s first impeachment trial in 2020, over allegations that the president abused his power by seeking Ukraine’s help for his first re-election bid. Trump has previously called for Schiff’s prosecution.
The three Democrats say they received information about Kirkland & Ellis’s free services for the Trump administration two days after the midterm race.
Some $4m in services was reportedly offered to the Department of Commerce. Another $2.2m went to the Department of Defense, and $1.6m was dedicated to the US Postal Service.
Kirkland & Ellis also reportedly gave $2m in services to the US International Development Finance Corporation, an agency that provides loans and development assistance to overseas projects.
The Democrats also said $1.8m went to an “investment entity negotiated between the Trump Administration and Japan to create a $550 billion slush fund”.
Law firms cut deals
In 2025, Kirkland & Ellis agreed to settle with the Trump administration after the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) opened an investigation into the law firm’s employment practices.
It accused Kirkland & Ellis of embracing diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI), a slogan for building greater opportunities for under-represented groups in education and the workplace.
The Trump administration, however, has characterised DEI as illegal discrimination, disadvantaging men and white people.
“The EEOC is prepared to root out discrimination anywhere it may rear its head, including in our nation’s elite law firms,” the commission’s acting chair said at the time.
In a Truth Social post on April 11, 2025, Trump revealed that Kirkland & Ellis had pledged $125m in free services. He also indicated that the EEOC would halt its investigation as a result.
Other law firms likewise entered into agreements to avoid the consequences of Trump’s executive actions or employment-related probes.
Estimates indicate that they collectively pledged nearly $1bn in pro bono services.
The handful of law firms that fought Trump’s executive orders, however, won their cases, with judges ruling the president’s actions to be unconstitutional.
In the case involving the law firm Perkins Coie, Judge Beryl Howell said the executive order against it was an “overt attempt to suppress and punish certain viewpoints”.
Fears of corruption
The Democrats in Thursday’s statement highlighted other concerns with the agreements.
The deals, they said, were announced on Truth Social, Trump’s social media platform. That made “the President the sole judge of whether those firms were complying with their obligations – putting these firms at the political mercy of the Administration”.
The Democrats also warned that law firms like Kirkland & Ellis might be dissuaded from taking on certain clients, for fear of upsetting Trump.
“For people and communities who rely on pro bono lawyers to defend their rights, that could mean facing the full power and intensifying fury of the federal government alone,” they said.
In a November letter obtained by the Reuters news agency, Kirkland said it began negotiating with the Trump administration after rival firm Skadden reached its own deal in March 2025.
It added that its White House agreement has had “little impact” on its pro bono work, telling lawmakers that the firm “still devotes substantial pro bono resources to interests that could be considered ‘progressive'”.
The law firm is represented by prominent Washington litigator Beth Wilkinson of Wilkinson Stekloff. She did not immediately respond to Reuters’s request for comment.

noticias.titulo: ‘Completely messed up everything’: Malawi’s fuel crisis causes chaos
noticias.resumen: Motorists and businesses struggle as shortages disrupt daily life.
noticias.texto:
‘Completely messed up everything’: Malawi’s fuel crisis causes chaos
Motorists and businesses struggle as shortages disrupt daily life.
Blantyre, Malawi – Finding fuel in Malawi has become a daily struggle, with motorists spending hours, sometimes entire nights, waiting for tankers that may never arrive.
As shortages persist, filling stations across the country have become flashpoints for frustration and violence as motorists compete for dwindling supplies.
Ken Mhango, 40, a car flipper in Blantyre, recently drove to a nearby filling station after a friend told him a fuel tanker was on its way. He had gone several days without fuel.
Twelve people were already waiting when he arrived, but the situation soon turned chaotic.
“Minibus drivers and motorcycle taxi operators started arriving and jumping queues. They were so reckless they didn’t care if they bumped your vehicle. A scuffle erupted and I saw others, especially women, desperately trying to keep their place in the queue. It took me four hours to get 20 litres but others spent the night in the queue,” he told Al Jazeera.
Violence at filling stations
The scramble for petrol has increasingly turned violent in Malawi’s cities and towns. Although the Malawi Energy Regulatory Authority publishes daily schedules indicating which filling stations are expected to receive fuel, motorists say uncertainty over deliveries makes it difficult to plan their journeys.
Videos of confrontations have circulated on social media, including footage appearing to show people attacking a man at a filling station. Al Jazeera could not independently verify the circumstances surrounding the incident.
The mayor of Blantyre has also been sued for assault following an incident at a fuel queue, while an attendant was killed after being struck by a vehicle during a commotion at a filling station, according to local media reports.
Purchases are reportedly rationed to 20 litres (5.3 gallons) a day, while motorists sometimes pay attendants for an additional five litres, Mhango said.
“The whole chaos that this has created is hectic. It is very hectic and it has created an atmosphere of uncertainty. This is happening when money is scarce, you have to make sure that you plan properly to survive,” he said.
On another occasion, Mhango arrived at Nyabadwe filling station in Blantyre at 5pm after joining a convoy of motorists searching for fuel. The tanker arrived at 9pm, and did not leave until 1am.
“My schedule has been completely altered. Now commuting is no longer a norm but a luxury. I have two parcels in town but I can’t even manage to go and get them,” he said.
Unable to find sufficient supplies at filling stations, Mhango turned to the black market. He paid 30,000 Malawian kwacha (about $17.31) for two litres of petrol for his father. On another occasion, he suspected fuel bought for his garage had been mixed with water after an engine malfunctioned.
“The crisis has completely changed and messed up everything. As a businessperson who deals with vehicles at my garage, people are no longer bringing their vehicles any more because of lack of fuel. And we can’t take our equipment to follow the client,” he said.
He added that his business was unlikely to meet its monthly targets, forcing him to consider docking the salaries of employees who assist him.
Black market dangers
Selling fuel without the required permits is illegal in Malawi, but shortages have created opportunities for vendors to sell petrol at inflated prices.
Motorists who need to travel for work, business or medical care are increasingly turning to informal sellers despite the high prices and safety risks.
According to GlobalPetrolPrices, petrol in Malawi costs about $3.24 per litre, more than double the global average of approximately $1.52.
The informal trade has also proved deadly. Authorities have stepped up arrests of illegal vendors, while fires and explosions caused by unsafe fuel storage have killed people.
Earlier this year, petrol vendors and motorcycle taxi operators protested in Lilongwe after a suspected black market fuel seller was burned alive in an explosion following a police chase, local media reported.
Malawi’s Nation newspaper has documented at least six deaths from fuel explosions this year, including incidents involving families and children.
Calls for accountability
The shortages, alongside foreign-exchange problems and electricity blackouts, have fuelled demands for government accountability.
The Human Rights Defenders Coalition (HRDC) planned nationwide demonstrations on November 17, calling for the resignation of the energy minister over persistent fuel shortages and power cuts.
The protests were postponed after police said they could not provide adequate security because officers were committed to a governing-party parade scheduled for the same day.
Michael Kaiyatsa, HRDC chairperson, told Al Jazeera that the decision reflected “genuine concerns about public safety”, rather than a retreat from the coalition’s demands.
He described the fuel situation as “heartbreaking”, saying its effects extended beyond transport and commerce to people’s access to essential services.
“It affects access to healthcare, education, food, employment and other essential services; ultimately this is a human rights issue,” he said.
“People are struggling to get their children to school. We have small-scale businesses that are losing money. We have employees that are failing to get to work, and ordinary motorists that are spending hours and sometimes entire days just looking for fuel.”
Kaiyatsa said the shortages were pushing people to buy fuel on the black market, not necessarily because they wanted to break the law but because they were trying to meet their daily needs.
“We must therefore be clear that this is the responsibility of the government to ensure that fuel is normalised,” he said.
While acknowledging the dangers of illegal fuel trading, he said law enforcement must respect human rights and due process.
“We have seen tragic incidents recently involving explosions and fires resulting from petrol being kept in homes. These incidents are serious public safety concerns. However, our position is that law enforcement must be exercised within the confines of the law with respect to human rights, proportionality and due process,” he said.
Livelihoods on the line
In a statement issued hours before the planned demonstrations, the Ministry of Energy acknowledged the difficulties caused by the shortages but rejected accusations of government inaction, saying interventions were under way to restore fuel supplies.
“The current fuel supply challenges are largely attributable to a combination of financial, foreign exchange and logistical constraints affecting the country’s capacity to consistently import petroleum products,” the statement said.
For motorcycle taxi operator Tadala Kachingwe in Limbe, the shortage has meant dwindling earnings and depleted savings. He said he could no longer set aside money to buy relish for his wife in the morning.
“The business has been affected because previously, when fuel was available, I could have some savings but now it’s impossible,” he told Al Jazeera.
Getting his motorcycle into a filling station has also become difficult, with minibuses blocking the entrances.
“I have no idea which queue I should be joining because the minibuses have blocked off all sides of entry into the filling station. I will need to pay caller boys to sneak this motorcycle into that filling station,” he said.

noticias.titulo: El Salvador’s Bukele expected to formalise bid for third presidential term
noticias.resumen: The Salvadoran president has won popularity through a crime crackdown that has granted the state enormous power.
noticias.texto:
El Salvador’s Bukele expected to formalise bid for third presidential term
The Salvadoran president has won popularity at home and abroad through a crime crackdown that has granted the state enormous power.
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele is set to formally register his candidacy for his country’s upcoming presidential race, as he seeks a third consecutive term.
Thursday was the registration deadline for the election, which is slated for February 28, 2027.
The 45-year-old president has been widely expected to seek re-election, a move that would further consolidate his party’s leadership in the Central American country.
Bukele is the founder and leader of the Nuevas Ideas party, which controls El Salvador’s Legislative Assembly by a wide margin.
While El Salvador’s constitution previously prohibited presidents from seeking immediate re-election, the Supreme Court overturned that rule in 2021, paving the way for Bukele to run for a second term in 2024.
Then, in 2025, the Legislative Assembly passed a constitutional amendment allowing Bukele to seek a third term. The amendment also extended the length of a presidential term from five to six years.
Bukele secured his party’s nomination for the 2027 race in July. He is expected to return to the ballot alongside his current vice president, Felix Ulloa.
Bukele’s time in office has been defined by a crackdown on criminal gangs that has won him massive popularity at home and turned him into an icon for the political right across Latin America.
In 2022, his government announced a so-called state of emergency to address high levels of crime in the country.
It empowered the police to make sweeping arrests, but it also heralded the suspension of key civil liberties. Some people were detained without charge. Mass trials have been carried out, with hundreds of defendants being sentenced at a time.
More than 1 percent of the country’s population is estimated to have been arrested as a result, with little due process for those seeking to contest their guilt, according to human rights groups.
Advocates also warn that rights abuses, torture and poor conditions are systematic in Salvadoran prisons.
The state of emergency has been extended for years, although it was initially intended as a temporary measure and the government claims El Salvador’s gangs have been all but dismantled.
The United States Treasury has also accused Bukele’s government of negotiating with the gangs in secret, offering incentives to help lower crime.
But experts say human rights activists and members of the news media have seen their ability to monitor abuses and corruption in the country hampered under Bukele.
Some, like human rights lawyer Ruth Lopez, have allegedly been detained for their work without access to legal support. She has spent more than a year in “incommunicado detention”, according to the group Amnesty International.
Under Bukele, El Salvador has also passed a Foreign Agents Law that allows the government to restrict civil society groups that receive funding from abroad.
Those efforts have prompted allegations that Bukele has weaponised the state against his critics.
But those concerns have done little to dent his popularity, and Bukele is considered the clear favourite to win the election.
A handful of candidates, including Maytee Iraheta of the right-wing Nationalist Republican Alliance and Rafael Aguirre of the left-wing Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front, are also set to contest the presidency.

noticias.titulo: Four bodies recovered after Senegal boat capsizes amid migration surge
noticias.resumen: Search for survivors continues near Yenne as migrant arrivals in Spain's Canary Islands surge by nearly two-thirds.
noticias.texto:
Four bodies recovered after Senegal boat capsizes amid migration surge
Four bodies have been recovered after a migrant boat capsized off Senegal’s coast, as authorities continue searching for survivors amid fears that the death toll could rise significantly.
Boubacar Seye, president of the nonprofit Horizons Sans Frontieres, confirmed the latest death toll to the Reuters news agency on Thursday, a day after the vessel capsized near the coastal town of Yenne, south of Dakar.
A local official said at least 50 people were aboard the boat, which struck a rock while migrants were being transferred from smaller fishing vessels to a larger wooden pirogue.
The number of people still missing remains unclear.
Canary Islands
The incident comes amid an intensifying wave of attempted Atlantic crossings from West Africa to Spain’s Canary Islands, with migrant boats being intercepted or rescued almost daily.
New figures from Spain’s Interior Ministry show that 24,364 migrants reached the Canary Islands between January 1 and November 15, compared with 14,690 during the same period last year, an increase of nearly two-thirds.
The ministry had recorded just 13,327 arrivals by the end of October, meaning 11,037 people reached the archipelago in the first 15 days of November alone.
The surge has persisted despite extensive maritime operations. Senegal’s navy said it had rescued or intercepted 1,424 people on November 16 and 17, including passengers aboard nine fishing boats, according to the Senegalese Press Agency (APS).
Cheikh Sadibou Senghor, head of Senegal’s National Division for Combating Migrant Smuggling, said authorities had intercepted 6,889 people in operations linked to irregular migration, prevented 107 departures and dismantled 88 smuggling networks between January and November, APS reported.
Just days before the boat capsized, authorities announced the dismantling of a suspected migrant-smuggling network in Yenne itself, arresting 14 people and seizing two boats, three engines and 12.5 million CFA francs ($22,000), according to APS.
Nearly 600 dead
The United Nations refugee agency said nearly 600 people had died trying to reach the Canary Islands from West Africa so far this year, highlighting the dangers of the increasingly busy migration route.
As authorities struggle to contain the surge, Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has called for greater efforts to improve employment opportunities for young people.
At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Faye requested a detailed assessment of the challenges facing efforts to curb irregular migration, according to a government statement cited by Reuters.
But Seye warned that tougher enforcement measures alone would not prevent further tragedies.
“We need to wake up to the gravity of the situation. The strategy deployed until now is not working,” he told Reuters.
“We need to fix the root causes of this problem.”

noticias.titulo: Six killed in suspected gas explosion at Georgia apartment building
noticias.resumen: Georgian Interior Minister Sulkhan Tamazashvili said rescuers had recovered six bodies from the wreckage.
noticias.texto:
Six killed in suspected gas explosion at Georgia apartment building
Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze said authorities would temporarily relocate 28 families.
Six people, including a child, have been killed after a suspected natural gas explosion caused part of a five-storey apartment building to collapse in Georgia’s capital, Tbilisi, according to the AFP news agency.
The blast struck the residential building in the suburban Ponichala district on Thursday morning, trapping several residents beneath the rubble.
Georgian Interior Minister Sulkhan Tamazashvili said rescuers had recovered six bodies from the wreckage, including that of a young child.
A three-year-old girl was pulled alive from the rubble after several hours of rescue operations, prompting applause from onlookers gathered at the scene.
Emergency Management Service chief Teimuraz Mgebrishvili said one of the women found dead was believed to be the girl’s mother, according to AFP.
Doctors at Ingorokva University Clinic said the rescued girl was in stable condition and scans had revealed no serious traumatic injuries, Georgian Public Broadcaster (1TV) reported.
An 11-year-old boy was also being treated in intensive care, although his condition was described as relatively stable, according to the broadcaster.
Tamazashvili said preliminary findings indicated that the explosion occurred on the fifth floor when a resident attempted to switch on a gas heater.
However, gas supplier Tbilisi Energy said the apartment identified as the likely source of the explosion had been registered as unoccupied and had recorded no gas consumption over the past year, according to 1TV. The company said it had not yet been able to inspect the damaged property.
Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze said authorities would temporarily relocate 28 families, comprising more than 100 residents, to hotels after structural assessments found two sections of the building unsafe, according to Georgia’s Interpressnews agency.
Prosecutor Levan Vepkhvadze said a criminal investigation had been launched into possible violations of safety regulations.

noticias.titulo: US signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months
noticias.resumen: US House committee releases chip export data amid scrutiny of former Nvidia CEO's alleged links to a Chinese spy.
noticias.texto:
US signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months
The US House Foreign Committee released the chip export licensing data amid Nvidia’s ex-CEO’s affair with alleged Chinese spy.
The administration of United States President Donald Trump approved exports of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026, the House Foreign Affairs Committee has said.
The Department of Commerce’s approvals covered exports of 879,000 chips, including 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD, the committee said on Thursday.
Companies had sought permission to ship 3.4 million of them to China during the period, committee documents show.
The unusual release of chip export licensing data comes as the Trump administration faces heightened scrutiny following revelations about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which fuelled renewed calls for a tougher stance against Chinese technology threats.
All four of the Chinese companies highlighted in the committee report are on the Pentagon’s list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies.
The committee chair, Brian Mast, has “exercised his authorities under the Export Control Reform Act to publicly reveal export control license application information regarding NVIDIA and AMD’s AI chip licenses for the People’s Republic of China”, the committee said in a statement. It was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipments of the chips, which included Nvidia’s H200 and AMD’s equivalent MI325X.
News surrounding Huang has turned a spotlight on instances of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialling up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech threats.
“The fact that over 30 percent of the AI chips sent to China were shipped to companies that the Department of War has designated as Chinese military companies is astonishing, and calls into question whether Commerce conducted any serious national security review before approving these licenses,” said Chris McGuire, a former US official and expert on the US-China technology battle.
Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were “subject to strict conditions and limited volumes”. It added that “despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China”.
AMD did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Former US President Joe Biden had restricted Chinese access to the prized chips over fears that they would supercharge China’s military and erode the US lead in artificial intelligence.
But Trump in December gave the green light for Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to China, rolling back Biden-era restrictions and drawing fierce criticism from China hawks across the US political spectrum.
Nvidia’s stock ended the day down 3.3 percent, while AMD slumped 7.7 percent and the broader Nasdaq and S&P 500 were down 2.2 percent and 1.8 percent, respectively.

noticias.titulo: Haiti police say at least 34 suspected gang members killed in raid
noticias.resumen: Police say the raid targeted the Martissant area, located on a key route out of Port-au-Prince held by gangs since 2021.
noticias.texto:
Haiti police say at least 34 suspected gang members killed in raid
Police say the raid targeted the Martissant area, located on a key route out of Port-au-Prince held by gangs since 2021.
At least 34 suspected gang members were killed in a police operation in Martissant, a neighbourhood in Haiti’s capital that has been under gang control for more than five years, Haitian police said.
Haiti’s National Police, which posted footage of armoured vehicles moving through the neighbourhood, said their officers carried out the raid on Thursday with an anti-gang task force that includes personnel from Vectus Global, the private security firm founded by Blackwater founder Erik Prince.
Police reported no other casualties and said none of the roughly 2,500 Salvadoran troops in Haiti took part.
The Martissant neighbourhood is located along a key road that connects Port-au-Prince to Haiti’s western and southern cities, and was used by thousands of people daily before rival gangs began fighting to control the area in 2021.
The subsequent violence forced at least 19,000 people to flee their homes, according to a July 2022 UN report.
Armed groups have since demanded payment for using the road or shot at cars that have tried to pass through, making it difficult to bring goods in and out of the city.
Separately, the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force said it was stepping up operations in Tabarre after months of night patrols and efforts to identify gang positions.
“The objective is clear: not just to displace gangs, but to dismantle their hold on communities, reclaim territory, and prevent their return,” the force said on X.
In the central Artibonite region, the force said their troops had come under fire while clearing barricades and filling in trenches that gangs had dug along National Route 5, north of the town of Gros-Morne.
“During the operation, gang members opened fire on GSF personnel, who responded and forced them to withdraw,” said the update on X.
The raid in Martissant comes as Salvadoran troops have been carrying out joint operations with Haitian police. El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele initially sent troops to search for four Salvadoran aviation technicians who went missing after an October 18 ambush near Port-au-Prince.
What began as a search for the missing men has since grown into a broader offensive against Haiti’s gangs.

noticias.titulo: US appeals court lets Trump end TPS deportation protections for Venezuelans
noticias.resumen: The appeals court's ruling prevents a lower-court decision from taking effect, which would block Trump from lifting TPS.
noticias.texto:
US appeals court lets Trump end TPS deportation protections for Venezuelans
The appeals court’s ruling prevents a lower-court decision from taking effect, which would block Trump from ending the TPS programme.
A United States appeals court has allowed the administration of President Donald Trump to move forward for now with the removal of deportation protections for Venezuelans.
The ruling on Wednesday cancels out a previous order by a lower-court judge that required the government to restore the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) of Venezuelans, which shields recipients against deportation.
The effort to end the TPS protections has proceeded despite humanitarian concerns.
Since taking office for a second term, Trump has sought to carry out what he calls the largest deportation effort in US history. Part of that agenda has been to roll back programmes like TPS.
But in September 2025, US District Judge Edward Chen blocked the expiration of TPS protections for Venezuelans, arguing that deporting those individuals would put them in harm’s way.
He also ruled that the Trump administration had overstepped its authority by seeking to shorten TPS extensions granted under the preceding president, Joe Biden. Such decisions, Chen added, needed to be taken with “careful study and analysis”.
Some 600,000 Venezuelans in the US were protected under TPS programmes.
The Supreme Court paused Chen’s ruling in October 2025. But that pause expired this month, and Chen’s order was set to take effect on Friday.
On Wednesday, the Trump administration filed an emergency request to the Supreme Court to extend the pause before Thursday’s appeals court ruling.
The appeals court’s decision does not nix the ongoing legal challenges to Trump’s efforts to revoke TPS extensions. But it allows the administration to suspend deportation protections while the challenges make their way through court.
The Trump administration has sought to strip large numbers of immigrants of their legal protections in a bid to render them deportable. Other programmes, like humanitarian parole, have also come under the administration’s scrutiny.
TPS allows foreign nationals already in the US to remain while conditions in their home countries are too dangerous or unstable to return to.
Humanitarian parole, meanwhile, allows people outside the US to come in on a temporary basis, often to escape similarly perilous conditions.
The Trump administration has argued that TPS designations are meant to be temporary — and that previous presidencies extended such protections without cause.
It has also maintained that conditions have improved in places like Venezuela, where a US military action on January 3 resulted in the abduction of President Nicolas Maduro.
Human rights advocates, however, have noted that Maduro’s government remains largely intact. That leadership has been accused of abuses ranging from arbitrary imprisonment to the torture of political dissidents.
The US Department of State currently warns against travel to Venezuela, citing issues such as crime, kidnapping and poor health infrastructure.

noticias.titulo: Why are Bukele’s Salvadoran troops in Haiti and what have they achieved?
noticias.resumen: With crowds rallying behind El Salvador's deployment in Haiti, analysts question whether civilians are any safer.
noticias.texto:
Why are Bukele’s Salvadoran troops in Haiti and what have they achieved?
With crowds rallying behind El Salvador’s deployment in Haiti, analysts question whether civilians are any safer.
The streets of Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince, rang out on Tuesday and Wednesday with chants from local residents in support of a president who was not their own: El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele. In a country where the scars of foreign intervention run deep, some Haitians are placing their hopes on another foreign force, this time from El Salvador, to help take their neighbourhoods back from armed gangs.
Thousands turned out to cheer on the roughly 2,500 soldiers Bukele has sent since October. What began as a narrow mission to rescue four missing Salvadoran aviation technicians has grown into a much broader military operation.
For some of those who marched, the intervention is exactly what the country needs after years of kidnappings, killings, and displacement, with little sign of relief.
But even with the Haitian government’s backing and a warm reception from the public, questions are growing about what the troops are doing on the ground and what kind of mark Bukele will ultimately leave on Haiti.
Why are Salvadoran troops in Haiti?
The immediate trigger came on October 18, when four Salvadoran aviation technicians working with the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) went missing after armed men attacked their vehicle near Port-au-Prince.
The force was created to help Haitian authorities deal with a security crisis that has grown more severe since the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moise. According to Reuters, gangs now control more than 80 percent of the capital region, with Haitian and international forces struggling to reclaim that territory.
Shortly after the technicians went missing, Bukele announced a new military operation in Haiti, sending 100 special forces soldiers to rescue them. Since then, he’s sent about 2,500 in total.
Most of them are operating outside the UN-backed force and outside the UN support office’s monitoring mechanisms, according to UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric.
And the deployment itself has turned from a narrow rescue operation to a broader offensive against Haiti’s gangs, with Salvadoran soldiers joining Haitian security forces, the GSF, and private contractors, including Blackwater founder Erik Prince’s Vectus Global.
Bukele, who gained international notoriety for a crackdown on gangs in El Salvador that led to a sharp decline in crime but has drawn widespread condemnation over human rights abuses, has been aggressively promoting the deployment on social media.
He has posted dramatic videos of helicopter attacks on gang leaders’ properties and, more recently, footage of rallies cheering on his troops.
“I never expected anything like this,” he wrote in a Tuesday post accompanying a video of a rally. “I hear you loud and clear. I love you, too.”
Neither the Haitian government nor the Salvadoran government replied to Al Jazeera’s requests for comment about the troops in Haiti.
Why are some Haitians cheering on the Salvadoran troops?
The troops have landed amid a worsening humanitarian crisis in Haiti, with nearly 1.5 million people displaced from their homes, and violence making it difficult to access food and basic services. More than 22,000 people have been killed in gang-related violence, including security operations, since 2022, according to Reuters.
At rallies in Port-au-Prince and other parts of Haiti, demonstrators voiced support for the deployment. Some who spoke to The Associated Press news agency described losing loved ones to gang violence and being forced to leave their homes.
“The support we see from many Haitians comes from sheer desperation after years of failure and widespread terror,” Louimann Maceus, president of the human rights organisation Ensemble des Citoyens Competents a la Recherche de l’Egalite des Droits de l’Homme en Haiti (ECCREDHH), told Al Jazeera. “People are exhausted.”
“There is a genuine hope, especially among the hundreds of thousands of internally displaced people we work with who just want to return safely home,” said Maceus, who lives in Port-au-Prince.
That hope, he said, follows years of frustration with UN-backed forces, which he said had done little to improve security.
The Salvadoran deployment already outnumbers the GSF, according to numbers from the GSF’s special representative Jack Christofides, on October 18, when it had just surpassed 2,000 personnel.
International Crisis Group analyst Diego Da Rin also links some of the enthusiasm to what he describes as a really effective communication campaign by Bukele, whose videos of strikes on gang leaders’ homes are all over Haitian social media.
“These are symbolic wins that everybody was waiting for,” he said, adding that AI-generated videos were also circulating of gang leaders being arrested.
But support for the deployment is not universal. Da Rin pointed to the residents of gang-controlled areas.
“Many of these people, who clearly see the risks in these iron-fist operations, are extremely scared of being attacked and being collateral damage of any of these operations,” said Da Rin.
What have Salvadoran troops actually achieved?
Security force clashes and drone strikes targeting gangs increased by 46 percent in the 21 days after the start of the deployment, compared to the 21 days before it, according to the conflict monitoring group the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED).
ACLED estimated more than 100 people were killed in the same period, including at least 26 civilians.
Haiti’s Justice Minister Patrick Pelissier, however, said on Monday that the government had received no reports of civilian casualties in the latest operations, which it described as professional, according to Reuters.
Bukele has used social media to highlight what he sees as the offensive’s successes.
After Salvadoran troops joined Haitian police and a government task force in a November 8 attack on a house belonging to Wilson Joseph, leader of the powerful 400 Mawozo gang, Bukele posted video of helicopters repeatedly firing at the building, as people ran away from the area.
Joseph reportedly was not there and survived the attack.
A few days later, Haitian national police and Bukele announced that they’d retaken control of the national football stadium. Bukele shared video of robot dogs armed with rifles moving through the corridors of the stadium alongside troops, although it’s unclear how exactly they were used in the operation.
Da Rin said it was worth noting that police initially credited their officers and the task force with retaking the stadium before handing control over to Salvadoran troops, who set up a base there.
The stadium is a useful spot to launch operations against nearby gang strongholds, he added, but it represented a relatively small gain from positions Haitian forces had already secured.
On Wednesday, Bukele posted another video showing a helicopter attack on the home of Jeff Larose, leader of the Taliban gang, which controls the area of Canaan in northern Port-au-Prince.
It was not clear whether the attack had killed Larose or whether Haiti’s police or army had participated. The GSF was not involved, according to The Associated Press.
For displaced people looking to return home, the gains have yet to make a tangible difference, said Da Rin.
After the attack on Joseph’s house, none of the security forces set up a permanent presence in the area, he said.
“Armed groups were able to return and are now intimidating residents, searching their phones, threatening people suspected of sharing information with the security forces,” Da Rin told Al Jazeera.
He warned that forces appeared to be “in a race” to show results without a unified strategy to sustain them.
Salvadoran officials have said they plan to leave once the missing technicians are found. Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, told the Associated Press earlier this month that they were dead, but their fate remains officially unknown.
“The priority should be to plan the most difficult part, how the forces will work together to establish lasting control,” said Da Rin.
Why are some experts concerned about the deployment?
The terms of the Salvadoran deployment haven’t been made public.
Amnesty International has called on both governments to explain who oversees the troops, what rules govern their use of force, and how civilians can safely report abuses.
On Monday, Salvadoran Vice President Felix Ulloa said the agreement would be kept under wraps until diplomatic conditions allowed its release and accused critics of having a “hidden agenda”.
Sam Vigersky, a fellow with the Council on Foreign Relations who studies emergency relief in response to armed conflict, said the lack of monitoring or publicly shared rules of engagement for Salvadoran troops operating outside the GSF means “we do not know what collateral damage might come of these offensives”.
For Vigersky, the lesson from past interventions, including a UN peacekeeping mission whose personnel brought cholera to Haiti and were implicated in widespread sexual abuse, is that “oversight matters”.
“Absent that,” he said, “the deep scars that Haiti has already from these past UN or other operations are only likely to grow.”

noticias.titulo: Will the Shenzhen summit safeguard world peace?
noticias.resumen: Xi, Putin and Trump issue 'Peace Declaration' after historic summit.
noticias.texto:
Inside Story
Will the Shenzhen summit safeguard world peace?
Xi, Putin and Trump issue ‘Peace Declaration’ after historic summit.
A three-way meeting between the leaders of China, Russia and the United States has yielded a number of commitments.
Xi Jinping hosted Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in the city of Shenzhen, China on Thursday.
In a joint statement called a “Peace Declaration”, the three countries’ presidents pledged to safeguard international security and increase the production of refined petroleum products.
They also stressed that a nuclear war should never be fought because it cannot be won.
And they agreed to keep channels of dialogue open to resolve conflicts such as the war in Ukraine.
But how will Xi, Putin and Trump turn these commitments into actions?
Presenter: James Bays
Guests:
Andy Mok – Senior research fellow at the Center for China and Globalization
Aaron Glasserman – Distinguished fellow at the Weatherhead East Asian Institute at Columbia University
Alexander Bratersky – Independent journalist and specialist in Russian foreign policy and Russia-US relations

noticias.titulo: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling
noticias.resumen: A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay , if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya. noticias.texto:
Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.
The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.
Lawyers representing Rohingya survivors say patterns of behaviour by Myanmar’s military, including killing people as they fled, show clear attempts to destroy the group during assaults on Rakhine state in 2016 and 2017.
It is the role of independent judges to interpret the genocide convention. However, judges at the court have taken advice on how to protect their assets from potential US sanctions, as a genocide ruling could be interpreted by Washington as lowering the “legal threshold” for the crime.
The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, an influential thinktank close to the White House, has predicted a genocide ruling will lead to the US imposing sanctions on the ICJ.
The US and Israel fear the final judgment may clarify how to establish a government’s intent to commit a genocide, and so set a precedent that makes it more likely the court will later rule that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Myanmar, which has denied carrying out a genocide, claims its actions targeted a military uprising by insurgents.
The ICJ, sometimes described as the UN’s top court, is responsible for settling interstate disputes, unlike the international criminal court (ICC), which prosecutes individuals accused of war crimes and other international crimes.
The US has already imposed crippling sanctions on judges at the ICC after the court issued arrest warrants against the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The US has also announced sanctions against the entire ICC as an institution, which it described as a “rogue court”. Washington fears the ICC could go after US troops.
The Gambia, as a litigant, was entitled to appoint an ad hoc judge in the case against Myanmar and chose the South African lawyer Pillay, who in October was awarded the Nobel peace prize. She is required to act as a jurist and not an advocate for the Gambia.
Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, has sent a warning shot to Pillay and the 15 ICJ judges, saying Washington “will not allow globalist, faux judges to weaponise the law against our troops”.
Waltz asserted last month: “The ICJ ad hoc judge Navi Pillay is tipping the scales on the ICJ’s current proceedings on Myanmar, intending to lower the legal threshold for proving genocide so that weakened and false standard can later be weaponised against American and allied soldiers whenever they raise a finger against terrorists that hide behind civilians.”
In remarks addressed to Pillay, he said: “We see your agenda and we’ll be watching the ICJ’s handling of these proceedings very closely.”
In a speech last Friday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said: “For this global elite, international law … is an instrument to advance their interests under the pretence of universal principles.”
He warned the ICC against quoting laws to “men with swords”.
Israel has previously criticised adverse advisory opinions issued by the ICJ and refused to implement 2024 orders requiring Israel to admit more aid into Gaza, and to cooperate with Unrwa, the UN relief and works agency.
In the Myanmar case, a 24-page submission jointly filed by the UK and five other mainly European states, argued that the ICJ, in judging intent to commit genocide, should examine a range of “facts and circumstances” assessed “comprehensively and holistically”.
It also stressed that genocide was not solely defined by killings, and that the treatment of children, gender-based violence and forced displacement were also relevant.
The US until recently had taken a relatively more benign view of The Hague-based ICJ, and under Antony Blinken as US secretary of state determined that Myanmar had committed genocide.
The 15 ICJ judges are elected for nine-year terms by the UN security council and the UN general assembly.
Rubio has given the ICC until April to respond to his criticisms before he imposes sanctions.
On Friday, the ICC formally decided to drop plans to prosecute US soldiers and intelligence agents for potentially unlawful acts in Afghanistan. The shelving of the near-dormant inquiry came after it was agreed evidence would be hard to obtain, but one side-effect may be a greater willingness on the part of the US to abandon its plan to impose sanctions on the ICC.

noticias.titulo: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
