noticias.texto:
The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.
The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.
The disclosure raises broader questions about the EU-Egypt relationship, as Egyptian authorities face scrutiny over shrinking press freedom following the jailing and alleged torture of six journalists, the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, a factchecking and investigative platform, and the closure last month of one of the country’s last independent news outlets and conviction of its high-profile editor, Lina Attalah.
Attalah is appealing against that conviction and will be in court this week as she seeks to overturn other charges including “publishing false news”, for which she was sentenced to a year in prison in absentia without her knowledge.
The spotlight is on €5bn in EU “soft” loans to Egypt – lending with easy repayment terms, known as macro-financial assistance, that is meant to be available only to countries that respect human rights and democracy. While the EU conditions on democracy and rights are vague, the loans impose much more specific requirements on Egypt to carry out economic reforms.
Separate data sources – from leaked EU documents and deleted from an Egyptian government website – raise questions about the European Commission’s claims that Egypt met targets linked to social welfare programmes, which enabled the EU to release €2.5bn in assistance.
In confidential documents, the commission told EU lawmakers that Egypt had “broadly fulfilled” and then “fulfilled” two separate targets to increase the numbers of poor people on social welfare programmes between 2024 and 2026. But data points to a net reduction of 85,734 households as the Egyptian government removed people from its welfare programmes rather than expanded coverage.
If Egypt had expanded the programmes in line with the EU’s apparent conditions – and not removed any households – about 245,000 households, equivalent to roughly 909,000 people, would be getting these benefits. (The Guardian used World Bank data to make this rough calculation).
According to the leaked documents, the commission wanted Egypt to “further expand cash transfer programmes”, but despite a net reduction in beneficiaries it gave the green light anyway to two separate “soft” loans totalling €2.5bn.
In response to the Guardian’s findings, one of the European parliament’s leading spokespeople on EU-Egypt relations, the Dutch MEP Tineke Strik, said she was introducing a question to the European Commission demanding clarification.
“The finding by this investigation that the commission is seemingly sugarcoating Egypt’s performance is worrying,” Strik said. “From the beginning, the commission has used macro-financial assistance primarily as a tool to lure Egypt into migration cooperation, while considering formal conditions and its reporting obligations towards parliament as an inconvenient formality.”
Under the plan, Egypt has so far received €3.5bn in soft loans in three instalments, with a final payment of €1.5bn expected before the end of 2027.
The charge of sugarcoating figures relates to two social welfare programmes: the Takaful and Karama cash transfer programmes for poor and vulnerable households.
The Takaful (Solidarity) programme gives poor families cash payments as long as recipients have regular health visits and good attendance at school. The Karama (Dignity) programme gives unconditional cash payments to people living with a disability, older people, orphans and widows.
One of the EU conditions for Egypt to gain the first €1bn loan was to increase the number of Takaful and Karama beneficiary households by 100,000 to 4.7 million.
In a leaked report to lawmakers in the EU council of ministers and the European parliament, the commission described that requirement as “broadly fulfilled”.
The data in that report, however, reveals a net fall of 62,281 households during this period, owing to what the EU officials describe as “a multi-annual recertification process”. Some beneficiaries were added to the list but a larger number were removed because they were deemed ineligible.
In order to achieve a later instalment of €1.5bn, Egypt was required to “further expand” the programmes, adding 60,000 households to the Takaful and Karama beneficiaries list. A second leaked report to EU lawmakers shows that the commission concluded the target was “fulfilled” because 442,118 families were added to the list.
On this occasion, the commission did not report on numbers removed. Figures from Egypt’s ministry of social solidarity, however, show a net reduction of 23,453 beneficiaries to the programmes in the 11 months until June 2026, the period leading up to the release of that payment. The EU announced the release of the €1.5bn payment in July 2026.
The data has since been deleted from the Egyptian ministry website but the Guardian has seen screenshots and archived webpages.
During a period from 2024 to 26 when the EU required Egypt to add 160,000 households to the rolls of the Karama and Takaful programmes, there was a net decline of 85,734 households.
Timothy Kaldas, the deputy director of the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy, said the commission had generally “done a poor job of leveraging the funds of European taxpayers to support genuine stabilisation” on the other side of the Mediterranean. “The strategic interest of Europe is seeing a more economically stable Egypt with a population that is less precarious,” he said.
Sandra Gómez López, a Spanish socialist MEP who recently visited Cairo to assess human rights in Egypt, said the data presented by the Guardian raised important questions. “The commission must explain transparently why it considers these commitments to have been fulfilled and demonstrate that European funding is genuinely contributing to improving social protection for the Egyptian population,” she said.
She stressed that the EU should not withdraw support, “but neither can we allow the country’s strategic importance to lead us to lower our standards when it comes to human rights”.
For critics, the questions about the EU’s willingness to hold Egypt accountable on very precise socioeconomic targets do not bode well for the broader but less defined goals for democracy and human rights.
Strik said: “The fact that Egypt and the commission even seem to ignore the crystal-clear socioeconomic conditions doesn’t increase my expectation that they adhere to the vague precondition on democracy and the rule of law.”
Claudio Francavilla, an associate EU director at Human Rights Watch, said: “Without benchmarks, the EU has turned a human rights conditionality into a blank cheque for Egypt’s authoritarianism.”
In a statement to the Guardian, the European Commission said the policy target on Takaful and Karama referred to new beneficiary families “and not to its net increase”. The spokesperson said there was “no contradiction” between this statement and that in a confidential document that said Egypt was required to “further expand cash transfer programmes”.
Asked about the release of the remaining €1.5bn in promised loans, the commission said it “will be made once all conditions have been met”, referring to 24 economic policy conditions, keeping an IMF programme on track and “taking concrete and credible steps towards respecting effective democratic mechanisms, including a multiparty parliamentary system, and the rule of law, and guaranteeing respect for human rights”.
It added: “Compliance with the conditionality is examined thoroughly” by EU officials and diplomats based on “information provided by the Egyptian authorities and other relevant sources”.
Egypt’s mission to the EU in Brussels did not respond to a request for comment.

noticias.titulo: Hegseth uses Venezuela visit to boast of Maduro’s capture by US military
noticias.resumen: Defense secretary asserts US dominance on trip that would have seemed ‘impossible, almost unbelievable’ a year ago Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro, to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”. Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ru
noticias.texto:
Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro, to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”.
Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ruled since 1999.
Speaking outside the recently reopened US embassy in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Wednesday, Hegseth said: “It’s a great honor to be here as the first United States secretary of war this century to set foot in Venezuela. Just one year ago my presence here … would have been deemed impossible, almost unimaginable.
“In fact, exactly one year ago today … [Maduro] stood on a stage not too far from here and yelled mockingly, ‘Come and get me!’” Hegseth recalled, before adding sarcastically: “Well, we answered that call.
“The reality is that … January 3 is the day that will go down in history as a day of liberation for Venezuela,” Hegseth claimed, although Maduro’s allies continue to hold power with US support.
Earlier in the day, Hegseth was welcomed to the Miraflores Palace by Maduro’s former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who became acting president with Donald Trump’s blessing after his abduction.
In the aftermath of the deadly US attack, Hegseth was one of the bluntest Trump administration voices when it came to celebrating the invasion. “Maduro had his chance … he effed around and he found out,” the defense secretary bragged.
Speaking at the palace, Hegseth struck a more conciliatory tone as he vowed to deepen cooperation with Venezuela’s new leaders in brief comments that were broadcast by the state broadcaster VTV.
“I stand here on behalf of President Trump, who sends his greeting and looks forward to the opportunities, not just militarily … but also economically: the incredible resource capabilities that your country has, that we look forward to unlocking together with you,” Hegseth told Rodríguez and senior cabinet members, including the defense and foreign ministers, Gustavo González López and Oliver Blanco.
Hegseth said his visit to Rodríguez’s “beautiful country” was designed to re-establish and increase “defense cooperation” between “two great militaries” that less than a year ago were briefly at war. Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that Trump officials were trying to negotiate a long-term US troop presence in Venezuela as part of their push for regional hegemony.
“I appreciate your leadership and commitment to your country,” Hegseth told Maduro’s successor, a once outspoken anti-imperialist leftist who has overseen an unlikely realignment with Washington since her ally was grabbed.
During her five-minute address, Rodríguez, whose oil-rich country is widely seen to have become a US protectorate after January’s invasion, made no mention of Maduro, who is behind bars in New York City.
But referring indirectly to his capture and the subsequent reconciliation with Washington, she told Hegseth: “Thanks to the political and geopolitical maturity of our governments, we have – in a very short period of time, just a few months – turned what were very difficult and very tough times for our people, into an extraordinary space for cooperation and mutual benefit.”
Rodríguez hailed the “historic” energy deal her government recently struck with Trump, who has called it “the biggest oil deal in world history” as well as “the spoils” of his “conquest” of Venezuela.
Hegseth claimed the agreement, which reportedly involves 65bn barrels of reserves, “makes the strait of Hormuz a non-factor for the western hemisphere”.
Critics of Rodríguez’s political movement painted Hegseth’s visit as a humiliating act of genuflection for a president with no choice but to roll out the red carpet for the man whose troops captured her boss.
Writing on X, Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent Venezuelan journalist, said Hegseth’s visit was designed to underscore Washington’s “direct administration” of her country.
“Ten months after Nicolás Maduro’s capture, Washington no longer needs to fire shots to remind everyone who is in charge: the mere presence on Venezuelan soil of the architect of the January incursion reaffirms that the country’s operational sovereignty is subject to the White House’s directives,” Reyes said.
Reyes suspected the visit also carried a message for members of Venezuela’s armed forces. “Domestically, the trip forces the military high command to legitimize the man who directed the extraction of their former commander in chief,” she said. “In this regard, I wonder whether it might be a message of discipline intended to prevent any pockets of resistance in the barracks.”
Trump’s attempts to expand his Shield of the Americas anti-cartel coalition of Latin American governments suffered a major blow last month with the defeat of his far-right ally, Flávio Bolsonaro, in Brazil’s presidential election. The leftwing winner, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has indicated his country will not join the initiative.
But Venezuela’s interim government is in little position to resist. During his surprise visit to Venezuela, Hegseth said Venezuela had gone from being “our most aggressive regional threat to [being] a compliant security partner”. He praised Rodríguez for working “closely, pragmatically, and diligently with the United States to stabilize Venezuela”. Hegseth claimed US and Venezuelan armed forces would work together to attack “narco-terrorists” operating on Venezuelan soil, vowing: “We will hunt you down. We will find you. And we will kill you.”
Concluding her speech at the palace, Rodríguez told her foe-turned-friend: “Thank you, secretary, and I wish you a lifetime of happiness.”

noticias.titulo: Apec summit as it happened: Xi welcomes Trump on China visit as Putin claims Europe in ‘humiliating decline’
noticias.resumen: This blog is now closed, you can read more on this story here Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up? That is the question the Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour seeks to address in his piece about the expected, Putin, Trump and Xi, meeting at Apec on Thursday. It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran
noticias.texto:
Apec summit as it happened: Xi welcomes Trump on China visit as Putin claims Europe in ‘humiliating decline’
This blog is now closed, you can read more on this story here
Wed 18 Nov 2026 12.48 EST
First published on Tue 17 Nov 2026 22.46 EST
Wed 18 Nov 2026 12.48 EST
First published on Tue 17 Nov 2026 22.46 EST
Closing summary
- The Associated Press is reporting that Donald Trump plans to hold a meeting with Vladimir Putin on Thursday, citing an anonymous US official. The meeting would be in addition to the blockbuster trilateral talks the two will hold with host Xi Jinping on Thursday.
- Meanwhile, a meeting between the leaders of China, the United States and Russia planned for Thursday in Shenzhen is set to last less than 60 minutes, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media on Wednesday. “No more than an hour” has been set aside for the historic summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, Peskov was quoted as saying by Russian state news agencies.
- Xi Jinping told Donald Trump he hoped their talks would help advance a “constructive, strategic and stable relationship” between China and the US, based on “respect, fairness and reciprocity”, according to China’s state news agency Xinhua. Xi also recalled Trump’s personal welcome at the airport during his visit to the US in September, saying China’s own welcome for the US president reflected its tradition of reciprocity.
- Xi personally greeted Trump on the airport tarmac in Shenzhen, reciprocating the welcome the US president extended to the Chinese leader during his visit to the US in September.
- Before landing in Shenzhen, Donald Trump enjoyed lunch in Manila with Philippine president Ferdinand Marcos Jr at the Malacañang presidential palace. Speaking during a meeting ahead of lunch, Marcos revealed that he had arranged for fried chicken from Filipino fast food chain Jollibee to be delivered to the US delegation as a late-night snack last night, praising Trump for “working very hard”.
- Chinese state media have released a readout of Xi Jinping’s earlier meeting with Vladimir Putin. In it, Xi is quoted as saying China-Russia relations are “unshaken by storms and steady as a mountain”, and have set “an example of a new type of major-country relationship characterised by equality, mutual respect, trustworthiness, and win-win co-operation”.
- Canada’s Mark Carney has hit back at Vladimir Putin’s earlier assertion that sanctions no longer work in this day and age. “Mr Putin can ask his financial institutions, he can ask his oligarch friends, he can ask his hockey players whether or not sanctions are a thing of the past. I think he’ll find out that they’re very real, they’re biting,” Carney told reporters.
- Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum won praise and went viral on Chinese social media on Wednesday for taking an economy flight to attend a regional summit in Shenzhen. World leaders this week descended on the southern Chinese city to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings – many arriving in specially chartered commercial airliners or dedicated government aircraft like US president Donald Trump’s Air Force One.
- It is unclear whether North Korean leader Kim Jong-un will attend the talks, but Trump has floated the possibility. On Wednesday US secretary of state Marco Rubio said the US president was willing to engage, but he did not confirm whether a meeting had been set in Shenzhen.
- Trump said on Wednesday that the US has just concluded a “very big trade deal” with the Philippines, but he did not provide any details, and Manila did not announce any agreement. “We’ve just consummated a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made so far, and it is a fair deal for both countries,” Trump said during a state luncheon at the Philippine presidential palace. Trump is set to arrive in Shenzhen on Wednesday evening.
Trump landed in China on Wednesday seeking to reinforce America’s status as the world’s leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left his administration scrambling to calm the US public.
The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty before the meeting with Xi and Putin.
As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the US worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.
“It’s fine,” Trump said Tuesday from the Philippine capital of Manila, suggesting it was all just a consequence of being a nation that is “big and powerful.”
The meeting between the leaders of China, the United States and Russia planned for Thursday in Shenzhen is set to last less than 60 minutes, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media.
“No more than an hour” has been set aside for the historic summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, Peskov was quoted as saying by Russian state news agencies.
The Associated Press is reporting that Donald Trump plans to hold a separate meeting with Vladimir Putin on Thursday, citing an anonymous US official.
The meeting would be in addition to the blockbuster trilateral talks the two will hold with host Xi Jinping on Thursday.
If confirmed, it would be their first bilateral since they met in Alaska in 2025 for talks that failed to reach a deal on the war in Ukraine.
Trump had already suggested he might meet with Putin, as well as with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, but neither option had been added to his official schedule.
Trump treated to fried chicken by Philippines president
Before landing in Shenzhen, Donald Trump enjoyed lunch in Manila with Philippine president Ferdinand Marcos Jr at the Malacañang presidential palace.
Speaking during a meeting ahead of lunch, Marcos revealed that he had arranged for fried chicken from Filipino fast food chain Jollibee to be delivered to the US delegation as a late-night snack last night, praising Trump for “working very hard”.
The gift may have gone down particularly well with Trump, who has something of a reputation for his love of fast food. The US president has long been associated with McDonald’s and KFC, with his former campaign aides revealing in 2017 that his usual McDonald’s order included two Big Macs, two Filet-O-Fish sandwiches and a chocolate milkshake. The Guardian reported on their revelations at the time in this article:
Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum won praise and went viral on Chinese social media on Wednesday for taking an economy flight to attend a regional summit in Shenzhen.
World leaders this week descended on the southern Chinese city to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings – many arriving in specially chartered commercial airliners or dedicated government aircraft like US president Donald Trump’s Air Force One.
Sheinbaum, however, flew in economy class from Mexico City to Shenzhen on a China Southern Airlines flight, media reports said. She arrived in China on Monday.
Posts on Chinese social media platform Weibo showed the Mexican leader in the plane chatting with passengers, though the photos could not be independently verified by AFP. A hashtag on Weibo about her arrival in China garnered 10.2m views as of Wednesday.
Meanwhile, Sheinbaum said on Wednesday she had a “very good meeting” with her US counterpart Trump as the two countries pursue negotiations aimed at easing trade tensions.
“We continue to make progress on our shared agenda,” Sheinbaum added in a post on X.
Carney and Trump discuss trade deal in meeting on sidelines of Apec summit, PM's office says
The Canadian prime minister’s office has issued a statement following Mark Carney’s meeting with US president Donald Trump on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen.
It said:
 This evening, the Prime Minister, Mark Carney, met with the President of the United States, Donald J. Trump, on the margins of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting, in Shenzhen, China.
The leaders discussed the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement that would create good jobs, boost affordability, and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture, and sovereignty. They agreed to continue the work and to stay in close contact.
Here is more of Xi’s speech (as per Xinhua):
 At tomorrow’s Leaders’ Meeting, we will discuss measures to expand mutual openness, explore pathways for innovation-driven growth, broaden opportunities for pragmatic cooperation in various fields, and promote the implementation of more outcomes. I look forward to discussing the grand plan for Asia-Pacific cooperation and jointly advancing the cause of Asia-Pacific development with you all.
Now, I propose that we raise a glass together.
For the common prosperity of the Asia-Pacific region,
For the success of this informal leaders’ meeting,
For the health of all guests and their families,
Cheers!
Xi hails Shenzhen's transformation in Apec banquet speech
China’s state news agency Xinhua has published the text of Xi Jinping’s welcome speech at tonight’s Apec banquet in Shenzhen.
In his remarks, Xi praised the city’s transformation into an international economic and innovation hub, describing it as a symbol of China’s development.
Here are a few passages from his address:
 This evening, the shores of the South China Sea are aglow with lights, and autumn is in full swing here in Shenzhen, the City of the Phoenix. As the 33rd Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting is about to commence, I would like, on behalf of the Chinese Government and the Chinese people, to extend a warm welcome to all our distinguished guests.
I have often said that to see a thousand years of China, one should visit Xi’an; to see five hundred years of China, one should visit Beijing; and to see a hundred years of China, one should visit Shanghai. Today, I would like to say to you all: to see fifty years of China, come to Shenzhen.
Shenzhen is a place with a rich history. In 1978, when I first came to Shenzhen, it was still a small fishing village. More than 40 years have passed in the blink of an eye, and now it is filled with high-rise buildings and bustling traffic. The changes are truly remarkable.”
Trump and Putin shake hands ahead of Apec welcome banquet
US president Donald Trump shakes hands with Russian president Vladimir Putin, as China’s Xi Jinping looks on, ahead of the welcome banquet at the Apec summit in Shenzhen, China:

noticias.titulo: Religion should be removed from terrorism definition under Australian law as it gives ‘false credibility’, watchdog says
noticias.resumen: Independent National Security Legislation Monitor says reference to religion has ‘contributed to discrimination and violence against religious minorities’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Religion should be removed from Australia’s terrorism definition and making bomb threats should not result in life imprisonment, the country’s national security laws watchdog has said. The highly anticipated report from the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor (INSLM), released Thursday, reviewed how terrorism has been defined in Australia over the past 25 years after
noticias.texto:
Religion should be removed from Australia’s terrorism definition and making bomb threats should not result in life imprisonment, the country’s national security laws watchdog has said.
The highly anticipated report from the Independent National Security Legislation Monitor (INSLM), released Thursday, reviewed how terrorism has been defined in Australia over the past 25 years after a suite of laws were introduced following the September 11 attacks in the United States.
It comes as the Australian Federal Police (AFP) and the Australian Security and Intelligence Organisation (Asio) warn the rise of extremist, violent nationalism has changed the threat landscape and the motivations behind some terrorist attacks cannot be categorised into single ideologies.
Among the recommendations are suggested changes to the definition of terrorism to remove religion, which the INSLM head, Jake Blight, said gives accused terrorists “false credibility” and has a detrimental impact on religious minorities.
“Having a law that requires proof that terrorists were advancing a ‘religious’ cause gives these terrorists false credibility and reinforces their narrative that they are doing holy work,” the report said. “The same individuals will still be able to be prosecuted, but should be described as violent ideologues.
“Reference to religion in the definition of terrorism has also, in practice, contributed to discrimination and violence against religious minorities, especially Muslim Australians. This has a negative impact on social cohesion.”
The current definition of terrorism under the federal criminal code requires agencies to prove an act intends to cause serious harm to people or property in order to advance a political, religious or ideological cause.
A change in terrorism laws to remove religion as a primary motivation and place it as an example of a broader “ideology” category is in line with international best practice, Blight’s report said.
The INSLM noted the UN special rapporteur’s report earlier this year recommended defining terrorism acts by political and ideological causes and omitting religious motives, as references to religion have “discriminatory and stigmatizing effects that outweigh the benefits of criminally denouncing them”.
In his submission to the INSLM, Australia’s special envoy to combat Islamophobia, Aftab Malik, said keeping religion in as a terrorism motivation created a “climate of suspicion” around Muslims and “provided ammunition for far-right extremist narratives”.
Eleven Muslim advocacy and community groups, including the Australian Muslim Advocacy Network, welcomed the report’s recommendations and urged the Australian government to amend the laws.
“Every time someone in authority says that a motivation is ‘religious’, it uplifts ISIS, far-right and harmful media narratives all at once, by officially perpetuating the false premise that Islam encourages terrorism,” their joint statement said.
“This makes all Muslims feel under siege.”
The Executive Council of Australian Jewry, Australia’s peak Jewish body, described the report as “high-quality” but said removing religion as a motivating factor made “little sense when so many notorious terrorist acts have featured motifs, words and images that unmistakably refer to religious doctrines and beliefs”.
“The inclusion of ‘faith’ as a type of ideology does not solve the problem. Faith is not the same as religion and religion is more than an ideology,” the organisation’s co-chief executive, Peter Wertheim, said.
“It is clearly not appropriate for Australian law to decide which beliefs are an authentic expression of a religion and which are not. Even the adherents of a religion may have divergent views about such matters.”
The INSLM’s report made six other recommendations, including separating credible threats of terrorism from actual acts.
Under existing laws, a person found guilty of making a credible terrorist threat can be sentenced to life imprisonment with a mandatory minimum sentence of six years.
The report said the punishment was “disproportionate, unnecessarily complex and out of step with international standards” and recommended terrorism threats be treated as a separate charge with a maximum sentence of no more than five years.
The legislation monitor also recommended raising the bar on designating damage to property and electronic system as acts of terrorism while excluding advocacy, protest, dissent and industrial action.
Asio’s director-general, Mike Burgess, has warned of the rise in violent nationalist extremism in recent years. In an October submission to a parliamentary inquiry into radicalisation, Asio said around 65% of its counter-terrorism caseload related to religiously-motivated violent extremism while 35% related to ideologically-motivated extremism.

noticias.titulo: US warned supplying nuclear-powered submarines to Australia would diminish its own fleet for ‘many years’
noticias.resumen: Congressional Budget Office also questions whether Australian-flagged vessels could be compelled into a conflict with China under Aukus deal Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Providing nuclear-powered submarines to Australia would diminish the US navy’s own fleet for “many years”, a new report for the US Congress has cautioned, questioning whether Australian-flagged vessels could be compelled into service in a conflict with China. The US navy’s latest shipbuilding plan does not countenance the Aukus agreement in its forecasts at all, noting only in a footnote that th
noticias.texto:
Providing nuclear-powered submarines to Australia would diminish the US navy’s own fleet for “many years”, a new report for the US Congress has cautioned, questioning whether Australian-flagged vessels could be compelled into service in a conflict with China.
The US navy’s latest shipbuilding plan does not countenance the Aukus agreement in its forecasts at all, noting only in a footnote that the transfer of any Virginia-class submarine to Australia “has not been factored into the plan”, the report says.
But the Congressional Budget Office has evaluated the impact of Aukus, releasing detailed analysis on Friday morning, finding “the US submarine industrial base is currently struggling to meet the Navy’s demand for submarines”.
“Increasing production further to replace SSNs [attack submarines] sold to Australia would increase the challenges that the Navy and the shipyards are facing,” the report found.
“The sale of SSNs to Australia would reduce the number of attack submarines available to the Navy for many years.”
Under the so-called “Pillar One” of Aukus, the US has agreed to sell between three and five in-service Virginia-class submarines to Australia, beginning in 2032.
The CBO analysis questioned whether any submarines transferred to Australia could be utilised in the event of a US conflict with China.
“Would China be less deterred if the United States reduced the number of its attack submarines to help Australia develop its own submarine force?”
The report argued that because of the longstanding, and robust, alliance between the US and Australia, boosting the Australian navy’s submarine fleet could help offset the US Navy’s “potential loss of capability”.
“That loss might even be more than offset because the Australian submarines would be based in the Western Pacific region and therefore could respond more quickly to any conflict with China over Taiwan or other issues in the South China Sea.
“However, Australia would control its own submarines, and their participation in any particular conflict would not be guaranteed.”
In 2023, Australia’s defence minister, Richard Marles, said Australia would make no promises it would deploy its submarines in support of any US conflict with China, and that any future Australian submarines would be “under the complete control of the Australian government of the day”.
Submarine-building rates in the US have been tenaciously laggard. The country’s shipyards are currently producing Virginia-class submarines at a rate of 1.13 a year: that rate needs to lift that to two submarines a year to service America’s own needs, and 2.33 a year to have additional boats to transfer to Australia.
The CBO report said submarine-building rates had slowed over the past two decades, and Virginia-class submarines were delayed between 24 and 36 months.
“Building … submarines took five to six years in the 2000s but now takes an average of 10 to 11 years, according to current schedules.”
The US legislation governing Aukus states that the president of the US can only transfer a submarine to Australia if losing that submarine from US service “will not degrade the United States undersea capabilities”.
The US can refuse to transfer any submarines to Australia without penalty, under the terms of the Aukus agreement.
Critics of Aukus have said there is vanishingly little chance the US will have the capacity to sell any of its in-service submarines to Australia.
The former foreign affairs minister Bob Carr told Guardian Australia both countries were “living a lie” in upholding the fiction that the submarine deal would happen. “It’s now conventional wisdom in Washington as well as in Canberra that we’re not going to get the subs.”
But the deal has avowed, bipartisan broad political support across both the US and Australia. Marles said earlier this month: “Aukus is happening, our alliance is happening, and all of that continues unimpeded.”
Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, affirmed his support for the Aukus agreement, and the two countries’ commitment “to advance the alliance and strengthen deterrence in the Pacific” at a meeting with Marles in September.
The US Congressional Research Service has openly countenanced an “alternative division of labour” under which no Virginia-class submarines are ever transferred to Australian control.
The research service’s latest report on Aukus, issued in January, considered a revision of the Aukus deal under which the submarines earmarked for sale to Australia were instead retained under US command to be sailed out of Australian bases.
The report argued both for and against the US selling three Virginia-class submarines to Australia, beginning in 2032. But it makes the case that, in the event of a “conflict or crisis” with China over Taiwan, submarines under Australian command could not be ordered into operation, whereas US-commanded vessels, operated out of Australian bases, could be immediately deployed.

noticias.titulo: Israel delays building contracts for West Bank settlement after UK sanctions

noticias.texto:
Israel has postponed issuing contracts for the construction of a large settlement on the West Bank seen as likely to render a two-state solution unviable, days after the UK imposed sanctions against building firms operating in the area.
Israeli diplomats insisted the move was not in response to the measures from Downing Street. Gali Baharav-Miara, the attorney general, said any decision on settlement expansion should not be taken by the caretaker government led by Benjamin Netanyahu but by whatever new administration was formed.
She ordered the Israel land authority and ministry of housing not to open the tender process. Israeli diplomats suggested the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, had acted prematurely on Monday in sanctioning the eight construction firms. But UK diplomats believe the growing political pressure on Israel over settlements, including from US Democrats, is having an impact.
The deferral puts the E1 settlement expansion in the mix for any coalition negotiations. The leader of the Change bloc, Gadi Eisenkot, seen as Israel’s most likely next prime minister, has been clear in opposing violent settler activity, as has the newly elected Knesset speaker, Matan Kahana, an ally of Eisenkot.
Eisenkot has also opposed the E1 settlement expansion, describing it as a mistake likely to alienate international opinion. He said of the plan: “I recall that Netanyahu himself opposed this for a long time, and due to coalition pressure, he gave in and approved it.”
The EI settlement expansion, due to have been announced on Thursday, has long been seen as qualitatively different since the land – between Jerusalem and Ma’aleh Adumim, a West Bank settlement city of nearly 40,000 residents – bisects the West Bank and cuts it off from East Jerusalem.
Miliband has said it would mark the death knell of a future Palestinian state. The UK, along with a group of European countries, has recently recognised Palestine, and the preservation of a two-state solution has been described as the north star of Labour policy towards the region.
The construction tender was published for more than 3,401 housing units in the area. At the beginning of November, the Israel Defense Forces began demolishing homes in a Bedouin community within the E1 area.
Israel has already enforced the downgrading of the UK consulate in East Jerusalem as a reprisal for Miliband’s decision in September to try to end trade links with the illegal settlements.
Bennett said: “The British Labour government’s hostility, bias and one-sided approach are particularly glaring given its failure to take any action against the Palestinian Authority, which continues to encourage terrorism through financial payments, promote incitement in its education system and engage in illegal construction in violation of signed agreements.”
Although the Israeli election was largely fought on domestic security-related issues, Eisenkot seems to be more sensitive to the implications of Israel’s crumbling global reputation, and the need to make efforts to be seen to be listening to the criticism.
If he becomes prime minister, Eisenkot will, indirectly at least, also have to take account of the views of the Arab parties even if these parties are not going to become members of the government.
The group Peace Now welcomed the attorney general’s decision: “A government that lost the elections is not permitted to exploit its final days in power to advance destructive moves that will endanger Israel’s future and its international standing.
Construction in E1 is liable to eliminate the possibility of a two-state solution and drag Israel into a severe diplomatic crisis and international sanctions. The AG’s decision is an important step, but the struggle is not over yet.”

noticias.texto:
An expert has determined that Thomas Markle, the 82-year-old estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex, is mentally competent to face charges of keeping child sexual abuse material in storage in California, a judge said on Thursday.
Markle’s defense lawyer said they would not contest the finding by Dr Amie Gerodimos. The exam was ordered after his arrest at a senior care center in Lakeland, Florida, on 6 November.
Investigators seized approximately 78 items from two storage units rented by Markle in the Los Angeles area, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse images, according to the FBI.
Some images appear to depict him with children, the FBI said.
Markle is in custody while the case remains in federal court in Tampa. It will eventually shift to a similar court in southern California.
Markle was initially released on bond but was arrested again when authorities accused him of cutting off his electronic ankle monitor on 10 November.
He had a stroke earlier this year while living in the Philippines and had to have his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the US and settle in Florida.
The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, reported that Meghan’s half-brother found child sexual abuse images while clearing out their father’s home in the Philippines. The discovery led to a search of the two US storage units in California, which Markle had rented since 2008.
Meanwhile, in the Philippines, Markle is under investigation for possession and intent to distribute images. The Women and Children Protection Center, a branch of the Philippine national police, filed a formal criminal complaint against Markle on Monday, police spokesperson Brig Gen Allen Rae Co said in a written statement.
The complaint was filed with the prosecutor’s office following an investigation into digital devices found at Markle’s former home in Cebu City, the statement said. The prosecutor’s office will assess the case for possible charges.
Markle did not attend his daughter Meghan’s 2018 wedding to Prince Harry at Windsor Castle. She said at the time he needed to tend to his health. Meghan is an American citizen who starred in the US television drama Suits.

noticias.texto:
Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year on a man convicted of killing a pregnant woman and her husband during a home invasion, while Texas put a man to death for the killing of a Houston jeweler during a $3.6m diamond heist.
Thomas Mitchell Overton, 71, was pronounced dead at 6.19pm after receiving a three-drug injection at Florida state prison in Raiford. In a final statement, he denied ever breaking into the couple’s home and attacking them, saying: “I never killed anyone.”
Soon after, Texas conducted the day’s second execution. Reinaldo Dennes, 70, became the ninth person executed by that state this year, receiving a lethal injection at the penitentiary in Huntsville. The executions of the two septuagenarians in one day reflect the ageing of the US death row population.
Overton was convicted of killing Michael and Susan MacIvor and their unborn child during an August 1991 break-in at their Florida Keys home. Dennes was convicted of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his office in January 1996.
On Thursday, Overton woke up at 5am and remained compliant, a Florida department of corrections spokesperson, Jordan Kirkland, said during a news conference. He did not meet with any visitors or a spiritual adviser.
Florida has now carried out more than half the country’s 39 executions this year under Ron DeSantis, the state’s outgoing Republican governor who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors. Thursday’s executions come amid renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the US after Tennessee’s failed execution of Christa Pike in October.
Texas set a record for executions there when 40 people were put to death in 2000.
On Thursday, the US supreme court denied a final appeal in the Florida case while an appeal remained pending in the Texas case.
Overton was convicted in 1999 of two counts of first-degree murder and received a death sentence for each. Defense attorneys had argued that investigators had planted the DNA evidence.
The MacIvors were found dead in their Tavernier, Florida, home in August 1991, according to court records. Autopsies determined both were strangled and that Susan MacIvor, who was eight months pregnant, had been raped. The medical examiner said her unborn male child likely survived for about half an hour after her death.
Investigators collected DNA evidence from the scene but initially found no match with samples in the state’s database. But Overton, who had worked at a gas station near the MacIvors’ home, was arrested on an unrelated burglary charge in 1996. Authorities said a sample taken from him matched the sample collected at the MacIvors’ home, and he was charged with their killings.
In the Texas case, Dennes, a jewelry designer, had an office in the same building as Szucs, according to court documents. A cleaning woman testified at trial that Dennes had arranged for her to open the building’s back door after hours. According to court records, she opened the door for him and his brother the night of the shooting and also distracted the security guard at Dennes’s request.
The guard, who was shot twice but recovered, identified Dennes as his attacker.
Police found the jeweler’s body upon entering his office, according to court filings. The documents said officers found the jeweler’s safe empty with no sign of the diamonds or the $200,000 in cash he was supposed to have on hand. The diamonds have never been recovered.
Dennes’s attorneys later argued there was insufficient evidence to prove that he killed Szucs.
Prosecutors noted in a recent court filing that Dennes admitted guilt during a Spanish-language interview with Telemundo in 2022.
“I did those things, so I am guilty,” Dennes told Telemundo, adding that he regretted taking a man’s life, the prosecutor’s filing said.
A year after Dennes was convicted, his brother, Jose Albert Dennes, pleaded guilty to murder in the case and was sentenced to 45 years in prison. He was released on parole in 2019.

noticias.titulo: White House cyber director ousted after US hit by wave of tech outages
noticias.resumen: Sean Cairncross exits after outages that sparked fierce criticism, with DoD official Kirsten Davies to take over White House national ⁠cyber director Sean ⁠Cairncross ​was ousted from his job, a person close to the White House told Reuters on Thursday, ⁠days after tech outages hit US air travel, banking and national security systems. Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and ⁠strategy across the federal government. Department of Defense chief information officer ​Kirsten Davies will ‌assume the position ‌temporarily, according to the source. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross was ousted from his job, a person close to the White House told Reuters on Thursday, days after tech outages hit US air travel, banking and national security systems.
Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the source.
“The president fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position,” said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Cairncross declined to comment on his departure.
Axios first reported Cairncross’s departure from the White House, citing anonymous officials claiming White House chief of staff Stephen Miller pushed for the personnel change because Cairncross “lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job”.
Technology-related outages have hit regularly over the last week, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage that hit email services and a temporary disruption to the US National Security Agency’s network.
The Trump administration has faced criticism over its response to the outages. The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday the disruptions to critical systems over the past week were separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes and not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.
Cairncross was an executive at the Republican National Committee before assuming the cyber director role. His successor will need to be confirmed by the Senate, which will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.
