noticias.texto:
Religious messages that US agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins emailed to the agency’s 100,000 employees were unconstitutional, and she must be careful to avoid proselytizing when communicating with workers, a federal judge ruled Thursday.
Rollins sent the messages, which included Christian messages and images, from her official email account on holidays such as Independence Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas and Easter. She did not send messages commemorating holidays from other religions.
“And so, like the very first disciples to encounter our risen Lord in the Upper Room almost two thousand years ago, this Easter let us too be alive with hope, full of Paschal joy, and confident in the mission each of us has been called for,” Rollins wrote in a 5 April email, marking Easter.
US district judge Trina Thompson in San Francisco said the emails violated the first amendment’s establishment clause, pointing to her position of authority, her use of an official email account and the messages suggesting that Christianity is the shared faith of Department of Agriculture (USDA) workers.
The USDA did not respond to a request for comment.
Employees cannot realistically opt out of reading emails from their agency director, and the messages could coerce them to hide their own faith or feel pressure to adopt Rollins’ Christian faith, Thompson ruled.
When disseminating religious messages, Rollins must stop if a colleague asks her to. “Cannot create a hostile work environment through persistent unwelcome advances” and “cannot use official authority to pressure subordinates” are commands that were quoted directly from a USDA policy on workplace religious expression that Rollins herself adopted.
Rollins may discuss her faith with interested colleagues, share why her faith is meaningful to her, politely invite co-workers to religious events and express her views in appropriate conversations, Thompson ruled, again quoting directly from Rollins’ policy.
Six USDA employees and the National Federation of Federal Employees, a labor union representing 19,000 USDA workers, brought the suit in May.

noticias.titulo: Fiona the hippo dies after ingesting knitted hat at Cincinnati zoo
noticias.resumen: Zoo staff tried a colonoscopy, vibration plate and other procedures to aid the hippo in passing the hat to no avail Fiona the hippo, one of America’s most famous zoo animals, has died after efforts to remove a knitted hat that she swallowed after it fell into her enclosure proved unsuccessful. “It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo wrote in a post on social media . Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Fiona the hippo, one of America’s most famous zoo animals, has died after efforts to remove a knitted hat that she swallowed after it fell into her enclosure proved unsuccessful.
“It is with extreme sadness that we share with you the devastating news that Fiona did not make it after multiple attempts from our amazing vets and keeper team to help her through what ended up being a medical emergency,” the zoo wrote in a post on social media.
With surgery too risky for full-grown hippos such as Fiona, who weighed in the region of 2,500lb (1,113kg), veterinarians tried an alternative method of getting the hat to pass through her system.
The hat fell near Fiona when a visitor to the Cincinnati zoo tossed it in the air, after which it bounced off a ceiling fan and fell into the enclosure, according to the Associated Press. Fiona ate the hat and was initially asymptomatic.
Days later, however, she began to lose appetite and staff at the zoo were forced to feed Fiona more in the hope that she would eventually get the hat through her digestive system.
“Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome. The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover,” the zoo statement said.
The zoo announced on Wednesday that the animal care team was using a vibration plate from a horse farm to help move things along, according to the Associated Press.
Fiona was sedated a second time on Tuesday for evaluation. After an ultrasound, veterinarians could see her intestines still trying to push the hat through. They also used a 9ft scope colonoscopy to view her intestines.
“The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the zoo had said on social media. Fiona remained out of her enclosure while she was receiving treatment.
Footage from the procedure released by the zoo on Wednesday shows her snorting and moving around her enclosure, which vets said was a sign of progress. Her hydration levels were being monitored.
“Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she has always liked, and they were happy to see her respond. Thank you for your continued love and concern for Fiona and her dedicated care team,” the zoo said.
This wasn’t the first time Fiona’s health had been at risk. She became a global sensation after her premature birth in 2017, when she couldn’t stand on her own.
Hopes for Fiona’s recovery had garnered support from across the country including, apparently, from Timothy, another hippo at the San Antonio zoo. Timothy had sent well wishes via Instagram. “I know you’ve got some amazing people looking after you. We’re sending lots of love from Texas to the most beautiful hippo in the world. Hope you’re feeling more like yourself soon!”
Zoo staff published a message on social media reminding visitors to be careful when near habitats and to secure belongings.
Fiona was born six weeks premature at just 29lb (13.2kgs), falling below the lowest recorded birth weight for her species at the time. Because she was initially too weak to nurse, Cincinnati Zoo staff hand-milked her mother while documenting Fiona’s recovery through photos and videos that captivated the internet.
Her survival then offered a much-needed positive chapter for the zoo following months of intense public backlash over the fatal shooting of Harambe, the silverback gorilla killed after a child breached his enclosure.
Wildlife facilities have long warned of the dangers posed by foreign objects dropped or blown into animal habitats. Past incidents have demonstrated the fatal risks involved, including a rare antelope that choked to death on a plastic cap of a snack pouch at a Tennessee zoo two years ago, and a polar bear at a German zoo that died in 2014 after swallowing a visitor’s dropped jacket.

noticias.titulo: New Ukraine talks including Europe to be held 'soon' — Merz
noticias.resumen: Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz says European leaders could take part in fresh Ukraine talks on "neutral ground." The UK and EU countries have urged a seat at the table in meetings between the US, Russia and Ukraine.
noticias.texto:
New Ukraine talks including Europe to be held 'soon' — Merz
November 20, 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Friday he believes new talks regarding Russia's invasion of Ukraine with European leaders taking part will occur "soon."
What did Merz say about the next Ukraine talks?
"Of course we are prepared to hold talks with Russia, we have always said this. These talks are now set to take place soon," Merz said after a meeting of Ukraine's allies in Berlin. He did not give a concrete date for the next talks, but said Europe's interests would be represented by Germany, France, the UK, Poland and Italy.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was present at the Coalition of the Willing summit in the German capital, along with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, French President Emmanuel Macron, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff.
Merz said the talks including Europe would take place on "neutral ground," such as the United Arab Emirates.
Merz along with other European leaders have been critical of meetings between US, Ukrainian and Russian representatives regarding the conflict, arguing that Europe needs a direct seat at the negotiating table.
Putin, in talks with Trump, says European leaders invited to Moscow
Russia's invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, with the Trump administration prioritizing an end to the war.
Trump took part in a bilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Friday, with Trump saying the two leaders would discuss the war in closed-door talks. Putin acknowledged that Europeans want a seat at the table, and said Russia invited European leaders to Moscow.
"We understand that discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without Europeans," Putin said, while rejecting any military cooperation between Europe and Ukraine.
Merz: 'Yalta format cannot bring peace' to Ukraine
Trump also took part in a historic trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The Trump-Putin-Xi meeting raised fears that the US, Russia and China are looking to carve up the world into spheres of influence. It drew comparisons with the February 1945 Yalta Conference, where US President Franklin D. Roosevelt, UK Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet Union leader Joseph Stalin discussed Europe's future as Nazi Germany's defeat was imminent in World War II.
Following the Trump-Xi-Putin summit, Merz said a "Yalta format cannot bring peace" to Ukraine. He downplayed the Shenzhen summit between the three leaders as a "photo opportunity."
Merz handed out pieces of the Berlin Wall to leaders at the Coalition of the Willing summit, saying the Yalta structure had brought "oppression, insecurity and a lack of peace."
"This is exactly what Yalta stood for," Merz said.
The Yalta format sought to divide post-war Germany into four zones: US, UK, France and the USSR. This later led to the construction of the Berlin Wall dividing the city into West and East Berlin, with city residents attempting to cross the barrier shot dead by border guards.

noticias.titulo: Cincinnati's famous hippo Fiona dies after eating visitor's hat
noticias.resumen: Fiona was a global sensation at the Cincinnati Zoo in the US. The hippo, who was born prematurely, was named after the "Shrek" film character.
noticias.texto:
Cincinnati's famous hippo Fiona dies after eating visitor's hat
November 20, 2026
Fiona the hippo has died at the Cincinnati Zoo in the US after swallowing a visitor's hat which was accidentally thrown into her enclosure. She was nine years old.
"Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome," the zoo said. "The team performed necessary supportive care today in an attempt to save her, but it was not successful and she did not recover."
Fiona was born in 2017 prematurely, with the hippo becoming a social media sensation. At the time of her birth, she only weighed 29 pounds (13 kilograms) and was in a fight to survive.
Social media users watched Fiona's daily activities as grew up. She was named after the character in the "Shrek" film series.
US second lady Usha Vance, Ohio Governor-Elect Acton remember Fiona
Fiona's death was met with reactions from her fans and political leaders.
Second lady Usha Vance, the wife of Vice President JD Vance, posted a photo of their kids face-to-face with Fiona at her enclosure.
"We are so sad to hear the news about Fiona," Vance said. Vice President Vance hails from the greater Cincinnati area and the US second family has a home there.
Cincinnati Mayor Aftab Pureval lauded Fiona as "a symbol of perservance and joy" in the city.
Ohio Governor-Elect Amy Acton said: "Fiona captured the hearts of millions and became one of Cincinnati's most beloved icons."
"Her story brought joy, hope and a little extra magic to our state," Acton added.

noticias.titulo: Price tag for US war in Iran barrels past $48 billion
noticias.resumen: A Pentagon budget officer has said the price of the Iran war surpassed $48.3 billion last week. That does not include costs sustained in Iranian attacks on US bases — lawmakers want details the Pentagon is loath to give.
noticias.texto:
Price tag for US war in Iran barrels past $48 billion
November 20, 2026
The cost of the US war in Iran, which Donald Trump launched without Congressional approval on February 28, blew past $48.3 billion (€44 billion) on November 13, according to Pentagon budgetary official Arthur Miller.
Miller laid out the figures during Thursday testimony before the US Senate Armed Services Committee as his nomination to become Navy comptroller is considered.
Miller said the costs cover US military operations, equipment and munitions but not damage sustained at US military installations across the Middle East.
How much damage has Iran inflicted on US military installations in the Middle East?
According to news agency AP, damage to hundreds of aircraft hangars, barracks, radar systems, warehouses and other US military infrastructure has run up into the billions of dollars, however, Miller failed to provide an estimate of the total cost when pressed during the hearing.
Committee Chairman Roger Wicker, a Republican from Mississippi, called on Miller to provide the figures as soon as possible.
In October, the Wall Street Journal cited Pentagon sources who said damage to US facilities in the region could range from $5 billion to as much as $15 billion.
The Washington-based think tank Center for Strategic and International Studies put the cost for repairing buildings alone — excluding equipment and systems inside — at more than $4 billion.
A war by any name, is still a very expensive undertaking
The Trump administration has variously argued that the war is not a war, that it has been won, and that it will be over soon. There is currently no end in sight and on top of the US military's costs, the global economy is getting pummeled every day as a result of the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz — which is the direct result of US attacks on the Islamic Republic.
The Trump administration is calling on Congress to pass the Pentagon's $1.5 trillion 2027 defense budget — a 40% increase over 2026 — in order to fund America's military. Unlikely prior to the November 3 midterm elections, the prospects of that figure being approved now that Democrats have taken control of both houses of Congress from Republicans would seem nigh impossible.

noticias.titulo: 'Humanitarian mission' for Kostiantynivka: Is it a trap?
noticias.resumen: Russian President Putin has proposed an evacuation of the Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka, like the recent operation in Oleshky. Experts warn this could serve military, not humanitarian, aims. What should Kyiv do?
noticias.texto:
'Humanitarian mission' for Kostiantynivka: Is it a trap?
November 19, 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a humanitarian mission in the city of Kostiantynivka similar to a recent operation in Oleshky. According to Putin, Russia has control of the city in the Donbas; the remaining civilian population, he says, could be evacuated. It would take five days to clear the access roads. The Russian leader has suggested that human rights organizations from Ukraine and Russia and delegates from the foreign press be incorporated into the mission.
Putin's proposal comes after discussions between the Russian government and US representatives, who have been negotiating to try to bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. Experts say that while Russia is indicating a readiness to make agreements, at the same time it is propagating its own depiction of the situation on the front line.
In July, Russia announced that it had taken Kostiantynivka but did not provide any proof. Ukraine says the fighting there is still ongoing. Experts from the Ukrainian open-source interactive map of military operations project DeepState say that the city is still controlled by the Ukrainian army, but that the situation there is "extremely difficult."
Responding to the proposal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists: "Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city." He emphasized that Ukraine had always given the civilian population in Kostiantynivka opportunities to leave, and said that Russia had used the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky to bring military equipment and weapons into the city.
What is the situation for civilians?
Kostiantynivka is the southernmost city in the so-called Donetsk "fortress belt," which also includes Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. Taking Kostiantynivka would open the way for Russian troops to advance to Druzhkivka, and on to the conurbation of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military expert at the Dmytro Tymchuk Center for Security Studies, a Ukrainian think tank, said Kostiantynivka's role is similar to that of Bakhmut, Avdiivka or Chasiv Yar — towns whose defensive installations were able to hold back Russian enemy forces for years.
Local authorities say the humanitarian situation in the city, whose population before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion was around 70,000, is catastrophic and that some 340 civilians remain. They add thatKostiantynivkahas no central water, electricity or gas supplies, there is no public transport, and since the spring of 2026 people have only been able to evacuate on foot.
"Those who stayed in Kostiantynivka need to be evacuated, they need a chance of a better life," military analyst Denys Popovych told DW. However, he added that an evacuation was virtually impossible without a ceasefire, as Russian troops had occupied the road between the town and Druzhkivka and drones were being deployed throughout the region. Ukraine, therefore, could not carry out such an operation unilaterally. "It still takes two to tango — to evacuate the people, that is," he said.
Humanitarian proposals as leverage
Kovalenko believes that Moscow is simply using the humanitarian issue for purposes of manipulation and to strengthen its negotiating position. The Russian army, he said, wants to gain time in order to reinforce units fighting in the vicinity.
Yevhen Zakharov, the director of the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group, has similar concerns. "I'm afraid that this proposal by the Russians has very different objectives to those they claim to pursue," he told DW. He described Putin's initiative as suspect, and said the Ukrainian side should treat it with the utmost caution.
Kyiv is in a difficult position, as the idea of a mission for Kostiantynivka is also being pushed by US intermediaries. "If we reject it, they'll say to us: 'You're rejecting peace proposals, you're not taking care of your own citizens, why should we keep talking to you, Zelenskyy wants to continue the war.' This is precisely the calculation behind it all," said Popovych.
Ceasefire as military tactic
After the end of the ceasefire in Oleshky, which was in place from October 27 to November 1, the Ukrainian General Staff announced that, in that time, the Russians had rotated their troops, entrenched their positions, reinforced measures to repel drones and brought in ammunition.
Kovalenko is convinced that the reason Russia is proposing a ceasefire is because its army is gradually losing ground in Kostiantynivka. From Moscow's perspective, the Russian troops that are meant to be storming the city are in urgent need of reinforcements, which they can't get because of the fighting on the ground.
"If a so-called humanitarian mission were to take place in Kostiantynivka, it would be a disaster for Kyiv, because Russia would use that time to consolidate forces that would enable it to take the city," he warned.
How should Kyiv respond to Moscow's proposal?
Popovych, however, does not think Ukraine should reject the Russian proposal. In his view, Kyiv should base its tactics on experiences with previous ceasefires and insist on very clear conditions in advance. "If there is a ceasefire, soldiers currently at their posts should stay there and not move," he suggested.
Oleksandr Pavlichenko from the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union believes Ukraine should submit a counter-proposal, which envisages the withdrawal of Russian troops from the Ukrainian city and the unimpeded departure of the civilian population.
The human rights activist said that, for a genuine humanitarian mission to be put in place, a strong, neutral third party should be brought in to supervise and ensure safe passage. In his view, the only party with such a mandate is the International Committee of the Red Cross. "If a proposal comes from only one side, and from a side such as Russia, it doesn't inspire confidence," he said.
This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

noticias.titulo: Borussia Dortmund bows to fan pressure and end Rheinmetall deal
noticias.resumen: Borussia Dortmund has reluctantly ended its association with a major sponsor after long-term fan protests. They are not the first Bundesliga club to u-turn, as commercial interests clash with politics and fan culture.
noticias.texto:
Borussia Dortmund bows to fan pressure on Rheinmetall deal
November 18, 2026
Two years of fan pressure and criticism has forced Borussia Dortmund to drop a sponsorship deal with Germany's largest arms manufacturer, Rheinmetall.
The Bundesliga club will not renew its deal with Rheinmetall beyond its expiry in June 2027, at the end of this season. Dortmund chairman Carsten Cramer confirmed the news on the club's website ahead of its AGM on Sunday, which may have proved a potential flashpoint. He acknowledged that "our partnership has been controversial from the outset" but lamented the loss of income.
"It reduces our financial room for manoeuvre. We will have to reprioritize planned investments and carefully examine how we can find viable solutions."
Though he welcomed the news, one of the leaders of the fan revolt against the partnership, Michael Schulze von Glaser, warned this is likely not the end of the road.
"I think in the end it was a victory for the fans. But I'm also a bit skeptical about what the future will bring us," the Dortmund fan and former head of the German Peace Society told DW. "Football fans in Germany always must be skeptical and always must watch what the club is doing.”
Long held opposition
Many Dortmund fans have opposed the deal — which has seen Rheinmetall's logo on advertising boards and other surfaces at locations such as Dortmund's 83,000-capacity Westfalenstadion — from its beginnings in 2024. It was estimated to be worth between €7 ($7.68 million) and €9 million per year.
At the club's AGM that year, 556 of 855 members present voted against the deal in a non-binding vote. There were 247 votes in favour, with 52 abstentions. This, said Cramer, informed the eventual outcome.
Rheinmetall sells arms mostly to Germany, Ukraine and NATO but fans and critics feel that platforming any arms manufacturer goes against the club's statement of its core values. In that, Dortmund states its desire for "a club and a society that operate free of racism, anti-Semitism, LGBTQIA+ hostility, sexism, violence and discrimination."
It has always been clear, said Schulze von Glaser, that this deal did not chime with that.
"In the end, they kill people. They are for war," he said of Rheinmetall. "The slogan of Borussia Dortmund is true love (Echte Liebe). But for me and many others, our love ends there…. I know some fans who have put fan merchandise in the trash because they were so shocked.”
In the Q and A on the club's website, Cramer said he was still a "personal advocate" of the deal but that Dortmund's commitment to the 50+1 model, which means German clubs are majority controlled by the members, meant they had to listen to fan voices. But he also warned that Rheinmetall must be an "absolute exception and an isolated case."
That set off some alarm bells for Schulze von Glaser.
"It's a bit concerning that there are constantly these attacks on professional football — a new sponsorship, investment deals," he said.
Dortmund not the first to climbdown on sponsors
Indeed, Dortmund's climbdown is not the first of its kind in Germany's top flight. Last year, after fan and media pressure, Bayern Munich ended its commercial deal with the tourism arm of the Rwandan government before its conclusion.
Fans had objected to the promotion of Rwanda, which many felt sought to divert attention from its poor human rights record and actions in the war with DR Congo, through sporting partnerships. Two years earlier, Bayern withdrew from a similarly controversial deal with Qatar Airways.
Elsewhere in the league, Werder Bremen fans objected to their long time shirt sponsor, Wiesenhof. Many supporters took issue with the factory farming practices of Germany's largest poultry producer. Though it was not given as a direct reason for the end of a shirt sponsorship deal in 2023, it likely played a part.
Union Berlin fans have also made their voices heard. When the club signed a new shirt-sponsorship deal with Luxembourg real estate company, Aroundtown, upon promotion to the top flight in 2019, many fans were frustrated at the tie up in a city where rent prices were skyrocketing.
German football's battle between commerce and 50+1
"It's a problem for a lot of people," fan Sven Dobberstein told DW at the time.
"We have to try to find a way between commercialization and what we have at the moment. It isn't easy."
Striking that balance can often be a source of tension for Bundesliga clubs. 50+1 ensures fans have a voice, preventing rich owners, or nation states, from taking control as they do in England's lucrative Premier League or in France or Spain. Indeed fan protests have also stopped the league signing a €1billion private equity partner and seen Monday night matches scrapped. For Schulze von Glaser, this needs to be protected.
"In Germany, the fan culture has an impact," he said.
”If there is something bad or terrible happening in your club and in the Bundesliga, there are the organized fans and they can have an impact if they want, if they stand together and, yes, they can stop the Rheinmetall deal."
Additional reporting by: Emmie Eernisse

noticias.titulo: 'Coalition of the Willing' meets in Berlin: Europe remains committed to Ukraine
noticias.resumen: The "Coalition of the Willing" supporting Ukraine is gathering in Berlin. One of the key issues under discussion is whether Europe will be able to play a role in future negotiations over the country's future.
noticias.texto:
'Coalition of the Willing' meets in Berlin over Ukraine's future
November 18, 2026
Once again, Berlin is rolling out the red carpet, and once again the focus is on Ukraine: Around 20 heads of state and government, primarily from across Europe, are set to gather in the German capital on Thursday (November 19). They will discuss the future of the Eastern European country that has been under attack from Russia since February 2022 and is now facing yet another harsh winter.
Extensive security measures have already been announced for Berlin's government district, pointing to the presence of high-ranking participants. It remains unclear whether Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will be among them. What does appear certain, however, is the attendance of chief US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, according to several media outlets.
The "Coalition of the Willing" is a group of 36 countries determined not to be deterred from supporting the nation under attack. Unlike other international forums, the group is focused not only on how to support Ukraine militarily and financially in the here and now.
Led by Germany, France and the United Kingdom, the coalition is also prepared, in principle, to help monitor a possible ceasefire within Ukraine itself and to contribute to the complex security guarantees the country would then require, should such a scenario come to pass. The effort dates back to March 2025, when the countries involved first met in London.
But what can the coalition realistically achieve? Stefan Meister of the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) is not overly optimistic.
"The fundamental problem is that Europe has yet to put forward a proposal," he told DW. "There is no plan outlining what security guarantees Europe would offer, what troops it would be prepared to deploy, what measures it could provide to safeguard a ceasefire, or where it would be willing to make compromises."
Merz: 'Germany has a seat at the table'
Nevertheless, the meeting comes at a moment when some observers believe there may finally be movement toward ending the war. During talks in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates a few days ago, Russia, Ukraine and the US managed to agree only on a prisoner exchange. It was a modest step forward.
Further talks are planned, and it has been a long time since the prospects appeared as favorable as they do now for Europe to secure a role in future decisions on war and peace in Ukraine.
It has repeatedly been argued, both by US officials and by those in power in Russia, that Europe does not speak with a single voice.
This has sparked a debate among EU heads of state and government over who, exactly, could represent Europe in such talks. Could it be German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU)?
After the EU summit in Dublin, Ireland, on Friday, Merz said: "For the first time, concrete peace talks are expected to take place in the coming weeks with Europe represented. Germany has a seat at the table, that is absolutely clear."
Europe has yet to speak with one voice
But what exactly did that mean? That Germany alone would speak for all of Europe? Hardly. As was also made clear in Berlin on Monday, Europe would be represented by the E3 countries, namely Germany, France, and the non-EU member United Kingdom, joined by Poland and Italy. Official EU representatives, including European Council President Antonio Costa, would also take part.
Stefan Meister of the DGAP believes the debate says a great deal about the pressures Europe itself is under.
"Europe's positioning has more to do with domestic political considerations than with developments in the negotiations," Meister said. "Everyone needs to show that they are participating in the talks in some way. Elections will be held next year in France and Poland, and it is still unclear whether French support for Ukraine will continue in its current form after that."
German Deputy Government Spokesperson Sebastian Hille, meanwhile, sought to downplay the debate on Monday over a possible role for Friedrich Merz as chief negotiator.
At the federal government's regular press briefing, he said: "This is not about discussing individuals. What matters is that Putin finally understands that he must come to the negotiating table so that we have a chance of achieving peace in the first place."
German government spokesperson: Europe now needs stamina
US negotiator Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of President Donald Trump, struck a rather different tone last week.
Speaking in Abu Dhabi, he said: "If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations."
Government spokesperson Hille responded on Monday: "Europe's strength lies precisely in the unity and cohesion of many countries. We should not allow ourselves to be drawn into debates that others want to frame around this question."
Hille emphasized that the situation remained unchanged: Peace in Ukraine could only be achieved step by step. Europe, too, would need stamina, perseverance and a willingness to undertake the painstaking work required to bring it about.
Declining support for Ukraine in German polls
European supporters of Ukraine are also under pressure as public opinion on the issue is shifting, including in Germany. While a broad majority favored helping defend the country in the immediate aftermath of Russia's invasion in the spring of 2022, support has since fallen markedly.
According to the latest DeutschlandTrend survey on the issue, conducted or German public broadcaster ARD in September 2026, 52% of eligible voters still support weapons deliveries to Ukraine, while 42% believe such support has gone too far. That is the highest level of opposition recorded since the start of the war.
A further study conducted for public broadcaster WDR in November 2026 found that support for Ukraine has become a more polarizing issue in Germany than immigration. According to the survey, 54% of respondents favor continued support for Ukraine, while just under 29% would prefer a rapprochement with Russia, despite its war of aggression against Ukraine.
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment
noticias.resumen: The depiction of the birth of the goddess Athena above the Parthenon's entrance is considered a masterpiece of ancient art. Now, a German research team has pieced together all the surviving fragments.
noticias.texto:
Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved?
November 18, 2026
The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most important temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.
Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.
The Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art. The sculptures adorning its pediments, created under the direction of the legendary sculptor Phidias, are considered unparalleled examples of proportion and grace. They have influenced artists from ancient Rome through Neoclassicism to the modern era.
'Very confident we've solved the mystery'
The east pediment above the temple entrance depicted the birth of the goddess Athena from the head of her father Zeus, surrounded by the Olympian gods. A total of 39 figures adorned the roughly 29-meter-long work of art. At its center stood a colossal Zeus figure, measuring 3.8 meters in height.
For centuries, scholars have puzzled over exactly what the arrangement looked like, as the pediment was destroyed during the Christianization of Greece.
But now there has been a breakthrough.
After decades of painstaking detective work and with the help of modern technology, archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann and his team have managed to piece together all the surviving fragments of the Parthenon's east pediment.
Brinkmann heads the Antiquities and Asia department at Frankfurt's Liebieghaus sculpture collection. "We're very, very confident that we've solved the mystery," he told DW.
The results are now on display in an exhibition at the Liebieghaus titled "Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle."
Only around 20% of the original marble sculpture's volume is known to have survived. The fragments are scattered across various European museums, with most located in Athens. The British Museum also holds numerous pieces.
Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, have spent more than 40 years working on this ancient puzzle, with so many of its pieces missing.
And they were far from the first to attempt it: "Already in the 19th century, many scholars studied the subject and developed well-founded theories based on their deep knowledge of ancient sources," Brinkmann explains.
In 1910, a study documenting the many fragments held by the British Museum was published. The research team was able to build on that earlier work, but progress remained slow for years.
Then, in 2014, a visit to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg provided Brinkmann with a crucial clue. There, he encountered a Roman sarcophagus featuring a relief of Athena's birth. "That's when it suddenly clicked: They're all there!"
Nine such sarcophagi are known to exist, almost all of them in Rome. Each depicts a different section of the Parthenon's east pediment.
Brinkmann emphasizes that other scholars had already noticed this connection in the 19th century. "But we really seized on the idea and never let go."
A handy tool: the iPhone
The researchers also benefited from 21st-century technology: 3D scanners and printers. Brinkmann and his team visited numerous destinations to examine around 60 original fragments at different locations — traveling light. An iPhone was all they needed to scan the pieces.
Digitally fitting the fragments together led to another important discovery. "We know these figures we're putting together!" Brinkmann recalls thinking at the time.
The Romans had repeatedly made individual copies of all the sculptures from the pediment. "These copies matched the fragments perfectly. Suddenly, we found ourselves surrounded by old acquaintances we had never suspected had come from the pediment." This finally enabled the researchers to reconstruct all the figures and their original arrangement.
Using a 3D printer, the team created a 4-meter-long model at a scale of 1:7.7. For the exhibition, they also produced life-size 3D prints of the most important fragments and mounted them on panels depicting the complete figures at their original size. An animation brings the reconstructed composition to life, digitally assembling the fragments to reveal how the east pediment once looked.
Alongside works from the Liebieghaus collection, the exhibition features loans from other institutions, including the Vatican Museums and the Louvre. Objects from the Acropolis Museum in Athens had originally been expected as well. But Greece withdrew its participation after learning that the British Museum was also planning to lend fragments to the Frankfurt exhibition. The Liebieghaus ultimately decided to forgo the British-owned fragments, too.
The dispute between Greece and Britain over the Parthenon sculptures
There is a reason for this controversy. Britain holds a substantial portion of the Parthenon frieze as well as fragments from both pediments.
Greek authorities have been campaigning for their return for decades.
In Britain, the 56 sections of the frieze are known as the "Elgin Marbles," named after Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople.
In the early 19th century, Elgin had sculptures removed from the exterior of the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. They were taken to Britain with the consent of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Greece at the time.
Britain maintains that the sculptures were legally acquired.
Greece, however, considers them stolen.
For years, the dispute remained deadlocked. Since the Labour Party came to power in Britain, there has been some movement toward resolving it. But apparently not enough to persuade Greece to lend artworks to an exhibition in which the British Museum might also participate.
The exhibition "Athena, the Stage is Yours. The Parthenon Puzzle" runs through July 25, 2027, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt.
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: How a green economy could help reverse climate change
noticias.resumen: Green growth promises a future in which economies thrive without destroying the environment. But is this vision realistic?
noticias.texto:
How a green economy could help reverse climate change
November 18, 2026
Human civilization is currently profoundly unsustainable. Earth has already crossed seven of the nine planetary boundaries critical for sustaining life, including climate change, ocean acidification and biosphere integrity.
If economies and societies keep to business as usual, the Earth's vital processes will continue to be thrown wildly out of balance, threatening the future of humanity.
It's now largely accepted that if humans are to have any chance of slowing global warming and nature loss, those social and economic models must change. That's where the idea of green growth comes in.
Its promise is to keep growing the economy while reducing emissions and resource use. That involves, for instance, running factories, businesses and homes on wind, solar and other green energy instead of coal and gas, replacing gas-fired furnaces with heat pumps and recycling and reusing resources and raw materials.
"Basically, the idea is: business as usual, but with more sustainable technologies," said Helmut Haberl, a social ecology professor at BOKU University in Vienna. Along with his colleagues, he published a major report in 2020 evaluating more than 800 studies on green growth.
Can economies grow while emissions fall?
In principle, the world's economic output could continue to grow in the long term and generate significantly fewer emissions from the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas. That's been shown in scenarios modeled by researchers with the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, or IPCC.
Thanks to renewable energy and green technologies, those scenarios have already become reality in several countries and regions.
The economies of developed countries like the United Kingdom, the United States, Japan and Australia have experienced years of growth alongside sinking CO2 emissions. That's even when offshore production is included.
In the European Union, the bloc-wide economy has grown by more than 70% since 1990. Meanwhile, the EU's carbon emissions have dropped by around 40%.
But such a complete decoupling of growth and emissions is, according to Haberl and his fellow researchers, relatively rare.
In India, and in several countries in Africa and Southeast Asia, economies are becoming more efficient. But while economic performance is outpacing emissions growth, emissions are still rising in those countries and globally. This is not compatible with preventing the worst impacts of climate change.
"That doesn't mean, however, that it couldn't work in the future," said Haberl, referring to decoupling of growth and emissions.
And even though economic growth has been shown to be compatible with emissions reduction, eliminating all greenhouse gases from a polluting industry like steel or chemicals is complicated.
These sectors don't just release emissions by burning fossil fuels for energy; carbon is also a key part of the chemical processes used to create their products, notably in the steel industry.
Replacing it with greener substitutes, or an alternative energy source like green hydrogen, requires significant investment.
Emissions aren't the only problem with economic growth
There's another hurdle: the world's high consumption of resources. A productive economy depends on many raw materials and other products: ores, chemicals, wood, cement, glass and agricultural products.
Many countries are now using green technologies to reduce the amount of resources needed to manufacture a product, for example, and are making their economies more efficient.
But that doesn't mean overall fewer resources are being used because falling costs can encourage businesses to produce more things and people to consume more. This can partially offset green savings and is called the rebound effect.
The British economy has been growing for years, emissions have been dropping and efficiency has increased, but the UK still used 7% more resources in 2023 than it did in 2001.
Global resource consumption has tripled over the last 50 years. If the world continues on the current pathway, that could increase by another 60% by 2060. It remains unclear whether green growth can deliver the emissions and resource reductions needed to stop climate change and biodiversity loss rapidly enough.
"We really need to move beyond efficiency gains in our existing production practices to look more broadly at what we consume," said Catherine Ganzleben, a sustainability and fair transitions expert at the European Environment Agency.
She told DW that people also need to reconsider how they consume and whether they really need to own everything they use in their daily life — cars, for example.
"But we can shift towards models where we share cars, so we pool our resources and have significantly lower resources per person through sharing the goods that we need."
Is degrowth the future?
Some researchers have concluded that unrestricted economic growth is no longer possible in the long term, even if it's sustainable.
Instead, they've called for degrowth. This posits slower economic growth, no growth at all or even negative growth, so that the world's ecosystems and the climate have a chance to recover and stabilize.
That applies mainly to economies in richer countries, which would need to take targeted steps to reduce their energy and resource use. Poorer countries would continue to grow until their economies and quality of life improve significantly.
Under the degrowth theory, a society's prosperity is not measured solely by the growth of its gross domestic product, but by values such as quality of life, education and community. The idea is that once countries develop to a certain point, additional growth doesn't translate into greater well-being.
Ultimately, the concept is based on the idea that human well-being and ecological sustainability is only possible in the long term with a planned, socially just reduction of material production and resource consumption. Degrowth advocates argue this would be preferable to an unplanned and potentially catastrophic economic contraction caused by escalating climate extremes.
A 2020 study by researchers from the universities of Leeds and Lausanne showed that the concept of degrowth supported the world's climate goals — and that a high quality of life didn't have to be sacrificed in exchange for a significantly lower consumption of energy and resources.
However, there is still no conclusive evidence that an entire modern economy could continue to function entirely on the degrowth principles in the long term.
Is an environmentally friendly economy possible?
Nevertheless, Haberl doesn't assume that an environmentally friendly economic model automatically goes hand in hand with sacrifice, arguing instead for a needs-based economy.
"A society isn't necessarily better off when it's producing more goods and services," he said. It all depends on how prosperity and quality of life are measured in the future, and how states decide to do business.
Today, a successful economy is measured by the growth of a country's gross domestic product — put simply, the worth of all of its goods and services. This calculation doesn't account for income distribution, unpaid work, quality of life or environmental damage.
"The highest possible real incomes for every individual would probably not be compatible with ecological goals in the long term," said Haberl. "On the other hand, an increase in prosperity — related to a higher quality of life — would be."
An analysis by the European Environment Agency (EEA) pointed out that the idea of steady growth is part of the world's economic cycle, and deeply anchored in our institutions, norms and societal discourse. The job market and tax system are also closely tied to gross domestic product growth. A shrinking economy would therefore require a fundamental shift in our way of thinking.
Countries face a dilemma: a steadily growing economy is not compatible with ecological goals, according to the EEA. On the other side, a sharp decline in growth could trigger enormous social upheaval.
And the correlation is much more complex than the idea of "less is more," as highlighted by an EEA study in November 2021. "The fact that GDP growth has been harmful for the environment does not necessarily mean that declining GDP would be good for the environment," noted the report.
Achieving green growth while respecting environmental limits would require an "unprecedented decoupling of economic activity from environmental and climate pressures. Whether this is feasible is currently uncertain."
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: Top House Democrat questions what Trump accomplished in Xi-Putin summit
noticias.resumen: Rep. Gregory Meeks raises concerns about U.S. alliances after Trump's summit with Xi and Putin. He also discusses Chinese espionage amid the Nvidia scandal.
noticias.texto:
Top House Democrat questions what Trump accomplished in Xi-Putin summit
Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., on Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping
Rep. Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, questioned Thursday what President Trump accomplished in his summit with the leaders of China and Russia, warning that the meeting could undermine U.S. alliances.
"I wish he had a plan and a strategy if he was going to meet with them and goals. Apparently, he does not," Meeks told Morning Edition.
His comments followed Trump's meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, which ended with few signs of progress on nuclear arms control or the war in Ukraine.
Meeks said he feared the leaders were discussing dividing the world into spheres of influence, potentially sidelining U.S. allies. He also questioned the lack of meaningful agreements on nuclear weapons and artificial intelligence safety.
Asked about the Nvidia scandal, Meeks said he would confront Xi over Chinese espionage and intellectual property theft and warn of possible retaliation.
"When it comes to our national security, that's where we draw a red line," he said.
Meeks argued that U.S. diplomats should have raised concerns about Chinese espionage and intellectual property theft before the summit to establish clear goals for the talks. In his conversation with NPR's A Martínez, Meeks also called for reducing tariffs on U.S. allies while pressing China to end its support for Russia's war in Ukraine.
Listen to the full interview by clicking the blue button above.
The radio interview was edited by J Mai and Olivia Hampton. The web version was adapted by Majd Al-Waheidi and edited by Treye Green.

noticias.titulo: Ukraine: Russian strikes damage Austrian and Dutch embassies in Kyiv
noticias.resumen: Russian strikes damaged the Austrian and Dutch embassies in Kyiv on Thursday. Windows were shattered and vehicles damaged, but diplomatic staff escaped unharmed.
noticias.texto:
Shattered windows, wrecked cars and a blast crater marked the aftermath of a Russian bombardment in Kyiv, on Thursday 19 November 2026. The strikes damaged both the Austrian and Dutch embassies, though staff at both missions escaped without injury. Ukrainian authorities said Russia fired anti-ship missiles and 98 drones across the country, logging strikes in 18 locations and damaging several diplomatic premises and historic sites in the capital.
Around 10 people were working inside the Austrian embassy when an explosion rocked the area during office hours, deputy head of mission Daniel Ruethlin said, as footage showed workers covering damaged vehicles with plastic sheeting amid the debris. Nearby, the Dutch embassy was hit by a projectile, according to Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen, with no casualties reported there either.
Notably, the Dutch mission was struck two days after Dutch weapons manufacturer Destinus revealed that Ukraine had used its arms in recent attacks on the Crimean Bridge, prompting Russia’s embassy in the Netherlands to accuse The Hague of openly participating in the war. No evidence has been provided linking the embassy strikes to that announcement, which nonetheless laid bare the relentless danger facing civilians and diplomatic staff in Kyiv.

noticias.titulo: 10,000 identical inflatable rings raise questions over Ceuta migrant crossing
noticias.resumen: The report estimates that between 8,000 and 10,000 identical inflatable rings were used during the mass migrant crossing in July, suggesting they may have been purchased and distributed in advance.
noticias.texto:
The report estimates that between 8,000 and 10,000 identical inflatable rings were used during the mass migrant crossing in July, suggesting they may have been purchased and distributed in advance.
A police report points to possible logistical preparations ahead of the mass arrival of migrants in Ceuta at the end of July, after detecting the use of thousands of inflatable rings of the same model, black with a printed design, during the crossing at Tarajal beach.
The officers believe that "it does not seem possible" for the migrants themselves to have bought the rings directly from shops or online, as there would not have been enough stock to meet a sudden purchase of thousands of units on the same day without prior planning or orders.
The analysis, based on aerial images and photographs from different points along the Tarajal border, suggests that a single large batch had been purchased in advance, then distributed at specific locations and widely used during the crossing.
Images on social media and in the press do not make it possible to clearly identify points of sale. However, some migrants interviewed said they had bought the rings in the Moroccan town of Fnideq, while others said they had acquired them on Tarajal beach itself, before entering the breakwater.
The judge requests information on the rescues
Judge María Tardón, who is handling the case at the National Court, has asked the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in Tarifa for information about the rescues carried out on 30 and 31 July, when the mass crossing took place, including the times, locations, identities of the people rescued and the units involved.
The magistrate has also asked the organisation Hazte Oír, which has joined the proceedings as a popular prosecution, for photographs and videos of a Ford Focus with a Spanish number plate in order to identify its two occupants.
According to the complaint, the vehicle was parked on the Tarajal breakwater in the early hours of 30 July and its occupants provided assistance to only some of the people who were crossing.

noticias.titulo: Nobel economist Joseph Stiglitz deems youth protests across Europe 'legitimate'
noticias.resumen: Nobel Prize-winning economist Joseph Stiglitz says young people are right to be worried and that youth protests across Europe are "legitimate".
noticias.texto:
Nobel Prize-winning economist Joseph Stiglitz says young people are right to be worried and that youth protests across Europe are "legitimate".
Hundreds of thousands have taken to the streets in France, Denmark, Italy and Spain in recent weeks to speak out against rising living costs, housing crisis and poor pay.
Nobel Prize-winning economist Joseph Stiglitz said he understands the youth's worries and that their concerns were "legitimate".
"Part of the problem [...] is inequality across generations," said Stiglitz.
"They can't afford housing. They're not given the education that would make them productive. AI is giving rise to new sets of anxieties," he said.
The former World Bank chief economist said that the world the next generation is inheriting is filled with uncertainties linked to rising inequality, climate change and other issues.
Protests have filled European countries' streets in recent months, fuelled by widening wealth gaps. "I think those are legitimate complaints," said Stiglitz. These pressures drive fear within younger generations that they may never match the living standards their parents enjoyed.
'I pay €460 for 5 square metres'
Last week, hundreds of thousands of protesters took to the streets in Spain for the first nationwide 24-hour strike since 2012.
Marching through pouring rain, protesters in Madrid carried signs chanting "we have no home", speaking out against rising living costs.
"People work a lot, and it isn't enough to pay the rent, to pay for a house," said Paula Diaz, a 25-year-old theatre technician who lives with her parents.
Arturo Leon, 24, is a student in Barcelona and pays €460 a month for a 5-square-metre bedroom in a shared apartment with four others. "We do not have a contract, and there are lots of things in the flat which are broken, but the landlord refuses to fix," he told Al Jazeera.
Sanchez called this month's election, initially scheduled for 2027, after his minority government failed to secure parliamentary approval for a package of housing measures proposed in response to the demonstrations.
'We don't want mice in our schools'
In Italy, thousands of students called for more school funding as they marched, set up tent camps and occupied schools to make their demands heard.
"We don't want windows falling on our heads, and we don't want mice in our schools. We want clean buildings, and I want to live in a better world than this one," said Sofia Cataldi, a 16-year-old Roman student.
This call for a better life sounds like an echo of student protests that have been rumbling in France since the beginning of September.
"The state of schools, the state of hospitals, staffing levels in schools and hospitals, the way things are getting worse and worse across all public services — these are issues that really resonate with us," said Aurelane Thos, a 38-year-old nurse.
"We're stressed about our studies, but when you have a bunch of cops in front of the high school every morning, you only want to keep protesting," said Mathilde, a 17-year-old pupil in Paris.
Stiglitz backs taxing the rich
The 83-year-old American economist has been a long-time advocate of taxing the ultra-wealthy. He argues that governments would have room to respond to social demands if they were willing to raise more revenue.
"There is so much money at the top that even a small tax rate on the top generates a huge amount of money," he said.
Stiglitz backs proposals such as the suggestion by French economist Gabriel Zucman for a minimum levy of around two per cent of fortunes above €100 million.
Such tax revenues would allow more money to be spent on public services and should be levied at the European Union level. He argues the bloc's free movement of people and capital made tax avoidance easier.
But the Columbia University professor warned that tax alone won't solve Europe's challenges. European countries should rethink parts of their public spending and implement more flexible pension systems that reflect longer life expectancy, while taking into account physically demanding jobs.
"Students may not fully understand," Stiglitz said, that beyond the usual budget pressures, "this is a particularly difficult time."

noticias.titulo: Four men found guilty of raping woman drugged by husband in UK
noticias.resumen: Police uncovered hundreds of intimate images of Joanne Young after investigating her husband in 2024 for uploading images depicting bestiality, exposing a wider pattern of sexual abuse.
noticias.texto:
Police uncovered hundreds of intimate images of Joanne Young after investigating her husband in 2024 for uploading images depicting bestiality, exposing a wider pattern of sexual abuse.
Four British men were found guilty on Thursday of multiple sexual offences, including rape, against a woman whose then-husband drugged her and advertised her for sex online.
Her then-husband, Philip Young, also filmed her without her knowledge at their home in Swindon, in a case bearing striking similarities to that of Gisèle Pelicot in France.
Joanne Young, who waived her right to anonymity, expressed her "relief" at the verdict and urged other women who have experienced similar abuse to come forward, saying they "can be believed and understood."
“Knowing what has happened to me without my knowledge or consent has been incredibly difficult to process, and this abuse has cost me my life as I knew it,” she said outside Winchester Crown Court in southern England.
“The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way."
The 49-year-old mother of three spoke after a jury found the four men, aged between 32 and 62, guilty of sexually abusing her at her home in Swindon after being recruited online.
The verdicts and guilty pleas
Philip Young, had previously pleaded guilty to dozens of offences, including 11 counts of rape and 11 counts of administering a substance with intent.
Norman Macksoni, 48, was convicted of rape, while Richard Wilkins, 62, was found guilty of rape and assault by penetration.
Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, was convicted of assault by penetration and sexual touching, while Mohammed Hassan was found guilty of sexual touching.
A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, admitted one count of assault by penetration, two counts of sexual assault and one count of rape.
Justice Pushpinder Saini said the four men faced “significant” prison sentences and praised Joanne Young for her "amazing bravery throughout these proceedings.”

noticias.titulo: Europe Tonight: Theresa Fallon on whether world leaders could redraw global spheres of influence
noticias.resumen: Euronews' Europe Tonight welcomes Theresa Fallon, founder and director of the Centre for Russia Europe Asia Studies, to discuss the APEC summit with presenter Mared Gwyn-Jones, including comparisons with the Yalta Conference and the possibility of leaders redrawing global spheres of influence.
noticias.texto:
Euronews' Europe Tonight welcomes Theresa Fallon, founder and director of the Centre for Russia Europe Asia Studies, to discuss the APEC summit with presenter Mared Gwyn-Jones, including comparisons with the Yalta Conference and the possibility of leaders redrawing global spheres of influence.
Historic talks between the leaders of China, the US and Russia concluded earlier today without a major breakthrough. China has published what it describes as a “trilateral peace declaration”, in which the three countries commit to reforming the UN and increasing the production and supply of oil and gas.
US President Donald Trump also praised his “great relationship” with Russian President Vladimir Putin after both leaders held their first face-to-face talks since they met in Alaska last year.
On his way back from China, Trump called into a separate meeting of Ukraine’s European allies in Berlin, where he questioned Europe’s decision to continue funding Ukraine. However, the US President has assured that he will not make decisions without consulting Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Euronews' evening show Europe Tonight welcomed Theresa Fallon, founder and director of the Centre for Russia Europe Asia Studies, to discuss the topic in depth alongside our presenter Mared Gwyn-Jones. Among the questions raised were whether the Yalta Conference – where the Soviets did walk away with a good deal – is a fair comparison to the recent talks, and whether these leaders could redraw spheres of influence.
Discover the full conversation in the video above.

noticias.titulo: Turkish court blocks jailed Istanbul mayor from 2028 presidential race
noticias.resumen: Imamoglu's office has released a copy of his business management degree from Istanbul University, awarded in 1995.
noticias.texto:
Imamoglu's office has released a copy of his business management degree from Istanbul University, awarded in 1995.
A Turkish court ruled on Thursday that jailed Istanbul mayor Ekrem Imamoglu's university diploma was invalid, preventing him from running in the 2028 presidential election, according to media reports.
Imamoglu, considered one of the strongest opposition challengers to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, was arrested in March 2025 on corruption charges that his party says are politically motivated.
Turkish law requires presidential candidates to hold a valid university degree.
The State Council's decision to reject his appeal over his diploma is the latest legal setback for Imamoglu, a member of the opposition Republican People's Party (CHP). He was elected Istanbul mayor in 2019, defeating Erdogan's preferred candidate.
The CHP later nominated Imamoglu as its presidential candidate.
Arrest sparks widespread protests
His arrest on 19 March 2025 on multiple corruption charges triggered widespread protests. Critics saw the move as an attempt to remove one of Erdogan's main political rivals.
A day before his arrest, Istanbul University cancelled Imamoglu's degree, claiming it had been obtained fraudulently.
Police raided his home hours later and detained him. He was subsequently jailed on the same day the CHP officially named him its presidential candidate.
Imamoglu defends his university degree
The diploma case went to trial in September 2025. Imamoglu told the court he had been admitted to a university in the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), which is recognised only by Turkey, when he was 18.
He said he later transferred to Istanbul University to complete his degree, following the rules set by Turkey's Council of Higher Education (YOK).
Imamoglu defended the transfer, saying he had followed the university's application process.
"I saw the announcement for a horizontal transfer to Istanbul University, met the requirements, applied and was accepted, studied and graduated," he said.

noticias.titulo: EU-UK summit — live updates

noticias.texto:
Andy Burnham heads to Brussels Friday for his first formal summit with the European Union as British prime minister.
More than a decade after the U.K. voted for Brexit, the two sides are hoping to move a little closer, eying deals on food and drink rules, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. London and Brussels are also seeking agreement on the thornier question of reduced tuition fees for European students in the U.K.
The long-in-the-works summit comes as Burnham eyes a wider reset in Britain’s relationship with the bloc in the coming years. POLITICO’s team on the ground will be poring over Friday’s deals, parsing leaders’ words, and asking what comes next in the post-Brexit rapprochement.

noticias.titulo: The web is held together by volunteers. AI could tear it apart.
noticias.resumen: As AI reveals deeply hidden vulnerabilities, idealist coders and non-profits say they’re running on fumes trying to maintain the web's core vitals.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — Long before the fresh spate of hacks and website shutdowns, the inherent instability of the web was depicted in an internet-famous cartoon of a rickety tower propped up by a single small block. Now a near-daily rhythm of outages suggests the supporting block may have come loose. POLITICO revealed Thursday that internal services at EU institutions had gone offline after a major AI-fueled cyberattack . That came after service interruptions at U.S. national security offices and the federal aviation authority, global outages at Microsoft and a succession of internet-activated attacks on supermarket refrigerators in Europe. Authorities blame the sudden wave of instability on the capacity of new AI tools to detect vulnerabilities in existing code and for bad actors to exploit them. Interviews with more than a dozen cybersecurity leaders and those working on maintaining the internet show the scale of the challenge to keep the web up and running, in a world where the pace of finding vulnerabilities has rapidly and permanently accelerated. Since the web’s early days, an unruly cast of idealist engineers and non-profit foundations have been essential for looking after decades-old critical code that’s been used to build our digital world. This small army of largely volunteer coders now say they can’t keep up with the power and pace of AI. “We’re running on fumes,” said Robin Bender Ginn, executive director of the OpenJS Foundation, which looks after JavaScript, among the most widely used programming languages. “It keeps me up at night.” Cybersecurity agencies around the world rang the alarm last month about major flaws detected in PHP, another critical coding language that underpins 70% of the web. This week, similar scares have spread over Java and NGINX, which also fuel large swathes of technology. Helmut Reisinger, the European chief executive of cybersecurity giant Palo Alto Networks, said in an interview that the company is seeing “more or less” ten times as many incidents compared to about four months ago. He predicts the constant drumbeat of attacks and scares in the last month is going to become the “new norm.” The PHP Foundation, which was only established in 2021 despite the coding language itself existing since the early 1990s, has two members of staff and 13 contractors. “Having very few individuals responsible for some key piece of infrastructure is just problematic,” said Nils Adermann, a PHP Foundation board member. Out of office Many tools like PHP have their origins in the 1990s, when foundational software and programming languages were developed in the messy, community-minded early days of the web. Those that worked well or were useful were gifted as a common good, picked up by other software developers and became building blocks for a vast number of digital technologies on which governments, critical infrastructure and citizens now rely. Many open-source software libraries form the basis for widely used software like Android. Facebook was originally built using PHP, and household names like Spotify , Etsy and Wikipedia are just some top destinations that still use it as the basis for their services and websites. The homepage of the PHP website is seen in Singapore on Oct. 22, 2026. | Yong Teck Lim/Getty Images When cybersecurity agencies and companies issued an urgent warning in October that there were major flaws in PHP identified with the help of AI , and that they should either update their systems or shut them down, it was a public revelation that the architecture upon which our digital world relies is almost comically fragile. Adermann explained that it is common for people who have worked on a PHP project for years in their spare time — developing a level of specific expertise that’s very hard to replicate — to duck out when they start families or can no longer find spare time. That became especially apparent during the process of fixing the recent PHP flaws: One person involved in pushing out technical updates had a scheduled medical procedure and “was simply not available,” he said. “It was like, ‘okay, how do we figure it out, who can even do this now?’” “That was one of these things where it became clear that we have a pretty limited budget and a lot of this is just barely working,” he said. The discovery of the flaws did not, in the end, result in a doomsday scenario, in part because many organizations took themselves offline or fixed their systems, and also because the PHP flaws turned out to be harder than expected to exploit. Free riders Along with the PHP Foundation, numerous other non-profit foundations exist to act as guardians of open-source software, including the Linux Foundation, Python Software Foundation and the OpenJS Foundation. They are typically funded through a mix of government grants and donations from technology companies. Funding can be used to pay full-time staff to carry out security audits, rather than relying on volunteers who, though committed, may suddenly become unavailable. Tech firms have been among the biggest donors because they benefit from the open source software on which their own offerings are based, and continue to contribute to many projects. Some of the world’s largest companies, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Microsoft, have clubbed together to back a Linux Foundation project called Alpha Omega , which provided funding that ultimately led to the PHP flaws being fully identified and fixed. The project has been a “tremendous help,” said Adermann. Another key donor often cited by open-source figures is the German government-backed Sovereign Tech Agency , which invested €205,000 in PHP in 2023 to 2024, with another €223,680 committed for 2025 to 2026, Powen Shiah, a spokesperson for the agency, said in emailed comments. Germany is widely seen as a leader in open source, and the agency considers the funds it hands out to be investments in “chronically underfunded” critical infrastructure rather than donations. “Improving a single foundational component can strengthen thousands of downstream applications and businesses, delivering benefits across entire industries,” Shiah said. Juhan Lepassaar speaks at an event in Kyiv on Feb. 7, 2024. | STR/NurPhoto via Getty Images Yet even between government and private funds, the sums remain small, particularly when dispersed among so many organizations. Tech firms can also be capricious, cutting funding when they lose interest in a particular project. “More organizations need to understand how fragile this infrastructure can be and see investment in it as part of their own security,” Shiah said. “Some companies already invest substantially, but the scale of their financial contributions usually doesn’t reflect the value they derive.” Only a “tiny fraction” of the companies that depend on PHP contribute financially, Adermann said. By his calculations , companies make hundreds of billions each year using PHP but contribute nothing. Ginn said one Big Tech company dropped out of her OpenJS Foundation’s top membership tier just recently, leaving only Microsoft remaining. She noted that an issue in recent months is that more cash is being funneled toward AI-focused open-source foundations. The AI deluge The rise of AI models and their capabilities of finding software flaws is putting more pressure on open-source software engineers, who are inundated with reports of vulnerabilities — some of which are false or exaggerated. Reports of flaws discovered by AI are “quite verbose,” Ginn said. Juhan Lepassaar, the head of EU cyber agency ENISA, said in an interview that the agency has observed a similar pattern of false positives. ENISA is making a list of the most critical open source components that should be made more secure, either by providing “skilled people, or AI models and tools,” Lepassaar said. The EU also has an open source strategy, in part with a view to weaning itself off U.S. tech. Those plans were made before AI rattled cybersecurity defenders worldwide. Some, like the German Sovereign Tech Agency, hope that the incident will put the needs of open source software on the map and prompt an intervention. But many of those steeped in the ecosystem, like Adermann, have their doubts. “I’m a bit pessimistic,” he said. “I worry that people will just not care enough to actually do anything about it.” Kilian Hocke contributed to this report.

noticias.titulo: What kind of ECB is Europe getting after Lagarde?
noticias.resumen: Now that Paris and Berlin appear to have lined up Spanish central banker Pablo Hernández de Cos for the ECB presidency instead of his Dutch counterpart Klaas Knot, whether a dove or a hawk sits at the top may matter less than it seems, including for France.
noticias.texto: This week, eurozone finance ministers are expected to choose who will replace Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank (ECB). Lagarde is stepping down early, on 7 February, to weigh in on the French elections and to allow EU governments to choose a new leadership team before next year’s presidential vote in France, which could well see the far-right Marine Le Pen take over the reins of power. Speculation has been going on for months, and the Dutch former central bank chief, Klaas Knot, as well as Spain’s ex-central bank governor, Pablo Hernández de Cos, quickly emerged as frontrunners. For a long time it seemed Knot, with conditional support from Paris, stood the best chance, but in recent days it has become clear that Paris and Berlin appear to have struck a deal, and that De Cos will almost certainly be Lagarde’s successor. Another southerner at the top This came as a disappointment in The Hague, where the feeling was that southern countries are overrepresented in European financial institutions. As the Dutch daily newspaper de Volkskrant said , “the Eurogroup is chaired by a Greek, the European Investment Bank is headed by a Spaniard, the European supervisory body for financial markets is chaired by an Italian, and the European Banking Authority has a Frenchman as president.” And now the ECB’s top spot will be filled by another southerner. noticias.titulo: Xi keen to look ‘neutral’ on Ukraine at Shenzhen summit, as China risks spoiling EU relations by helping Putin to wage war
noticias.resumen: As Xi, Putin, and Trump gather in Shenzhen, Beijing is stretching its “neutral” pose to maintain a war‑fuelling trade lifeline for Moscow.
noticias.texto: Chinese president Xi Jinping and his Russian and US counterparts, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump, are meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday (19 November) to discuss the war in Ukraine. China is seen as having considerable economic and diplomatic influence over Russia, but has so far shown little appetite to use this leverage to push the Kremlin towards concessions in peace talks. Xi and Putin began talks in Shenzhen on Wednesday, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, but whether Ukraine will dominate the agenda of Thursday’s trilateral summit remains uncertain. US officials had initially signalled that Ukraine might not be discussed, but Trump later said it would be. Beijing, for its part, has framed the summit more broadly, with China’s foreign ministry saying the three leaders would discuss “safeguarding world peace.” The meeting in Shenzhen comes after discussions in Abu Dhabi among the US, Russia, and Ukraine last week ended with an agreement to exchange 314 prisoners. And with peace talks gaining momentum, Beijing is positioning itself as an indispensable mediator, while avoiding responsibility for delivering a settlement. Beijing is trying to preserve a strategic relationship with Moscow, while maintaining its economic relations with Europe and presenting itself as a responsible global power. “These objectives are not always compatible, and the war in Ukraine has made those contradictions increasingly visible,” said Maria Adele Carrai, an international relations professor and a member of the Oxford School of Global and Area Studies ( OSGA ), at the University of Oxford. Dimitar Lilkov, a senior research officer at the Wilfried Martens Centre for European Studies in Brussels, also told EUobserver: “It is interesting to see if and how Xi Jinping is actually involved in a potential meeting, given that he considers Vladimir Putin as a junior partner.” Analysts have often called Russia China’s “junior partner”, given Moscow’s growing dependence on China for trade, energy, and technology after Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. China abstained from a United Nations Security Council vote denouncing the invasion in 2022, and Xi has maintained close political ties with Putin ever since. Portraying itself as an outsider to the conflict, Beijing has repeatedly said it is ready to promote peace talks and has conducted diplomatic shuttle missions and multilateral initiatives through its special representative Li Hui, but its diplomatic activity has not been matched by public pressure on Putin. “Its public support for talks stays at the level of general principles,” said Alicia García Herrero, a senior fellow at Bruegel Institute in Brussels. Status without responsibility China has consistently maintained that it is neither “the creator of the Ukraine crisis” nor “a party to it”, while calling for dialogue based on principles outlined by Xi, including respect for sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the UN Charter, as well as attention to the legitimate security concerns of all sides.
