noticias.titulo: US army warns detonation of unstable explosives will create toxic plume
noticias.resumen: The Army has delayed the controlled explosion of unstable lead azide in eastern Iowa to Monday after concerns from residents and lawmakers.
noticias.texto:
US army warns detonation of unstable explosives will create toxic plume
- Published
The US Army is set to detonate five tonnes of degraded explosive material in Middletown, Iowa, and have urged locals to vacate the area or stay indoors for their safety.
The detonations will result in an air plume that could send toxic dust, containing lead particles, over eastern Iowa and into neighbouring Illinois, with the potential for contaminants to settle on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces, the army said.
The two controlled explosions will be powerful enough that they could damage buildings and shatter windows nearby.
On Thursday, environmental groups sued in an effort to stop the detonations, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives or give adequate notice.
The detonation was originally scheduled for noon local time (1800 BST) on Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown - a community of about 360 people about four hours west of Chicago, Illinois.
The plant produces medium- and large-calibre munitions for the US Department of Defense.
On Thursday evening, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle delayed the detonation to Monday, saying that "public safety is the Army's top priority".
The planned detonation will be "the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material", he said on X.
The army said that the detonation is part of "a planned and controlled safety operation" to dispose of degraded lead azide. It added that the detonation has been permitted by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) under conservation and recovery laws.
Residents have been asked to leave their homes for about six hours - between 08:00 and 14:00 local time - while the operation takes place and the dust settles. The army said that "all humans" should avoid outdoor activities within affected areas.
Residents in Middletown will hear a loud noise, feel vibrations from two consecutive, rapid detonations and will see a plume of dust, the advisory said.
According to Iowa Public Radio, external, the IAAAP found earlier this year that the lead azide - a highly volatile compound used as a detonator - stored in underground concrete tanks is degrading, becoming too unstable to safely move.
Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place is the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.
The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".
Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command, said that the substance has been stored at the plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers.
It sits in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, but a routine check earlier this year found that some of the water had evaporated, Barati told the Associated Press.
The army said the lead azide barrels will be detonated inside earth-covered magazines made of concrete, and surrounded with barriers full of sand. The soil above will be saturated with water in an effort to reduce the lead in the air.
On Thursday, two environmental groups sued to block the detonation, challenging the validity of the EPA's emergency permit, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.
"The EPA itself admits that there is no safe level of lead exposure for humans," said Michael Schmidt, General Counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council.
"When our federal government makes decisions that result in a potentially toxic plume of lead dust that could cover much of southeastern Iowa, Iowans deserve to know that every available alternative was considered before choosing this method of disposal."

noticias.titulo: China issues Mount Fuji warning as family of missing climber offers reward
noticias.resumen: The $75,000 reward offered by Chen Jie's family has sparked fears of more reckless climbing attempts.
noticias.texto:
China issues Mount Fuji warning as family of missing climber offers reward
- Published
The Chinese embassy in Japan has warned its citizens against off-season ascents of Mount Fuji amid concerns that the hefty reward offered by a missing hiker's family could encourage more reckless climbing.
Chen Jie, 25, vanished on 8 November on the mountain. His family is offering 500,000 yuan ($75,000; Â£57,300) to anyone who finds him alive, and 100,000 yuan to anyone who recovers his body, say Chinese and Japanese media reports.
Strong winds and blizzards pose serious risks during the closed season, especially as shelter and first-aid centres are not operational, the embassy said on Tuesday.
Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from around early July to early September.
Earlier this year, authorities of Yamanashi province, where the northern part of Mount Fuji sits, had said that people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have to pay for the service from next year on.
Authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season to submit detailed climbing plans.
"We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Kotaro Nagasaki, the prefecture governor, said at the time.
On Wednesday, Nagasaki told reporters that attempts to find the missing climber could lead to "secondary disasters"
According to Japanese news outlet the Mainichi Shimbun, Nagasaki appeared to appeal to Chen's family, saying: "I understand that your family is important, but please refrain from doing anything that could endanger others."
Some social media users in Japan have similarly expressed fears would entice people to venture into the mountains ill-prepared and lead to more accidents,
Yamanashi police said Chen had set out on his hike on 8 November with two friends, who turned back after they realised the mountain was closed and that they weren't suitably equipped for the conditions of the trails.
Chen pressed on alone from the fifth station of the Yoshida Trail, which sits at around 2,300m (7545ft) above sea level.
A friend last heard from Chen at 10:30 that day, when he sent a video message saying: "I'm going up the mountain... There's no one in sight."
The highest point of Mount Fuji, which is Japan's tallest peak, stands at 3,776m.
Local authorities launched a search for Chen on 10 November, but it had to be halted several times because of poor weather.
Chen's father reportedly arrived in Japan on 13 November. It is not clear when he posted the reward offer.
  - Published16 September

noticias.titulo: US appoints new cybersecurity chief after series of tech failures
noticias.resumen: Appointee Kirsten Davies says US has the chance to 'dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come'.
noticias.texto:
US appoints new cybersecurity chief after series of tech failures
Appointee Kirsten Davies says US has the chance to ‘dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come’.
The White House has fired the United States’s cybersecurity chief and appointed a replacement, days after widespread outages disrupted air travel, banking and national security systems.
Kirsten Davies, chief information officer at the Department of Defense, was appointed on Thursday to replace Sean Cairncross, who was reportedly sacked.
President Donald Trump’s administration has come under scrutiny over its handling of outages that hit Microsoft, the air industry and banks.
A communications failure disrupted air traffic late last week, grounding all flights in the US for about four hours and causing more than 10,000 flights to be cancelled. The disruption is expected to have cost travellers more than $1.9bn in lost time and expenses, according to the Anderson Economic Group.
Microsoft has apologised after governments, businesses and individuals around the world were affected as server failures caused outages of email and websites.
This week, bank customers across the US reported problems accessing services after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase disrupted transactions involving other banks.
The incidents have renewed questions about the vulnerabilities of critical infrastructure, most of which depends on modern-day technology.
“Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected,” Davies said in a social media post.
“Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come … but only if we modernise and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future. Under President Trump’s leadership we will have a more secure, resilient; and supercharged technological future.”
US officials have said the outages were not caused by a cyberattack.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Wednesday that the disruptions were likely due to organisations using artificial intelligence to fix security flaws and carry out maintenance updates.

noticias.titulo: EU and UK seal reset deal
noticias.resumen: This is a breaking news story.
noticias.texto:
EU and UK seal reset deal
The European Union has struck agreements on three policy areas with Britain in a move seen as the start of a reset of relations a decade after the Brexit vote.
Following a summit in Brussels on Friday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s office said negotiations had concluded and a reset deal had been sealed.
Downing Street said both sides had agreed timelines for implementing a youth mobility scheme, a sanitary and phytosanitary agreement and a link between their emissions trading systems. Details are due to be published in a joint statement.
A UK government spokesperson told Al Jazeera: “The deal is done – negotiations have concluded. Now, both sides will work towards implementation.
“As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place,” the spokesperson added. “And talks will continue on some areas.”
Despite the agreements, months or years of negotiations – on topics ranging from student fees to manufacturing rules – lie ahead in order for a deeper reset in relations to take effect.
Burnham has previously told the British public all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation bloc.
However, he has stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome, and far from imminent.
That possibility, and the agreements sealed so far, will incur anger from the significant section of the British public that remains Eurosceptic.
More to come…

noticias.titulo: Kushner says Russia OK with ‘NATO-like’ security pact for Ukraine: Is it?
noticias.resumen: NATO Article 5 says attack on one member is an attack on all. Analysts say inclusion of Ukraine 'stretches credulity'.
noticias.texto:
Kushner says Russia OK with ‘NATO-like’ security pact for Ukraine: Is it?
NATO’s Article 5 says an attack on one member of the alliance is treated as an attack on all. Analysts say inclusion of Ukraine ‘stretches credulity’.
The United States has pitched a new plan to secure post-war Ukraine when its almost five-year war with Russia finally comes to an end.
At a meeting on Thursday with European leaders in Germany’s capital, Berlin, US President Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said he believes Russia is “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for post-war Ukraine.
Kushner’s comments came just hours after an unprecedented summit involving Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China. At that meeting, Putin promised to retaliate against Ukraine’s attacks on Russia.
Following the Berlin summit, French President Emmanuel Macron said Ukraine’s membership of NATO should be considered again, prompting Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov to push back.
Ryabokov said any form of “quasi membership” for Kyiv of the Western military alliance was totally unacceptable for Moscow, Russian state media reported.
Ukraine applied to become a member of NATO in September 2022, seeking to fortify its borders with Russia.
But the Kremlin has repeatedly stated that Ukraine becoming a member of NATO would trigger “a harsh response” from Russia.
So could NATO-like security guarantees really work for Kyiv in light of Russia’s opposition?
Here’s what we know:
What has Kushner said?
European countries have been angered by the European Union being largely sidelined in the stop-start US negotiations with Russia and Ukraine since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.
Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi on Thursday has added to apprehension about whether the US president is serious about ending Russia’s war on Ukraine, particularly after his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his apparent recent overtures to Putin by relaxing sanctions on Russian oil.
But at a meeting of the “coalition of the willing”, a nearly 40-nation alliance of Ukraine’s European allies, in Berlin this week, Kushner and fellow US envoy Steve Witkoff tried to reassure European leaders, telling them Trump had held discussions in Shenzhen on ending the war on Ukraine.
“Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side,” Kushner said.
“We do believe that Russia having Europe at the table will be essential for ending the war,” he added.
Kushner also said Russia is “comfortable” with the idea of security guarantees for post-war Ukraine modelled on NATO’s Article 5, which says an attack on one member of the alliance is treated as an attack on all.
“I think we’ve gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5,” he said, adding that Trump was “open” to the idea but “obviously, it has to be in America’s interest” and part of “a broader security package”.
Kushner said Trump also called in to the Berlin talks after his meeting with Putin and the latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi last week had produced no major breakthrough.
What is NATO’s Article 5?
Described as the “cornerstone” of the military alliance, NATO’s collective defence principle, contained in Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, was developed in 1949 to create a mutual protective pact to counter risks posed by the Soviet Union at the onset of the Cold War.
According to NATO, committing to Article 5 means that each member of the alliance knows that if one of them is the “victim of an armed attack, each and every other member of the alliance will consider this act of violence as an armed attack against all members”.
That means that each NATO member is obligated to “take the actions it deems necessary to assist the ally attacked”.
When Article 5 is invoked, NATO allies are free to provide whatever form of aid and assistance is deemed “necessary to respond to the situation”.
However, it is not an automatic process. The article must be invoked and then agreed upon by NATO members and can take time to implement. First, there must be a meeting of the North Atlantic Council to assess whether the attack meets Article 5 criteria. Then there must be a unanimous political decision and declaration to invoke the article. This can be slowed down by deliberations, intelligence gathering and legal reviews.
After that, determining what is necessary to respond to a given situation is the individual obligation of each NATO ally and may not necessarily include military action. As NATO states: “It is therefore left to the judgement of each individual member country to determine how it will contribute.”
Each country consults with all other alliance members in terms of response and with the ultimate aim “to restore and maintain the security” of alliance members.
Article 5 has been invoked only once, after the September 11, 2001, attacks on the US by al-Qaeda.
The triggering of Article 5 saw “NATO engage actively in the fight against terrorism, launch its first operations outside the Euro-Atlantic area and begin a far-reaching transformation of its capabilities”, according to the alliance.
“By invoking Article 5, NATO members showed their solidarity toward the United States and condemned, in the strongest possible way, the terrorist attacks against the United States.”
What could ‘NATO-like’ security guarantees look like for Ukraine?
It is very unclear.
Ukraine applied to become a NATO member seven months after Russia’s full-scale invasion began. Since then, Zelenskyy, his officials and Ukrainians around the world have been lobbying NATO nations to speed up Kyiv’s accession process.
But NATO members remain divided about offering Ukraine alliance membership during an ongoing war despite a broad consensus to signal strong support for Kyiv.
NATO members bordering Russia, such as Lithuania and Poland, have been most enthusiastic about backing Ukraine’s ambitions. Several other nations in the alliance have also been supportive of an expedited process for Kyiv to join despite concerns about corruption in Ukraine and while seeking an end to the war with Russia as a condition for the country to become a NATO member.
Under Trump, the US has been far less receptive to Ukraine’s calls for NATO membership. Indeed, Trump has publicly told Ukraine to give up its hopes of joining the alliance.
Yet last week, Kushner and Witkoff suggested that Kyiv could join the alliance in exchange for relinquishing eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region to Russia.
At the Berlin meeting on Thursday, French President Emmanuel Macron revisited the topic of Ukraine’s NATO membership. “Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine’s accession to NATO,” Macron said.
Also at the meeting, Kushner pitched NATO’s Article 5-like security guarantees for Ukraine without specifying how they would work.
This year, Zelenskyy stressed that for Ukraine, guarantees of security first need to come from the US. In October, the Ukrainian president and Witkoff discussed US security guarantees for Kyiv similar to Article 5.
But on Thursday, Zelenskyy told reporters that at the Berlin meeting, there was no common understanding of what Article 5-style security guarantees for Kyiv would entail.
He questioned whether giving Ukraine such security guarantees would mean that US and European troops would be based on Ukrainian land because that was his understanding of Article 5.
“For me, the most important thing is how countries will react on aggression,” he said.
Harry Nedelcu, partner and senior director of geopolitics at the Rasmussen Global consultancy, who previously served on the NATO secretary-general’s policy planning staff, said there is inconsistency in US strategy.
“On one hand, they are proposing NATO membership to Ukraine in exchange for Kyiv entirely withdrawing its troops from the Donbas, and now they are saying Ukraine could get NATO-like security guarantees. It is clear Washington wants to show some kind of progress and get a peace deal done, also perhaps in light of the situation in Iran,” he told Al Jazeera.
“But Russia has to agree to this proposal,” he said, adding that so far, Washington only appears to be pressuring Ukraine to negotiate and not Russia.
He noted that Russia has long been strongly opposed to Ukraine joining NATO and stressed that it is time for the US and European powers to pressure Moscow to come to the negotiating table.
What is Russia’s position?
After the trilateral summit in Shenzhen, Putin said discussions about post-war security guarantees must address both Ukraine and Russia.
“We acknowledge that Ukraine has a right to security, just as Russia has. It is simply that no one wants to discuss Russia’s security, and that is a matter of considerable importance to us, to put it mildly,” he told journalists.
Historically, the Kremlin has maintained a strict position that Ukraine’s NATO membership is a red line for Moscow and a direct threat to Russia’s national security. Putin has previously cited Ukraine’s NATO aspirations as one reason that Russia launched its war in 2022.
In Shenzhen, the Russian president reiterated that Ukraine becoming a NATO member and getting the alliance’s security guarantees would be “unacceptable” to the Kremlin.
Putin noted how in 1991, when the Soviet Union broke up, Russia was promised that NATO would not expand eastwards but has since been “deceived”. Since then, 16 countries in Eastern Europe and Scandinavia have joined the alliance.
“We were deceived then, and so it began – five or six waves of expansion. Ultimately, they reached Ukraine,” he said.
“I have already spoken about this more than once. When Ukraine gained independence, its Declaration of Independence stated that Ukraine was a neutral state. Then suddenly – bang! – came the push for NATO accession, both on the part of NATO and on the part of Ukraine itself,” he said.
“But we repeated this a thousand times: Wait, there is no need for this [Ukraine joining NATO]. This is unacceptable to us,” Putin stressed.
Could NATO-style security guarantees work for Ukraine?
This remains unclear because the US and other NATO members have not specified what these security guarantees would look like.
Analysts are also sceptical.
In a November 10 report for the United Kingdom-based defence think tank, the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), Eric Ciaramella, senior fellow in the Russia and Eurasia programme at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, wrote that an Article 5 security guarantee for Ukraine makes little sense.
“The notion that the US and European nations would obligate themselves to defend Ukraine from a future Russian attack – the essence of Article 5 – strains credulity,” he wrote.
“A pledge by Trump to do so would be especially implausible considering how his administration has cut American support for Ukraine and is intent on reducing the US role in Europe’s security,” Ciaramella said.
“A more realistic course would be for the US and Europe to commit, through a set of legally codified agreements, to a steady supply of weapons, training, defence industrial cooperation, and intelligence sharing for at least a decade after the war ends,” he added.
Ian Lesser, distinguished fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, told Al Jazeera that it is hard to make Article 5-like commitments practical and credible at a time when NATO itself is grappling with its own rearmament strategy for European defence.
“Much depends on US participation, and the American commitment to European defence is unfortunately in flux. It is also important to remember that there is nothing automatic about Article 5. It is a political decision taken by member states,” Lesser said.
“The good news is that security guarantees for Ukraine are being seriously discussed on both sides of the Atlantic,” he added.

noticias.titulo: Can the Rohingya genocide verdict deliver justice?
noticias.resumen: The ICJ has ruled against Myanmar, but safe return, citizenship and reparations remain far from guaranteed.
noticias.texto:
Can the Rohingya genocide verdict deliver justice?
The ICJ has ruled against Myanmar, but safe return, citizenship and reparations remain far from guaranteed.
On Thursday, the International Court of Justice did something it had never done in its 80-year history: It held a state responsible for committing genocide. By nine votes to six, the court found that Myanmar’s 2017 campaign against the Rohingya crossed the gravest threshold in international law.
That matters because Myanmar’s defence was never simply that nothing terrible happened. It argued that its “clearance operations” followed attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) and were, however brutal, fundamentally counterterrorism. Genocide requires more than proof of killing, rape or village destruction; it requires specific intent to destroy a protected group.
The court found that Myanmar’s government forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, committed widespread sexual violence, inflicted extreme violence on children and attacked people fleeing towards Bangladesh. Taking the evidence together, it concluded that the “only reasonable inference” was an intention to destroy a substantial part of the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine state.
That strips away the central evasion of the past decade. The ARSA attacks were real. So was armed conflict. But rebellion is not a legal alibi for genocide. Nor can the atrocities now be dismissed as excesses by rogue soldiers. This was a judgement about what Myanmar, as a state, did to a people.
The 9-6 split will inevitably be used by Myanmar to cast doubt on the ruling. But the judgement is final and binding. And by 10 votes to five, the court went further, ordering reparations, including safe, voluntary and dignified return, family reunification, restitution of property and compensation where restitution is impossible.
For Rohingya survivors, that is extraordinary vindication. Yasmin Ullah, a Rohingya rights activist who sat in the courtroom, called it “a great day for the Rohingya”. In Cox’s Bazar, refugees had been making an equally practical demand: They want to go home, but with rights, citizenship and dignity.
But here is the problem: You cannot eat a judgement. You cannot live inside one. You cannot rebuild a burned village with one or raise a child safely inside one.
The ICJ has no enforcement arm. Under Article 94(2) of the United Nations Charter, noncompliance can be taken to the UN Security Council (UNSC), where China or Russia could block action. That makes pressure outside the UNSC essential: Targeted sanctions, ASEAN diplomacy, the ICC investigation and Argentina’s universal-jurisdiction case, where arrest warrants have already been issued for 25 suspects.
Who governs the map has also changed. In 2017, Myanmar’s military dominated Rakhine. Today, the Arakan Army controls most of it, and UN investigators have documented forced recruitment, movement restrictions, arbitrary killings and other abuses against Rohingya under its rule.
Any serious return framework must therefore deal with whoever controls the ground. Bangladesh should tie cross-border trade, humanitarian access and political engagement with the Arakan Army to measurable Rohingya benchmarks: Freedom of movement, restoration of land, an end to forced recruitment, international monitoring and a pathway to citizenship. Dhaka should also press Myanmar’s authorities, ASEAN, China, India, Gulf states and Western governments to support a monitored return-and-reparations mechanism. For too long, ports, pipelines and trade corridors have been treated as “strategic” while the Rohingya remain in the humanitarian file.
Everyone wants something from Myanmar. The Rohingya should finally be part of the bill.
None of this matters if the camps fall apart before return becomes possible. About 95 percent of Rohingya refugees are moderately to highly vulnerable and rely almost entirely on humanitarian assistance. The UN’s scaled-down 2026 response plan seeks $710.5m, 26 percent less than the previous year’s appeal. In April, the World Food Programme reduced support for about two-thirds of refugees under a new tiered system; about 17 percent now receive only $7 per person per month.
Donors applauding the verdict should fund the wait as seriously as they praise the destination. The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, which backed The Gambia’s case, and Gulf donors have a particular responsibility. Western governments should restore cuts, while lenders and donors should support Bangladeshi host communities. Underfunded camps feed trafficking, exploitation and dangerous sea journeys towards Malaysia and Indonesia. A judgement that opens a path home is worth little if the people it was meant for cannot survive the wait.
Reparations now have legal force, not merely moral appeal. Property claims should be documented; land restored where possible; compensation paid where it cannot. Aid says: You are suffering, so we will help you survive. Reparations say: A wrong was done to you, and someone is obliged to repair it.
The verdict is enormous. The test now is simpler: Can the Rohingya go home as citizens, reclaim their land, receive compensation and raise their children somewhere other than a refugee camp?
The court has established the truth. Now justice has to bring it home.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: Drone operator removes Man United training footage and issues apology
noticias.resumen: The footage, filmed during new manager Mauricio Pochettino's first training session, was uploaded online.
noticias.texto:
Drone operator removes Man United training footage and issues apology
The footage, filmed during new manager Mauricio Pochettino’s first training session, was uploaded online.
A drone operator who filmed Manchester United’s training session this week has apologised for what he called a “total error of judgement” and removed the footage from his YouTube channel.
The footage, filmed at United’s Carrington training ground during new manager Mauricio Pochettino’s first training session on Thursday, was uploaded online under the username “CC OVERVIEW”.
In a statement posted on his YouTube channel on Friday, the drone operator said that while the flight was legal under drone regulations, filming the session had been “unethical”.
“My aim was to picture Mauricio Pochettino in his United training kit for the supporters to see for the first time,” he said.
“I fully accept it was unethical on my part. I would like to apologise to Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino and the players for my actions and sincerely hope those actions do not affect the outcome of any match.”
The operator added that he had wrongly assumed only warm-up activities would be visible and that the training session would be open to various media outlets.
He also said neither Liverpool nor any other football club had been involved in his decision to film at Carrington.
“The video has been removed from my channel,” he said.
Pochettino arrived from the US men’s national team this week after United sacked Michael Carrick, and faces an immediate test with a trip to Liverpool on Sunday.
United are languishing 18th in the league table after winning just one of their 10 games. Liverpool are fourth.

noticias.titulo: Russia unleashes retaliatory barrage on Kyiv bridges
noticias.resumen: The attack follows Putin's pledge of 'painful' response to Ukraine's attack on symbolic Crimean bridge.
noticias.texto:
Russia unleashes retaliatory barrage on Kyiv bridges
The attack follows Putin’s pledge of ‘painful’ response to Ukraine’s attack on symbolic Crimean bridge.
Russia launched a barrage of air attacks on Ukraine, killing eight people, as it targeted Kyiv’s bridges and infrastructure across the country.
The attacks overnight on Thursday into Friday hit vital transport bridges spanning the Dnipro River in the capital and knocked out power generation in several parts of Ukraine, officials said.
The missile and drone swarms came shortly after Russia’s President Vladimir Putin threatened retaliation for Ukraine’s targeting of a symbolic bridge linking his country with the Crimean Peninsula, which Moscow illegally annexed in 2014.
Eight people – including six in Kyiv – were killed in the overnight attacks, and 28 wounded, Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said in a social media post.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said ballistic missiles had damaged the Podilskyi, Darnitskyi, and Southern bridges, requiring traffic restrictions across the Dnipro.
Buildings, transport and logistics infrastructure were hit in several districts of the city, the Kyiv City Military Administration said in a statement. Citywide electricity disruptions were also reported.
Elsewhere, Ukrainian sources reported that one person was killed as a strike hit a hospital in the Zaporizhia region. Nuclear power plants across the country were forced to reduce operations, causing outages in Kyiv and 10 regions, First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said on Friday that road and rail bridges in Kyiv used to transport weapons and military equipment to the battlefield were targeted. It added that its forces hit defence industry facilities as well as energy and transport infrastructure in several regions of Ukraine.
The large-scale attack came hours after Putin pledged a “painful” response to Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch Bridge earlier this week. The attack severed the key road link across the Kerch Strait.
“We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that,” Putin told reporters on Thursday in China, where he attended a summit with the Chinese and United States presidents. Putin said the roadside of the bridge had been “seriously damaged” and pledged to rebuild it.
Ukraine continued its efforts to target energy and military infrastructure overnight. Russia’s Defence Ministry reported that its forces had intercepted 310 Ukrainian drones.
A Ukrainian drone attack damaged an industrial facility in Russia’s western region of Smolensk, Governor Vasily Anokhin said on the Telegram messaging app, without identifying the facility.
The commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces said on Friday that 40 Russian oil facilities and defence industry targets have been hit over the past 50 days.
Moscow-installed officials in occupied eastern Ukraine also reported three people had been killed during an attack.
‘Unacceptable’
The overnight hostilities illustrate the lack of progress in US-led efforts to mediate a ceasefire.
US envoy Jared Kushner said on Thursday that Russia is comfortable with Europe joining the negotiations, and also with the idea of security guarantees for post-war Ukraine that are modelled on NATO’s Article 5, under which an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.
Early on Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said cooperation between Ukraine, the US and Europe on negotiations is “becoming closer” and that he hoped the US would organise the first multilateral meeting involving the Europeans “as soon as possible”.
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said later that a visit by three European Union representatives to Russia is “under consideration”.
However, he added that any form of Ukrainian membership of NATO is unacceptable to Moscow.
“[E]ven the notion of a formula for Ukraine’s quasi-membership of NATO, and the search for some sort of – in inverted commas – ‘creative solution’ in this area, is an option that is unacceptable to us. We discuss security guarantees first and foremost in terms of ensuring the security of our own country,” Ryabkov was quoted as saying by the Interfax news agency.
“As far as Ukraine is concerned, let them recognise the irrevocable nature of our demand that this state must not join NATO. When that happens, I think the issue of security guarantees can be discussed in one way or another,” Ryabkov was quoted as adding.

noticias.titulo: Kenya’s growing doping crisis overshadows legacy as athletics powerhouse
noticias.resumen: More than 140 Kenyan athletes suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit since 2017, most of them distance runners.
noticias.texto:
Kenya’s growing doping crisis overshadows legacy as athletics powerhouse
Since 2017, more than 140 Kenyan athletes have been suspended by the Athletics Integrity Unit, most of them distance runners.
Over decades, Kenya built a legacy of producing elite runners who dominated distance running. The recipe for success was simple: High-altitude training, a whole-foods diet, early nights, consistency.
But a quiet, underhanded addition over the past few years is threatening to tarnish its legacy and the dozens of global accolades that stemmed from it – doping.
The African nation’s latest doping scandal is perhaps the most shocking; Peres Jepchirchir, world and Olympic marathon champion, was handed a three-year ban on Thursday for testing positive for banned blood booster EPO.
The Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) said Jepchirchir’s sample was taken before her Sydney Marathon victory in August, where she stormed to her fourth World Marathon Majors win after triumph in New York (2021), Boston (2022), and London (2024). She’s also a former half-marathon world record holder.
Jepchirchir, who admitted to breaching anti-doping rules, is arguably the most prominent and successful in a string of Kenyan athletes who have faced formal doping sanctions over the past decade. Since 2017, more than 140 Kenyan athletes have been suspended by AIU, most of them distance runners.
How has Kenyan athletics ended up at this point and what comes next? Al Jazeera Sport spoke to experts to find out.
Why has there been a rise in doping violations among Kenyan runners?
Rather than seeing it as a rise, the reality is that more athletes are being tested, caught, and publicised for doping violations, former Kenyan middle-distance runner Martin Keino told Al Jazeera.
“Testing has expanded, particularly out-of-competition testing, and the AIU now goes after suspicious patterns instead of waiting for a positive sample,” said Keino, a former pacer who helped set seven world records.
“The problem is real, but the visibility is new.”
What drives athletes to dope?
Financial insecurity, fear of decline in performance, and pressure to deliver are some of the biggest factors, Keino explained.
“Kenya produces a huge number of runners chasing a very small number of life-changing contracts. When one breakthrough can lift a whole family out of poverty, the pull to find an edge gets much stronger.
“Add weak local controls on banned substances, unqualified ‘coaches’ and agents who push for quick results, and doping can spread quietly.”
For Kenyan Olympic champion Wilfred Bungei, men’s 800m champion at the 2008 Beijing Olympics, the rise in doping violations hits closer to home.
Bungei is a relative veteran compared with contemporary Kenyan greats like Eliud Kipchoge, Sebastian Sawe and Faith Kipyegon, who have continued the legacy built by the likes of Martin’s father Kip Keino, one of Kenya’s first Olympic champions in the 1960s. He says doping violations by the likes of Jepchirchir and Ruth Chepngetich jeopardise the legitimacy of future victories while tarnishing the current legacy.
“For decades, Kenya has built its athletics on solid hard work from dedicated athletes. Now, some athletes are choosing the shortest way to make it big in athletics, by cheating,” Bungei said.
“I can only describe it as greed, selfishness and above all just plain stupidity to not understand that it’s not you the doper who is damaged but thousands of Kenyan athletes who built their careers on pure sweat and discipline.”
Caroline Mwanzia, an international sports lawyer practising in anti-doping, safeguarding, and sports governance, had a more straightforward view.
“For some athletes, it is because of intentionally wanting to gain an unfair advantage over other athletes competing,” she said.
“Others may have taken medicinal drugs without first obtaining a Therapeutic Use Exemption [TUE], but most athletes are simply being ignorant.”
Are athletes always at fault for doping violations?
This is where the lines get blurred on whether athletes or their support personnel are responsible for what goes into their bodies. Bungei insists that the responsibility “sits squarely on the athlete”.
“I don’t believe that an athlete with integrity would be encouraged by anyone to do what is wrong,” he said.
Keino held a similar sentiment. “Most elite athletes know the basics: The prohibited list, testing, whereabouts rules, the penalties. You can’t compete at World Marathon Major level and claim total ignorance of the rules.”
But knowing the rules is different from understanding every product, injection, supplement, or “recovery treatment” handed to you, Keino explained.
“Some athletes take things without really understanding the risks, the dosages, the detection windows, or who is supplying them. Others take banned substances knowingly and hide behind ignorance later.”
Per a 2016 investigation, the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) found two Kenyan athletes who attempted to escape their sanctions by providing falsified medical records, one of which WADA termed the “culminating peak in an overall strategy of cover-up and concealment by the athlete”.
“That’s why education has to be practical. A seminar where someone reads out the WADA code isn’t enough,” Keino emphasised.
“Athletes need to hear it plainly: Never take an injection or unknown substance without checking it, keep records, ask questions, and walk away from any coach or agent who can’t explain what they’re giving you.”
WADA also concluded in its investigation that “athletes in Kenya are insufficiently educated on doping and/or wilfully blind as to the consequences of doping.”
Why do elite athletes risk doping?
Experience doesn’t make you immune to pressure, fear, or bad decisions, Keino explained.
“Established runners actually carry a different kind of pressure. They have a reputation to protect, a lifestyle to maintain, and people depending on them.
“An injury, a dip in form, or a few poor races can hit contracts, appearance fees, and sponsorship fast.”
Keino went on to explain that for veteran athletes like Jepchirchir and Chepngetich, doping is not to break into the elite circle but to stay on top longer, keep up with younger athletes, or bounce back from a setback.
“None of that excuses it – at that level, nobody can credibly say they don’t know what EPO is, how it works, or why it’s banned.”
Should Kenya be sanctioned by global bodies?
“Back in 2009 when a few doping cases had been reported, I advocated for the criminalisation of doping and people thought I was too harsh. Almost 20 years later, Kenya’s image is on the line,” said Bungei, who still believes the government should make doping a criminal offence in Kenya.
In September, Kenya signed the Anti-Doping Amendment Bill 2026 to align with WADA’s updated code, a decade after it was first signed into law after WADA declared Kenya non-compliant with global anti-doping rules and regulations.
“Better options [than sanctions] are stronger audits of Kenya’s anti-doping system, funding for testing and education, bans for repeat enablers, and conditions attached to hosting major events,” Keino said.
“Nairobi’s award of the 2029 World Athletics Championships should come with real accountability, not just prestige.”

noticias.titulo: Pakistan minister visits India for first time since 2025 war
noticias.resumen: Islamabad and New Delhi insist the visit is strictly multilateral, despite hopes it could open a channel for contact.
noticias.texto:
Pakistan minister visits India for first time since 2025 war
Islamabad and New Delhi insist the visit is strictly multilateral, despite hopes it could open a channel for contact.
Islamabad, Pakistan — Pakistan’s climate change minister, Musadik Malik, arrived in New Delhi on Friday, becoming the first Pakistani federal minister to visit India since the neighbours fought a four-day war in May 2025.
Malik is attending the first Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum, a three-day gathering that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is due to inaugurate on Friday evening. Malik is expected to address the forum on Saturday.
No bilateral meeting has been announced. Pakistan’s Foreign Office said on Thursday that its participation was “reflective of its contribution as an active SCO member State to promote dialogue, cooperation and understanding in line with ‘Shanghai Spirit’”.
It is the first such visit since then-Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari travelled to Goa in May 2023.
Both governments have framed these exchanges as routine SCO business.
With Pakistan due to host the bloc’s leaders next August, the question is how far contact confined to a multilateral forum can go — and whether this could set the stage for Modi to travel to Islamabad for the summit.
The choice of minister
Indian media, quoting diplomatic sources, reported that India’s invitation was for Pakistan’s minister for national heritage and culture, Aurangzeb Khan Khichi.
Neither government has confirmed this.
Pakistan’s Foreign Office said on November 6 only that it had received an invitation and would decide after consultations. Islamabad has not said why it sent Malik.
The Foreign Office said Malik would “share Pakistan’s perspective on the salience of dialogue among civilisations” and meet SCO member states on the sidelines.
Jauhar Saleem, president of the Islamabad-based Institute of Regional Studies (IRS) and a former foreign secretary, said the choice was Pakistan’s to make.
“There is no hard and fast rule about who represents a country at such fora, and it is the prerogative of the invited state to nominate the representative it considers most appropriate,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Civilisation is not only about heritage and culture; it is about how societies relate to their land, their rivers, and one another,” Saleem added.
Khurram Dastgir Khan, a former federal minister for foreign affairs and defence and senior leader of the governing Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N), said the choice was deliberate.
Sending a minister of its own choosing “lets Pakistan take part as an SCO member without being seen to buy into India’s framing or showcase,” he told Al Jazeera.
He said it also signalled Pakistan’s aim “to be seen as a constructive host for the 2027 summit; thereby nudging the door open an inch for PM Modi’s participation”.
Pakistan took over the SCO’s rotating chairmanship on September 1 and will host the leaders’ summit in Islamabad in August 2027, the month both countries mark 80 years of independence.
New Delhi’s position
New Delhi has sought to keep the visit within a narrow SCO frame.
At an October 28 briefing, foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India had invited “all SCO members” “as per established practice”, along with dialogue partners and one observer.
Asked whether New Delhi was reviewing its Pakistan policy ahead of upcoming multilateral engagements, he said: “Post the Pahalgam attack, we have a Pakistan policy. That Pakistan policy remains in place; there has been no change.”
India blames Pakistan for the April 2025 attack in Pahalgam, in Indian-administered Kashmir, in which gunmen killed 26 civilians, setting the stage for the war that followed. Islamabad denies any involvement.
Sharat Sabharwal, India’s high commissioner to Pakistan from 2009 to 2013, said the invitation followed from India’s role as host.
“This is a meeting in the SCO framework, where India, as the organiser, has to invite all member countries. Therefore, at this juncture, there is no reason to look for any deeper meaning in this visit,” he told Al Jazeera.
Modi proposed the forum at last year’s SCO summit in Tianjin, China.
Irfan Nooruddin, a professor at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, said the initiative gave New Delhi a narrative of its own.
“If anything, it will be spun as further indication of India’s leading role in the region and its magnanimity in terms of including Pakistan in the dialogues,” he told Al Jazeera.
Rezaul Hasan Laskar, foreign affairs editor at The Hindustan Times newspaper in New Delhi, said there was little appetite at home for anything more.
“The government has maintained this is a multilateral engagement under the SCO framework, and that there will be no bilateral engagements with Pakistan till the issue of terrorism is addressed,” he told Al Jazeera. “There doesn’t appear to be widespread public backing for a fresh approach towards Pakistan.”
A history of contact
The SCO has been one of the few forums bringing the two countries together since they joined in 2017.
Bhutto-Zardari’s visit to Goa ended in public sparring. In his speech, he warned against “weaponising terrorism for diplomatic point scoring”, without naming India.
Jaishankar later described him to reporters as a “promoter, justifier and spokesperson of a terrorism industry”. The two did not hold a separate bilateral meeting.
Jaishankar’s subsequent visit to Islamabad in October 2024, for an SCO heads of government meeting, passed more quietly, with pleasantries but no talks.
In September this year, Alok Dimri, India’s SCO coordinator, spent three days in Islamabad and shook hands with Pakistan’s Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar. He described the visit to reporters as “an annual rotational ritual of the SCO”.
Dastgir said such contact had done little to change the course of relations.
“The Indian External Affairs Minister’s October 2024 trip to Islamabad for SCO proved a dead-end, despite the hoopla. It did not prevent open hostilities in May 2025,” he said.
Salman Bashir, a former Pakistani high commissioner to India, was blunter. “SCO is an opportunity to maintain a semblance of civility. Don’t think that it is a pathway to normalcy,” he told Al Jazeera.
Frozen ties
Beyond the SCO calendar, nearly every bilateral link remains frozen.
India has held the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty “in abeyance” since the Pahalgam attack.
On August 31, a court of arbitration in The Hague ruled that India could not suspend the treaty unilaterally. New Delhi rejected the court’s jurisdiction.
In September, Indian and Pakistani naval vessels collided in the Arabian Sea, prompting India to summon Pakistan’s chargé d’affaires in protest. Neither country has had a high commissioner in the other’s capital since 2019.
Contact has continued below the official level.
Laskar pointed to “several Track 1.5 and Track 2 engagements right from a few months after the conflict in May last year,” referring to semi-official and unofficial meetings only partly involving government representation.
The road to Islamabad
Pakistan’s chairmanship will bring a series of tests before next August.
At its summit in Bishkek, the SCO named Lahore its tourism and cultural capital for 2026-27. During his visit, Dimri said he hoped to see the city.
The biggest test will be the leaders’ summit itself. Indian officials have told local media that New Delhi will decide its level of representation closer to the date.
Laskar said a breakthrough was hard to predict, but such a visit “could be the pathway to opening all sorts of possibilities”.
Dastgir said SCO meetings “can provide the pretext for bilateral communication, however rudimentary. Sidelines encounters need no announcement and no concession.”
Nooruddin did not rule out a visit by Modi.
“If there’s a single leader in India’s context who could do that, and get away with it, it is he. A sort of Nixon goes to China, if you would,” he said.
“But, again, so much will happen between now and next August that prognosticating so far into the future is pretty pointless. Let’s just say that it’s entirely possible that Modi goes but I wouldn’t bet on it.”

noticias.titulo: El Salvador’s Bukele seeks third term after constitution change
noticias.resumen: Critics accuse populist president of engineering a de facto one-party state in El Salvador.
noticias.texto:
El Salvador’s Bukele seeks third term after constitution change
Critics accuse populist president of engineering a de facto one-party state in El Salvador.
El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele has officially launched a re-election campaign that critics say illustrates his bid to make El Salvador a one-party state.
Supporters gathered outside the Supreme Electoral Tribunal on Thursday as Bukele arrived to register his candidacy for the February elections.
The populist is widely expected to win the race thanks to the huge political support earned by his crackdown on El Salvador’s violent cartels.
However, the launch of the campaign comes after his party Nuevas Ideas used its supermajority in the country’s congress to remove term limits on the presidency and extend the length of terms from five to six years.
Critics accuse the president of consolidating power by removing checks and balances. The Bertelsmann Transformation Index and others accuse Bukele of creating a de facto one-party state.
The 45-year-old has made uprooting El Salvador’s cartels a core part of his presidency and political persona.
“In El Salvador there is total, complete open democracy,” Bukele told the crowd on Thursday. “We’re sending a message to the world that El Salvador will never return to the past.”
He has now begun exporting the model. Last month, he sent about 2,500 soldiers to Haiti after four Salvadoran members of a United Nations-backed force went missing. The deployment has been welcomed by gang-wracked Port-au-Prince.
However, many analysts question Bukele’s motives, accusing him of exploiting the crisis on the island nation to enhance his reputation.
“Bukele is running for a third consecutive term after packing the court, rewriting the constitution to his liking and jailing or forcing into exile those who dare criticise him,” Juan Pappier of Human Rights Watch said, according to The Associated Press news agency.
“The absolute concentration of power in his hands has been the defining feature of his administration.”
Last year, Nuevas Ideas used its supermajority in Congress to abolish second-round votes and bring forward national elections by two years, to February 2027.

noticias.titulo: Islam set to be the largest religion by 2035: Where will most Muslims live?
noticias.resumen: Pew Research projects Muslim population in Pakistan will overtake Indonesia by 2070, with India next and Nigeria third.
noticias.texto:
Islam set to be the largest religion by 2035: Where will most Muslims live?
Pew Research projects the Muslim population in Pakistan will overtake Indonesia by 2070, with India second and Nigeria third.
Muslims are projected to outnumber Christians worldwide by 2035, according to projections released by the Pew Research Center.
Both religions will keep growing. Between 2020 and 2070, the number of Muslims is expected to rise by 80 percent, from 2.02 billion to 3.64 billion. Christians are projected to grow by 30 percent to 2.96 billion, roughly in step with the world population.
Which religions are growing fastest?
Muslims are projected to grow faster than any other major religious group. Hindus and Jews are expected to grow more slowly than the world population, while the number of Buddhists and people with no religion is projected to shrink.
The main reason is birth rates. Between 2020 and 2025, Muslim women had an average of 3.1 children, compared with 2.5 for Christian women and 1.6 for all other women. A population needs about 2.1 children per woman to replace itself.
Births minus deaths are projected to add 1.6 billion Muslims and 792 million Christians by 2070.
Which countries will have the most Muslims?
Most of the growth will happen where Muslims are already the majority. The 53 Muslim-majority countries are expected to gain 1.2 billion Muslims by 2070, 74 percent of the global increase.
Indonesia had the world’s largest Muslim population in 2020, at 239 million. Pakistan, just 12 million behind, is projected to take the top spot. Pew’s figures compare 2020 with 2070, so they do not say exactly when, but with Pakistan’s Muslim population set to double to 461 million while Indonesia’s grows 15 percent, the switch is likely to come well before 2070.
By 2070, India’s Muslim population is projected to rise from third to second, growing from 213 million to 334 million. Nigeria jumps from fifth to third, more than doubling to 282 million and pushing Indonesia to fourth.
Four of the top 10 in 2070 are in Africa: Nigeria, Egypt, Ethiopia and Sudan. Ethiopia and Afghanistan join the list, replacing Iran and Algeria, while Sudan’s Muslim population more than doubles to 116 million and climbs above Turkiye.
Pew’s projections cover 201 countries and territories, home to 99.98 percent of the world’s population. They assume current trends in fertility, mortality and religious switching continue, and could change with wars, disasters or economic shifts.
