noticias.resumen: Argentinian football legend Messi, who joined Miami in 2023, signed a contract extension through 2028 last year.
noticias.texto:
Lionel Messi of Inter Miami tops Major League Soccer salaries
Argentinian football legend Messi, who joined Miami in 2023, signed a contract extension through 2028 last year.
Lionel Messi remains the highest-paid player in Major League Soccer, with $28.3m in guaranteed compensation, according to a salary release on Thursday by the players’ union, with Chicago’s Robert Lewandowski second.
Argentinian legend Messi topped the league list revealed by the MLS Players Association with compensation almost $8m higher than last year, although his figures include only playing compensation, not income from other sources.
Messi signed a contract extension through 2028 last year.
Poland’s Lewandowski, who joined the Chicago Fire earlier this year, was second overall with $19.51m, followed by Orlando’s Antoine Griezmann of France at $13.94m, South Korean star Son Heung-min of Los Angeles FC at $11.15m and Swiss international Breel Embolo of Atlanta United at $10.81m.
Among MLS clubs, Miami topped all teams in total guaranteed compensation at $59.37m, with Chicago second at $41.29m, Atlanta third at $38.35m, the Los Angeles Galaxy fourth at $34.91m and LAFC fifth at $32.91m.
The league’s lowest total team compensation was Philadelphia Union at $12.64m, with Sporting Kansas City second-lowest at $13.30m and DC United third-lowest at $14.55m.
The figures are through October 9 and are annualised for players who arrived in the summer transfer period.

noticias.titulo: The Gambia stood up for the Rohingya, now the world must act
noticias.resumen: The ICJ has delivered a historic judgement, but justice will depend on what happens next.
noticias.texto:
The Gambia stood up for the Rohingya, now the world must act
The ICJ has delivered a historic judgement, but justice will depend on what happens next.
There are moments in history when a nation is defined not by its size, wealth, military strength or political influence, but by the courage of its conscience.
On Thursday, the International Court of Justice found that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine State, in breach of its obligations under the Genocide Convention. For the Rohingya, it is a long-overdue recognition. For The Gambia, it concludes a case our country brought to the Court seven years ago.
The Rohingya have lived in Myanmar’s Rakhine State for generations. Their basic human rights have been systematically denied over time, leaving them stateless and subject to dehumanising rhetoric, hate speech and legal persecution. Following the Myanmar military’s “clearance operations” in 2016 and 2017, over 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh. The military killed an estimated 10,000 civilians, raped and sexually assaulted women and girls, and burned villages to the ground. There are currently 1.2 million Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh, the majority in the camps of Cox’s Bazar, and 520,000 remain in Myanmar.
When confronted with reports of unimaginable suffering, persecution, displacement and the destruction of communities, The Gambia chose to act. In 2018, our then Minister of Justice, Abubacarr Tambadou, visited the camps in Bangladesh as part of an Organisation of Islamic Cooperation delegation. As a former prosecutor at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, he recognised the signs of genocide in the accounts of the survivors.
With the support of the OIC’s 57 member States, The Gambia brought the case to the International Court of Justice in November 2019. It was the first time in the court’s history that a state with no direct connection to the alleged crimes had filed a case under the 1948 Genocide Convention, which obliges all state parties to prevent and punish genocide wherever it may occur.
Yet, The Gambia’s action before the Court was never only about legal obligations or diplomatic considerations. We asked ourselves one fundamental question: if we remain silent in the face of such suffering, what does our silence make us?
As Gambians, we know the value of dignity. We understand what it means to yearn for justice. We know the pain that comes when our rights are denied, and voices are silenced. Our own history of political struggle taught us that freedom, accountability and human rights are lived realities that shape the lives of us all.
Perhaps that is why this case has resonated deeply with many Gambians: it speaks to our common humanity. In January, Rohingya survivors of the violence testified before the court about what they had lived through. We recognise that the fear of being driven from one’s home knows no nationality, and compassion does not stop at national boundaries.
The years since the case was filed have required patience and perseverance. International justice can often move frustratingly slowly. However, the court’s order in January 2020, the rejection of Myanmar’s objections in 2022, and the interventions from 11 states (Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands, the UK, the Maldives, Slovenia, the DRC, Belgium, and Ireland) on how the Convention should be interpreted have reaffirmed our shared commitment.
The judgement by the world’s highest court today is a reminder that the obligation to prevent genocide applies to every state, large or small, near or far. This is the first time in the history of the court that a state has been found responsible for committing genocide. The court concluded that the widespread rape and sexual violence committed by Myanmar’s security forces were part of the genocide, and that Myanmar failed to prevent genocide and to punish those responsible.
Myanmar is now under a clear obligation to comply fully with the judgement. It is required to investigate and prosecute those responsible, to facilitate the safe, voluntary and dignified return of displaced Rohingya and to protect them from discrimination and persecution. Justice for the Rohingya will also require the restoration of their citizenship and the recognition of their right to be called Rohingya.
Parliamentarians also have a role to play. As the court made clear today, punishing genocide requires laws that explicitly criminalise it. The court has held Myanmar to that standard, and we must hold ourselves to it, too. We must ensure that genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes are fully incorporated into our domestic laws, and that our courts can try them wherever they are committed.
In our National Assembly, we will ask our government about the next steps, monitor Myanmar’s compliance, and ensure that The Gambia continues to press for that compliance at the United Nations and within the OIC. Other states must now step in by ensuring that Myanmar complies, supporting Rohingya refugees and ensuring they will not be sent back into danger.
As Gambians, we have chosen empathy over indifference, principle over convenience, and action over silence. The Rohingya have shown extraordinary courage and determination in their search for justice, and today international law has finally answered them. Our collective responsibility now is to call for compliance and prevent any future acts of genocide.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: EU and Britain to agree steps towards relations reset
noticias.resumen: A decade after Brexit, London is signalling a willingness to align more closely with the EU on various policies.
noticias.texto:
EU and Britain to agree steps towards relations reset
A decade after Brexit, London is signalling a willingness to align more closely with the EU on various policies.
British and European Union leaders are set to meet at a summit billed as a chance to reset relations a decade after the Brexit vote.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will meet with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa, who heads the European Council, on Friday in Brussels. In the second such meeting since Britain formally left the bloc in 2020, deals on food, emissions and youth mobility are expected to be sealed.
The previous summit in 2025 was billed as a “stable foundation” upon which to rebuild the relationship between London and Brussels. Friday’s meeting is being sold as a chance to start on a reset of relations.
Burnham said earlier in the week that it was an “obvious truth” that Britain had lost more than it had gained from Brexit, which followed a non-binding referendum in 2016 in which 52 percent of the British public voted to leave the EU. He has signalled that a reformed relationship with Brussels is on his agenda.
The most valuable agreement on the table concerns the cross-border exchange of animals, plants and related products. Britain has estimated that the removal of the current controls could be worth 5.1 billion pounds ($6.7bn) annually.
A potential deal on emissions trading systems could see London and Brussels mutually exempt each other from carbon border levies on goods like steel.
An agreement on youth mobility, which would allow 100,000 people from the EU to live and work for up to three years in the UK, and vice versa, is also reportedly set to be signed. The UK had originally wanted half that number.
The EU is also pushing for students to qualify for “home fees” at British universities – often one third of the international price. London, however, has only agreed to apply “significantly reduced” fees.
The UK also wants to be part of the EU’s “Made in Europe” rules. Brussels has said it may be open to this, but it would require the UK to accept its policies. That could prove tricky for Burnham, given that the UK still hosts a significant Eurosceptic population.
Nigel Farage, leader of the populist radical right-wing Reform UK party, accused Burnham of a Brexit “betrayal”.
“We don’t need to be in political union of any kind at all to do business and have good relations with our neighbours,” he told the BBC. “I’m afraid that the great Brexit debate has just started again.”

noticias.titulo: Sandpapergate: Australian gov’t demands CA to ensure transparency in forum
noticias.resumen: Cricket Australia's Sandpapergate forum for players to give their accounts has been ridiculed by former cricketers.
noticias.texto:
Sandpapergate: Australian gov’t demands CA to ensure transparency in forum
Cricket Australia’s Sandpapergate forum for players to give their accounts has been ridiculed by former cricketers and pundits.
Cricket Australia (CA) should ensure its forum into Sandpapergate is handled as independently and openly as possible, a government spokesperson said on Friday, as former players slammed the governing body’s attempts to defuse an escalating controversy surrounding the 2018 ball-tampering scandal.
CA bosses said on Wednesday that an independent forum would be set up to allow players to give their accounts of the incident, but the results would not necessarily be made public and no sanctions would follow.
The move has been ridiculed by past players and pundits, including former captain Michael Clarke, who said the Australian public had been lied to about who was party to the cheating during the 2018 South Africa Test series.
A spokesperson for Sport Minister Anika Wells said integrity mattered to “every kid with a bat or a ball”.
“This is Cricket Australia’s process to run and it is a matter for them to work through. Australians will expect this to be run independently and as openly as possible,” the spokesperson said in a statement.
“We have a summer of cricket to look forward to and I’m sure all of Australia will get behind our team.”
No prior knowledge
CA did not provide immediate comment when asked by the Reuters news agency on Friday for more details about its forum.
The eight-year-old Sandpapergate scandal has reignited this month following allegations by former Australia batter Usman Khawaja that other players and staff knew of the ball-tampering – not just the three who were found culpable and sanctioned after a rapid investigation by CA’s integrity unit during the South Africa tour.
CA banned then-captain Steve Smith and David Warner for 12 months, and Cameron Bancroft for nine.
Test captain Pat Cummins and fellow pace bowler Mitchell Starc have since rejected Khawaja’s allegations, saying they had no prior knowledge of ball tampering.
But three other players involved in the 2018 tour came forward to back up Khawaja’s account, including Warner and Bancroft, who said “the whole team” knew, including coaching staff and a media manager.
Bancroft claimed the idea to rough up the ball with sandpaper to make it swing was Warner’s, but that the conversation had taken place “within a wider team environment”. He added that he had lied about the extent of the plot to protect CA’s investigation into the incident.
Clarke, who captained Australia from 2011 to 2015, said Bancroft’s explosive 4,000-word statement shared with the media on Wednesday had made CA’s forum redundant.
“The public don’t want any more bullshit,” he said on his podcast, Beyond23.
“The public want the complete truth to allow us to move on.”
The scandal has heaped pressure on Cummins, one of the game’s most devastating pace bowlers, who boasts a strong portfolio of corporate sponsors.
Cummins called Khawaja’s allegations “complete and utter nonsense” in an hour-long news conference last week, and criticised his former teammate for being “casual” with others’ lives and reputations.
He declined to comment to a large media scrum camped outside his Sydney home on Thursday and at training, but his manager said Cummins’s position remained steadfast and he had no need to respond to Bancroft’s statement.
A poll of 13,000 readers of Melbourne’s Herald Sun newspaper had 82 percent saying they believed Khawaja’s, Warner’s and Bancroft’s accounts of Sandpapergate, versus 18 percent for Cummins and Australia’s bowlers who denied prior knowledge.
A majority of 6,000 readers in a poll in the Sydney Morning Herald said they did not expect Cummins to remain as captain for the first Test of the home summer against New Zealand, which starts December 9.
Former Australia bowler Mitchell Johnson said the public pressure on Cummins to stand down as captain would be too much.
“I just can’t see how his captaincy and personal brand survives this,” Johnson wrote in a column for The West Australian newspaper.

noticias.titulo: ‘We don’t want our future decided by the military’: Young Germans protest
noticias.resumen: Ahead of Friday's nationwide rallies, German teenagers explain why they are resisting conscription.
noticias.texto:
‘We don’t want our future decided by the military’: Young Germans protest
Ahead of Friday’s nationwide rallies, two German teenagers explain why they are resisting conscription and growing militarisation.
Berlin, Germany – Last month, high school student Phil Werring received a letter from the German Armed Forces, known as the Bundeswehr.
In an official document, a military registration form, Werring was asked to answer compulsory questions – and optional ones if he was interested in joining the army.
After initially ignoring the first letter, two weeks later he received another, warning him of a 250 euro ($275) fine if he did not answer.
Logging in via a QR code, he started working his way through the questionnaire.
“The mandatory questions included ones on whether you have any diseases, your weight, height and whether you played sports, while other questions asked about whether you had a driving licence and what languages you spoke,” the 18-year-old, who lives with his three younger siblings and parents in Muenster, western Germany, told Al Jazeera.
“I only answered the mandatory questions, so it took me around 15 minutes to complete, but if I had filled it all out, it would have taken me a lot longer. I know that not answering all the questions can increase my chances of being called in by the military for a check-up, but I still didn’t want to answer them all.”
Official figures show that by the end of October, nearly 600,000 letters had been sent out this year to young Germans, of which about 286,800 were sent to young men and 271,700 to women and people of other genders. The form is only mandatory for men to complete.
Military conscription, meanwhile, has been a headline-grabbing issue in Germany since the start of the year, after the Military Service Modernisation Act came into effect on January 1 . It set out new targets to grow the army by the mid-2030s, increasing its full-time force to about 260,000, plus 200,000 reservists.
The recruitment drive is one element of Germany’s broader military expansion plans, initiated in 2022 after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Berlin is also increasing defence budgets and surveillance powers for intelligence services.
According to the Ministry of Defence, its efforts are yielding positive results. Official figures indicate that the Bundeswehr has already exceeded the statutory force build-up range for 2026, with personnel numbers in October about 6,400 higher than the same month last year.
Yet as recent protests have shown – including a series of school strikes and a large-scale demonstration organised by a loose alliance called “Gen Z Regelt” (Gen Z Sorts It) – many young people are pushing back against the plans.
Gen Z Regelt is rallying again on Friday, with nearly 20,000 people across 40 cities, including Berlin, Cologne, Frankfurt and Munich, signed up so far.
“The military questionnaire had many personal questions, and I found the experience quite scary, and it made me angry,” Werring said. “As I filled out the form, I realised how serious the government is about taking these steps to reintroduce compulsory military service, and that I may have no choice but to serve and risk my life for companies making millions selling arms. It made me realise that I must be active against these steps towards militarisation and support resistance efforts against these war preparations.”
‘Students worry about the roof falling on them’
Linus Schneider, 16, fears that as more money goes towards rearming Germany, the less there is for schools like those in his home city of Munich, which are not in good shape.
“The roofs have been leaking at my school for three years now,” he told Al Jazeera. “Something wasn’t installed properly when the building was built a few years ago, and the city has been saying that they don’t have as much money as they did a few years ago, so they can’t fix the issue. This has led to a lot of problems at school; for example, sometimes we can’t have gym class at all because there are buckets of water in the sports hall.”
Munich is the largest city in one of Germany’s wealthiest states, Bavaria.
Schneider added, “I also hear from friends in other schools that their roofs are in such a bad condition that they are worried about the roof falling on them. We literally don’t have good roofs over our heads. There are big cuts to education and healthcare, while at the same time, military spending has increased drastically.”
According to the current draft budget for 2027, to be agreed on later this month, defence spending is expected to rise to 109.7 billion euros ($120.5bn) from 82.7 billion euros ($90.8bn) the year before. The Ministry for Education and Family, meanwhile, projects a budget of 15.9 billion euros ($17.5bn) compared to 16.6 billion euros ($18.3bn) this year.
Sebastian Koos, a sociologist at the University of Konstanz who researches youth and protest movements, said the wave in Europe was an “important spark” for the German movement.
“There are some similarities and overlaps with the problems, such as the cost of living and cuts to education. But I think the issue of military conscription makes the situation for young people here unique,” he told Al Jazeera.
Koos said that while several different organisations participate in the Gen Z Regelt protests, a common thread is a sense of hopelessness.
“There are also many issues and demands that are being put together. They are also worried about economic and social inequality, right-wing extremism, the cost of living, as well as climate change. This is a lot to digest, and it is very difficult to get a sense of hope if you are confronted with so many different conflicts.”
Friday’s protest will include thousands of students protesting against compulsory military service, organised by the youth-led alliance, School Strike Against Conscription.
Werring will be among those taking to the streets in his local area.
“I’m still figuring out what I want to study, but I am interested in the medical sector. I want to help people, not shoot or harm anyone. I don’t want my future to be interrupted by the military,” he said.
Schneider is in trouble with the school head teacher for getting involved in the protests, but he still plans to join Friday’s rallies.
“We want to make our own decisions about our future,” he said. “We don’t want our future to be decided by the military or the state. And I think that’s quite an important reason why we’re protesting. We also didn’t want war. I think it’s crucial that we stand together in the face of these increasing state repression that [Chancellor] Friedrich Merz is overseeing.”

noticias.titulo: Tashima says Balogun red card row at World Cup prompted FIFA presidency bid
noticias.resumen: Tashima is one of three names on the ballot for the March election, along with current President Infantino and Diallo.
noticias.texto:
Tashima says Balogun red card row at World Cup prompted FIFA presidency bid
Tashima is one of three names on the ballot for the March election, along with current President Infantino and Diallo.
Japanese football official Kozo Tashima said on Friday that the handling of Folarin Balogun’s red card at the 2026 World Cup was what prompted him to run for FIFA president against Gianni Infantino.
FIFA suspended forward Balogun’s automatic one-match ban for a red card in July, allowing the American striker to play against Belgium after United States President Donald Trump said he had personally asked President Infantino to review the sanction.
The decision triggered a swift and fiery backlash and, along with an aborted attempt to sell a stake in FIFA tournaments, led to opposition to Infantino’s re-election as president.
Tashima said he wanted to restore trust in FIFA, drawing parallels with 2016, when Infantino took charge after a corruption scandal.
“Ten years ago something similar happened, and Mr Infantino became president to reform and improve things,” the Japan Football Association (JFA) honorary president told a news conference.
“He has certainly done wonderful things. But in this year, 2026, 10 years later, events have occurred that ignored governance.
“I have worked in football, especially as a player and coach. As such, I cannot accept Balogun’s red card in any way. On top of that, no explanation has been given even now. I felt very indignant about this, and that is why I decided to stand here.”
Following the Balogun incident, FIFA’s disciplinary committee said it had the authority to suspend the one-match ban, and that it operated independently.
FIFA last month said it would amend the rule in its disciplinary code, which had allowed for the reversal of the ban.
Working with Diallo
The election, set to be held in March next year, will be the first time since he won the post in 2016 that Infantino will face a challenge after being re-elected unopposed in 2019 and 2023.
French Football Federation President Philippe Diallo also announced a challenge on Monday with the backing of European governing body UEFA. Infantino has the support of Asia and Africa’s confederations.
“I have not actually received a nomination from any continental confederation. So I’m well aware that I’m at a considerable disadvantage in this race,” Tashima said.
“It’s a fact that Gianni’s support has been gradually declining. I will keep appealing to voters.”
Diallo said at a news conference on Tuesday that he would reach out to Tashima to “unite forces”. Tashima said he was open to the idea of coordinating with the Frenchman’s team to avoid splitting the anti-Infantino vote.
“I don’t think the French candidate’s entry puts me at a disadvantage. In fact, France has ties to Africa and other regions, so Mr Diallo’s entry may bring those votes,” he added.
“Watching his press conference, I saw that he pointed out FIFA’s accounting and other figures in great detail. I find it reassuring that such a professional has joined.”
‘Least conspicuous’ FIFA president
Tashima is a former Japan international and youth coach and the first Japanese candidate to stand for FIFA president. He has served on the FIFA Council since 2015.
The 68-year-old said that if elected, he would shun the spotlight.
“A foreign media person described me very accurately. They said that if I’m elected, I might become the least conspicuous president ever,” he said.
“That may have been a bit of irony, but I’m fine with it. It’s not the president who should stand out, but the players.”
He added that he would need to be modest in his campaigning, much of which would be funded by his own money.
“The JFA’s budget for this year is already set, so of course, I would like support from the JFA, but we’ll also have to gather funds, for example by creating a fund or running crowdfunding,” he said.
“I won’t spend wastefully. I also have no intention of flying by private jet or anything like that.”

noticias.titulo: US maritime agency warned Iran blockade was adding to rising Gulf premiums
noticias.resumen: US Maritime Administration acknowledged naval blockade's impact on insurance premiums and cargo capacity, memo shows.
noticias.texto:
US maritime agency warned Iran blockade was adding to rising Gulf premiums
US Maritime Administration acknowledged naval blockade's impact on insurance premiums and cargo capacity, memo shows.
The United States government’s maritime agency flagged the disruptive impact of Washington’s blockade of Iran on commercial shipping in an internal memo, documents obtained by Al Jazeera reveal.
In an alert, the US Maritime Administration (MARAD) acknowledged the Iran war’s negative impact on insurance premiums and cargo capacity after US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced that it had disabled a Panama-flagged bulk carrier for attempting to breach the blockade.
MARAD administrator Stephen M Carmel shared the alert with a subordinate on October 12, following CENTCOM’s attack on the vessel Ocean Molica and unattributed attacks on three other tankers in and around the Strait of Hormuz.
“Why it matters: This materially escalates the previous alert: merchant ships now face kinetic action from both sides, and the threat has spread to Gulf anchorages and the Gulf of Oman,” said the memo, titled “Alert – Hormuz risk expands beyond the strait”.
“That increases the likelihood of further war-risk premium spikes, crew refusals and effective tanker capacity contraction.”
Carmel shared the alert with MARAD colleague Michael Yarrington in an email requesting information about the impact of the attacks on insurance premiums and an update on the agency’s efforts to “rebuild” war risk insurance.
It is unclear whether the alert originated within MARAD or another agency.
“How is the insurance market responding to all this?” Carmel wrote to Yarrington, an official at MARAD’s Office of Marine Insurance.
Yarrington replied that a colleague had reached out to contacts in London for information and forwarded a summary of rising insurance premiums compiled from news reports.
Yarrington also shared a description of “core deliverables” considered crucial to MARAD’s work on war risk insurance, the details of which were redacted from the emails before their release.
Al Jazeera obtained the documents through a Freedom of Information Act request to MARAD, which is responsible for promoting the US maritime industry.
MARAD, which sits under the US Department of Transportation, the White House, the Department of Defence and CENTCOM, did not respond to requests for comment.
The emergence of the memo acknowledging the negative fallout of the blockade comes as a definitive end to the Iran war remains elusive after months of on-again, off-again negotiations between Washington and Tehran.
US President Donald Trump last week dismissed the need for a peace deal with Iran, days after suggesting that the conflict could end “fairly soon” and that renewed US strikes were “highly unlikely”.
“Those days have long since passed,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”
Todd Huntley, a retired US Navy captain who leads the National Security Law Program at Georgetown University Law Center, said MARAD’s monitoring of the blockade was likely aimed at informing its advice to other branches of the US government.
“As far as I know, MARAD will issue general alerts on incidents or threats, but will not then discuss the consequences, eg, increases in insurance rates,” Huntley told Al Jazeera.
“I do think that some US officials either didn’t consider this risk or ignored it when ordering and implementing the blockade.
“To me, it was pretty obvious this was a likely development given past Iranian actions and threats.”
Ian Ralby, the CEO and founder of maritime security consultancy I.R. Consilium, said the Trump administration appeared to be less concerned about the “strategic considerations” of the blockade than preventing ships from contributing to Iran’s economic survival.
“The President has made it clear that he is unperturbed by the global economic fallout from the War – including the blockade – so it may also be the case that the potential consequences of the blockade were considered but dismissed as unimportant,” Ralby told Al Jazeera.
Global shipping has been roiled by attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28.
Some 130 attacks on vessels have been recorded in the region since the start of the conflict, resulting in the deaths of at least 25 seafarers, according to the International Maritime Organization (IMO).
October was the worst month for shipping since the war began, with 35 vessels targeted, according to the IMO.
While most attacks during the war have been blamed on Iran or Iranian-aligned forces, CENTCOM has claimed responsibility for destroying or disabling at least two dozen vessels, some of which it has identified as belonging to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) shadow fleet.
The turmoil in the strait has sharply driven up costs for shipping lines.
The cost of insurance for an oil tanker carrying crude from the Middle East to East Asia surged about 200-fold from January to the end of October, reaching $12.29 per barrel, according to the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).
As of July, insurers charged 3.5 percent–7.5 percent of a vessel’s market value for war risk cover, up from 0.10-0.25 percent before the war, according to industry estimates cited in the Parliament of Singapore, a major logistics and shipping hub.
Amid rising shipping costs, prices of crude oil and fertiliser have surged as much 60 percent and 112 percent, respectively, at various points during the war.
Boon Chuan Lim, an independent researcher in Singapore whose research on the turmoil in the Strait of Hormuz has been published in the Borsa Istanbul Review, said it was noteworthy that the Trump administration had placed enforcement of the blockade alongside other attacks when assessing disruption risk.
“A disabling strike adds a potential source of loss for vessels exposed to that enforcement, though the implications depend on each vessel’s circumstances,” Lim told Al Jazeera.
He added that danger was not limited to the narrow corridor in the strait.
“Geography matters, too,” Lim said. “Risk is not confined to the strait: Ships at anchor, bunkering or approaching ports can also be exposed.
“Insurance terms depend on the vessel, route, area and duration of exposure, so a wider threat can raise costs and complicate operations beyond the transit itself, but it does not mean every vessel faces the same additional premium.”
The Republicans’ crushing defeat in the US midterm elections on November 3 has been widely attributed to the fallout of the war, particularly higher fuel prices.
US Democrats achieved their best electoral performance in decades in a stinging rebuke of Trump ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Democrats have so far secured 56 seats in the 100-member US Senate and at least 257 seats in the 435-member House of Representatives.

noticias.titulo: Tears of joy, prayers for return home: Rohingya react to genocide ruling
noticias.resumen: For refugees, the ICJ ruling that Myanmar committed genocide is a vindication. But will they be able to return home?
noticias.texto:
Tears of joy, prayers for return home: Rohingya react to genocide ruling
For refugees, the ICJ ruling that Myanmar committed genocide is a vindication. But for many, the relief comes with a question: will they be able to return home?
Dhaka, Bangladesh — Umme Ruman was watching the news on her mobile phone from her shelter in Camp 1E of the Rohingya refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh. She had been waiting for the International Court of Justice (ICJ) verdict since the afternoon. But poor internet connectivity kept interrupting the live broadcast.
Then she opened Facebook and saw a headline: “ICJ confirms Myanmar committed genocide.”
Overwhelmed, she jumped. Her sister-in-law was cooking. Ruman rushed to hug her. Before she could explain what had happened, she broke down in tears.
“I celebrated with tears of joy because, for the first time, the world acknowledged what happened to us,” she said.
On Thursday, the ICJ found Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya during brutal military operations in 2017, in which the court found more than 10,000 people had been killed.
The landmark judgement in the case, brought before the court by The Gambia, recognised the atrocities committed against the community after years of denial. For refugees who have spent nearly a decade waiting for justice, the ruling brought a wave of relief, emotion and renewed hope.
“For me, this is not simply a legal verdict. It is proof of our suffering,” Ruman said.
Across the camps, people followed the announcement on mobile phones, laptops and large screens. Some watched with friends. Others gathered with their families. Many turned to Facebook and YouTube to follow the proceedings.
Eighteen-year-old Mohammad Rehan watched with his community teacher and friends on a laptop. “Some women were crying, while others were praying to Allah,” he said. “I did not do anything special. I just sat there and listened, hoping to hear some good news that would give us a peaceful life in the future.”
For Rehan, the first thought was that the verdict could potentially open the door for the Rohingya to return home. “Just imagining that made me so happy,” he said.
The news soon spread through the blocks. Rehan said people were celebrating, while elderly refugees discussed the case and The Gambia’s role in bringing it before the court. The small West African nation was not directly affected by the violence against the Rohingya. Still, it acted as a party to the 1948 Genocide Convention, under which all member states have an obligation to prevent and address genocide. In 2022, the court ruled that The Gambia had standing to bring the case.
Rehan’s mother was also delighted when he told her about the ruling. “She was saying that we had won and that we would be able to return to our homeland,” he said.
The celebrations came against a backdrop of difficult living conditions. Rain fell over the camps on Thursday as Cyclone Akvan bore down on the Bay of Bengal, adding to the discomfort of families living in cramped shelters.
It was a reminder that while the verdict had brought recognition to their suffering, it had not changed the daily realities of refugee life. Nurul Amin, a Rohingya youth, said he was happy when the court recognised the genocide, but the announcement also brought back painful memories.
“I was happy, but I was also remembering what happened to us in 2017. I was remembering the horrific military operation, the violence I experienced and the home I had to leave behind,” he said.
Rohingya activist Rohimullah said the announcement was difficult to put into words. It reminded him of those the community had lost and the darkest days of their displacement. He described the judgement as a moment of relief and renewed hope, but said it could not bring back loved ones or erase painful memories.
Nasir Uddin, a professor of anthropology at the University of Chittagong who researches the Rohingya crisis, said the ICJ ruling was important to ensure justice and accountability from the victims’ perspective.
“In the 21st century, we talk about liberal democracy, globalisation and global justice. Yet such a massive genocide happened before our eyes. The judgement was essential to establish the concept of global justice,” he said.
Michael Kugelman, a resident senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council, said the ruling meant that Dhaka would need stronger assurances from Myanmar about the safe return of Rohingya refugees under any repatriation arrangement.
“I think that this will also have some impact on the dynamics around negotiations between Bangladesh and Myanmar on the return of Rohingya refugees, now that an international court has said that they experienced genocide,” Kugelman told Al Jazeera.
For the Rohingya, however, the hope of going home remains central. They want accountability for those responsible for the atrocities, the restoration of their rights and citizenship, and a safe and dignified return to Myanmar.
Nurul Amin said he hoped the international community would look beyond the humanitarian crisis and address the political causes of their displacement. He said he wanted freedom in Myanmar, democracy and an end to discrimination and military dictatorship.
“We are hoping this judgement will lead to something more – that we will finally be able to return home with our rights and dignity,” he said.
Maung Solaiman Shah contributed to this story.

noticias.titulo: Gaza Civil Defence struggles to rescue lives as vehicles break down
noticias.resumen: More than 85 percent of Gaza Civil Defence vehicles are out of service as crews struggle to reach trapped people.
noticias.texto:
Gaza Civil Defence struggles to rescue lives as vehicles break down
More than 85 percent of Gaza Civil Defence vehicles are out of service, leaving crews struggling to reach trapped people.
Gaza City, Gaza Strip – Palestinian Civil Defence crews heard an explosion nearby and rushed to respond. But instead of taking a fire engine – the only vehicle available to the team at the time – they had to grab their equipment and rush to help on foot. The fire engine wasn’t working.
“We heard the strike, opened the vehicle, took our equipment and ran,” said Abdullah al-Majdalawi, a Civil Defence field officer, describing the response to an Israeli attack near the al-Qattan Centre on November 3. It took about 10 minutes for the crew to reach the site, carrying their equipment, and then carrying injured people back. They also recovered the body of someone killed in the strike.
It was another example of how the breakdown of emergency vehicles is affecting rescue teams’ ability to reach people quickly.
In a separate incident in southern Gaza City’s Sabra neighbourhood last month, the vehicle the Civil Defence team was using broke down while the crew was responding to an Israeli air strike on the area.
By the time they were able to reach the scene, several people had been killed, and others were critically injured. Al-Majdalawi believes that arriving sooner could have given some of the injured a better chance of survival.
During another mission, in 2024, the crew had to rely on a man with a donkey-drawn cart to transport them and their equipment.
“People were astonished to see Civil Defence personnel travelling that way… but this is what we can do,” al-Majdalawi said.
An ageing fleet, dwindling capacity
The only dedicated rescue vehicle in Gaza governorate, a Toyota Hilux pick-up truck, has been out of service for weeks. It is more than 20 years old, according to al-Majdalawi, and has been worn down by years of use and the intense workload during Israel’s genocidal war, which began in October 2023.
The crew has tried everything to keep it running, including patching its tyres with flour dough when proper repairs were not possible. The vehicle needs a power steering pump, tyres and other parts. Its turbo system is also faulty, while problems with its lights make night-time missions more dangerous.
“We have exhausted every means and every method to keep this vehicle running,” al-Majdalawi said.
Without it, crews have to rely on larger fire engines for rescue operations. These are harder to manoeuvre through streets crowded with tents, makeshift shelters, and market stalls.
If emergencies happen simultaneously in different areas, and there aren’t enough vehicles available, teams have to choose where to respond first.
The situation reflects a wider collapse in the capacity of Gaza’s Civil Defence.
Emergency teams are still responding to strikes, fires, and building collapses, but their ability to reach people is increasingly constrained by a lack of functioning vehicles and equipment.
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned in a May 1 report that restrictions on the entry of engine oil and spare parts for vehicles and rubble-removal machinery were having an increasingly severe impact on humanitarian operations in Gaza.
It said prolonged shortages were causing vehicles and generators to break down beyond repair, affecting the movement of humanitarian teams, ambulance services, and other essential operations.
Raed al-Dahshan, director of Gaza City’s Civil Defence, said more than 85 percent of the department’s vehicles were out of operation, leaving only about 15 percent working across the territory.
Many vehicles have been in service since 1994, when the Palestinian Authority was established, and have carried out tens of thousands of missions. Years of use, damaged roads, and the demands of the war have left much of the fleet worn out.
Al-Dahshan said many Civil Defence vehicles have exceeded their expected service life and urgently need replacing. International fire-service guidelines generally recommend replacing front-line fire engines after 15 to 20 years of operation.
Repairs without the parts
Repairing the vehicles has become increasingly difficult. Local workshops have limited capacity, and the department often has to refurbish old parts or find alternatives because replacement parts are unavailable.
At the department’s maintenance workshop, maintenance officer Abd al-Fattah al-Nimra works alongside a team trying to keep the ageing fleet operational.
With proper parts unavailable or prohibitively expensive, mechanics resort to temporary fixes and substitute components. These may get a vehicle moving again, but they cannot offer the reliability or performance of the original parts.
“Since the beginning of the war, we have faced many problems with spare parts and their high prices,” al-Nimra said. “The parts that run out are not replaced because the occupation prevents them from entering.”
He said the team tried to find temporary alternatives wherever possible, but they did not perform as well as original components. Even basic items such as tyres had become extremely expensive, while the cost and shortage of engine oil added another burden to already limited maintenance budgets.
Since the beginning of the war in October 2023, Israeli restrictions on the entry of essential supplies into Gaza, including vehicle spare parts and engine oil, have made it increasingly difficult for emergency services to maintain their fleets.
OCHA warned that shortages of these supplies were causing vehicles and generators to break down, in some cases beyond repair, while also affecting heavy machinery needed to remove rubble and keep essential services running.
The only rescue vehicle serving Gaza governorate needs a power steering pump, tyres, a turbo component and warning lights identifying it as a rescue vehicle, al-Nimra said. Although some parts can be found in the local market, their prices are beyond the department’s available budget.
Every second counts
The shortage of equipment comes as Civil Defence teams continue to respond to the consequences of Israel’s war on Gaza, including air strikes, fires, and buildings at risk of collapse.
With winter now under way, officials fear that heavy rain and strong winds will further weaken already damaged structures, creating more emergencies at a time when rescue teams have fewer vehicles and limited equipment to respond.
Those fears have already been borne out. Heavy rains in early November caused damaged buildings to collapse and flooded displacement sites across Gaza. But Civil Defence teams were only able to respond to a minority of the distress calls they received.
Most other callers were given guidance over the phone, highlighting the gap between the growing needs and the department’s capacity to respond.
More than 140 Civil Defence personnel have been killed during the war, al-Dahshan said.
The department has fewer than 1,000 employees across Gaza’s five governorates, and many continue working despite inadequate resources and a lack of regular salaries.
Civil Defence personnel and equipment are entitled to protection under international humanitarian law, including Article 62 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, which provides for the protection of civilian civil defence organisations and their personnel.
Al-Dahshan warned that without urgent support, the department could reach a point where it is unable to respond to people’s calls. The time it takes to reach an injured person can determine whether they survive, he said.
For al-Majdalawi, the immediate needs are basic: functioning vehicles, spare parts, tyres, engine oil and fuel.
“We are not asking for much,” he said. “We need tyres, engine oil and fuel. We are ready to dig through the rubble for hours and days to rescue people, but we need the equipment to do that.”
“If the world cannot stop the war on Gaza,” al-Dahshan said, “at the very least it should enable humanitarian services to rescue the injured before they die.”

noticias.titulo: Contaminated petrol leaves Yemeni drivers struggling to make ends meet
noticias.resumen: Drivers in Houthi-controlled areas face rising fuel prices and costly repairs as contaminated petrol damages their cars.
noticias.texto:
Contaminated petrol leaves Yemeni drivers struggling to make ends meet
Drivers in Houthi-controlled areas face rising fuel prices and costly repairs as contaminated petrol damages their cars.
Sanaa, Yemen – Yazan, 28, filled up his car at a petrol station in Sanaa and began a trip towards the city of Ibb to the south.
The journey would usually take about two and a half hours, but as he accelerated along the road, Yazan noticed that the car was struggling to pick up speed.
Yazan, who did not want to give his full name, explained that the harder he pressed the accelerator, the more the engine vibrated. The unusual engine noise and vibration forced him to stop several times on the road.
It eventually took Yazan six hours to reach his destination. He believes the problem was caused by contaminated petrol – fuel mixed with oil and impurities – that he bought in Sanaa.
“The petrol left numerous cars, including mine, with many faults,” Yazan told Al Jazeera. “We pay for the expensive petrol that damages our engines.”
Yazan is not alone. Other drivers in Sanaa have reported similar problems with contaminated and increasingly expensive petrol.
The cause of the issue is disputed. In June, the Sanaa-based Yemen Petroleum Company (YPC), run by the Houthis who have controlled northwest Yemen since 2014, said contaminated fuel was the result of inadequately equipped fuel storage facilities in Hodeidah.
Fuel storage tanks in the port city and the nearby Ras Isa oil terminal have been attacked by Israeli and United States air strikes since 2024, in response to Houthi attacks on Israel and shipping in the Red Sea.
The YPC said that the tanks allowed the company to remove impurities before pumping fuel to the market. With the facilities not functioning, the quality of the fuel is impacted.
But many Yemenis dispute that explanation. According to the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies, restrictions on fuel imports have led the Houthis to partly rely on importing lower-quality Iranian fuel.
Mohammed Ansi, a Yemeni academic, said regular people were being exploited.
“Fuel shipments are being brought in without any accountability, oversight, or conscience – driven solely by the desire for profit and commissions,” he said.
Fuel imports fell sharply from January to May this year. Compared to the same period in 2025, they fell 73 percent through Houthi-controlled ports and 60 percent through ports controlled by the Yemeni government, according to the World Bank.
The drop is partly a result of the impact of the US-Israeli war on Iran on oil shipments passing through the Strait of Hormuz, as well as damage to Yemen’s ports from the various attacks it has faced.
Costly repairs
With the crisis continuing, its financial toll on families is mounting amid the escalating war in Yemen.
“Paying for expensive petrol and vehicle repair is a fresh war on our livelihoods. It is draining us,” said Yazan.
A few weeks ago, 20 litres (5.3 gallons) of petrol cost 9,500 Yemeni riyals ($18 at rates set by the Houthis) in Sanaa. The price has since risen to 11,400 Yemeni riyals ($21), an increase of 20 percent.
That is not taking into account the additional repair costs necessary if contaminated fuel gets into a vehicle’s engine.
Yemenis are already struggling to make ends meet, a situation that has gotten worse over a decade of war.
An April report by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said that Yemen’s conflict has led to significant macroeconomic vulnerabilities and a marked decrease in income per capita, leaving more than half of the population in urgent need of humanitarian assistance.
Akram Naji, a taxi driver in Sanaa, is among those struggling to get by, and he is now having to figure out how to pay to fix his car.
Naji said he visited a mechanic in Sanaa’s Maeen district after he heard a strange noise coming from his vehicle’s engine.
“The mechanic identified mechanical problems, including a faulty fuel pump, clogged fuel injectors and reduced engine performance.”
Repairing the damage cost him 55,000 Yemeni riyals (about $100), he said.
“For many taxi drivers here like myself, paying this amount of money immediately is a challenge,” Naji said. “I had to not pay my rent in full and decreased my family’s daily expenses to cover the maintenance costs.”
Ali Beidhani, a mechanical engineer in Sanaa, explained what happens when the contaminated petrol enters a vehicle.
“As I observed, when this oily substance or impurities enter the engine along with the petrol, they accumulate in the combustion system,” Beidhani said. “As this substance is exposed to high temperatures, it becomes highly viscous, almost like glue. This leads to damage to engine valves, clogged fuel injectors, and engine vibrations.”
In severe cases, it can even lead to complete engine failure, Beidhani noted.
He said he had seen many drivers struggle to afford repairs.
“The repair cost could force drivers to borrow money or sell possessions like gold, especially if the engine gets damaged or completely fails. Those who rely on their vehicles to eke out a living suffer the most,” said Beidhani.
Deepening humanitarian crisis
Wafiq Saleh, an economic researcher and executive director of the Taiz Centre for Yemeni-Gulf Studies, told Al Jazeera that the spread of contaminated fuel heightens the misery of civilians in the war-torn country.
“Bus or taxi driver or delivery riders or farmers struggle every day to make ends meet. With the spread of contaminated petrol, their jobs are disrupted, and they may find themselves incapable of feeding their families,” said Saleh.
He argues that the authorities in Sanaa “bear full responsibility for importing substandard fuel or supplying the market with adulterated petrol, taking advantage of the lack of accountability”.
“The proliferation of adulterated fuel drains citizens’ savings and threatens the livelihoods of thousands of drivers. Breadwinners shift their focus from feeding their children to fixing their vehicle engines,” said Saleh.
Naji is now cautious whenever he approaches a petrol station to fill up his taxi. He checks the colour of the petrol, hoping to spot any signs of contamination.
“A fault in my car is like a wound in my child’s body; I cannot bear to see either go untreated,” he said.

noticias.texto:
Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.
Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.
Nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.
After a yellow level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.

noticias.titulo: ‘Traumatizing’: hunger striker in ICE detention tells of force-feeding ordeal – and what made him crack

noticias.texto:
The text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”
A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Perez, 32, said in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.
The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Perez. But the detainee sent more details – and his is far from an isolated case.
Cora Perez was one of two men on hunger striker at a Texas facility for whom ICE sought and received a federal judge’s permission to force-feed in recent weeks, a Guardian investigation found.
Cora Perez and the other man were locked up inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an ICE detention facility in south Texas, just a few miles from the US-Mexico border, on the coast near where Elon Musk’s SpaceX launches rockets. Cora Perez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out. At first he only drank water, then after three weeks, he says he began to drink one Ensure nutritional shake per day.
On 30 October, court records show ICE received permission to forcibly feed and hydrate him, and to restrain him while doing so.
The next day he says six guards at the center held him down, while medical staffers inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach – a process he called “traumatizing, both physically and psychologically”.
On 3 November, ICE then received permission from a federal judge to force-feed another hunger striker at Port Isabel, from Uzbekistan, federal court records show. DHS says the Uzbek man has not been subjected to the practice, however.
On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Perez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas. His relative says neither of them were alerted to any plans to transfer him, or a reason for it.
DHS did not specify why Cora Perez was transferred, adding that ICE makes custody determinations on a “case-by-case” basis based on “various factors”.
The revelations come as ICE’s detention practices continue to come under fire amid allegations of mistreatment, and as an increasing number of sporadic hunger strikes have been breaking out in ICE facilities across the country.
The two men’s cases in Texas, revealed here for the first time, are some of the most recent instances of government lawyers seeking a federal judge’s permission, as required by ICE policy, and receiving the go-ahead to force-feed detained hunger strikers. The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Perez via a facility phone. It further reveals how the Trump administration is increasingly obtaining such court orders to force-feed detained immigrants, a secretive practice widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and medical ethics groups.
Detainees driven to hunger strike are typically using it as a last resort to protest against poor conditions and the Trump administration’s preference for arrest and prolonged detention while their civil immigration cases proceed through the system.
Cora Perez said detention center staff inserted the feeding tube and left it in his body, a not uncommon practice, according to experts, and introduced nutrition – first a “clear liquid”, followed by a “milky liquid”, he recalled – through the tube twice more that day, before he cracked and said he broke his hunger strike, citing what he called “horrific torture”. He began voluntarily drinking nutritional shakes the following day, he said.
“ICE does not hold back on anything, and they do anything they want, like we have seen, even killing their own US citizens,” he wrote to the Guardian, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good by an ICE officer and Alex Pretti by a border patrol officer in January of this year during Trump’s pivotal immigration crackdown on Minneapolis.
Detained hunger strikers subjected to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, have rarely spoken out about their cases or revealed their identities, much less while still detained. Cora Perez’s messages offer a rare glimpse at conditions inside a detention center’s restricted medical unit where hunger strikers and suicidal detainees are held.
“They just took [the Uzbek man] in an ambulance after [him] fainting in front of the medical lobby where they take our vitals, our weight and our temperature,” Cora said in an alarmed message last Monday morning.
The Uzbek man was returned the following day to the facility, Cora Perez said.
“I see him every day because I see him in the room in front of me, but they don’t let us talk to each other,” he added.
The Guardian independently confirmed the Uzbek’s man identity but is not publicly naming him, because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. The man arrived at the Mexico-US border in April 2022 and was released into the country while navigating his immigration case. He was arrested by border patrol officials in April of this year and placed in detention. The man does not appear to have any criminal record and DHS did not point to any criminal history.
In a statement, DHS said that after they received the court’s permission to force-feed the Uzbek man, he “has voluntarily taken in fluids and there has been NO force-feeding or forced hydration”.
Security operations at the sprawling Port Isabel facility in Los Fresnos, Texas are run by a private prison company, Akima Global Services, while healthcare is primarily handled by government workers.
“ICE respects detainees’ rights to exercise self-expression and medical autonomy by refusing nourishment and medical care,” DHS said in a statement. “ICE Health Services Corps may provide involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death. Medical staff may provide treatment only to medically stabilize the patient, bringing the detainee outside the imminent harm, incapacitation, or death.”
The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas, which represented ICE in its force-feeding request, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Virginia-headquartered Akima Global Services, and its parent company Nana Regional Corporation, based in Alaska, did not respond to a request for comment.
Force-feeding cases are shrouded in secrecy. After a detainee launches a hunger strike, ICE often sequesters them in medical isolation cells for monitoring, according to ICE’s detention standards. DHS said that ICE continues to offer hunger strikers three meals per day.
After a certain period of not eating, which varies per case, ICE will request a federal judge’s permission to force-feed the hunger striker. Many court records, and sometimes entire court dockets, are sealed and hidden from public view. In Cora Perez and the Uzbek man’s cases, like in others, they did not have any legal representation to challenge the force-feeding requests.
The Guardian found at least five instances in which ICE requested permission to force-feed hunger strikers in Port Isabel since January 2025. The federal judge who ruled on Cora Perez and the Uzbek man, Rolando Olvera, has similarly ordered in at least three other cases, records show. Olvera’s judicial assistant said the court had no comment for this article.
ICE is known to have requested permission to force-feed at least 21 detainees across the US since January 2025, the Guardian found, but the number is likely higher since an unknown number of records and dockets remain sealed, unsearchable and not feasible to locate. Most of the cases coinciding with the second Trump administration and tracked by the Guardian are in Texas and Florida, with others in Georgia, Arizona and Washington state. Under the Biden administration, ICE force-feeding requests were also made in Louisiana and California.
Amy Zeidan, an emergency medicine physician based in Atlanta and an expert on healthcare in immigration detention, said force-feeding hunger strikers can amount to “torture”, and lead to significant psychological distress. She also said it is a violation of medical ethics.
“Essentially it’s like inserting a straw into your nose,” Zeidan said. “You have a gag reflex, so most times people will gag, and that’s really uncomfortable. And people will even vomit repeatedly if it continues to irritate their gag reflex.”
Zeidan added that the forceful insertion of a feeding tube can lead to the swelling of the nostrils and the throat, and even tear them, leading to bleeding.
“It is like torture – somebody is doing a painful procedure to you that you don’t consent to,” Zeidan added. “Autonomy is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. We can’t do something to patients if they don’t want to, even if we think it’s good for them.”
There are numerous cells and rooms inside the Port Isabel medical unit, including isolation cells and shared rooms for ill detainees, according to Cora Perez. In recent weeks, there were five people in the Port Isabel medical isolation cells used for hunger striking or suicidal detainees, he added. He described the cells as “practically freezing”, constantly surveilled with a security camera, and with just a bed, toilet and sink. As well as himself, he says he observed the Uzbek man, a Middle Eastern man, a “tall” eastern European man and a Black man of unknown nationality in the isolation cells. Unit detainees are escorted by facility staff to showers and sometimes receive yard and television access, he said.
Cora Perez worries for the other detainees. The Black man, whose identity or nationality he does not know, seems to have “serious mental health problems”, Cora Perez observed.
“He harms himself and spends the night yelling and hitting the door, and does not let anyone sleep,” he said.
The Guardian has independently confirmed the eastern European and Middle Eastern men’s identities, but is not publicly naming them because efforts to contact them have been unsuccessful. DHS did not comment on the other men inside the medical isolation unit, saying they could not comment without the Guardian providing their identities.
Cora Perez had left his son and parents in Cuba and requested asylum at the Mexico-US border in 2023, according to a relative who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity due to fear of retaliation by immigration authorities. Cora Perez went to live with the relative in Florida, where he worked in maintenance at a hotel and as a food delivery worker, he said.
In March 2025, Cora Perez was arrested by local police and later convicted of two misdemeanors, including “breach of peace” and “obstructing an officer without violence”, according to local records. He was sentenced to two months in jail, his relative said. But ICE placed a hold on him and as he was being released in June 2025, immigration officials took him into custody – a common system – and soon transferred him to the Adelanto detention center, a privately-run facility in California.
Days in Adelanto turned to weeks, then months, then a over year, according to a federal court order denying one of his petitions requesting his release. His multiple requests to immigration and ordinary federal courts for release from detention, while he fights his asylum case, have been unsuccessful.
“All his claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law,” DHS said. “Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”
In August, he stopped eating to protest against his protracted detention.
“I have spent two birthdays behind ICE’s bars,” he wrote. “The reasons I did the hunger strike in Adelanto are for my political asylum, for the time I have spent detained, [and] because I have a 14-year-old son who is starving to death in Cuba because he does not have my help.”
“Also due to the mistreatment by the officials,” he added.
Cora Perez did not tell his family about the hunger strike, so as not to further worry them. It was not until he was transferred to Port Isabel in late September that he confessed to his relative he had been on a prolonged hunger strike.
“He doesn’t share details so that I won’t get upset or worry,” the relative said in a phone interview.
Cora Perez’s mother, who is in Cuba, “does not know anything, because she is sick, and with his detention she has gotten worse”, the relative added, between tears. “I don’t want her nor his grandmother to know anything about it,” the relative added.
On October 30, the federal prosecutors requested permission for ICE to forcibly feed and hydrate Cora Perez. Hours later, a federal judge approved the procedures without hearing from Cora Perez. Cora Perez told the Guardian in various instances he felt it was unfair he was not given the opportunity to present his case to the judge before the judge approved his force-feeding.
“It’s very disturbing because the judge is basically making a decision on information that is only provided by one side,” said Linus Chan, a professor of clinical law and the director of the detainee rights clinic at the University of Minnesota law school. “That just seems ridiculous.”
Cora Perez was force-fed the following day, he said in his messages and in a phone call, adding that he did not physically resist because he “had seen a lot of mistreatment of others detained”.
“[ICE does] what they want with us, whatever they want, because a federal judge gave them permission,” he added. “I have suffered on the island [of Cuba] and now at the hands of ICE.”
After asking Cora Perez about DHS’s denials that he was force-fed, he repeated that he was. “Brother, ICE says and does whatever they want. They deny, punish, retaliate and do everything at their own will. They have even sent Cubans to Africa,” he said.
The number of people detained by ICE has soared under the Trump administration. And due to policy and legal changes, tens of thousands of people are forced to stay in detention for long periods while they fight their immigration cases.
Chan, from the University of Minnesota, says prolonged detention and delays in their cases lead to logical conclusion. “That’s exactly when people protest,” he said.
“And the only form of protest, for many of these people, is a hunger strike,” he said.
As Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown continues and people are detained as a first resort while their cases play out, Chan said: “Hunger strikes will become more common.”
