noticias.texto:
The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations.
Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate.
Despite countries not being required to reveal how they voted, it is thought Grynspan’s candidature has been resisted by Russia and the US, two of the five permanent security council members that can ultimately wield a veto against a candidate. Knowledge among the security council delegations of how countries are voting is down to private intelligence, leaks and a process of elimination.
The intensive lobbying over the job has spread across the globe, but Friday is especially important since the poll is slated to differentiate the voting of the P5 from the 10 elected members (E10) of the security council. To be recommended as secretary general to the UN general assembly, a candidate needs nine votes and no vetoes. In Friday’s colour-coded secret ballot, the P5 will cast red ballots and the E10 white.
One diplomat said: “The electoral system means it is important how many votes you win, but equally how many of certain votes you don’t lose.”
The protracted 140-day deadlock confirms the polarisation that has hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres, but also belies claims the role is now an irrelevance.
Friday’s secret ballot may also reveal whether the United Arab Emirates’ campaign for its diplomat, Lana Nusseibeh, is about to blow up in its face due to the hostility to the UAE’s brand of active, commercially driven diplomacy, not just in Sudan, but also Somalia, Western Sahara, Libya and Yemen.
A late entrant, in the two straw polls in which she has contested so far, Nusseibeh secured only seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” and two “no opinions”. This is despite prestigious big-power backing and her acknowledged personal diplomatic skills.
Nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. The French foreign ministry may have misgivings about the UAE, but Emmanuel Macron, the French president, travelled to the UAE in the midst of French riots to see the UAE president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and secure 100,000 metric tons of diesel a month.
In the UK, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has kept his counsel, but he shares a Polish-Jewish refugee heritage with Grynspan and cannot be an admirer of the UAE’s human rights record or its evasion of EU sanctions on Russia. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has UAE connections from his time as mayor of Manchester, and Nusseibeh is a fellow alumnus of the University of Cambridge. At the UN she worked closely with the UK in an informal group called “Friends of the Future of the UN”.
Yet 68 British MPs, including the Labour chair of the international development select committee, Sarah Champion, last week signed a letter calling on Burnham to veto Nusseibeh, describing her as “a tainted and compromised figure”.
Some of the opposition to her from elected security council members is not wholly political. Latin American countries believe an informal rotation system means it is their turn to lead the UN. As a result Panama and Colombia, currently on the security council, will oppose her. China has also been supportive of this rotation principle.
But others deeply object to what they consider to be the UAE’s dollar diplomacy and preparedness to use its extraordinary wealth to exacerbate and exploit pre-existing divisions in a country to gain a commercial foothold. Somalia, for instance, has a seat on the Security Council, and its president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, this week went on TV to accuse the UAE of buying ports, establishing military bases and supporting armed forces outside Somalia’s national security framework without federal approval.
It is also possible that Finland and Latvia, the two elected members with the greatest stake in Ukraine, are unimpressed that the UAE gave Vladimir Putin red carpet treatment when he visited Abu Dhabi in December 2023, nine months after the international criminal court had issued an arrest warrant for child trafficking. Greece, less engaged in Ukraine, may be more flexible.
Since the last poll, Nusseibeh has been to Bahrain, Britain and Pakistan, a clue as to where extra votes may be harvested. She also had a “thoughtful exchange” with Zeng Jixin, the Chinese ambassador to the UAE.
The two hurdles are whether someone so deep inside the UAE inner circle would have the courage in office to show true independence, and whether her active denials of UAE involvement in arming the RSF in Sudan leave her irretrievably tainted. From a Palestinian intellectual family, she insists she would make peace in Sudan her number one priority.
In the last ballot on 5 November, Grynspan won 12 votes in favour and three negative. But on 16 October – the only colour-coded ballot so far – which distinguishes between permanent and elected members – she received two discourage votes from permanent members, the equivalent of a veto. Nusseibeh had not joined the race at that point.
In an administration as personalised as the US, it has been hard for Grynspan to gain influence, with many sensing that Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, is the key influencer.
Grynspan has been reluctant to make the fact she is Jewish a feature of her candidacy, but the election of a Jewish person to run the UN might be seen as something the US could embrace as transformative. Her age – she is 70 – could be considered a drawback among those calling for a younger generation to renew the institution.
Although there are other Latin American candidates, Grynspan is seen as a more viable candidate than her rival, the Argentine Rafael Grossi, the head of the UN weapons inspectorate. Russia has opposed Grossi, objecting to his interventions over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine.
One way or the other, the logjam has to be broken soon.

noticias.titulo: Global stock markets slump as Anthropic IPO fails to stem AI sell-off
noticias.resumen: Asian markets on track for their worst week since 2020, with European and US stocks also way down Business live – latest updates Global stock markets have slumped as Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies. Asian stock markets were on track for their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell on Friday. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Global stock markets have slumped as Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.
Asian stock markets were on track for their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell on Friday. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.
In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets were heading for their worst week since March, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.3% in the first 90 minutes.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.
Anthropic’s shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the frontier AI firm began. But they were heading for losses on Friday, down 6% at $91.30, falling back towards the IPO price of $83.
Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI build out.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.
“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index hit a five-month low on Friday morning. It has dropped by 4.8% this week, and is heading for its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

noticias.titulo: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
noticias.resumen: State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang. Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.
Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: companies cannot mislead their investors.”
The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.
Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China.
Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.
Bonta said the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.
“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he said. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”
Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.
Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, said the company had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back.
Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.
Shares in rival chipmaker AMD closed down almost 8% on Thursday after the publication of reports connected to short seller Hunterbrook warning about its links to China and the “circular financing” of customers.
The company, which has been targeted amid the Nvidia scandal, is looking at a further fall of more than 5% in pre-market trading.
Hunterbrook Media published allegations on the use of AMD’s software by a Chinese server maker blacklisted by the US. Sister publication, The Bear Cave newsletter, alleged that AMD’s use of datacentre lease guarantees and backstops for unsold cloud computing capacity could leave it exposed to a pullback in AI spending.
AMD said the reports’ claims “misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships”.
“AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” the company said. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.”
AMD’s share price has more than doubled so far this year, giving the company a market capitalisation of more than $800m.

noticias.titulo: Vape users hospitalised after losing consciousness, prompting public health warning in New South Wales
noticias.resumen: Testing confirms presence of etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Three people who lost consciousness and were hospitalised in New South Wales after using certain vapes have tested positive for the unregulated anaesthetic agent etomidate, health officials said. NSW health on Friday issued a public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for
noticias.texto:
Three people who lost consciousness and were hospitalised in New South Wales after using certain vapes have tested positive for the unregulated anaesthetic agent etomidate, health officials said.
NSW health on Friday issued a public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia.
The three people who were hospitalised had used non-nicotine refillable vapes, the state health department said. Testing of their blood and urine confirmed the presence of etomidate.
The department would not confirm how old the three patients were, where they were hospitalised, or their condition on Friday.
The discovery of etomidate in vapes in NSW comes about four months after Victorian health officials announced they had found the powerful anaesthetic agent in an illicit vape sold in Melbourne.
On Friday, NSW health warned vapes sold as space pods, space oil, kpods, piu piu vapes, or zombie vapes may contain etomidate, or other substances, including ketamine, THC and potent opioids.
The medical director of the NSW poisons information centre, Dr Darren Roberts, said etomidate’s effects were unpredictable when used in a vape.
Roberts said etomidate could cause confusion, drowsiness, slow breathing, vomiting, muscle spasms or movements that were hard to control, and people who took it could become unresponsive.
These effects could be life threatening, especially if used with other drugs that could cause sedation, such as alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, and GHB, Roberts said.
He said etomidate could also cause long-term harm when used regularly, including the disruption of hormones produced by the adrenal gland.
These hormones are important in regulating stress responses and need to be replaced if they aren’t produced naturally, he said.
“The contents found in non-nicotine vapes vary,” Roberts said. “You can’t assume what’s inside.”
He urged anyone considering using a vape to ask themselves what could be in it.
“You won’t get into trouble for seeking medical care,” he said. If you feel unwell, or if your friend feels unwell, after using a vape, do something about it.”
NSW health officials said it recommended people administer Naloxone to anyone who became responsive after using any drug, in case they had ingested opioids.
Naloxone is an opioid overdose treatment, which is free at pharmacies and does not require a prescription.
Naloxone won’t reverse the effects of etomidate, as the sedative does not belong to the opioid class of drugs, but it is still safe to give, health officials said.
The officials said anyone who witnessed someone experiencing unexpected symptoms after using drugs should call triple zero immediately or seek urgent medical attention.

noticias.titulo: Baby born with heart abnormalities ‘didn’t have a chance’ after non-medical free birth, NSW inquest hears
noticias.resumen: Inquest into the deaths of four babies after free and home births hears routine checks and follow-up may have saved their lives Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Four babies who died in New South Wales – three after free births and one after a home birth – might have survived if they had had routine checks and follow-up , a coronial inquest has heard. Baby DH , Baby D , Baby R , and Baby B died in the state’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Four babies who died in New South Wales – three after free births and one after a home birth – might have survived if they had had routine checks and follow-up , a coronial inquest has heard.
Baby DH, Baby D, Baby R, and Baby B died in the state’s northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024.
The inquest in Lismore has heard women chose free or home births for reasons including traumatic experiences, a lack of trust in clinicians, and a lack of services.
Baby DH died about eight hours after he was born in a free birth – with a doula but no medical professionals present. The court earlier heard he turned purple, was struggling to breathe and had became floppy.
His parents gave evidence they were worried but the doula kept reassuring them their baby was OK, then left.
The doula denied many of their claims, and denied that she gave them any clinical advice.
Expert neonatologist and associate professor Nicholas Evans said on Friday that Baby DH’s complex heart abnormalities “would have been readily detectable” in a routine pregnancy scan after which he would have been referred to a paediatric cardiologist.
It was a “missed opportunity”, he told the court.
Paediatric cardiologist Dr Paul Brooks said it was “highly likely” all the abnormalities would have been identified in a routine scan before birth.
Even if the extent of the abnormalities wasn’t clear, he told the court, the scan would have shown the baby needed to be born at a major hospital with cardiac surgery capabilities.
“The site of [Baby DH’s] birth meant that he didn’t have a chance.”
Baby D’s mother did not know she was having twins, and at first thought she’d delivered Baby D’s placenta, only to realise it was a stillborn second twin.
Experts at the inquest agreed it was impossible to know exactly why Baby D died. They discussed the possibility it was because self-described birth keeper Sita Tara Kali did not clamp the umbilical cord before cutting it, but Evans told the court that it was ultimately most likely from respiratory distress because of his compromised heart function.
Baby D might have survived if someone who could do advanced resuscitation had arrived in under 10 minutes, he said, but the “root cause” was that it was not known the mother was carrying twins before the births.
“If [twins] had been diagnosed, at 18 weeks, as it would usually in pregnancy, there would have been very close monitoring.”
Baby R likely died of “severe post-maturity” after being born at 43 weeks and one day in a free birth. The standard is to induce birth or perform a caesarean section at 42 weeks, as the ageing placenta puts the baby at risk.
The mother had been for an ultrasound at 12 weeks, which had put the date of birth at 28 July, 2020.
But the mother distrusted hospitals and trusted Kali, her birth keeper, the court previously heard.
Kali told her to calculate her due date from the date of conception, an unreliable measure that put the date of birth in mid-August.
That recalculation, Evans wrote in his report to the court, was the “root cause” of the issue.
“The standard practice now is that you don’t allow a pregnancy to go beyond 42 completed weeks,” Evans said on Friday.
Expert midwives earlier told the court they didn’t have statistics for babies born beyond 43 weeks because it was so rare.
A 19 August ultrasound showed the pregnancy had become a medical emergency – but Kali advised her to “go home and rest”. It is “more likely than not” that the baby would have survived had she gone to hospital after the ultrasound, Evans said.
Baby B’s mother was warned multiple times she needed to go to hospital to give birth to her twins, but she was determined to have a home birth. Rather than let her have a free birth, four midwives assisted her and the head midwife repeatedly counselled her about the risks.
The mother declined ultrasounds as well as a test for early onset group B streptococcus (GBS) – an organism present in 15 to 20% of women that infects the babies of about 2% of carriers.
Baby B likely died of GBS, pneumonia and sepsis, Evans told the court on Friday, while his twin fell ill but survived. Many infected babies survive in hospital thanks to antibiotics, he added.
The inquest is ongoing.

noticias.titulo: Beau Lamarre-Condon’s explanations of body disposal ‘ring hollow’, court hears
noticias.resumen: Former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Paddington in February 2024 Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Beau Lamarre-Condon knew he had murdered two men and his attempts to explain the disposal of their bodies “ring completely hollow”, a court has heard. Lamarre-Condon is accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Beau Lamarre-Condon knew he had murdered two men and his attempts to explain the disposal of their bodies “ring completely hollow”, a court has heard.
Lamarre-Condon is accused of fatally shooting Jesse Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024.
The former officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.
On Friday, Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC went through Lamarre-Condon’s attempts to clean up the alleged crime scene and dispose of the bodies as the trial wrapped up its ninth week.
The defence does not dispute Lamarre-Condon’s actions in the aftermath of the deaths, instead arguing he did so because he “panicked considerably”.
But Hatfield told the New South Wales supreme court his conduct was not that of a person who panicked after something unintended, but behaviour that was “deliberate, sustained and very purposeful”.
The crown prosecutor said Lamarre-Condon took extensive steps to distance himself from the deaths, manufactured evidence to make it look like Baird was alive by texting people from the dead man’s phone, and “disposed of the bodies in an utterly callous manner”.
“The lies, concealment and disposal of the bodies are not equally explained by manslaughter or accident,” Hatfield said.
“His conduct is immediate and the steps are so extreme you might think it’s only consistent with having intentionally killed both men and a planned murder.
“His explanations in his evidence … ring completely hollow.”
Lamarre-Condon claimed his initial steps came out of concern for the housemates, but by leaving the bodies in the courtyard, he risked them making a “completely terrifying discovery”, Hatfield told the court.
Hatfield said the accused had an understanding that “exactly what he’d done was murder”.
“His conduct was an exercise in avoiding accountability in what he knew he had done,” he said.
Earlier on Friday, Hatfield re-iterated the prosecution’s arguments about the day of the alleged murders, playing the audio of the two gunshots that killed Baird.
The lawyer invited the jury to consider what they could do in the four seconds between the shots.
Making a gun gesture with his own hand, Hatfield argued there was only time to walk a few steps and fire and “not opportunity for much more than that”.
Lamarre-Condon then came up with a “pathetic moral dilemma” and claimed he feared he could be killed in jail, when he knew he would be in protective custody, the prosecution alleged.
His decisions to go to Sushi Train for dinner with his friend and undergo a minor elective surgery in the aftermath of the alleged murders showed Lamarre-Condon was calm and at points “completely relaxed”, Hatfield alleged.
But within days, the accused must have been “feeling the world closing in”, the prosecutor said.
“He wants credit for handing himself in to police … but even in his last hours he’s there going to Bunnings, buying paint and painting the inside of the van … still trying to cover up what happened,” Hatfield told the court.
Lamarre-Condon eventually helped police locate the bodies, but only after being told about the state’s no body, no parole laws.
“The bodies were left … for a further four days after he’s arrested,” Hatfield said. “Evidence all the while being destroyed.
“Imagine the grief [of the families] on those four days.”
The defence alleges Baird and Davies were killed in two separate struggles when Lamarre-Condon was acting in “self-defence”.
Going through forensic evidence, Hatfield noted Davies’ DNA was found on the gun, but says this is “entirely unremarkable evidence”, alleging Lamarre-Condon had handled his body at the scene and then touched the weapon.
“It’s just something he’s grabbed on to in order to weave this invented narrative about Mr Davies shooting himself,” the lawyer said.
Earlier evidence provided by a weapons expert indicated it would take the force equivalent to almost 3kg to pull the trigger, which would not happen without a conscious movement on behalf of the person holding the gun, the prosecution alleged.
The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.

noticias.titulo: NextDC vows to keep future datacentres away from homes after community backlash in Melbourne
noticias.resumen: Public expectations around datacentres have changed in the age of AI, chief executive Craig Scroggie says Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Community backlash to a datacentre expansion in inner Melbourne that resulted in NextDC’s share price dropping 40% will change the way the company engages with communities – and it says it will no longer pursue new developments near homes. The company held its first annual general meeting since it was forced to delay the controversial expansion of its M3 site in West Footscray after power provider Jemena paused construction of ne
noticias.texto:
Community backlash to a datacentre expansion in inner Melbourne that resulted in NextDC’s share price dropping 40% will change the way the company engages with communities – and it says it will no longer pursue new developments near homes.
The company held its first annual general meeting since it was forced to delay the controversial expansion of its M3 site in West Footscray after power provider Jemena paused construction of new 22-metre power poles amid community protest.
The share price has since recovered to over $9 a share, but not before rival Goodman Group bought a nearly 10% stake in the business.
Shareholders revolted against the company at the AGM, issuing a second strike against executive pay, but the resulting motion on whether to spill the board was resoundingly defeated on Friday.
The chief executive, Craig Scroggie, said it was his “hardest AGM” in 15 years, and that he ultimately took responsibility for “delivery, power, planning, approvals, construction and community support”.
“At M3, we needed to work more closely with our power and construction partners, and with the community,” he said. “We are now doing that.”
Scroggie said the community deserved to be heard earlier than they had been during the Jemena construction works, and it was NextDC’s job to do that.
“M3 has certainly changed how we plan, build and operate alongside our neighbours,” he said.
“For more than 15 years we’ve built datacentres right across the country, and what earned trust then is not enough now. Community expectations have moved in the age of artificial intelligence and we must move with them.”
In addition to a new community consultative committee, including a standing forum for residents and local stakeholders, NextDC has said it will have a dedicated project website and contact channels with defined response times for complaints and inquiries.
NextDC’s chair, Doug Flynn, also revealed that the company would change where it builds in future.
“Given community sensitivities, we do not intend to pursue new development opportunities that are near residential properties,” Flynn said.
“The pushback against datacentres is very different right now than it was … six or so years ago.”
Flynn said that the M3 site in inner Melbourne had been an industrial site for 100 years, and had petrochemical works on it before NextDC built the datacentre.
After the blowback to taller power poles led to a delayed expansion, Flynn said the Jemena employee overseeing community engagement left the business.
“They recognise that they were just charging ahead regardless of community,” he said. “And they got a bloody nose.
“Unfortunately, we did as well.”
A spokesperson for Jemena declined to comment, but pointed to a September statement announcing its general manager for electricity networks had decided to step down.

noticias.titulo: UK says EU reset deal agreed but talks will continue ‘in some areas’ – live
noticias.resumen: UK statement comes after EU said deal would not take effect without future agreement over university tuition fees Senior correspondent Making today’s reset deal contingent on a further agreement on the level of tuition fees for EU citizens is designed to neutralise the leverage London gets in the next six months, EU sources have said. Senior diplomats had already confirmed this week that the EU would defer the deal on the level of tuition fees for another six months , a move designed to give the UK leverage in parallel negotiations to have the UK included in Made in Europe legislation designed
noticias.texto:
'Deal is done,' No10 spokesperson says, but talks 'will continue in some areas'
Peter Walker
Senior political correspondent
The UK and EU have agreed a reset deal on food and drink, emissions trading and a new youth mobility scheme, Downing Street has said, although talks on the level of tuition fees EU students will pay remains unresolved.
“The deal is done – negotiations have concluded,” a No 10 spokesperson said, less than an hour after Andy Burnham arrived at the summit venue in Brussels, where he was greeted by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, António Costa, the European Council president.
It went on:
“Now, both sides will work towards implementation of the youth mobility scheme, the SPS deal and the emissions trading scheme. Both sides have agreed when these will come into force. And those dates are set out in the joint statement, which will be published in due course.
As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place. And talks will continue on some areas – these will be set out in the joint statement later.”
Talks “will continue on some areas”, it added (10:40).
Everyone expects the overall reset deal to be done and a compromise to be eventually reached on tuition fees.
But the EU has form with the UK on linking bad behaviour with penalties so the EU statement that the SPS deal and the electricity deal will not be “adopted” until the tuition agreement is achieved needs to be seen as a real threat.
Back in 2020 the EU and the UK agreed that Britain could have associate membership of Horizon Europe. It was a hard fought deal with the UK almost pulling out over a row on the level of rebate owing to London if it did not receive research grants to the value of the UK’s contribution.
The EU, much to the amazement of the UK and the science community, withheld that associate membership until late 2023 in a broader row over the UK’s failure to implement the Northern Ireland protocol in full.
UK officials push back against suggestions reset deals could be jeopardised by tuition fees disagreement
Peter Walker
Senior political correspondent
in Brussels
After the deal was announced, UK officials pushed back strongly against the idea that the three plans could be jeopardised if there was no agreement on tuition fees, saying they were completely separate.
Earlier, EU officials had indicated that progress on the main deals would be contingent on tuition fees.
But while talks on tuition fees are scheduled to last another six months, even if there was not agreement by March 2028, when the new arrangements on food and agriculture come into force, this would still happen, UK officials insisted.
They said the UK had also won agreement in principle for sign-up to the EU’s still-to-be finalised “Made in Europe” policy, a protectionist plan intended to limit China’s increasing influence on European industry, with one official calling this “a big win”, especially as this had happened before a deal on tuition fees.
'Deal is done,' No10 spokesperson says, but talks 'will continue in some areas'
Peter Walker
Senior political correspondent
The UK and EU have agreed a reset deal on food and drink, emissions trading and a new youth mobility scheme, Downing Street has said, although talks on the level of tuition fees EU students will pay remains unresolved.
“The deal is done – negotiations have concluded,” a No 10 spokesperson said, less than an hour after Andy Burnham arrived at the summit venue in Brussels, where he was greeted by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, António Costa, the European Council president.
It went on:
“Now, both sides will work towards implementation of the youth mobility scheme, the SPS deal and the emissions trading scheme. Both sides have agreed when these will come into force. And those dates are set out in the joint statement, which will be published in due course.
As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place. And talks will continue on some areas – these will be set out in the joint statement later.”
Talks “will continue on some areas”, it added (10:40).
Tuition fees hold up mostly political - snap analysis
Jakub Krupa
Just to highlight Jennifer’s point there (10:40): the “hold-up” over tuition fees is nowhere near as catastrophic or dramatic as some headlines elsewhere would have you think – and, in fact, was pretty anticipated.
The three sectoral deals are still getting signed today and it counts as a genuine step forward in the post-Brexit relationship; it’s just that their full implementation get suspended until the tuition fee issue is resolved.
The explicit link on their implementation does create a new high-pressure political deadline in six months’ time, adding urgency for the two sides to resolve the tuition fees issue and unblock the whole process.
Ah, classic EU-UK negotiations stuff. Nothing is agreed until everything is agreed.
Just like the good old days (gets Brexit flashbacks).
'Heavily choreographed' welcome ceremony with several ministers in attendance
Peter Walker
Senior political correspondent
in Brussels
The arrival of Burnham and his European hosts was heavily choreographed – there were no words to the assembled media, or any shouted questions – but one notable element was the sheer number of ministers the UK PM has brought with him, in a sign of how seriously the summit is being treated by London.
These included Lou Haigh, the first secretary of state; John Healey, the chancellor; Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary; Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary; Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, and Anneliese Midgley, the chief whip.
Three sectoral deals to be signed, but won't enter into force until tuition fees issue resolved
Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels
Andy Burnham’s Brexit reset deals will not materialise unless the UK reaches a settlement with the EU over tuition fee rates for European students.
EU sources said on Friday that the three deals – on food and drink, emissions trading and youth mobility – will not enter into force without equal treatment for European students at British universities.
In a statement seen by the Guardian from the EU council and European Commission spelt it out:
“The Council and Commission consider that this agreement is to provide for equal treatment with nationals as regards tuition fees for all students. The Council and Commission acknowledge that these four agreements form a package of the 2026 EU-UK summit.”
The EU wants to ensure its students pay UK domestic rates of tuition fees, rather than the far higher international rate. In a concession last night, the bloc agreed to defer agreement on tuition fees by six months, but that does not mean they have accepted the UK’s position that their students pay higher rates
As the Guardian has reported, it intends to use its leverage, by making the three deals contingent on an acceptable agreement on tuition fees.
An EU official said:
“I think our position has been clear. We think this is an issue that needs to be addressed.”
The European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and the European Council president António Costa are now in position and waiting for UK’s Andy Burnham.

noticias.titulo: Senior Tories urge Badenoch to drop Brexit talk in major strategy shift, sources say

While the Tory leader still gives views on Brexit – in an opinion piece in the Daily Mail on Thursday she condemned Andy Burnham’s ongoing reset with the EU as a “backwards” move – sources say it is now seen as a second
noticias.texto:
Kemi Badenoch has been advised by her team to limit the amount of time she spends discussing Brexit and Europe, the Guardian has been told, moving the Conservatives away from an issue that defined the party for many years.
While the Tory leader still gives views on Brexit – in an opinion piece in the Daily Mail on Thursday she condemned Andy Burnham’s ongoing reset with the EU as a “backwards” move – sources say it is now seen as a second-order subject.
Instead, Badenoch intends to focus on areas the party believes are more fertile electoral ground, in particular the economy, the cost of social security and defence.
One source said Badenoch had been advised to shift the narrative away from Brexit by Stephen Gilbert, a former Conservative official who is now a peer and who joined the Tory leader’s team as a senior political adviser a year ago.
Although another party source said Gilbert’s advice was “more nuanced” than this, Badenoch’s recent run of speeches and interventions appears to demonstrate the change.
In eight sets of prime minister’s questions since Burnham entered No 10 over the summer, Badenoch and her deputy, Alex Burghart, who took one session when Burnham was away, have focused on Europe just once, on 28 October, when she challenged the PM on whether or not he wanted a new Brexit referendum.
Every other outing has focused on various aspects of the welfare state, the cost of living, or defence, also including subjects such as the budget, debt and whether or not the UK should drill for more North Sea oil and gas.
“The way I see it, this is less of a conscious attempt to sideline Europe than it is a way to talk more about the subjects we think are our strong points, like the economy and defence,” one senior Conservative said.
One Tory shadow minister said the wider party was firmly behind the idea: “Europe does still come up from time to time, but as a former remainer even I think we should move on. I’m not sure what is likely to change by us talking about it all the time.”
Another shadow minister said: “We don’t want to be talking about Brexit for multiple reasons – including the simple one that it was so awfully divisive.”
Badenoch does still at times defend Brexit to selected audiences, for example in Thursday’s Daily Mail piece, where she disputed Burnham’s charge that it had hampered the UK’s economic growth, saying the prime minister “wants to reopen arguments from 2016 because he has no answers for the world as it is”.
At other times her language on links with the EU has been more nuanced than the period when the Conservatives liked to disparage the continent as economically moribund and less relevant than more distant economies.
Asked about Burnham’s attempt to renegotiate the post-Brexit trade agreement during a press conference on defence earlier this month, Badenoch said: “They say they want to end red tape on food checks – that’s a good thing”, while then predicting this would not actually happen.
Badenoch also said she accepted that the deal with the EU could and should be updated: “The free trade agreement that we have with the EU, like many others, is one that needs constant negotiating. So I want to see Labour negotiating and improving on deals with all countries. That’s what you do when you have your own trade policy.”
A Conservative spokesperson said: “As Kemi has said, the last thing the country needs is to be dragged back into a debate on Brexit. That absolutely does not mean Kemi and the Conservatives won’t discuss the EU, but we will be very clear that Andy Burnham is only trying to reopen old wounds on Brexit because he doesn’t have anything to say about the challenges facing the country.
“Bringing down the welfare bill, funding defence, cutting taxes to promote growth can all be done outside the EU. Burnham’s reset is one big distraction and we will never shy away from saying so.”

noticias.titulo: Iraq university’s removal of male professors teaching women sparks weeks of protests
noticias.resumen: Al-Qadisiyah University’s move a sign of the country’s slide into a Taliban-like gender segregation, say activists The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in southern Iraq has sparked protests and been criticised by activists as a Taliban-like gender segregation policy. As many as 400 women are estimated to have joined protests over the past two weeks calling for the return of their professors at Al-Qadisiyah University in a move that appears to have surprised its administrators. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The removal of male professors teaching female students at a university in southern Iraq has sparked protests and been criticised by activists as a Taliban-like gender segregation policy.
As many as 400 women are estimated to have joined protests over the past two weeks calling for the return of their professors at Al-Qadisiyah University in a move that appears to have surprised its administrators.
The university said the move was necessary to “prevent the mixing” of men and women and had been requested by the families of female students. But students said their families had known since before they enrolled that there were men on the teaching staff and supported their daughters’ protest.
Students said university bosses had mocked their protests and refused to discuss their concerns about the sudden loss of their academic supervisors. On social media, commentators also accused the women of seeking to keep male professors to “establish immoral relationships with them”.
“My classmates and I went to demonstrate, and the university president, Rahi al-Yasiri, blocked our path with his bodyguards, who then began making fun of us. He ordered them to take photographs of our faces, in an attempt to intimidate us and punish us later,” said Huda, 22, one of the female students.
Huda said the students tried to explain how men and women still worked together in society in Iraq. “Aren’t there doctors who treat both men and women? Why then do you prevent male professors from teaching us, too?” In response, Huda said Al-Yasiri replied: “Even if you hit your heads against the wall, I will not bring back the professors.”
The students said a large number of them were tied to graduation projects and research supervised by the professors. They said they had grown accustomed to their professors’ teaching methods, who also knew their students’ strengths and weaknesses, which made replacing them at this stage more complicated.
Female students said they had been told by the university that if they were not happy with the change, they should drop out.
An Iraqi-British feminist researcher, Balsam Mustafa, from the University of Cardiff, said the female students were “treated as if they are minors without the right to object to decisions affecting their academic lives”.
Mustafa said the removal of the male professors was a part of a worrying trend in women’s rights in the country, with “growing discussion about women’s clothing and chastity reflected in the celebration of female students who wear the abaya”.
An Iraqi lawyer and human rights activist, Israa Salman, said the restrictions on women was a “societal catastrophe”.
“Attempts are being made to suppress women’s talents and turn Iraqi society – a society that has produced remarkable minds and expertise, with women playing pioneering roles in many fields – into something resembling Kabul under Taliban rule.
“This contradicts Iraq’s constitution and the international treaties and conventions the country has signed and ratified,” said Salman.
Produced in collaboration with Jummar, an independent Iraqi media platform

noticias.titulo: ‘You’ve got me for life’: first ceremonies in England cement care leavers’ relationships
noticias.resumen: Lifelong guardianship ceremonies were announced in July as way to publicly affirm chosen connections Allan was 14 years old and had been through eight foster families and a stint in a children’s home when he began living with foster carer Russ in Kettering – a move that would change the course of his life. Russ, 63, fought for Allan to get the school placements he needed and took him to kickboxing every week, eventually joining in himself. When Allan turned 18, he moved out into his own flat, but the pair have stayed close. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Allan was 14 years old and had been through eight foster families and a stint in a children’s home when he began living with foster carer Russ in Kettering – a move that would change the course of his life.
Russ, 63, fought for Allan to get the school placements he needed and took him to kickboxing every week, eventually joining in himself. When Allan turned 18, he moved out into his own flat, but the pair have stayed close.
“You’ve got me for life now, I’m coming to your wedding,” said Russ. “I think what makes our relationship so special is that we choose to be part of each other’s lives. It’s no longer defined by fostering, it’s just simply who we are together.
“He still comes back for me to take his braids out every six weeks. And he still comes and searches my cupboards for food.”
In Allan’s words: “Moving out meant leaving the house, but not the family.”
The pair were some of the first in the country to take part in a lifelong guardianship ceremony, launched by the government in July as a way for care leavers to publicly affirm a chosen relationship with significant person in their life.
That person could be former foster carer, a mentor, a member of a faith community, a friend, or a wider family figure, and ceremonies can be faith-based, secular or community-led.
Speaking in Northampton before the first ceremonies took place, the children’s minister, Josh MacAlister, said: “As human beings, we thrive through our connection with other people and we find these special moments to mark the people we care about and love.
“We do that with blessings, we do it with weddings, we do it at parties, and we’re doing it today for the first time in this country, with something that’s unique and distinct for care experienced people.”
Each of the seven pairs taking part delivered short speeches explaining their relationship and feelings towards each other, before being presented with a lifelong guardian certificate, designed as two jigsaw pieces that fit together.
Colin Foster, chief executive of Northamptonshire Children’s Trust, acted as celebrant and navigated people through the teary-eyed event. “Any dry eyes in the house?” he asked at the end.
Russ said that when he met Allan, he couldn’t have imagined how much they would change each other’s lives.
“Five years on, he’s taught me so much about relationships, about trust, about the importance of seeing the person and not just the circumstances that we came together,” he said. “Today, we train together, we share friendship, we share experiences, and he’s encouraged me to be a better version of myself.”
In his speech, Allan said: “What matters most is knowing that I still have someone I can turn to. Whether I have a problem, need advice or simply want to talk – having my own home and independence hasn’t meant losing the relationship we built.”
Justine, 55, who was a personal adviser to 28-year-old Jodie as she transitioned out of the care system into adulthood, said she found the ceremony moving.
“It sparked a lot of emotions for both of us,” she said. “It’s going to be a lifelong relationship. I’ve gained another daughter and I’ve gained another grandson [Jodie’s son, Riley]. That to me is absolutely priceless.”
In her speech, Jody talked about how “when you grow up in the care system, professionals come and go. You get used to things being temporary and chapters ending before you are ready for them to close”.
She said Justine “treated me like a human being who deserves stability and someone firmly in her corner”, and sat at the top table at her wedding in 2022.
“The only relationship that I’ve maintained out of the care system is with Justine,” she said. “When you’re in care, there are a lot of endings, but this was never made to feel like an ending. So the ceremony has been really amazing to show other people how important the relationship is.”
Research has shown that care leavers face huge challenges, particularly due to the “care cliff”, when supports drops away at 18. They are more likely to end up homeless, unemployed and in the criminal justice system.
A landmark review found that profound isolation contributed to the deaths of more than 100 care leavers in England in a year.
MacAlister said the ceremonies were one small part of his enduring relationships strategy, which is designed to make the care system “absolutely obsessed with building connections around young people”.
He has also introduced a new metric to Ofsted and the Department for Education: the quality of young people’s care will be measured on whether their relationships are getting stronger or weaker.
“So much of care is about the mechanics of it and talking about placements, and that can often lead to relationships breaking down,” he said. “These ceremonies are about giving relationships a gravity and an acknowledgment from other people that it’s seen and it matters.
“I think this is one of the most powerful signals in the shift of care that we’ve got in England at the moment.”

noticias.titulo: Home Office tells woman born and raised in London she is not British
noticias.resumen: Woman, 24, says she cannot work and faces destitution after it was found her mother had no right to UK passport A 24-year-old woman who was born and raised in London believing she was a UK citizen has been left in a state of shock after being told by authorities that she is not British . After the Home Office recently discovered that the woman’s mother, who is from Jamaica, had no right to a British passport, she received a letter informing her her UK passport was being revoked. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
A 24-year-old woman who was born and raised in London believing she was a UK citizen has been left in a state of shock after being told by authorities that she is not British.
After the Home Office discovered that the woman’s mother, who is from Jamaica, had no right to a British passport, she received a letter informing her her UK passport was being revoked.
She no longer has the right to work or rent a property and says she is facing homelessness and destitution.
The rules around who is eligible for British citizenship are complex and being born in the UK does not automatically entitle a person to it. Instead it is determined by when a person was born and their parents’ circumstances.
“As your mother and father were not British citizens at the time of your birth you have no claim to British nationality or entitlement to the passports issued,” the Home Office said in their letter.
The woman, who does not wish to be publicly named, was born at Guy’s and St Thomas’ hospital in London and was brought up in the capital. She struggled with her education due an unstable family life. Her mother spent periods in prison for drug-related offences and as a result she spent time in care, including a short period with family in Jamaica, and on the child protection register.
But she was determined to make something of her life worked hard at school, and secured a good job. “I have always believed I’m British. The UK is my home and the only home I have,” she told the Guardian.
“I don’t want to leave the UK and move to Jamaica, a place I hardly know. I want to continue with my life in the UK. I’ve lost everything because the Home Office is punishing me for my mum’s actions. I’m trying to find a way forward but this has been a horrendous change in my life.”
A legal challenge against the passport revocation has been rejected by the Home Office. Officials said they had acted lawfully. “Where evidence comes to light that citizenship or a British passport has been obtained on the basis of fraud or false information, we will take appropriate action in accordance with the law,” a Home Office spokesperson said.
When asked if officials were planning to deport the woman to Jamaica, Home Office sources said that any action concerning an individual’s immigration status or removal from the UK would be considered on the particular circumstances of their case.
The woman’s solicitor, Naga Kandiah of MTC Solicitors, said: “She was born and raised in the UK, educated here, and has held a British passport since birth. Britain is the only home she has ever known. To suddenly have her identity and citizenship called into question is devastating. She is innocent of any wrongdoing, yet she is the one being made to suffer. This decision raises profound questions of fairness and justice and could have serious implications for others in similar circumstances.”
A spokesperson for the Project for the Registration of Children as British Citizens said: “The government must urgently do two things. First, it must take steps to ensure people can get on with their lives as swiftly as possible by resolving their citizenship. Second, it must raise awareness of citizenship rights so that far fewer people find themselves in this dreadful situation.”

noticias.titulo: Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as ‘biggest breakthrough in decades’
noticias.resumen: Cancer undetectable for one in 12 patients in daraxonrasib trial, while nearly all participants’ tumours stopped growing A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades. In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib , during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
A pill that can shrink and potentially eliminate pancreas tumours is being hailed as the biggest breakthrough treatment for the cancer in decades.
In one in 12 of the patients given the drug, daraxonrasib, during a trial, the cancer became undetectable, and the tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 patients. The trial participants had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.
Though doctors have said the pill cannot yet be considered a cure, and they do not know how long it can keep the disease at bay, they have said it is encouraging news because it appears it will offer patients more time, even if it does not cause full remission.
Half of all people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer die within three months, and only about 3% of patients survive for five years when the disease spreads to other organs. It has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK.
Patients were followed for a year and a half during the trial on average and some did not see the cancer return during this period. Longer studies will be conducted to see if any of the cancers can be put into remission. During the trial, tumours stopped growing in 90% of patients, just over 60% of patients had their tumours shrink or disappear, and for about 8% of patients tumours became undetectable on CT scans.
A year after starting treatment, 76.6% of patients were alive; usually 40-45% of patients given chemotherapy alone survive a year.
Dr Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, who presented the findings, said “this is the closest to cure”, adding that he had never seen so many tumours disappear in patients whose cancer had spread.
He presented the findings at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona. “We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival,” he said.
“The median follow-up is 18 months. Just imagine, in an average of 18 months your disease just disappears on the CT scan … that’s closest to complete remission … it’s incredible.”
Daraxonrasib is a KRAS inhibitor treatment, which works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations found in most pancreatic cancers. These mutations drive tumour growth.
There are hopes the treatment could work for dozens of other cancers because they can have similar mutations.
Michelle Mitchell, Cancer Research UK’s chief executive, said more research was needed, but added: “This is the biggest leap forward we’ve seen in decades for pancreatic cancer patients and could offer real hope to people facing one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat cancers.
“These results raise the exciting possibility that this breakthrough could eventually pave the way for treating other cancers that carry Kras gene mutations. More trials are now needed before this treatment can be assessed for use on the NHS and despite this advance, pancreatic cancer survival is still very low.”

noticias.titulo: British Library to outsource security and ‘repurpose’ reading rooms as business spaces

noticias.texto:
The British Library has sparked outrage over plans to outsource its security workforce and hand over to a private company three of its public reading rooms, to be “repurposed” as business spaces for hire – despite having reportedly received millions of pounds from the public purse to refurbish those spaces.
Almost 70 guards have been told that their jobs will be transferred to a private contractor, STM, on 1 December. Their union, the PCS, has in turn been informed that STM has rejected union recognition for those staff.
The union is balloting for strike action over what it describes as management’s “appalling approach to industrial relations”.
Nick Marro, the PCS culture group secretary, said serious questions around public money had been sparked because the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport was understood to be investing up to £14m in renovating the British Library’s reading rooms,“which the British Library is then going to immediately privatise”.
Marro said: “That’s absolutely ridiculous. We believe this raises important questions about the future of publicly funded cultural institutions, the treatment of workers and the government’s own commitments on insourcing and trade union rights.”
The library is proposing to close three of its 11 reading rooms – the science and social science spaces – turning them into a privately operated “flexible business workspace”. Sources believe this will involve the loss of 340 reader desks.
As one of the world’s most important research libraries, the British Library holds more than 150m items, including a copy of Magna Carta. Security staff affected by the latest plans include guards, supervisors and managers. Some patrol the reading rooms; others monitor CCTV.
Fran Heathcote, the PCS general secretary, has written to Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, calling for her “swift intervention”, saying that outsourcing is “in defiance of government policy”.
The letter, seen by the Guardian, reads: “What on earth is a government department doing investing in a resource only to privatise it, and outsourcing workers and stripping them of union recognition?”
She pointed out that at the Labour party conference, Louise Haigh, the first secretary, had announced an insourcing unit that promised to deliver on the pre-election pledge of “the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation”.
The PCS is questioning why the library is proposing to privatise reading rooms that are a vital resource for students and academics, among others.
On its website, the library notes a “huge demand in London for high-quality workspace”, while arguing that it is “running a financial deficit”. It says: “This year we expect to spend around £7m more than our total income … At the same time, research behaviours have changed. As online demand increases, in-person visits to our reading rooms have dropped.”
It estimates that the plans will affect about 20% of the more than 1,400 reading room desks across the St Pancras site, and that “the income generated by the new flexible business workspaces will make a vital contribution towards ensuring that our core library services – including reading room access – remain free to users”.
Charles Darwin is among famous scientists who have used the British Library, whether in its previous home in Bloomsbury or its current site in St Pancras. Marro said that these scientists would be turning in their graves over the latest plans, while today’s scientists would also be appalled as it was “already difficult to get a desk at the reading rooms”.
Marro added: “Any time I’m in the building, it’s hard to find a place to work. The library has pointed to falling use in the past five or 10 years, but that’s slightly disingenuous as there was a catastrophic security attack where they lost complete access to their systems and of course there was a drop in use when nobody could access it.
“The library has not stated that any jobs are at immediate risk of redundancy. However they have refused to rule out redundancies or a restructure in the future. It’s impossible to envision a situation in which they’re going to be closing reading rooms and losing hundreds of reader desks, without redundancies.”
Although the British Library’s chief executive, Paul Bate, announced the DCMS’s multimillion-pound refurbishment funding to dozens of staff members who attended a meeting last week, the DCMS yesterday denied that it has been allocated.
But documents seen by the Guardian include an internal slide from a British Library presentation delivered to staff, which states: “The cost of fitting out the space is £8m to £13m.”
Insiders said that the DCMS denial could mean that the funding simply had not been formally allocated yet.
The British Library declined to confirm the figures, initially suggesting that it does not recognise them. It said that its “commitment to science remains steadfast”, adding: “The new space will enable businesses, researchers, entrepreneurs and innovators to work and collaborate at the heart of London’s Knowledge Quarter, while generating income that can be reinvested in the library.”
STM has been contacted for comment.

noticias.titulo: Household rush to stockpile emergency supplies sends British retail sales soaring
noticias.resumen: Surge fuelled by ‘preppers’ heeding Be Ready campaign’s call for households to have three days of food and water for emergencies Business live – latest updates Retail sales in Great Britain surged last month as the public rushed to buy products including tinned food and long-life milk, after the government issued a warning to stock up in case of a disaster. noticias.texto:
Retail sales in Great Britain surged last month as the public rushed to buy products including tinned food and long-life milk, after the government issued a warning to stock up in case of a disaster.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said that the volume of goods sold jumped by 0.7% month-on month in October, defying economists’ consensus expectations of flat sales, as “preppers” took heed of the government’s Be Ready campaign to hold supplies to last 72 hours to survive a possible extreme weather event, cyber incident or another serious emergency.
The surge in sales is a welcome bounce back for the industry after a poor September, which the ONS has revised down from a 0.4% fall to a 0.6% fall, fuelled in part by poor online sales of autumn and winter clothing because of unseasonably warm weather.
“Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government’s ‘Be Ready’ campaign,” said Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS.
Food store sales, primarily supermarkets, rose by 0.8% month-on-month, the fastest rate since the 1.4% rise in April.
Textile, clothing and footwear stores reported a 1.5% month-on-month boost. An increase in visits to galleries, and a jump in sales of sports equipment, games and toys, lifted sales across other non-food stores by 3.1% month-on-month, the biggest rise since January.
The total non-food stores category – which includes department stores, clothing, household and other non-food stores – increased by 1.1% month-on-month in October.
Non-store retail sales, primarily online but also sellers such as street stalls and markets, bounced back too, rising 0.9% as a turn in the weather last month drove sales of autumn and winter ranges.
However, sales volumes of motor fuel fell by 2.2% last month, the steepest rate since April, as prices at the pump rose.
“October’s retail sales have exceeded expectations, despite low consumer confidence and growing pressure on household finances from higher interest rates and inflation,” said Erin Brookes, European retail and consumer lead at Alvarez & Marsal.
“Retailers will be feeling optimistic as the sector approaches the critical Black Friday and Christmas trading period, with October’s sales growth suggesting consumers are still willing to spend this festive season.
“Despite this positivity, retailers are caught between increasingly price-sensitive consumers and mounting operating costs.”

noticias.titulo: Emails reveal how Trump allies pushed pardons for election deniers

noticias.texto:
In the fall of 2025, Cleta Mitchell, a key lawyer in Donald Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential election, contacted a justice department official with an urgent request.
Criminal cases against people who signed certificates falsely claiming that Trump won the presidential election in their state – known widely as fake electors – were pending in Georgia, Michigan, Arizona, Nevada and Wisconsin. She knew the official, pardon attorney Ed Martin, was working on a memo outlining why those involved in the fake elector scheme should receive a presidential pardon.
Mitchell, a key figure in the movement to sow doubt about US elections, wanted the justice department to move forward with the pardons immediately before any of the cases went to trial. “Time is of the essence,” she wrote.
“If trials (and in the Michigan case, an appeal of the dismissal) are allowed to occur, the additional financial and emotional costs to these loyal Trump supporters will be enormous,” she added in the message, which was obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight via a Freedom of Information Act request, and provided to the Guardian. “It is essential that the pardons move forward as quickly as possible before trials are scheduled and before these defendants are subjected to further expense and mental anguish. Please let me know what else I can do to help get this done.”
Martin’s response to Mitchell’s email was brief. “Thank you for this,” he wrote. “Very helpful.”
While the president eventually did issue a blanket pardon to the fake electors weeks later, the pardon was largely symbolic and did not affect the state-level charges they faced.
The email exchange offers insight into the machinations that took place behind the scenes as key players in the election denial movement shaped the administration’s efforts to relitigate the 2020 election won by Joe Biden and to absolve loyalists of wrongdoing.
“While the pardons were federal, not for the ongoing state cases, the documents shed light on the extent to which Mitchell and other Trump allies were using their access to get President Trump to act. Protecting our democratic system requires ensuring that no one, regardless of political influence or proximity to power, is placed above the law,” said Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight.
A person close to the pardon effort said Martin had been pressing and working on the issue for months. Mitchell did not respond to a request for comment.
In Georgia, at the time, the criminal case against Trump and fake electors were pending before the prosecuting attorneys council after Fulton county district attorney Fani Willis was disqualified. Mitchell suggested that a federal pardon could get the case dismissed.
Other states, including Georgia, a slate of Republican electors had met privately and signed a certificate claiming Trump was the winner of the presidential election. Republicans sought to have those certificates recognized during the counting of the vote on 6 January 2021 – an effort that was unsuccessful.
“If the pardons are issued promptly, before a new prosecutor is appointed, the Council can move for dismissal of the only remaining charges in the case, being the charges against President Trump,” she wrote to Martin. The prosecutor who eventually took over the case dismissed the charges, though it was for reasons unrelated to the pardons Trump issued.
Mitchell’s interest in the Georgia case was notable. She was on the telephone call when Trump put pressure on Georgia secretary of state Brad Raffensperger to find enough votes to overturn the election. A special purpose grand jury in Georgia recommended criminally charging Mitchell for her involvement in the effort to overturn the election in the state, though she ultimately was never charged.
Mitchell is a key figure in the election denial movement that has spread since the 2020 election. She has helped organize a network of local activists who have spread false and misleading information about elections. She is also linked to organizations that have provided funding for groups that have spread misleading information about elections.
In Martin, Mitchell had a powerful ally. Prior to joining the justice department, he participated in the effort to overturn the 2020 election, speaking at a rally in Washington on 5 January 2021. “What they’re stealing is not just an election. It’s our future, and it’s our republic,” he said during the speech. On January 6, he posted on X: “I’m at the Capitol right now. Abd [sic] I was at the POTUS speech earlier. Rowdy crowd but nothing out of hand. Ignore the #FakeNews.”
Martin represented some of those charged for January 6, and served on the board of an organization that provided financial assistance to their families. Before being appointed pardon attorney, he served as the interim US attorney for the District of Columbia, a position from which he fired and demoted prosecutors who worked on January 6 cases.
Writing about the Arizona case, Mitchell urged a pardon before a grand jury could file charges, saying it would “be optimum to stop the persecution of these defendants, which include two of Charlie Kirk’s top lieutenants at TPUSA [Turning Point USA]”. Kirk had been slain in Utah only weeks earlier.
Summarizing the Michigan and Wisconsin cases, Mitchell wrote that a presidential pardon could save defendants further financial burden. “Some of them have already spent their retirement funds, mortgaged their homes to pay legal fees, and suffered significant emotional hardship over the past four years. Allowing a trial to proceed is simply unacceptable.”
The US constitution gives the president broad power to pardon people convicted of federal crimes. But not state ones. Nonetheless, Mitchell has publicly advanced a novel legal argument that a federal pardon for the fake elector scheme could wipe out the state charges.
“The U.S. Constitution created the presidential electors and the federal Electoral Count Act controls the proceedings by which the electors conduct their federal responsibilities,” she wrote in an op-ed in the Federalist in November 2025. “We can reach only one conclusion: These are not true state charges, these are not state actors, and the entire scheme to concoct some odd collection of purported violations of state law are a nullity.” Mitchell also publicly advocated for the pardons on X.
The Oversight Project, a rightwing group, published a memo in November 2025 making similar arguments.
Trump eventually did issue a blanket pardon for the fake electors on 10 November 2025, though those pardons didn’t legally affect the state-level cases. In Wisconsin, the criminal case against three architects of the fake elector scheme is still pending. The cases against fake electors in Arizona, Michigan and Nevada have stalled for reasons unrelated to the pardons.
The day Trump issued the blanket pardons, Martin received an email congratulating him on the pardons.
“It was a long project,” Martin wrote. “But I am glad we stuck the landing.”

noticias.titulo: Zohran Mamdani unveils plan to close Rikers Island jail complex
