noticias.texto:
Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island jail complex, with a goal to end all incarceration at the current facility and relocate its remaining jail population by the end of 2032.
“It is time to finally close Rikers Island,” Mamdani said in a statement. “For decades, New Yorkers have demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane. This plan puts us on a path to deliver just that: closing Rikers, reducing pretrial detention, tackling the case delays that deprive people of their right to a speedy trial and investing $146m in the evidence-based supports that helps break the cycles of incarceration.”
Described by Mamdani’s administration as “the city’s first comprehensive plan to close Rikers Island”,it comes as the city faces a legally mandated deadline to close the facility by August 2027.
That deadline was established under legislation passed by the city council in 2019 and signed into law by then mayor Bill de Blasio. The legislation called for Rikers to be replaced by four borough-based smaller, modern jail facilities located in Brooklyn, the Bronx, Queens and Manhattan.
However, the city is not on track to meet the August 2027 deadline, with construction behind schedule, and an increase in the city’s jail population since 2020, which has raised concerns about the city’s ability to reduce its population enough to accommodate the capacity of the four new facilities. The four facilities are expected to have about 4,500 beds, while roughly 6,600 people remain held in jails on Rikers Island as of early November.
Mamdani’s plan states that the Brooklyn facility is on track to open in 2029, followed by the Bronx and Queens facilities in 2031, and the Manhattan facility in 2032. It also states that his administration hopes to bring the 6,600 number down to no more than 4,100 people by the end of 2032, with a population of no more than 5,500 at the time of the Brooklyn Facility’s opening in 2029.
In a news release on Friday, the mayor’s office said the plan also includes the creation of hundreds of therapeutic beds “for New Yorkers with serious mental health conditions and complex medical needs”; and an investment of $146m from the city next fiscal year toward “mental health care, substance use treatment, educational and vocational programming both inside jails and in communities as well as victim services”.
As part of the proposal, the city will also work to reduce pretrial detention and case delays, modernize the department of correction, “and plan for the future reuse of the island”, per the release.
In the plan document, it states that Mamdani’s administration will “work closely with City Council on legislation to bring this plan into law, as well as the Remediation manager, federal monitor and the Board of Correction”.
The Mamdani administration cannot unilaterally decree a new legal closure date, it will require the city council to pass a new law extending the deadline, per Politico,
“We have a legal and moral obligation to close Rikers,” Mamdani said in a statement. “Working alongside the City Council, Courts and nonprofit partners, we will meet it – for the people in our custody, the staff who serve them, victims of crime, and every New Yorker.”
The Rikers Island complex has, for years, faced criticism over the conditions of the jails, the infrastructure, staffing challenges and reports of violence and deaths. The conditions have drawn sustained scrutiny from civil rights advocates, local lawmakers and more.
Last year, under former mayor Eric Adams, a federal judge moved Rikers Island out of the city’s direct control, and placed it under the authority of an outside official who was tasked with making the decisions affecting the jail facility. That official was appointed this January. In the plan on Friday, Mamdani’s administration said it would work with the federal monitor, as well as councillors and more, to “bring this plan into law”.
In a Friday statement, city council speaker Julie Menin said “delays under previous administrations have made it clear that more time is needed to fulfill the commitment the City Council made to New Yorkers in 2019 when we legislated closing Rikers Island”.
“With Rikers now under federal court-ordered oversight, we must bring this troubling chapter in our city’s history to an end once and for all” she said.
The proposal shared on Friday includes plans to restructure and modernize the department of correction, aimed at ensuring that “the operational challenges faced at Rikers Island are not transferred to the new facilities” per the report shared with press. It includes plans to “optimize jail staffing”, modernize data collection systems, improve processes for investigating, addressing and disciplining misconduct, and more.
The plan also proposes the administration invest $50m next fiscal year to “expand access to vocational training, educational programming, mental health counseling, substance use services and other supports”.
The news release states that the proposal includes plans for the city to restore its online bail payment portal in 2027, which it says has been unavailable since 2023. According to the news release, the city will also invest an additional $76m next fiscal year in “community-based services for New Yorkers” such as expanding access to “reentry services and community diversion programs, such as supportive housing”.
The plan also includes investment of $16m in support services for crime victims and survivors, to “expand access to mental health care and legal services”.
The lengthy proposal also discusses the planning “for the Future Reuse of Rikers Island” and said that the administration is “exploring near-term renewable energy and sustainability projects for Rikers Island”.
Since taking office, Mamdani has emphasized his administration’s commitment to closing the complex. He appointed a “Close Rikers Czar” and selected Stanley Richards to lead the city’s department of correction, making Richards the first formerly incarcerated person to head the department.
In June, Mamdani also announced the closure of North Infirmary Command, a facility at Rikers that first opened in 1932 and was described by the administration as a “vacant jail”. Officials said the facility was not housing people in custody, and it was transferred to the department of citywide administrative services, along with large portions of two other centers.
“This report is only the beginning,” the proposal unveiled on Friday states. “We are committed to demonstrating progress transparently and frequently, through quarterly updates.
“Together, these steps will result in the closure of Rikers Island, once and for all.”

noticias.titulo: Ukraine updates: Russian attack 'one of largest,' Zelenskyy says
noticias.resumen: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia launched one of the largest aerial attacks since the invasion began. Poland has said its airspace was violated in the process. Follow DW.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine updates: Russian attack 'one of largest,' Zelenskyy says
Published November 20, 2026last updated November 20, 2026
What you need to know
- Zelenskyy said the Russian attack included 400 drones and more than 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles
- At least 8 people were killed and several bridges and energy facilities were hit
- Poland said it's airspace was violated during the Russian attack
Below you can follow the latest updates from Russia's war in Ukraine on Friday, 20th November:
Ukraine says dozens of Russian oil and defense targets hit in past 50 days
The commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, Robert "Magyar" Brovdi said that his forces had hit 40 Russian oil facilities and defense industry targets in the past 50 days.
Brovdi said via the Telegram that among those targets, five of them had been hit more than once.
He went on to say that the Dorogobuzh chemical plant in Russia's Smolensk region was struck on November 10 and November 20.
Ukraine has managed to adapt on the battlefield with the use of drone technology which has allowed hundreds of drone sorties, in some cases deep inside Russian territory, on a daily basis.
Zelenskyy says overnight Russian attacks 'one of the largest'
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was targeted by more than 400 drones and more than 110 missiles, 27 of which he said were ballistic missiles.
"The Russians spread this attack across many cities and regions of Ukraine. Absolutely all the targets were ordinary civilian infrastructure – things that literally sustain people’s lives," Zelenskyy said in a detailed post on social media platform X.
Zelenskyy listed what had been hit during the overnight strikes
- Energy facilities, substations and power lines, which Zelenskyy said nuclear facilities depended on
- Logistics and bridges across the Dnipro, three were reportedly struck
- Regular residential buildings damaged
- Zelenskyy says Russians used missiles with cluster warheads and described it as "one of the largest attacks"
He accused Russia of carrying out second strikes on targets that had already been hit, in so-called "double-tap strikes."
"People had essentially already been killed by the time specialists were inspecting the initial damage to the facilities, as the Russians were carrying out double-tap strikes," Zelenskyy said.
Most Russian missiles reportedly intercepted
Zelenskyy said that in all 79 cruise missiles had been intercepted and that fighter jets had been scrambled to deal with the aerial threats involving F-16s, Mirages and MiGs.
"Ballistic missiles are, unfortunately, much more difficult to deal with, and that depends not on our capabilities but on the supply of missiles by our partners," Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine's leader called for a "clear response" from the global community.
It is important that our partners not only issue statements in support of Ukraine and Ukrainians, but also follow through on specific agreements on air defense," Zelenskyy said.
He pointed out the timing of the latest attacks and said Putin launched them "in a highly demonstrative manner – following weak meetings in China."
"Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic impotence with precisely this kind of terror, precisely these attacks on life," Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine death toll rises to 8 after Russian bombardment
Ukrainian officials said that the death toll has risen to at least 8 following an overnight Russian aerial bombardment.
Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said six of the eight people killed were in Kyiv. Two deaths were also reported at a railway station in the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia had launched 84 cruise missiles in the attack, adding that almost all of them were destroyed.
An unspecified number of ballistic missiles and more than 400 attack drones were also reported to have been destroyed.
Poland's defense chief confirms Russian attack on Ukraine 'impacted' Poland
Poland's Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said that several Russian flying objects entered Polish airspace during recent air attacks on Ukraine.
"Russian long-range aviation was operating, launching both Kinzhal and Kh-101 missiles, as well as a large number of jet-powered drones and conventional drones. … This Russian Federation attack on Ukrainian territory, which also had an impact on the Republic of Poland, was one of the largest since the beginning of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine," the Defense Ministry quoted Kosiniak-Kamysz as saying.
It comes after Polish prosecutors reported earlier that a flying object had crashed in Poland's eastern Lublin region.
Polish officials said it had taken place during heavy Russian airstrikes on neighbouring Ukraine.
In July, a missile entered Polish airspace and crashed in the same region near the village of Tarnawa Kolonia.
According to the Polish government, it was a Russian CH-101 cruise missile.
Poland probing 'violations' of airspace at three locations
Poland's Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski said that investigations were taking place at three sites after reporting that Polish airspace had been violated.
"In connection with violations of Polish airspace, authorities are conducting operations at three locations: Rudnik nad Sanem, Molodycz and Nowy Lipowiec (Lublin Province)," he said in a post on social media platform X.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that he had convened a meeting of senior government and military officials along with the heads of security services in a post on X. He said there was currently no danger from the air.
WATCH — Ukraine: Premature babies in a war zone
In war-torn Ukraine, premature babies remain at risk during air raids, while young architects work to save a forgotten gem in Romania.
Deaths and damage reported in Russian missile strikes on Kyiv
Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that a Russian missile bombardment in Kyiv has killed at least three people and injured 13 others.
Klitschko said in a post on Telegram that three bridges had also been damaged following the strikes on Ukraine's capital.
Experts would only be able to give a proper assessment of the damage caused to the structures once the aerial threat had ended, Klitschko added.
"Given the difficult traffic conditions between the left and right banks of the capital, I ask residents not to leave the city by private car unless absolutely necessary," the mayor said.
Klitschko also appealed to employers to allow remote-working arrangements, where possible.
Bridges have been key targets in Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine, but Kyiv's forces have managed to hit the Kerch bridge multiple times this week in what is being seen as a major psychological blow to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
He warned of a harsh response after the bridge linking occupied Crimea with mainland Russia was struck three times this week.
One of the archways and a section of roadway was destroyed in the attack.
Putin said he expected Moscow's response to be "far more painful" than the damage Ukraine had caused to the Kerch bridge.
Welcome to our coverage
Just a day after moves by world leaders to get warring parties to the negotiation table in the form of two summits — one in China, the other in Berlin — Russia has continued with its nightly attacks on Ukraine.
Kyiv has been been targeted by Russian missiles with local officials reporting deaths as a result and damage to at least three bridges.
The latest strikes follow ominous warnings from Russian President Vladimir Putin that Moscow's response would be "far more painful" than the damage done to the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia.
Follow here for the latest updates and analysis from DW's news team.

noticias.titulo: EU and UK hold a rare summit in bid to 'rebuild ties'
noticias.resumen: European Union officials and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham met in Brussels to discuss efforts to rebuild ties following Brexit.
noticias.texto:
EU and UK hold a rare summit in bid to 'rebuild ties'
November 20, 2026
European Union top officials and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham were set to announce deals on trade and youth mobility at Friday's Brussels summit.
This might be the first steps to rebuild ties, a decade after Britain voted to leave the EU.
In September, Burnham said he would seek a political consensus on the country's future relationship with the EU, even suggesting he could campaign to take Britain back into the bloc at the next election.
What did Burnham say at the EU-UK summit?
Brussels said the agreements would only take effect if a deal is reached to lower university tuition fees for EU students studying in the UK.
"Britain and Europe share values, interests and a global neighborhood. In a more dangerous world, we are stronger together. A closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe," Burnham said as he arrived in Brussels.
UK prime minister, who was greeted on arrival by a string quintet, said Britain should explore different options for its future relationship with the EU, including rejoining the bloc.
On Monday, he said it was the "obvious truth" that Britain had lost more than it had gained from Brexit.
What is on the agenda?
Three key agreements were being discussed in Brussels: one to simplify food exports by reducing red tape, another to link the UK and EU emissions-trading systems, and a third to establish a "youth experience scheme."
It aims to facilitate British companies exporting food to Europe, as well as enabling young people to travel between the UK and EU for work and study without being subject to existing visa requirements.
A key obstacle was securing a commitment from the UK to reach a future agreement that would reduce university tuition fees for EU students to the same level paid by British students. The EU made the implementation of the other agreements conditional on reaching such a deal.
The two sides had agreed on these initiatives shortly before the summit started, DPA news agency reported, citing EU diplomats and officials.
According to DPA, the agreements will only take effect if both sides reach a deal to lower tuition fees for EU students at British universities. They aim to reach an agreement on this issue within the next six months.
Speaking to AP news agency, a British government spokesperson said "the deal is done," adding that details would be published in a joint statement later.
Polling firm YouGov runs a regular tracker on whether the UK was right or wrong to vote to quit.
Since mid-2022, a majority of people surveyed said Britain was wrong to leave.In September, the "Bregret" camp rose to 60% — the highest ever.

noticias.titulo: Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?
noticias.resumen: German automakers are pulling back on investments at home, sparking fresh anxiety about the auto sector's future. Some industry watchers think there is still a narrow window to stem the decline. But how?
noticias.texto:
Can German auto manufacturing recover after Mercedes and VW cuts?
November 20, 2026
Mercedes-Benz's announcement last week that it would halt further investments at its factories in Germany has added to the sense that the country's best automaking days are behind it.
In a written interview for staff, production chief Michael Schiebe noted how the running costs of German plants are far too high.
Schiebe added that the automaker is "now forced to carefully examine which German sites we would have to close if we cannot achieve a change in the cost structure."
The decision came one day after Volkswagen (VW), Europe's largest carmaker, said it was shelving plans to modernize its massive Wolfsburg plant.
German auto industry faces restructuring
Germany's auto sector is in a deep crisis, amid fierce rivalry from ambitious Chinese automakers. VW alone is looking to cut 100,000 jobs globally by 2030, while four of its German factories are earmarked for possible closure.
Yet, many auto analysts doubt this really marks the beginning of the end for car making in the country.
"We have to admit that a third of our capacity [in German plants] is overcapacity and that needs to be cut," Thomas Puls, senior economist for transport and infrastructure at the Cologne Institute for Economic Research (IW Köln), told DW. "This will hurt a lot."
A report last month by Munich-based consultancy Roland Bergeragreed that domestic automaking needs an urgent "reset," but predicted that Germany could still "preserve a sustainably profitable core of automotive value creation."
In other words, car making in Germany may shrink, but what remains could be leaner, more specialized and more profitable.
Unions dig in amid fight for survival
Many doomsayers overlook the fact that Mercedes' investment halt is tied to tough negotiations with unions over cutting labor costs at its German plants. This includes scrapping the 35-hour workweek. The investment freeze could be lifted if a deal is reached.
Even so, Achim Kampker, an electric mobility engineering professor at RWTH Aachen University, sees the investment cuts as more than a negotiating tactic.
Kampker compared China's lightning-fast industrial strategy with Germany's, which he said was "too slow," as excessive bureaucracy and complex business structures prevent value creation.
"We need to become faster, more innovative and significantly more productive," Kampker told DW.
China's EV-makers can bring a new model to market in around 20 months, versus 48 to 60 months for Germany, according to Roland Berger. Plus, the Chinese have a 30% cost advantage.
Production costs at German plants are also much higher — between €3,500 ($3,840) and €5,000 per vehicle — than in Eastern Europe, where they range from €2,000 to €2,500.
Does Germany have a 'false sense of security?'
A separate report by consultancy PwC in September noted that despite German carmakers being well managed, well capitalized and knowing exactly what is coming, they may have a "false sense of security."
PwC said Germany needs to focus on four areas to ensure its auto industry is "future-fit" to compete with China.
These include splitting its internal combustion engine (ICE) business from the electric vehicle (EV) business, investing bumper ICE profits into those new technologies, redesigning workplace culture and training, and leveraging existing partnerships with Chinese automakers and US tech firms.
"The future viability of the German automotive industry depends significantly on decisions made in the next 12 to 18 months," wrote Harald Wimmer, global and German automotive leader at PwC Germany.
With the transition to EVs, some predict that automaking will become part of a much larger global electronics sector, which Germany must exploit.
Wimmer noted how top Chinese automakers were already benchmarking themselves against consumer electronics giants. These include smartphone maker Xiaomi, which now also produces around 400,000 EVs per year.
"Anyone who continues to base their competitive framework solely on their own industry is making a mistake that cannot be corrected once it becomes apparent," he warned.
Production remains resilient despite decline
Despite all the doom and gloom, car production within Germany is holding up pretty well.
Domestic manufacturing sits around 12% lower than pre-pandemic levels. This year, however, the auto sector is on course to meet a December estimate of 4.11 million vehicles, just 1% lower than last year, according to the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA).
IW Köln's Puls thinks German automakers must now avoid a trap Italy fell into in the early 2000s when its national auto champion, Fiat, struggled with profitability.
In Italy, "the politics and the unions blocked any attempt by Fiat to cut overcapacity," Puls told DW. "What's the result? They have a capacity of 1.1 to 1.2 million cars and utilization of about 250,000."
Last year, those same Italian plants built just 214,000 passenger cars, according to the FIM Cisl trade union, the fewest since 1954.
Analysts call for faster reform
For Germany, the issue isn't a lack of expertise or ambition; it's that reforms to huge industries often get weighed down by caution and red tape.
As the country's auto giants try to push through painful cuts, RWTH Aachen University's Kampker warned that if they fail to address their shortcomings, "we will see more production sites closing and a substantial shift of industrial investment and employment away from Germany."
"There is still an opportunity to reverse this trend, but the window of opportunity is narrowing," Kampker concluded.

noticias.titulo: COP31: UN Climate summit enters final phase with no deal in sight
noticias.resumen: After nearly two weeks of negotiations, countries remain divided on how to fight global warming. A new draft declaration doesn't mention the phaseout of fossil fuels, the main drivers of climate change. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
COP31: UN Climate summit enters final phase with no deal in sight
Published November 20, 2026last updated November 20, 2026
What you need to know
- Diplomats and delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey
- A new draft deal omits any mention of how to phase out fossil fuels, in what campaigners call a step 'backwards' and a 'glaring regression'
- Like in previous years, the climate summit is likely to be extended until a consensus is reached
These are the major developments from the closing phase of the UN's COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday, November 20, 2026:
EU slams COP31 draft as 'not acceptable'
European Union negotiators have told German news agency dpa that the current COP31 draft declaration, which omits any mention of fossil fuels, is "not acceptable," as they aired their frustration with the current state of negotiations.
The summit is formally set to end at 6 p.m. local time (1500 UTC), but it is likely that the deadline will be extended, as it has in previous years.
The draft declaration's main proposal aims to increase electricity's share of global energy consumption from 23% to 35% by encouraging nations to favor cleaner electric alternatives over fossil-fuel-powered cars, heating systems and industrial processes in order to cut emissions.
Some 90 governments, including many EU states, back the proposal, although it is likely to be watered down amid opposition from oil-producing states.
Meanwhile, a number of African countries have said they will only support the electrification target if they receive increased funding to help deal with the impacts of climate change.
Turkey to start offshore hydrocarbon drilling next year
A Turkish seismic research vessel is set to start searching for oil and gas off the coast of Pakistan next year, Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar said Friday.
The announcement that Turkey will start drilling offshore for oil and gas resources comes as the country hosts COP31.
"At a time when global oil and natural gas markets are experiencing a historic supply shock, we are bringing the experience we have gained in our own waters and our domestic engineering expertise to our friend and brother, Pakistan," Bayraktar said in a post on X.
Turkey's state oil company TPAO signed hydrocarbon exploration and production agreements last year with several Pakistani companies for three offshore fields in Pakistan, as well as two onshore fields.
WATCH — UN warns climate change could displace millions
Climate-related disasters are uprooting people at an unprecedented rate. From floods in Nepal to droughts, storms and wildfires across the globe, millions are being forced from their homes.
DW speaks with Atle Solberg of the Platform on Disaster Displacement and DW climate correspondent Tim Schauenberg, who was reporting from protests at COP31 in Antalya.
IN DEPTH — Fossil fuels dropped from latest COP31 draft deal
One of the most fraught debates at the UN climate talks in Turkey has revolved around the future of coal, oil and gas.
Now, all mention of fossil fuels has been removed from the summit's new draft agreement.
Learn more about why fossil fuels, the main drivers of global warming, were removed from the COP31 draft declaration in this report.
COP summit poised to be extended with no deal imminent
Delegations from nearly 200 countries have been meeting in the Turkish resort city of Antalya since November 9 to negotiate ways to tackle global warming and provide financial aid to the world's poorest and most vulnerable nations to climate change.
But, as in previous years, countries remain sharply divided, and consensus has proven elusive.
Three years ago, at COP28 in Dubai, nations pledged to move away from fossil fuels, although no target or timeline was ever set.
Oil- and gas-producing countries have strongly resisted attempts to bring that particular issue back to the negotiating table.
Last year's COP30 summit in Brazil concluded with no mention of fossil fuels, prompting some nations to pursue the fight outside of the UN's sphere.
This year's summit is being held against the backdrop of rising living costs and the US-Israeli war with Iran, which has sent shockwaves through global energy markets and sent prices soaring.
Those challenges have taken the focus away from long-standing issues like rising global temperatures and increasingly frequent and extreme weather disasters, which have been exacerbated by this year's record-breaking El Nino.
In an initial draft deal earlier in the week, the phaseout of fossil fuels was included.
But a new draft declaration released on Thursday night by Australia, which is co-hosting the summit, omits any mention of gas, oil and coal, widely recognized as the main drivers of climate change.
The omission is a "black mark," France's Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut said.
Climate activists have also slammed what they call a "glaring regression."
"You cannot solve a fossil fuel crisis by pretending we don't need to phase out fossil fuels," said Harjeet Singh, convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign.
The director of Power Shift Africa, Mohamed Adow, also condemned the slimmed-down draft text, which he said had "gone backwards."
Despite the current differences, Australia's Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who is leading negotiations, said, "We will be consulting and negotiating until it is very clear to us that we have a consensus."
IN PICTURES — Hotter seas, more plastic: High stakes for oceans
IN DEPTH — Have we missed our chance on climate?
From record-breaking heat to devastating floods and wildfires, the warning signs are everywhere. Can rising temperatures still be brought under control?
Learn more about whether the world is acting too late to stop catastrophic climate change in this report.
Welcome to our coverage
Thank you for joining us as we bring you live updates from what is scheduled to be the final day of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey's southern Mediterranean resort city.
Like in previous years, however, it is looking increasingly likely that the negotiations will have to be extended, amid significant differences between delegates despite nearly two weeks of talks.
A new version of a joint draft declaration unveiled on Thursday night omits any mention of how to transition away from fossil fuels — the main causes of global warming.
Stay tuned as we bring you more details on those talks in this blog.

noticias.titulo: Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports
noticias.resumen: According to a letter obtained by the media, Lufthansa's executive board said the German company is losing €20 million every month. In addition to job cuts, operational cuts are also planned.
noticias.texto:
Lufthansa to cut 1,000 jobs, citing ongoing losses — reports
November 20, 2026
Germany's flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its Frankfurt and Munich hubs, according to a company letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets.
The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa CEO Jens Ritter and four other board members.
Why is Lufthansa cutting 1,000 jobs?
This is reportedly down to ongoing financial losses. In the first nine months of the year, the airline recorded an operating loss of €180 million ($197 million).
The executive board said on average the loss amounts to €20 million every month, according to media reports. The board stated in the letter that "this is the third year in a row of not being financially successful."
"Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said.
At the end of 2025, the Lufthansa group employed some 67,100 people, up 1% from the previous year.
How else is Lufthansa planning to save money?
The company also plans to cut employee travel benefits, restructure its hub operations to reduce crew overnight stays abroad, and reduce short- and medium-haul capacity by replacing some A320 aircraft with A220 jets.
Furthermore, it plans to equip ten aircraft per month with Starlink, a satellite internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The airline hopes to generate "additional revenue” by monetizing onboard internet access, according to the letter.
The time frame of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were a part of a previously announced downsizing.
In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4,000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization.
In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook.

noticias.titulo: Have we missed our chance to stop climate change?
noticias.resumen: From record-breaking heat to devastating floods and wildfires, the warning signs are everywhere. Can rising temperatures still be brought under control?
noticias.texto:
Have we missed our chance to stop climate change?
November 20, 2026
When world leaders agreed to do what they could to stop the world from overheating back in 2015, it was heralded as a victorious moment. Hope rippled from Paris, where the historic deal was made.
Since then, efforts to curb the use of planet-warming fossil fuels have achieved some success, with coal, oil and gas falling to a record low share of global primary energy supply. But they still account for around 86% of the world's energy.
"We're still burning stuff like [it's] the 19th century," Mark Maslin, professor of Earth System Science at University College London, told DW.
And that has consequences. The United Nations now says overshooting the temperature threshold agreed in Paris 11 years ago is inevitable. That means even more extreme weather events, like storms, flooding, droughts and deadly heat waves and resultant crop failures and water shortages across the world.
The impacts are already being felt globally. This summer, Europe alone recorded 50,000 heat-related deaths in urban areas. In Delhi, India, summer heat waves saw temperatures soar above 45 degrees Celsius (113 Fahrenheit). Even in the relative cool of the evening, there was little respite.
"It feels like your eyes are burning," said Disha Ravi, co-founder of the India chapter of youth climate movement Fridays for Future (FFF). "I always describe it as being cooked alive in an oven."
Heat waves and other weather extremes are killing people now, says Ravi, and she is aware that as the global average temperature continues to rise, life is only set to become tougher.
"Even at this moment where we haven't even reached the worst of what it could be, it's already difficult," she said.
"We should have dealt with climate change 10, 20 years ago," Maslin said.
Shoulda, woulda, coulda: Is it too late to bring temperatures under control?
The UN now says that the world must keep the time it spends in overshoot as brief as possible, bringing global heating back down by the end of the century.
The longer the planet spends above the threshold, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible, self-perpetuating tipping points, such as massive forest die-back and permafrost melting that would release huge amounts of carbon into the atmosphere.
A recent report by science-based assessment Climate Action Tracker says limiting overshoot will require policies to rapidly and steeply reduce the emissions warping the climate.
"The stark choice for governments is to continue to support the fossil fuel industry, which would consign humanity to insurmountable economic damages, rising mortality from heat and climate-driven diseases and disasters that they are unable to adapt to — or pivot to the solutions which are available and cheaper than ever," the authors said.
Failure to cut emissions quickly has made it significantly harder to get climate change under control, and the window for doing so is rapidly closing. But Maslin refers to a Chinese proverb: "When is the best time to plant a tree? Yesterday. When's the next best time to plant a tree? Today."
He points to the massive expansion in renewable energy as reason not to despair. Wind, solar and hydropower accounted for around 34% of global electricity production in 2025 and are increasingly being used to meet rising demand.
Last year, record growth in solar power meant that clean energy met all new global electricity demand, stifling new fossil fuel generation, according to an analysis by energy think tank Ember.
"At the moment, $2 trillion is being invested in new renewable energy projects around the world, which is twice as much as fossil fuels," Maslin said.
But no country is weaning itself off fossil fuels quickly enough to limit the time spent in overshoot. "The transition is happening, it's just not happening fast enough," he added.
The countries pushing for a fossil fuel phaseout
One of the problems is that most climate and energy plans focus on building a green energy system rather than creating policy to shift away from fossil fuel use and production, according to a recent report on how to manage the transition by nonprofit research organization, World Resources Institute.
A group of 57 states is working together to manage and accelerate the complicated task of phasing out oil, coal and gas by creating specific roadmaps to do so.
Under the Transition Away from Fossil Fuels initiative (TAFF) initiative, Brazil has published a global roadmap that suggests various measures that can be tailored to each country's financial circumstances and capabilities.
So far, a small but growing number of countries, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Finland, have released national roadmaps.
Yet renewables advocacy group Oil Change International says they largely repackage existing commitments rather than offering new ones, when "what we need is an accelerated timeline for a clean, secure energy system."
France is sticking to a previously announced deadline of phasing out fossil fuels entirely by 2050. The Netherlands has not published binding dates for quitting oil and gas, and will continue to extract gas in the North Sea.
 
Germany, however, explicitly mentioned transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045 for the first time, in line with its existing climate neutrality target. The country has also reduced its emissions by 48% compared to 1990 levels. 
And while Finland has not set a hard and fast target for phasing out the fossil fuels that still account for 26% of its total energy consumption, it already generates more than 96% of electricity from non-fossil sources.
"None of these examples is a perfect template," according to the WRI report. "But together, they show that countries are already developing many of the core ingredients of a fossil fuel transition plan."
Every fraction of a degree matters
Limiting the time spent in overshoot would mean fossil fuel use falling 20% by 2030 and being phased out completely by 2070, according to research institute Climate Analytics.
It also means removing hundreds of billions of tons of CO2 from the atmosphere using carbon removal technologies that remain unproven at scale, as well as nature-based approaches like reforestation.
And it requires fast action on the short-lived but highly potent greenhouse gas methane. A 45% cut would reduce warming by 0.3%, according to the UN.
Scientists stress that every fraction of a degree matters as the world blows past the threshold of 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) of warming above pre-industrial levels. That's because every increment will bring more extreme heat, heavier rainfall, rising seas, and greater and more catastrophic risk for everyone around the world.
Still, even in the face of accelerating climate change, FFF co-founder Ravi rejects the idea that it is too late to act.
"I refuse to believe we'll ever run out of time. No matter how bad it gets," she said. "We owe it to ourselves. We owe it to each other to always try to get out of this mess."

noticias.titulo: India: Pakistani minister visits Delhi for SCO forum amid frozen ties
noticias.resumen: Pakistan's Climate Minister Musadik Malik has arrived in New Delhi for an SCO cultural forum, the first visit by a Pakistani federal minister since 2023. Meanwhile, Cyclone Akvan has made landfall.
noticias.texto:
India: Pakistani minister visits Delhi for SCO forum amid frozen ties
Published November 20, 2026last updated November 20, 2026
What you need to know
- Pakistani minister is in Delhi for SCO forum, the first ministerial visit since 2023, even as the opposition questions PM Modi's government
- US religious freedom panel has accused India of targeting Muslims in voter roll revision, urging a 'country of particular concern' label
- Cyclone Akvan has made landfall along India's eastern coast,
Here is a roundup of headlines from India from Friday, November 20:
Alleged Dawood aide Naseem Durrani killed in encounter in UP's Bulandshahr, police say
Naseem Durrani, a 37-year-old alleged gangster linked to Indian-born Pakistani mob boss Dawood Ibrahim's D-Company, was killed in an encounter with a joint team of Delhi Police and the Noida Special Task Force in Bulandshahr, Uttar Pradesh, late Thursday.
Durrani was accused of shooting 26-year-old Sameer, a Mustafabad resident, near Delhi Law Minister Kapil Mishra's office in Khajuri Khas on November 16, allegedly firing about 20 rounds, local media reported. Police tied the killing to an ongoing gang rivalry in northeast Delhi.
Durrani, also known as "Rizwan," faced more than 20 criminal cases, including murder, attempted murder and robbery, and carried a 50,000 rupees (about €500, $540) reward. He was reportedly in touch with Chhota Shakeel, a close Dawood aide, and was allegedly involved in a conspiracy to kill gangster Chhota Rajan.
Doctors declared Durrani dead at a hospital.
Rahul Gandhi says India has become a 'side player' in world affairs, BJP hits back
Congress leader Rahul Gandhi told students at the University of Chicago that India has become a "side player" in global affairs, prompting Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) to respond sharply.
"India, by its size, naturally has a global voice and India should be actively involved in global conversations. But frankly, India has become a side player," Gandhi said in his interaction with students and faculty at the university, citing neighbor Pakistan's role in US-Iran talks.
He also questioned Prime Minister Narendra Modi's reliance on personal ties with leaders like Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin: "Friendship is not the point. Who gives a damn about friendship? Do you really think that geopolitics is going to work because the guy is your friend?"
When asked by a Pakistani participant about relations between the neighbors, Gandhi said talks could begin if Pakistan stopped backing terrorism. "And it is impossible for us to accept our innocent people being murdered and having a conversation with Pakistan," he said.
Reiterating allegations about electoral rolls, he also ruled out an opposition election boycott: "If we were to say that we are not going to participate in elections, Indian democracy would end that very instant."
BJP spokesperson CR Kesavan took to social media to write, "Rahul Gandhi, the LoP [Leader of Opposition], sounds like an eager cheerleader and a shameless propagandist for Pakistan and his reckless remarks expose how clueless Rahul Gandhi is about global geopolitics."
WATCH — A woman in the well of death
Rehana Khan is one of India's women stunt drivers. She tours the country's fairgrounds, drawing crowds as she rips around the "Well of Death" on her motorcycle.
The danger is matched by difficulty making ends meet.
Watch for more:
Cyclone Akvan weakens after landfall
Cyclone Akvan made landfall on India's eastern coast on Friday, bringing heavy rain and strong winds with no major damage reported so far, Reuters said. It is the third cyclone to hit the coast in under a month.
The storm crossed the north Andhra Pradesh and south Odisha coasts near Gopalpur between 7:30 and 8:30 a.m. local time (0230 GMT and 0330 GMT), according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD). IMD said it had weakened to a cyclonic storm overnight and crossed with winds of 70-80 kph, gusting to 90 kph.
IMD said it weakened to a deep depression by 11:30 a.m. IST and is to develop into a depression in the next six hours, according to Reuters.
More than 300,000 people had been moved to relief camps in Odisha, local media reported. Odisha and Andhra Pradesh together evacuated hundreds of thousands.
"No damage or untoward incident has been reported so far," Odisha's Special Relief Commissioner Rajesh Prabhakar Patil told Reuters. Andhra Pradesh also reported minimal impact, disaster management official Prakhar Jain said.
Cyclone Murasu struck a fortnight ago, uprooting trees and electric poles, and Cyclone Arnab last month killed six people, Reuters said.
Pakistani minister in Delhi for SCO forum, first ministerial visit since 2023
Pakistan's Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik arrived in New Delhi on Friday for a Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) cultural forum.
It is the first visit to India by a Pakistani federal minister since Bilawal Bhutto Zardari attended the SCO meeting in Goa in May 2023, and the first since last year's conflict between the two countries.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi is set to inaugurate the Civilizational Dialogue Forum, which runs from November 20 to 22. India invited Pakistan's culture minister in October, but Islamabad sent Malik instead.
Pakistan's Foreign Office said he would present the country's views on dialogue among civilizations and meet other SCO members on the sidelines, local media reported.
Malik said the visit is not a bilateral negotiation, according to NDTV. No breakthrough in frigid relations is expected.
The visit comes after the four-day India-Pakistan conflict of 2025, set off by the Pahalgam attack, which killed at least 70 people on both sides, AFP stated. It also comes two days after Indian forces killed Lashkar-e-Taiba commander Lateef Bhat.
Opposition leaders criticized the government's move to host Malik.
"BJP always says that talks and terrorism cannot happen at the same time. But now, a Pakistani minister is visiting India for the SCO meeting," said Samajwadi Party leader Fakhrul Hasan Chand, NDTV reported.
Congress Member of Parliament Pramod Tiwari also recalled Malik's earlier remarks on the Indus Waters Treaty, calling his language that of a "terrorist," according to NDTV.
Earlier this year, Malik, referring to the Indus Waters Treaty suspension after last year's Pahalgam terror attack, had warned against "water aggression," pressing India to respect the 1960 treaty.
"Whoever touches our water, their hands would be cut off," he said at the time.
US religious freedom panel says India targeted Muslims in voter roll revision
The US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF) said Thursday that India has escalated its targeting of religious minorities during a voter list revision that struck off tens of millions of names, Reuters reported.
At 130 million names removed, it is the largest deletion in India's history, local media reported.
"The Indian government is targeting Muslim citizens by removing them from voter rolls, calling them 'foreigners,' and now illegally deporting them," USCIRF chair Asif Mahmood said in a statement.
The revision has become entangled with a separate drive to identify and expel suspected illegal immigrants, even though removal from the rolls does not itself establish that someone is a foreigner.
USCIRF commissioner Gene Mills urged the State Department to designate India a "country of particular concern."
The panel is a bipartisan US government body whose recommendations are not binding, and Washington has not acted on its recent ones on India.
India's Election Commission is overseeing a nationwide re-verification of the electoral rolls requiring voters to prove their eligibility to remain on them, removing duplicate, deceased, shifted and otherwise ineligible voters.
But critics say the ECI has gone far beyond that remit.
The Indian Express reported that more than 130 million names were removed from electoral rolls across the country. Before this, India had some 970 million eligible voters.
For scale, Germany has about 60 million eligible voters in total.
India's Foreign Ministry has cast USCIRF as biased, and New Delhi has called such criticism interference in its internal affairs.
Welcome to our coverage
Hello and welcome to our Friday coverage!
This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, once again, bringing you the latest news out of India.
As Prime Minister Narendra Modi prepares to kick off the First Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Civilizational Dialogue Forum in the national capital on Friday, the arrival of an unlikely guest is raising questions.
A US government religious freedom panel says India's voter list revision, which removed an estimated 130 million names, targeted Muslims, while the Election Commission has said it removed duplicate, deceased and ineligible voters.
Meanwhile, Cyclone Akvan has made landfall along India's eastern coast, the third cyclone to hit the region within a month.
For this and more, follow our live blog.

noticias.titulo: China's Xi praises 'turnaround' in relationship with Australia
noticias.resumen: The leaders of Australia and China have held talks on sidelines of APEC summit. Australian PM Anthony Albanese is also slated to meet Chinese Premier Li Qiang.
noticias.texto:
China's Xi praises 'turnaround' in relationship with Australia
November 20, 2026
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Chinese President Xi Jinping held talks on Friday, following which Xi hailed a "comprehensive turnaround" in the ties between two nations and Albanese said his country was engaging "constructively" with Beijing.
The leaders met on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Forum (APEC) summit in China's Shenzhen.
What did Xi say to Albanese?
Xi pointed out to Albanese that they had met four times since the latter became Australia's Prime Minister in 2022.
"I think it is fair to say that together we have brought about a comprehensive turnaround in China-Australia relations," the Chinese President said.
Xi also called for enhancing cooperation in agriculture, energy, the green economy and artificial intelligence, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported.
Why is China important for Australia?
China is Australia's top trading partner.
The relations between the two countries hit rock bottom under Canberra's former centre-right coalition government, which had called for an independent inquiry into the origins of the coronavirus.
An angry China retaliated by imposing import curbs worth $13 billion (€12.2 billion) on Australian timber, coal, barley, lobsters and wine.
Since Albanese's centre-left Labor party came to power, China has lifted most of its blocks on Australian exports.
But friction in ties has surfaced occasionally on issues such as China conducting a missile test in the South Pacific and Australia tightening a foreign investment screening in the critical minerals sector.
"It is important that Australia continue to engage in a constructive way with China, manage our differences, but not be defined by them," Albanese told the media on Friday.
"What happens in China does matter for Australia," he added.
Iron ore, a pressure point
Albanese is expected to travel to Beijing and meet China's Premier Li Qiang later on Friday.
On Monday, Australia, which is the world's biggest producer of iron ore, called out China's "manipulation" of trade in the commodity over Beijing's formation of a central buying body to purchase ore on behalf of its steelmakers.
A single buyer has increased bargaining power in negotiations with sellers.
Albanese and Li will attend a business roundtable comprising of senior executives from Australian mining giants Rio Tinto and BHP and Chinese company executives.

noticias.titulo: Germany news: Merz joins German-Ukrainian business forum
noticias.resumen: Chancellor Merz is taking part in a forum to boost business ties with Ukraine. Meanwhile, youth protests are expected to take to the streets again. DW has the latest.
noticias.texto:
Germany news: Merz joins German-Ukrainian business forum
Published November 20, 2026last updated November 20, 2026
What you need to know
- Further Gen Z-led protests are expected across Europe, including in Germany
- German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is set to attend a German-Ukrainian business forum in Berlin
- Lufthansa to reportedly slash 1,000 positions at Frankfurt and Munich hubs
Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines in Germany on Friday, November 20:
Germany's electricity exports rise
Germany's electricity exports rose in the first three quarters of this year, according to official data released on Friday.
According to the energy association BDEW, Germany has been a net importer of electricity since 2023.
The neighbouring countries Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands, were the most important buyers of German electricity in the first nine months of 2026.
Together, they bought about half of all German electricity exports.
The volume of German electricity exported rose by 25.5% compared with the same period last year, to 48.8 terawatt-hours, while its value increased by 51.3% to €4.3 billion ($4.7 billion). 
Electricity imports into Germany fell by 13.3% in volume, but at 49.2 terawatt-hours they remained slightly above exports.
While imported electricity cost an average of €116 per megawatt-hour, 39% more than a year earlier, exported electricity from Germany averaged only €87 per megawatt-hour, some 20.6% more than a year earlier.
With a high share of renewable energy sources, wind and solar, Germany tends to offer electricity when supply is high and prices are low, but in times of shortage it has to pay higher prices for imported electricity.
Finance ministry launches dialogue on economic future
Germany's finance ministry officials said the agency is launching a dialogue process, dubbed "Germany 2035," to develop proposals for the future
of the country's economy.
Officials want to study how Germany can secure growth and prosperity and what that could look like in terms of fiscal-policy.
Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil will begin the dialogue process on December 2, when he welcomes economists from around the world to Berlin.
Aditionally, think tanks, research organisations, universities and civil society groups have been asked to host workshops, which would take place in the first half of 2027.
Among 12 economic topics that the ministry seeks to explore are tax and fiscal policy, investment and domestic demand, industrial policy, energy and climate transition, foreign trade and sovereignty, and housing and local infrastructure.
The dialogue will culminate with a white paper, to be published in 2028, that can provide recommendations for Germany's economic future up to 2035.
Youth protests expected in German cities
A group called "Gen Z Takes Charge" (Gen Z regelt) has called for thousands of young people to demonstrate in many German cities.
The gathering comes almost three weeks after the first major youth protests hit Germany, inspired by the protests that took place in France in the last weeks.
Those protests, which took place on October 31, saw tens of thousands take to the streets across Germany, with crowds remaining largely peaceful, although rioting broke out in several cities, including Frankfurt, later in the evening.
Among the demands of the "Gen Z Takes Charge" group are increased funding for schools, addiction support and psychotherapy, affordable living, opposition to conscription and consistent action on climate change.
Another group, the Federal Pupils' Conference, has also organized its own demonstration at the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin, with police saying that some 5,000 people have already signed up.
The pupils' conference advocates for improvements in education policy in Germany, including school renovation, school social work, relief for teachers and the inclusion of climate action in curricula.
The demonstrations are set to begin in the morning and run until late afternoon.
President Steinmeier to welcome Emir of Qatar
President Frank-Walter Steinmeier will welcome him the Emir of Qatar Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani in Berlin with military honors.
Steinmeier will also hosting a state banquet for the emir and his delegation in the evening. Al Thani is also expected to meet with Chancellor Friedrich Merz during the day.
The visit comes in the midst of tensions in the Middle East, with the war in Iran likely to be a critical topic in the talks between the two governments. Qatar is currently one of the mediators in the deadlocked conflict between the US and Iran.
Economic and bilateral relations are also expected to take center stage.
On Saturday, the emir will visit Germany's most populous state of North Rhine-Westphalia, where he will be greeted by its state premier Hendrik Wüst at the military section of Cologne/Bonn Konrad Adenauer Airport.
During the visit, Al Thani and North Rhine-Wesphalia leaders will hold an economic conference in the small city of Königswinter, near Bonn, where the Emir will also visit Drachenburg Castle.
Merz to visit German-Ukrainian business forum in Berlin
Following a political summit on Ukraine in Berlin yesterday, the German Chamber of Industry and Commerce (DIHK) said it would host a German-Ukrainian business forum.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz and German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche are expected to be in attendance, along with Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi, among others.
Christian Bruch, deputy chair of the Eastern Committee of the German Economy and chief executive of Siemens Energy, said German companies are committed to invest in Ukraine, despite Russia's ongoing war and were open to expand their business partnerships.
Bruch said bilateral trade was expected to rise to around €13 billion ($14.1 billion) in 2026.
Lufthansa to slash 1,000 jobs in Frankfurt, Munich — reports
German flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its airport hubs in Frankfurt and Munich, according to a company letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets.
The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa Airlines CEO Jens Ritter and four other managers.
The timeframe of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were apart of a previously announced downsizing.
In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization.
Lufthansa's parent company Lufthansa Group had 67,100 employees in Germany by the end of last year. In the letter seen by news agencies, Lufthansa said financial struggles were the reason behind the planned cuts.
"Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said, while pointing out that the company operated at a €180 million ($197 million) loss in the first nine months of this year.
In addition, Lufthansa Airlines is now in its third straight year of being unprofitable.
In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook.
WATCH: Leaked files raise questions over Deutsche Bank's Russia ties
Leaked documents raise new questions about Deutsche Bank's dealings in Russia up to Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, adding to scrutiny over the bank's risk controls and past controversies.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Tag and welcome to DW's daily coverage of Germany-related news on Friday.
Lufthansa is reportedly planning on cutting jobs as the German flag carrier faces financial difficulties.
Meanwhile, youth-protests are expected across Germany and Qatari's emir is visiting Berlin, where he is expected to meet with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Stay tuned for the latest on all this and more throughout the day from the heart of Europe.

noticias.titulo: White House replaces cyber security chief after tech outages
noticias.resumen: Sean Cairncross is leaving his role as national cyber director after a chaotic week of tech outages. Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, will assume the position in an acting capacity.
noticias.texto:
White House replaces cyber security chief after tech outages
November 20, 2026
Sean Cairncross is exiting his post as White House national cyber director after a series of technology-related outages in the United States over the week led to disruptions in air travel, banking and national security networks.
Shortly after Axios and other US news outlets first reported Cairncross' departure on Friday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the Pentagon's Chief Information Officer, Kirsten Davies, as the new cyber director, congratulating her on X.
"Look forward to working together to strengthen America's cybersecurity," Rubio said.
Davies will assume the position in an acting capacity, media outlets reported citing White House officials.
"Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected," Davies wrote on X late Thursday night, as she thanked US President Donald Trump and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller for their "faith and steady confidence" in her.
"Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come …but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future."
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth referred to Davies' tenure at the Pentagon as one in which "she has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional."
"We are confident she will advance President Trump's America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape," the Pentagon chief said.
Cairncross leaves after US tech outages
The Trump administration came under scrutiny in recent days after the US witnessed a major tech meltdown as service outages affected not just travel, communications, and e-commerce, but also the National Security Agency.
Top US officials have since sought to assure people in the country that there was no evidence of a cyberattack.
In 2025, Trump nominated Cairncross to serve as his top adviser on cybersecurity and data protection policy. He was subsequently confirmed to the post by the Senate.
During Trump's first stint in the Oval Office, Cairncross took on various roles as a White House insider. He was also an executive at the Republican National Committee before becoming the cybersecurity chief.

noticias.titulo: Senate passes bipartisan energy bill amid environmental concerns
noticias.resumen: As Americans struggle with rising energy costs and increased demand driven by AI, the Senate passed a bipartisan bill that will speed up the approval process for data centers and power plants.
noticias.texto:
Senate passes bipartisan energy bill amid environmental concerns
As Americans struggle with rising energy costs and increased demand driven by artificial intelligence, the Senate on Thursday passed a bipartisan bill that will speed up the approval process for data centers and power plants.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, passed 62-33. Fourteen Democrats and one Independent joined most Republicans in supporting the bill. It now heads to the House. The bill was authored by two Democrats and two Republicans.
"Tonight, the passage of permitting reform in the Senate finally became reality and we took a major step towards addressing the affordability concerns of the American people," said one of the bill's co-authors, West Virginia Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune said the bill would "cut through decades of red tape" and "save the average household hundreds of dollars each year, and Americans will see better roads, more American manufacturing, and better-paying jobs."
Rhode Island Democratic Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, who co-authored the bill, said "Americans will quickly begin getting some relief on their energy bills if the House follows suit."
Nationwide, the cost of a kilowatt-hour has risen faster than overall inflation: more than 6% in the last year and 39% in the last five years.
Whitehouse also said the bill would make data centers pay for the power they use. There has been considerable pushback by the public against data centers in the U.S., cutting across party lines.
Some climate change advocates say the U.S. needs to speed up building renewable energy projects and transmission lines and argue that the bill will allow the country to build more solar, wind and battery projects.
But major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, have opposed the bill, arguing it will weaken environmental accountability.
Many Democrats have also opposed the bill. They say it will worsen pollution by making it easier to greenlight oil and gas projects and energy-hungry data centers, while weakening protections for clean air and water.
There is also concern the bill could undermine tribal rights.
"Don't sacrifice the Clean Water Act, hunting or fishing grounds, historic or sacred sites, or protections of tribal sovereignty," said Washington Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell on X.
California Sen. Alex Padilla had similar concerns. "I support cutting red tape and getting more energy projects built, but not at the expense of tribal sovereignty and California's environment," he said.
Jeff Merkley, a Democratic senator from Oregon, called the bill "a bad deal."
"It opens the gates to a flood of natural gas for data centers while leaving expanded transmission of renewable energy subject to Trump's obstruction," he said on X.
In a recent social media post, President Trump urged Congress to approve the bill, calling it a "BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE."
Julia Simon contributed reporting to this story.

noticias.titulo: New York City unveils a bold plan to move its jails off Rikers Island
noticias.resumen: New York City officials are moving forward with plans to close Rikers, the city's main jail complex, after years of discussion. The jail has been plagued by assaults and inmate deaths.
noticias.texto:
New York City unveils a bold plan to move its jails off Rikers Island
New York City officials on Friday unveiled their plan to close the troubled jail complex on Rikers Island, the city's main pre-trial detention center, which has been plagued with reports of abuse and neglect for decades.
"It is long past time to close what's been a moral stain on our city," Mayor Zohran Mamdani told NPR. "We cannot simply accept the old approaches to public safety just because they've always been done that way."
Rikers, which sits on a former garbage dump in the East River, has long been infamous for its dismal conditions – including crumbling infrastructure. Inmates have accused guards of excessive force, sexual assault and high rates of violence in multiple lawsuits.
Last year, a federal judge called the amount of violence at Rikers an "unconstitutional danger" for both the people held there and the staff.
Since 2022, more than 50 people have died in the custody of the New York City Department of Correction. Almost all had been held at Rikers. People have been found unresponsive. They have died by suicide and been beaten to death. Federal court records say Rikers is "significantly more violent" than comparable jails.
But now, city officials say they finally have momentum to close the jail for good, and the newly released plan details how they intend to do that.
The plan — which takes on both the conditions inside the jails and the size of the population behind bars — is ambitious. It seeks to transform how the city government thinks about crime prevention and safety overall, says Insha Rahman, president of the Vera Institute of Justice, a criminal justice reform nonprofit.
"If New York City can do this at scale, which it will, it is encouragement for places like LA, like Chicago, like Philadelphia, like Houston to do the same," Rahman says.
A goal set by the city years ago
In 2019, the New York City Council approved a plan to close Rikers by 2027, and to build in its place four smaller jails in Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens and the Bronx.
Rikers is on an island between Queens and the Bronx, out of sight for many New Yorkers. The borough-based jails will be closer to the courts and to public transit, making it easier for families, lawyers and service providers to visit people inside the facilities.
Since 2019, not a lot of progress has been made toward closing Rikers. City officials acknowledge they won't make the 2027 deadline. But Mamdani says the city is in a new moment.
"We're not the first administration to talk about this. We also know that the last administration had no interest in advancing this," Mamdani told NPR. "And we are also confident that we can be the first administration to deliver on it."
Earlier this year, he appointed a "Close Rikers Czar" dedicated to closing the jail and reducing the jail population. The mayor also appointed Stanley Richards as commissioner of the DOC, the first formerly incarcerated person to lead the department.
Mamdani says his administration has already taken concrete steps: The city revived plans for a housing initiative for New Yorkers released from jail with medical needs, for instance, and it opened a therapeutic housing unit at a public hospital in Manhattan.
'Human dignity at the center of incarceration'
Last year, a federal judge stripped the city of its authority over Rikers. Operations are now controlled by a remediation manager, who released his own initial plan earlier this year for bringing the jail system into legal compliance, independent of the city's plan.
Aspects of that plan took inspiration from carceral systems in Europe, a growing trend among correctional leaders across the U.S. The remediation manager, Nicholas Deml, traveled with Commissioner Richards to Germany earlier this year on a trip organized by the Vera Institute. There, they observed the country's prisons and jails, which are often regarded as an international model.
"While German correctional systems are not directly transferable to New York, they reflect a fundamentally different orientation — one that places human dignity at the center of incarceration," Deml wrote in his plan.
Last month, the Vera Institute took a second group of New Yorkers to Germany to see how jails can look when they're done right, including the Moabit jail in Berlin. Each member of that group had a part to play in reimagining New York City's criminal justice system: a prosecutor, a judge, a city councilmember, the chief who supervises officers at Rikers, among others.
At first glance, the group observed, Moabit looked like a lot of jails in the U.S., but key differences emerged on closer inspection. The jail was quiet. The cells had windows to the outside. In some of them, a door inside connected it to the adjacent cell.
"Some people are afraid of the first night here, and sometimes it really helps just to open the door to have someone to talk to," Katharina Spanaus, a staff member at Moabit, told the group.
There were also televisions in the cells to calm people down, and in the hallway, a vending machine selling cigarettes.
"I'll never forget the cigarette vending machine," says Christopher Watler, who was recently appointed chair of the New York City Board of Correction, which oversees the city's jail system.
What struck him wasn't really the cigarettes, but what the gesture communicates about treating people as human, Watler says.
It also showed him how far New York City has to go.
Just a week earlier, he sat at his first board meeting in New York, where he heard stories that evoked a different image. At the start, the board listened to anonymous phone calls from people held at Rikers.
The callers voiced concerns: A woman reported black mold. A man said he was denied his medications. Another pleaded for a less violent environment.
"New York City's a great city. Our jail system isn't great," Watler says. "It's a broken thing. But how do you repair broken things?"
'The sum of all the efforts will help'
The four new jails won't be fully completed for another six years. Each facility will have more access to natural light and fresh air, and more space for recreation, vocational training and education.
Together, the new jails will hold about 2,000 fewer people than the approximately 6,600 people Rikers holds now.
The city's plan invests more than $250 million across the next several years in efforts to reduce the number of people in jail, for instance, by expanding alternatives to incarceration like diversion programs and electronic monitoring.
It also aims to keep people from committing crimes, by expanding services like supportive housing and mental health treatment.
Another way to lower a jail's population is to shorten how long people stay there. The average length of stay of people in New York City DOC custody was nearly twice as long in 2025 as it was in 2015, according to the policy journal Vital City.
The vast majority of people at Rikers are awaiting trial, and many of their cases take longer to process than national standards dictate. Nearly a quarter have been in jail for more than a year.
Judge Joseph Zayas, chief administrative judge of the New York State Unified Court System, told NPR there are many factors that can lengthen a jail stay, including processing evidence during discovery and administering mental health assessments, for instance.
"The only way to solve this backlog problem is to hit each of these things. The sum of all of the efforts will help," Zayas says.
The city is planning a task force dedicated to speeding up court cases, but the forces affecting that are outside city hall's control. Judges act independently from the mayor, as do district attorneys. City officials say they are investing in those relationships.
'If you are wrong, then you have crowded jails'
Some people, including those with deep knowledge of Rikers, are concerned with what happens if the city doesn't lower the jail population enough.
Vincent Schiraldi, who was DOC commissioner under Mayor Bill de Blasio, says he can understand that.
"It's really hard to have the guts to forecast lower incarceration numbers. Because if you are wrong, then you have crowded jails and you're in trouble," says Schiraldi, who now runs a philanthropic fund to close Rikers.
Other cities have dramatically reduced their jail populations. After Hurricane Katrina in 2005, New Orleans reduced its jail population by more than two thirds in the decade after.
Schiraldi pointed out that aside from an increase during the pandemic, crime rates have trended downward for decades.
If crime increases again, Schiraldi says, "Then we deal with it. What is the scenario by which the government spends billions of dollars just in case?"
But Elizabeth Glazer, who led the Office of Criminal Justice under de Blasio, told NPR she hopes the mayor will be pragmatic when it comes to having contingency plans – including the possibility of building again on Rikers Island.
She says it is possible to shrink the jail population, but it's not going to be easy.
"It requires relentless attention, coordination and organization around a common goal to get it done," says Glazer, who is also the founder of Vital City. "Even if you hit that number, the question is, can that be sustained for the decades when all you have is that capacity?"
Still, for some people the city's plan is a crucial opportunity, after years of inaction have left thousands of people held at the jail under inhumane conditions.
"We wait for these perfect plans, and for all the reasons we know, including funding, those perfect plans never come to pass. And so what do we do? We do nothing," says Tina Luongo, who leads the criminal defense practice at the Legal Aid Society, which brought the class action lawsuit that resulted in the remediation manager's appointment.
Changing the culture at Rikers
Officials caution the new jails alone won't solve the systemic problems at Rikers.
Over the last decade, the federal government has documented a "culture of violence" among the guards. In 2023, more than 700 women sued the city alleging they'd been raped or sexually abused by staff at Rikers, according to a Gothamist investigation.
"People talk about culture change and that's really just a euphemism for the extraordinary brutality and violence that has plagued Rikers," Glazer says. "If you're going to move the very same system into the new buildings, you're going to move the problem of violence as well."
In their report, city officials outline plans for more training and mentoring for staff, tighter oversight, and more programming for people in jail.
Commissioner Richards told NPR he wants to see the jail's culture transform and become more like what he saw in Germany, where human dignity is non-negotiable for everyone. That includes staff, who Richards says have been demonized.
"Part of the work that I'm doing is showing value and appreciation to our staff. So they begin to expand their capacity to show that same value and humanity to the people who come to us," Richards says.
But he didn't offer specifics on what exactly will change. That may be in part because he has a more immediate focus: safety and security.
The plan set forth by Deml, the remediation manager, starts with the most basic correctional functions, including protocols for securing doors. Richards, who was incarcerated at Rikers himself 40 years ago, says they need to start somewhere.
"Everybody wants something to happen by tomorrow. And we are in a moment of urgency. But it takes time to turn," he says.
The larger goal remains the same: for the failures of Rikers to not be carried into the next generation of New York City jails.

This week, Alaska flipped, there was news about Starship and four actors were skipped … over to be the next James Bond. That tortured attempt to rhyme will have to do for the intro this week.
