noticias.titulo: Mysterious Mercury is about to get a visitor - after spacecraft's eight-year epic voyage
noticias.resumen: The mission is set to give us our best ever view of Mercury - the closest planet to the Sun.
noticias.texto:
Mysterious Mercury is about to get a visitor - after spacecraft's eight-year epic voyage
- Published
After an eight-year journey travelling almost six billion miles (10bn km), a spacecraft called BepiColombo is about to reach its final destination and get into orbit around Mercury.
It will be entering an extremely hostile environment: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and temperatures can reach a fierce 430C and then plunge to -180C, and it is constantly blasted with intense solar radiation.
Until now, the planet has been little explored but the hope is this mission will solve some of Mercury's major mysteries.
These include uncovering why there is ice in its craters despite its proximity to the Sun, and understanding the mysterious hollows that are dotted all over its surface.
"I think it's a little bit of an under-loved planet in the inner Solar System, but I think that's one of the reasons why it is so compelling," said Prof Emma Bunce, from Leicester University, who is a principal investigator on the mission.
"There are lots of reasons, scientifically, why we really want to understand Mercury, how it formed, how it evolved, what it looks like today, but also how it interacts with the Sun and the extreme space weather that it experiences."
The BepiColombo mission, which is a collaboration between the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japanese Space Agency (JAXA), blasted off in 2018, launching from French Guiana.
With the spacecraft heading deep into the inner Solar System, it has had to battle the Sun's immense gravitational pull.
So it has had its brakes on for the entire journey, and has also taken a very convoluted path - looping once around the Earth, twice around Venus and six times around Mercury - to slow it down enough to get into orbit.
This journey should have taken seven years, but a problem with BepiColombo's propulsion system meant the already epic voyage was extended by a year.
The final manoeuvre to get into orbit is a perilous one: it needs to perform a 37-minute handbrake turn to be grabbed by the planet's gravity.
If anything goes wrong, the spacecraft could hurtle past Mercury.
Only two spacecraft have visited Mercury until now - both Nasa missions.
Mariner-10 flew past the planet three times in the 1970s, and then the Messenger spacecraft arrived at Mercury in 2011 and spent four years in orbit.
But there is still much to discover about this tiny world.
Mercury is only a bit bigger than our Moon, and is covered in ancient volcanoes, towering cliffs and colossal craters.
And time on Mercury passes in a mind-bending way.
The planet zips around the Sun so quickly, a year on Mercury lasts just 88 Earth days. But it turns incredibly slowly on its own axis, so a single day there lasts 59 Earth days.
As well as investigating why Mercury has ice in its craters in the polar regions, the mission will also spend time studying strange dents in the planet's surface.
There are thousands of hollows all over it. They are shallow but with steep sides and often clustered together, and in planetary terms, they are young: about 100,000 years old.
Scientists know they are not impact craters - larger pockmarks on the surface caused by colliding space rocks - but they are not really sure what the hollows are or how they formed.
BepiColombo will also help to study another aspect of Mercury that has been puzzling researchers. Despite the planet's tiny size, it has a huge metal core.
Prof Emma Bunce said that the planet could once have been much bigger, but was potentially the victim of a "hit and run" early in its history.
"One of the explanations is that the mantle was stripped away in a large collision," she explained.
"Or it's a combination of collisions over a longer period of time that then strips away its outer outer regions, its mantle and its crust, and leads to the planet that we see today."
Or she said, it could have just formed that way in a metal-rich part of the early Solar System.
Unusually, this is a sort of "buy one get one free" mission - there are two spacecraft onboard.
A few weeks after arriving at Mercury they will separate.
An ESA craft will study the surface close-up, the other, which belongs to JAXA, will view the planet from a distance.
A life-size model of BepiColombo is on display at the Science Museum in London. It was used to test the craft while it was being put together.
Jessica Marshall, a systems engineer at Airbus, who built the spacecraft, showed us Bepi's key features - and said the moment of separation would be "nerve-wracking" for the team.
The two spacecraft had to be very securely attached together for their launch and long journey, but now, eight years later, they have to delicately disconnect.
"We have designed a special mechanism that we have thought very carefully about," said Marshall.
"It's been exposed to the harsh radiation of space and highly different thermal temperatures, and after eight years this is a spring mechanism that has to then release very gentlyâ¦ As it releases, it actually also twists in order to start the spin of that spacecraft as well."
With two orbiters at Mercury, both packed with instruments, the BepiColombo team hopes to find answers to Mercury's mysteries.
Of course, they may uncover many more once they arrive.
  - Published9 January 2025
  - Published19 October 2018

noticias.titulo: Israeli drone attacks kill seven Palestinians in central Gaza
noticias.resumen: Drones cause 'fear and panic' among Palestinians as Israel continues attacks on the Strip despite 'ceasefire'.
noticias.texto:
Israeli drone attacks kill seven Palestinians in central Gaza
Buzzing of drones causes ‘fear and panic’ among Palestinians as Israel continues attacks on the Strip despite ‘ceasefire’.
Israeli attacks have killed at least seven Palestinians and wounded others in the central part of the Gaza Strip, as attacks continue despite a “ceasefire” agreement.
Four Palestinians were killed on Friday when an Israeli drone struck the Bureij refugee camp in Deir el-Balah, medical sources told Al Jazeera.
Witnesses said the drone targeted a group of civilians within the camp.
Separately, a medical source at al-Awda Hospital reported the arrival of the body of a Palestinian killed by an Israeli drone strike in the Nuseirat refugee camp.
Two Palestinians were also killed when an Israeli drone struck civilians near the entrance to the city of Deir el-Balah.
Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud, reporting from Deir el-Balah, said the injured were brought to hospitals in central Gaza that operate at reduced capacity due to a lack of medical supplies and staff.
Mahmoud added that drones were “causing fear and panic” among Palestinians in Gaza.
“People cannot run simple errands because of the ongoing fear of being attacked and killed on the road,” he said.
The buzzing of drones adds to the sound of explosions from home demolitions and to that of fighter jets, our correspondent added.
The Israeli army on Friday carried out demolition operations near areas under its control in the al-Shuja’iya neighbourhood in the eastern part of Gaza City using explosive-laden drones.
It also carried out three large-scale demolitions near the “Yellow Line”, east of Khan Younis in southern Gaza.
By June 16, 2026, an estimated 201,290 structures in Gaza had been damaged or destroyed, about 82 percent of all structures in the Strip, according to the United Nations Satellite Centre (UNOSAT).
Israeli forces have continued demolishing buildings and homes in the Gaza Strip amid ongoing military operations and disputes over the “ceasefire” line.
Israel has repeatedly violated the so-called “ceasefire” agreement that entered into force on October 10, 2025.
Since then, Israeli attacks have killed more than 1,600 Palestinians in Gaza. Since the genocidal war began in October 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured 176,000 others.
Separately on Friday, which marks World Children’s Day, Palestinian prisoner groups said that around 350 Palestinian children were being held in Israeli prisons, where they face torture, starvation and deprivation of medical care, education, and family visits.
The Palestinian Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs and the Palestinian Prisoner Society said dozens of children from Gaza were detained during the war, but enforced disappearance and restrictions on visits have made it impossible to determine their numbers.

noticias.titulo: Nepali cricket fans in Qatar want to see their team competing with the best
noticias.resumen: As thousands from Qatar's Nepali community watch their team play, they hope that the team will rise in global rankings.
noticias.texto:
Nepali cricket fans in Qatar want to see their team competing with the best
As thousands from Qatar’s Nepali community watch their team play, they hope for the team to rise in global rankings.
Nepal cricket fans celebrate their team’s global rise
Doha, Qatar – On a warm Friday afternoon in Qatar, the country’s only international cricket stadium was a sea of Nepal’s uniquely triangular crimson and deep blue flags.
Nepal’s supporters arrived with flags draped across their shoulders, held them aloft to flutter in the breeze, cheering every delivery and waving them wildly in celebration of every wicket.
The events on the field seemed nearly inconsequential against the loud cheers of the thousands of fans who had filled the West End International Cricket Stadium on the outskirts of the Qatari capital, as the nation with the world’s highest mountain faced the most powerful force in cricket.
Nepal were bowling first against India A – India’s second XI – in their first group match of the Asian Cricket Council’s (ACC) Rising Star Asia Cup 2026 in Qatar.
Indian captain Tilak Varma and his batting partner Kumar Kushagra kept finding boundaries. Nepal’s bowlers faced the wrath and their fielders could barely keep up.
But the noise in the stands barely subsided.
The supporters followed every ball closely, their attention firmly focused on the team they rarely get to watch up close, especially living thousands of kilometres from home.
A cricket nation on the rise
Qatar is home to at least 367,000 Nepalis, according to the Non-Resident Nepali Association of Qatar, making them the Gulf country’s third-biggest diaspora community.
Pradeep Kumar Yadav was one of the few thousand Nepali fans who were on a mission to provide vociferous support to their cricket team this weekend.
Yadav arrived at the stadium with seven Nepali friends, who had been planning to come as soon as the tournament’s fixtures were announced.
“This is our first time watching Nepal play outside our country,” Yadav told Al Jazeera.
For Nepal’s sizeable diaspora in Qatar, the cricket team provides a reason to gather around a national passion and often draws large crowds.
The supporters are happy to travel to stadiums to back a team that has risen through the international ranks over the past decade.
Nepal’s modern cricketing journey can be traced back to 1996, when the country became a member of the International Cricket Council (ICC) and the men’s team first competed in an international tournament.
The turning point came when the South Asian nation qualified for its first ICC event at the T20 World Cup 2014.
Soon, Nepal’s players were being noticed on the international stage and leg-spinner Sandeep Lamichhane’s selection in major T20 leagues around the world raised the country’s cricketing profile.
Back home, cricket has spread far beyond the capital Kathmandu into towns and villages, backed by efforts to build the sport’s structure at grassroots level.
‘A passionate people’
For Qatar-based fan Himmat Joshi, the Nepali cricket team’s success has resulted in a sharp rise in the popularity of the sport.
“I feel a lot of happiness,” Joshi said while watching the team play against India. “In the past, fewer people followed it but it has grown over the years,” he said.
Mohammad Zahoor, who was among the thousands in the stands, sees the national team’s progress as a source of pride. He describes the Nepalis as a hardworking nation and says the country is building a domestic cricket system capable of competing with higher-ranked international teams.
“There is a lot of pride in seeing Nepali cricketers represent the country. We are a passionate people,” Zahoor said.
The ambitions extend beyond the T20 format.
Nepal’s supporters want to see the country compete against established cricketing nations and eventually earn a place among the teams playing Test cricket.
For Zahoor, defeating a Test-playing country would be an important step towards that ambition.
He also hopes cricket will become part of Nepal’s international identity, alongside its reputation for mountaineering, the Himalayas and being home to Mount Everest.
“Nepalis play the game like a festival,” Zahoor explained.
“Our expectations and hopes are that one day Nepali people are known for their cricket as they are known for their culture of mountaineering and Mount Everest.”
At the stadium in Qatar, the flags, chants and sheer number of supporters reflected that ambition.
In the end, India broke their hearts with a crushing 306-run win.
But it mattered little to the thousands cheering on their team, despite the loss.
For some, including Yadav and his friends, it offered a unique opportunity to watch Nepal play abroad.
Others were simply happy to get a chance to follow a team that has given the country, and its passionate supporters, a growing presence in international cricket.

noticias.titulo: Palestinian anti-Hamas groups accused of role in Israel Gaza operation
noticias.resumen: Israeli-backed Palestinian militias accused of expanding operations, raising concerns over their role in Gaza’s security
noticias.texto:
Palestinian anti-Hamas groups accused of role in Israel Gaza operation
Israeli-backed Palestinian militias accused of expanding operations, raising concerns over their role in Gaza’s future security arrangements.
Nuseirat refugee camp, Gaza Strip – It was late on Tuesday evening when a group of armed men stopped outside a house sheltering displaced Palestinian women on ad-Dawa Street, on the northern edge of the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza.
The streets were gradually emptying, and drones could be heard overhead. The men wore no military uniforms or insignia. They were Palestinians in civilian clothes carrying light weapons, believed to be members of Israeli-backed local militias, locals said.
The gunmen surrounded the house and forced the women into the street and questioned them by torchlight about a man they were looking for. They threatened those who refused to answer and fired into the air before withdrawing minutes later without detaining anyone.
Hours later, on Wednesday, the Israeli military launched a ground operation near the Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camps, west of the so-called “Yellow Line” that demarcates areas under Israeli military control following the October 2025 ceasefire.
The military closed Salah al-Din Street, Gaza’s main north-south thoroughfare. About 6,000 Palestinians fled, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office.
Israel said the operation targeted a tunnel that posed a threat to its troops. On Thursday, the military said that the operation had been completed. At least one Palestinian was killed in Israeli attacks near where the incursion took place.
The sequence of events raises questions about the extent of coordination between Israeli forces and Palestinian armed groups, whose activities have expanded across Gaza in recent weeks.
‘Engineering chaos’
A Palestinian security source in Gaza told Al Jazeera that security authorities had documented the local armed groups’ participation in this week’s Israeli military operation in central Gaza.
Their activities included “terrorising civilians and pressuring families to evacuate homes and shelters”, the source said.
Speaking on condition of anonymity, the source said the groups benefitted from Israeli military fire cover and the closure of Salah al-Din Street, which also impeded humanitarian operations.
The source described them as “gangs”, financed and armed by Israel to undermine Palestinian internal cohesion by “engineering chaos”.
Israel has publicly acknowledged supporting armed groups opposed to Hamas in Gaza, as it fought its genocidal war on the Palestinian enclave, killing more than 74,000 people. “What’s wrong with that?” asked Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu last year, claiming that the policy had saved the lives of Israeli soldiers.
Expanding military and intelligence roles
Palestinian political analyst Iyad al-Qarra told Al Jazeera that Israel had expanded the armed groups’ reach from Rafah and Khan Younis in the south to central Gaza and Gaza City.
He accused the groups of carrying out kidnappings and attempted assassinations targeting Palestinians, including members of Palestinian factions, in which they benefitted from Israeli aerial protection and fire cover.
Al-Qarra linked their expanding activities to Israel’s demolition of buildings and forced displacement of Palestinians, which have enabled the groups to operate in areas that Israeli forces would otherwise struggle to access.
He said the Israeli military uses the fighters in front-line operations before committing its own troops.
The groups also gather intelligence through local social and family networks while receiving information from the Israeli military, al-Qarra said.
Who are the Israeli-backed anti-Hamas groups?
The groups emerged during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, with some accused of looting aid supplies before taking on broader roles through Israeli funding, weapons and coordination with the military and intelligence services.
Published estimates point to about five main groups with several hundred members in total. In April, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) monitor reported that Israel had increased its support for them, including deploying attack drones during their clashes with Hamas.
The groups include the Popular Forces in Rafah, led by Ghassan al-Duhaini, since founder Yasser Abu Shabab was killed in December 2025; Hussam al-Astal’s group east of Khan Younis; and Shawqi Abu Nuseira’s group in central Gaza.
Two others, led by Rami Helles and Ashraf al-Mansi, operate in eastern Gaza City and northern Gaza, respectively.
A permanent security presence?
Palestinian political analyst Wesam Afifa told Al Jazeera that Israel seeks to establish local security influence that it could retain even after a partial military withdrawal.
He cited Israel’s historical support for the South Lebanon Army before its withdrawal from Lebanon in 2000, and more limited forms of collaboration during the first and second Palestinian Intifadas.
What distinguishes the situation in Gaza, Afifa said, is the groups’ transition from limited support roles to conducting armed operations outside areas under direct Israeli military control.
He pointed to their involvement in searching and obstructing travellers returning through the Rafah border crossing, which he said contradicted existing agreements and the role of the European Union monitoring mission.
In February, the United Nations Human Rights Office documented accounts from Palestinian returnees alleging intimidation, searches and theft by armed Palestinians purportedly backed by Israel.
Afifa warned that the groups’ continued presence could extend Israeli security influence beyond a military withdrawal, raising the possibility that Israel could push for their inclusion in Gaza’s future security arrangements.

noticias.titulo: Indian man sentenced to 19 years in US Sikh separatist assassination plot
noticias.resumen: Nikhil Gupta jailed for conspiring to hire a hitman to kill New York-based Sikh leader, Gurpatwant Singh Pannun.
noticias.texto:
Indian man sentenced to 19 years in US Sikh separatist assassination plot
Nikhil Gupta jailed for conspiring to hire a hitman to kill New York-based Sikh leader, Gurpatwant Singh Pannun.
An Indian national has been sentenced to more than 19-and-a-half years in prison in the United States in a murder-for-hire plot targeting a prominent Sikh separatist leader living in New York City.
Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to three conspiracy charges for plotting to hire a hitman to assassinate Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a US citizen, lawyer and vocal advocate for a sovereign Sikh state.
US District Judge Victor Marrero handed down the 235-month sentence at a federal court in Manhattan on Friday. Gupta faces deportation to India after completing his prison term.
Addressing the court on Friday, Gupta said he regretted straying from the nonviolent example set by Indian independence leader Mahatma Gandhi. “I’m sorry to Mr Pannun, I’m sorry to the communities I hurt, I’m sorry to my own family,” he said.
Prosecutors accused Gupta of conspiring with an Indian government official to kill Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer for the US-based separatist group Sikhs for Justice, in New York. Pannun is also a proponent of independence for Punjab, the northern Indian state where Sikhism was founded.
Court documents showed that Gupta and the Indian government official, Vikash Yadav, arranged to have $15,000 in cash delivered to someone who could kill Pannun. But the person turned out to be an undercover law enforcement officer posing as a hitman.
Gupta was arrested in Prague and has been held without bail since his extradition to the US in June 2023. A plea agreement called for him to serve at least two decades in prison.
Yadav is also charged in the case but is not in US custody. It is unclear whether he has hired a defence lawyer.
India’s government has denied any involvement in the plot against Pannun, saying it was against government policy.
However, multiple alleged assassination plots against Sikh separatists have been uncovered in the US and Canada, testing relations with India. New Delhi denies involvement in the plots.
‘A foot soldier’
Prosecutors with the Manhattan US Attorney’s Office had recommended a sentence of about 24 years in prison for Gupta.
“This case cuts to the very core of American values,” prosecutor Ashley Nicolas said in court. “We don’t condone the use of violence to silence voices in this country, ever.”
Pannun was in court on Friday to see the sentence handed down. He described Gupta as “just a foot soldier acting at the behest” of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a Hindu nationalist who has opposed the independence movement.
Pannun said the Modi government wanted him dead “because I lead the campaign openly, defy threats and intimidation”.
Pannun also told the court he would keep advocating for Sikh sovereignty.
“Self-determination for my people and my homeland, Punjab, is my lifetime goal,” he said.

noticias.titulo: Belgrade mayor charged with assaulting opposition politician in Serbia
noticias.resumen: Prosecutors say Aleksandar Sapic caused serious facial injuries to a female councillor and seek a three-year sentence.
noticias.texto:
Belgrade mayor charged with assaulting opposition politician in Serbia
Prosecutors say Aleksandar Sapic caused serious facial injuries to a female councillor and seek a three-year sentence.
The mayor of Serbia’s capital city, Belgrade, has been charged with injuring a female opposition politician during an argument they had in September.
Serbian prosecutors charged Aleksandar Sapic, a senior figure in the right-wing nationalist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), on Friday. He is accused of grabbing Belgrade city councillor Tatjana Micic by the arm and punching her in the face.
Prosecutors said Micic suffered fractures to her nose and part of her upper jaw, and injuries to her right arm and neck, which the prosecutors said constituted grievous bodily harm.
“Within less than two months of the incident, the Prosecutor’s Office examined witnesses, reviewed video surveillance footage, obtained medical records as well as the findings and opinion of a forensic expert, and filed an indictment proposal,” prosecutors said in a statement.
“In protecting the physical integrity and safety of citizens, the Prosecutor’s Office applies the same criteria to every defendant, regardless of the position they hold,” it added.
They are seeking a three-year sentence for Belgrade mayor Sapic, and are seeking to block him from approaching and communicating with councillor Micic.
Sapic denied attacking Micic, but acknowledged an argument and a scuffle with her husband. Opposition parties have demanded Sapic resign from his role, but he has resisted their calls. Sapic’s SNS party, which had headed up the government since 2012, lost an election to a student-led opposition movement in October.
The party, however, retains control of the capital, Belgrade.

noticias.titulo: What are the implications of the ICJ Rohingya genocide ruling?
noticias.resumen: Verdict against Myanmar may have implications for Israel's genocide in Gaza.
noticias.texto:
Inside Story
What are the implications of the ICJ Rohingya genocide ruling?
Ruling against Myanmar may have implications for Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Muslim Rohingya minority.
Thousands of people were killed in a 2017 crackdown that forced nearly one million Rohingya to flee to Bangladesh.
So, how significant is this ruling? And are there implications for Israel’s genocide in Gaza?
Presenter: James Bays
Guests:
Lucky Karim – Rohingya refugee, author and founder of Refugee Women for Peace and Justice (RWPJ)
Simon Adams – Professor of Human Rights at Murdoch University in Australia and former Executive Director of the Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect
Michael Becker – Assistant Professor of International Human Rights Law at Trinity College Dublin, who previously worked at the ICJ

noticias.titulo: Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge as Putin ally declares ‘no one needs Europe’
noticias.resumen: Russia-Europe tensions rise as Ukraine uses its own weapons and communications tech to hit the Kerch Bridge.
noticias.texto:
Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge as Putin ally declares ‘no one needs Europe’
Russia-Europe tensions rise as Ukraine uses its own weapons and communications tech to hit the Kerch Bridge.
Ukraine’s fourth and most complex operation on the Kerch Bridge brought down its road section and may have crippled its rail section over three days of strikes, taking a crucial Russian supply route into Crimea off the map.
“The short supply route from Russian territory has been destroyed,” declared Ukraine’s General Staff.
“Once again, the myth of Russia’s greatness has been shaken,” said Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), which took part in the operation.
It was part of a wider set of strikes against oil facilities and supply routes in the Rostov and Krasnodar Krai regions abutting Ukraine – an apparent strategy to asphyxiate Russian forces in southern Ukraine.
“The alternative route is overland, along the front line, where our drones are waiting for the cargo,” said the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence.
For a month, Ukraine’s military said it “systematically destroyed enemy air defence systems, radars, and electronic warfare equipment along the way to the target.”
On November 16, Ukrainian drones damaged the bridge’s road surface and compromised its steel arched span that allows shipping between the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea.
On November 17, the SBU said it used “Palyanytsia kamikaze drones to target the roadway section of the Crimean Bridge, causing it to collapse.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Neptune and Flamingo missiles and Ruta drones struck the separate railway span.
During this 48-hour period, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said it intercepted 4,305 Ukrainian drones compared with a daily average of 882 during the previous week.
On November 18-19, Ukraine again used Neptune missiles to strike the railway span, saying rail service had been suspended. It was unclear whether those strikes had permanently disabled the rail bridge.
Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed the operation as a strike against “a purely civilian facility … We haven’t even transported oil or petroleum products across the bridge.”
Ukraine’s General Staff disagreed, saying it had targeted the Kerch Bridge because it “was a vital artery, supplying fuel, ammunition, equipment, and personnel”.
The Ukrainian Defence Ministry called the bridge “a war machine”.
On the same day as the main strike on the Kerch Bridge, Ukraine also struck Russia’s main overland route to its southern forces, the M-14 Rostov-Crimea highway.
In addition, Kyiv also struck a series of refineries and oil depots in southwestern Russia that are nearest to the front, including in Azov, Ilsky and Afipsky.
“Fuel from such depots has a short route to the front,” it said.
Ukraine has already put Russia’s Black Sea and Azov Sea fleet of oil and fuel carriers out of action, striking at least 300 ships between July and September, leaving fuel supply dependent on road and rail transport.
Southern Ukraine is where Russian offensive efforts are now most active.
Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, has said Russian casualties are heaviest near Dobropillya and Huliaipole in Zaporizhia. Ukraine’s General Staff has also confirmed this is where the highest number of assaults takes place.
Defying two superpowers
Ukraine made a point of saying its Kerch operation was entirely autonomous.
“The strike was carried out exclusively with Ukrainian weapons – our technology, our solutions,” said Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhen Khmara.
This also meant that Ukraine did not rely on the US-controlled Starlink and Starshield satellite systems, on which it depends for short-range drone navigation. On November 6, those services began to cut out when drones exceed 160km/h (100mph). They were later restored, but Zelenskyy said they were again compromised beginning on November 13.
For the Kerch Bridge operation, Ukraine instead designed a system of drones that acted as signal repeaters. Video released by Ukraine showed an FP-5 missile relaying video up to the moment of impact, indicating that operators had control of it.
During the past week, Ukraine also targeted Russian refineries as far-flung as Volgograd and Samara, Salavat and Tatarstan, in an ongoing strategy to deprive Russia’s war machine of export revenue and diesel.
Almost half of the output of the Volgograd refinery is diesel, Ukraine said – a blow not only to Russia’s military, which consumes the fuel, but also to its promise to export 1.7 million tonnes of diesel this year as part of a deal struck with US President Donald Trump to lower fuel prices.
US negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have reportedly threatened Ukraine with an intelligence cutoff if it continues to strike Russian refineries.
As Ukraine defied them, Putin and Trump took to the global stage as the guests of Chinese leader Xi Jinping in the city of Shenzhen on November 19.
It was the first time Putin and Trump had met since their summit in Alaska in August 2025, and the first time all three men had met.
Kremlin-aligned media made much of the event, picking up Putin’s comparison with the Big Three conference in Yalta at the end of the second world war.
“The world’s three most consequential powers – have met. As the Big Three, they have emerged as the principal force in shaping a new architecture for international and European security,” wrote Putin’s deputy on the National Security Council, Dmitry Medvedev. “Today … no-one needs Europe.”
Asked whether peace in Ukraine was any closer as a result of the summit, Putin said he and Trump were still aligned on the proposals they discussed in Alaska. Those involved Ukraine handing over to Russia the one-fifth of the eastern Donbas region it cannot take by force, and to agree not to join NATO.
In the recent negotiations at Abu Dhabi on November 10-11, Ukraine was reportedly offered a green light to join NATO in return for the Donbas.
At those talks, Russia also turned its emphasis on Europe’s future security architecture.
Putin developed this further in Shenzhen, reported The New York Times and Bild magazine. He apparently offered Kremlin approval of Ukraine’s EU membership as long as Ukraine did not become part of EU defence policy, and as long as the United Kingdom and France refrained from offering a pan-European nuclear deterrent.
It would be “strange to discuss Europe’s security without Europe itself,” Putin said. On Ukraine’s however, he appeared to demand Europe sign onto whatever the US and Russia agreed.
Despite US and Russian attempts to appear to rearrange the world order, Europe did not appear to be listening.
During the past week, it provided Ukraine with a tranche of 1.7 billion euros ($1.97bn) from a 90 billion euros ($104.4bn) Ukraine Support Loan agreed in 2025, and another 8 billion euros ($9.28bn) from the Ukraine Facility, a 50 billion euros ($58bn) fund focused on Ukrainian economic recovery and financial support.
In addition to these two facilities, the EU agreed this week to raise 45 billion euros ($52.2bn), covering most of a 70-billion-euro ($81.2bn) shortfall that Ukraine says it will face next year. Of that amount, 25 billion euros ($29bn) will be for additional military assistance.
In addition to being a staunch supporter of Ukraine, however, Europe continued to be a divided supporter, deciding that its top diplomat should not represent it in talks with Russia and Ukraine, but representatives from its five biggest economies instead.
Kaja Kallas has argued that “all the member states actually agreed that I am the one who is representing Europe in foreign and security policy” when they appointed her to the job of chief of the External Action Service.
“We have institutions in place so we can’t just send any person that has no institutional role like the Americans are sending,” she said this week, in a clear reference to Witkoff and Kushner. “Clearly, we should not copy the same patterns.”

noticias.titulo: Zohran Mamdani unveils plan to close New York’s Rikers Island jail by 2032
noticias.resumen: The plan would replace the jail complex with four smaller jails and reduce the number of people behind bars.
noticias.texto:
Zohran Mamdani unveils plan to close New York’s Rikers Island jail by 2032
The plan would replace the jail complex with four smaller jails and reduce the number of people behind bars.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has unveiled a plan to close the notorious Rikers Island jail complex by 2032, setting out how his administration hopes to shut down a facility long criticised for violence, overcrowding and poor sanitation.
The plan, released on Friday, proposes closing the jail five years after a deadline of August 2027 that was set under then-Mayor Bill de Blasio.
With less than a year to go, the four smaller jails in four New York boroughs that are meant to replace Rikers are still under construction.
The jail complex mostly holds people awaiting trial rather than serving sentences after conviction.
“For decades, New Yorkers have demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane,” said Mamdani in a statement.
“We have a legal and moral obligation to close Rikers,” he said.
How does Mamdani plan to close Rikers Island?
The mayor’s strategy involves reducing the number of people held at Rikers from 6,700 to no more than 4,100 by expanding alternatives to detention, restoring online bail payments, investing in programmes that aim to reduce repeat offending, and shortening court delays.
Court delays can leave people “detained for years in what is essentially legal purgatory”, said Mamdani at a news conference on Friday. The city plans to set up a task force to deal with bottlenecks and improve how agencies share evidence.
Under the new timeline, the first replacement jail will open in Brooklyn in 2029, with the rest completed by 2032. The city plans to also make hospital beds available for people in custody who have serious mental health or medical needs.
“Any family member of someone held at Rikers will tell you how isolating that jail is, how it can take hours to visit a loved one,” Mamdani said, adding that the new jails would be closer to courts and public transport, and would help integrate imprisoned New Yorkers back into the city.
Why is Rikers Island notorious?
Rikers Island, near LaGuardia airport in New York’s East River, opened in 1932 and has long faced criticism over violence, abuse, and unsanitary conditions, with campaigners pushing for its closure for over a decade.
The facility has been tied to cases like that of Kalief Browder, who spent three years there awaiting trial before the charges against him were dismissed. He died by suicide in 2015 aged 22, two years after his release.
City lawmakers voted to close Rikers in 2019, and Mamdani has blamed the city’s inability to meet the 2027 deadline to build the replacement jails on the previous administration.
Once the jail closes, Mamdani said he wants the island to be used for renewable energy and projects to help the city withstand the effects of climate change.
“Our hope is that the new Rikers Island will be unrecognisable,” he said.

noticias.titulo: US tech sell-off continues as Anthropic tumbles after mega IPO
noticias.resumen: Anthropic's listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain its footing.
noticias.texto:
US tech sell-off continues as Anthropic tumbles after mega IPO
Anthropic’s listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain its footing but that was not the case on Friday.
Anthropic’s much-hyped arrival on Wall Street has fizzled out a day later, as a dramatic unravelling of the artificial intelligence trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector.
On Friday, the stock, the biggest public stock offering ever and which surpassed $2 trillion in value at one point, was trading at $87.95, about 9.5 percent down from Thursday’s close, at about 11:30am in New York (16:30 GMT).
Widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, Anthropic’s listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain its footing after a turbulent stretch. But the slump in price within a day of listing – though still higher than its offer price of $83.30 – while losses across other technology heavyweights suggested the IPO had done little to reverse the broader selloff.
“Investors still believe in AI but are becoming more selective about what they will pay for that growth,” said David Miller, chief investment officer at Catalyst Funds.
Among the Magnificent Seven stocks, Nvidia was down nearly 7 percent, Meta Platforms fell almost 4 percent, while Amazon and Microsoft dropped 2.1 percent and 1.7 percent, respectively.
Chip stocks also slid, with AMD down 11.2 percent, Sandisk down nearly 15 percent and Intel losing 4.3 percent.
More stocks were gaining ground within the S&P 500, but AI stocks with hefty market values have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.
AI stocks have been losing ground partly over worries that their big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also run up against the recent midterm elections, where there has been a shift in power after the Republican Party, seen as more friendly to the industry, suffered an electoral sweep.
Anthropic’s stock could find support later in the year; London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could account for purchases of up to 30 percent of Anthropic’s shares by year-end.
Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for the biggest IPO, rose nearly 50 percent in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later. On Friday, the stock was down about 7.4 percent.

noticias.titulo: Protests held across Europe over wages, services, high living costs
noticias.resumen: Workers and students take to the streets as protests inspired by demonstrations in France show no sign of abating.
noticias.texto:
Protests held across Europe over wages, services, high living costs
Workers and students take to the streets as protests inspired by demonstrations in France show no sign of abating.
Protesters have rallied across 25 European countries amid a wave of public discontent over issues ranging from high living costs to military spending and the climate crisis, ramping up pressure on political leaders they accuse of ignoring the concerns of young people.
Inspired by demonstrations that have shaken France in recent months, thousands took to the streets in countries including the United Kingdom, Austria, Germany, Spain, Italy, Sweden and Croatia on Friday.
Tens of thousands of workers and students protested in more than 100 Italian cities to demand higher wages and greater investment in public services.
The rallies coincided with a general strike by Italy’s largest trade union, CGIL, that involved workers in both the private and public sectors, including schools and healthcare.
“Across Europe and among ordinary people, the demand for change is growing,” CGIL leader Maurizio Landini said at a rally in Rome.
Demonstrators in Rome threw objects at the Ministry of Education, while in Bologna some protesters clashed with police, news agency ANSA reported. In Milan, demonstrators set fire to a cardboard tanker as well as cardboard figures depicting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and United States President Donald Trump.
The Italian rallies followed a nationwide mobilisation on October 17 that descended into rioting and looting and prompted the right-wing government of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to approve sweeping security measures and deploy the army alongside police in subsequent demonstrations.
Student groups have since continued protests and occupations at schools and universities, with opposition to higher military spending also emerging as a rallying cry.
Opposition leaders joining demonstrations on Friday criticised Meloni’s government and its budget policies amid rising living costs. Elly Schlein, leader of the centre-left Democratic Party, said the 2027 Budget Law “does not have a vision for the future of the country” as it does not help industries but slashes funding for public healthcare and education.
Meanwhile, in Germany, campaign group “Gen Z regelt” (German for “Gen Z sorts it”) said it was organising protests in 73 cities and towns.
In Berlin, roughly 4,000 people attended a protest in the city’s Alexanderplatz square.
The Cologne protest drew fewer than the 5,000 people expected, though demonstrators still numbered in the thousands, police said.
Protesters gathered to call for greater education funding and to oppose a possible return to compulsory military service.
In Austria, several hundred people gathered outside the University of Vienna for a youth-led protest calling for more spending on education and less on weapons. Police dispersed the event after reported disturbances, saying officers used pepper spray and made several arrests.
In Croatia, students boycotted classes and staged protests in about a dozen cities, demanding greater investment in education, housing and public services rather than military spending.
Demonstrations across Europe were inspired by much larger protests in France that began in September and descended into violent confrontations with the police and looting.
On Tuesday, France’s Interior Ministry said a total of 146,000 people took part in protests across the country, with 28,000 in Paris alone. The CGT trade union put the nationwide total at just over 500,000 demonstrators.
The prices paid for everyday items such as food, energy, transport and bills have risen by between 59 and 78 percent since 2000 in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal, according to Eurostat – the European Union’s statistics agency.
Once inflation is taken into account, the average full-time wage in Italy fell by almost 5 percent between 2000 and 2025. Over the same period, real wages rose by 7 percent in Spain, 11 percent in France and 20 percent in Portugal, according to OECD wage data adjusted with Eurostat’s price index.

noticias.titulo: Top US Democrat warns Trump admin against destroying records
noticias.resumen: In a new letter, Congressman Jamie Raskin says officials in the US government are ignoring federal recordkeeping laws.
noticias.texto:
Top US Democrat warns Trump admin against destroying records
In a new letter, Congressman Jamie Raskin says officials in the US government are ignoring federal recordkeeping laws.
A top Democrat, who will wield significant investigative powers in the United States Congress starting in January, has warned US law enforcement agencies to preserve records, including encrypted communications on digital messaging apps.
In letters sent on Thursday to the US Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Congressman Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the next likely chairman of the US House Judiciary Committee, wrote to the cabinet-level agencies to remind their employees of a legal obligation to “safeguard” records against destruction.
Letters were also sent to the heads of three subagencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Bureau of Prisons (BOP).
Raskin disclosed he has obtained evidence that government officials in the Trump administration have been using non-government apps, like Signal, to send disappearing messages.
The Maryland Democrat, who is currently the Judiciary Committee’s ranking member, appended a screenshot of a Signal exchange between FBI General Counsel Samuel Ramer and Drew Lynch, an associate of President Donald Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, showing a conversation where messages were set to automatically delete after one week.
“The FBI’s top lawyer should be ensuring that all 35,000 FBI employees are preserving government and law enforcement records”, Raskin wrote to US Attorney General Todd Blanche.
“Instead, he has conducted official business on a platform specifically configured to erase communications.”
The incident, Raskin wrote, is “just one of many” that have been reported to the Judiciary Committee, raising concern among Democrats that the Trump administration could be ignoring federal recordkeeping laws by destroying documents before likely congressional investigations.
“There is significant evidence that Trump Administration officials have engaged in the widespread destruction, mutilation, and concealment of government records”, Raskin wrote. “This attempt to evade transparency extends to the highest levels of federal agencies, including top-ranking law enforcement officials”.
Raskin instructed the federal officials to take “immediate action to recover these records” from data backups or “associated metadata,” asking them to comply by December 3.
The Trump administration has signalled it intends to fight any probes by US Democrats, who won control of both chambers of the US Congress earlier this month in the country’s midterm elections.
According to a letter viewed by Al Jazeera, the White House’s top lawyer, Will Scharf, wrote to US House Democrats on Wednesday, pushing back against demands from the incoming Democratic majorities, such as Raskin’s, because the new Congress has not yet been sworn in.
“Your demands do not reflect a request of the House, Senate, or a committee to which that body’s oversight authority has been delegated,” Scharf wrote. “As a result, Ranking Member requests in the 119th Congress do not trigger any obligation to ‘accommodate[e] … the needs of the conflicting branches'”.
In response to Raskin’s letter, a White House official told Al Jazeera the administration complies “with all federal record retention laws and regulations”.
The DOJ echoed the White House’s response, saying it “follows all legal requirements for the management of federal records involving its official functions and decisions.”
“The men and women of the DOJ who work tirelessly to arrest and prosecute criminals will not be intimidated by a congressman who once called 2020 riots ‘magnificent’ and ‘nonviolent'”, the agency said about Raskin.
Al Jazeera also reached out to DHS, FBI, ICE and BOP for comment but has not yet heard back.

noticias.titulo: UK far-right activist ‘Danny Tommo’ jailed for slashing migrant boat
noticias.resumen: Daniel Thomas livestreamed himself slashing a dinghy used to bring migrants from France to the UK.
noticias.texto:
UK far-right activist ‘Danny Tommo’ jailed for slashing migrant boat
Daniel Thomas livestreamed himself slashing a dinghy used to bring migrants from France to the UK.
A British far-right anti-immigration activist has been jailed for 15 months for criminal damage for slashing a small boat which had brought migrants from France to the United Kingdom.
Daniel Thomas, also known as “Danny Tommo”, is the founder of the British anti-migrant Patriot Platform group, which mobilised hundreds of protesters earlier this year. He pleaded guilty to criminal damage earlier this month, after slashing the inflatable vessel while a French emergency responder was on board.
Sentencing Thomas on Friday, judge James Newton-Price said the offence “amounted to flagrant interference and a deliberate disruption” of French and British authorities’ important activities in the English Channel.
“They do necessary, highly sensitive and difficult jobs, and which should not be disrupted by a publicity-seeker slashing with a knife a boat they were attempting to recover,” he added.
Thomas livestreamed himself on September 22 as he followed a small boat carrying migrants across the Channel, who were transferred onto another vessel and taken ashore.
The 37-year-old later approached the dinghy and slashed it with a knife, soon after a French rescue worker had stepped on board. British police arrested him shortly after the incident.
Prosecutor Joel Smith told Portsmouth Crown Court that Thomas had shouted “get off the boat, you’ve got time to get off the boat … take them back, no more of these”.
‘Thuggish’
Thomas appeared in court via videolink from prison, with his head bowed and rarely looked up as footage of the incident was played.
Judge Newton-Price accepted that “there was no immediate danger to the rescue worker”, but said Thomas’s actions were a deliberate attempt to disrupt rescue efforts.
The far-right activist had built a large online following and organised gatherings of protesters on the UK’s southern coast in response to the arrivals of small boats.
A government minister described the demonstrations as “thuggish”.
The court heard that Thomas had five previous convictions, including in 2016 for kidnapping.
Separately, he is set to stand trial in London next June accused of multiple offences, including entering a restricted zone at a migrant processing centre in Dover in March.
UK government data shows the number of people arriving in small boats to British shores has fallen, though the crossings remain a prominent political issue which has dogged successive governments. Right-wing opposition parties and anti-immigration activists have called for more action.

noticias.titulo: 10 years after divisive Brexit referendum, UK weighs a ‘Breturn’ to the EU
noticias.resumen: Prime Minister Andy Burnham returns from the UK-EU summit with a potential new deal and a new start.
noticias.texto:
10 years after divisive Brexit referendum, UK weighs a ‘Breturn’ to the EU
Prime Minister Andy Burnham returns from the UK-EU summit with a potential new deal and a new start.
A decade after the narrow vote to leave the EU, the United Kingdom is showing every sign of buyer’s remorse.
For many, the bitterly fought contest over the referendum on whether to leave the EU was unpleasant and divisive.
Couples and families reportedly split over where they stood on the referendum. Each side of the debate – Leave and Remain – became a cipher for how people saw themselves and their country in a changing world.
As the campaign unfolded amid accusations of foreign influence and dirty tricks, the murder of a politician, a debate over economics and political sovereignty, a visceral fight intensified over identity, belonging and competing visions of what it meant to be British.
Critics and pro-Brexit slammed various exit deals that successive governments negotiated with Brussels as somehow a betrayal of what had originally been a binary choice.
The EU, the trading bloc the UK sat uneasily within for nearly half a century, remains the country’s biggest trading partner.
On Friday, in a joint news conference with Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, following the latest UK-EU summit in Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham hailed the first in a series of expected deals with the EU as rebuilding “the bridges that were broken all those years ago”.
The agreements, which cover three main areas – easing trade restrictions, expanding opportunities for young people to live and work across borders, and addressing carbon levies – were characterised by Burnham as “a good deal for Britain” and regarded as first steps towards bringing the UK back into the EU’s orbit.
Does the UK want to rejoin?
Some in the UK believe that leaving the single market and customs union brought little tangible benefit while creating additional paperwork, border checks and barriers to trade with the UK’s largest export market. Others have no regrets about leaving the bloc.
According to polling expert Sir John Curtice, surveys show an average of 62 percent favour rejoining, against 38 percent for staying out, once undecided respondents are excluded.
“Whatever the nuances, the UK public are certainly in a different place on the EU than [they were] in 2016,” he told Al Jazeera.
Could the UK Breturn?
According to some analysts, the government – which is not bound by a single written constitution – could, with the EU’s agreement, begin the process of rejoining without holding another referendum, or even including the commitment in an election manifesto.
However, doing so would inevitably be politically difficult and, according to Professor Curtice, almost certain to be highly unpopular.
“The Brexit referendum in 2016 was not legally binding,” Sionaidh Douglas-Scott, the chair in Law at Queen Mary University of London, wrote by email. “Legally, it could have been ignored altogether. But it was thought to be politically unacceptable to ignore the public’s vote in the referendum. And political parties can ignore their election manifesto pledges at their peril,” she said, referring to parties’ reliance on public trust to support any agenda.
“I suspect Burnham might be tempted to have a referendum on the issue of rejoining the EU, feeling that public opinion had changed sufficiently to render a rejoin vote likely, although that’s by no means certain,” she said. “Some senior members of the [governing Labour] party … clearly feel that rejoining should be a manifesto pledge. So, politically, steps might be taken to make it more acceptable.”
Meanwhile, questions remained over the terms on which the UK might rejoin the bloc, whether it would be required to adopt the euro – a prospect it had previously resisted – and what form the EU itself might take following elections in some of its most influential member states, including France, Germany and Spain.
Polling suggests a distinction between support for closer relations with the EU as opposed to support for full membership.
While some surveys put support for rejoining at about 35 percent when closer ties were offered as an alternative, Curtice said support for closer relations was often less firmly held.
“Much of that support is soft – people say they somewhat support rather than strongly support” closer ties, he explained. By contrast, around half of those supporting rejoining the EU say they “strongly support” it, suggesting a deeper commitment to that option.
Similarly, at home, many of the more prominent figures of the original campaign to leave Europe have resurfaced and appear to be marshalling their forces against any return or realignment.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, one of Brexit’s most prominent campaigners, returned to Brussels on Thursday to oppose the prime minister’s efforts.
Other figures associated with the Leave campaign have also re-emerged, including former Prime Minister Boris Johnson and his former cabinet ally, Michael Gove, now a magazine editor. They have revived loosely sourced claims about the financial cost of rejoining the EU – or even of having remained a member. The campaign group Stay Out, for instance, puts the annual cost at 39.3 billion pounds (approximately $51.4bn), equivalent to 750 million pounds (about $982m) a week.
“I think we should think about two things when we think about Brexit and the potential to rejoin: trauma and salience,” Anand Menon, professor at King’s College London and director of UK in a Changing Europe, said. “Some people felt traumatised by the first debate and don’t want to revisit it. At the same time, the issue has lost its salience. The public don’t consider it one of the main issues facing the country,” he said.
“If you cast your mind back to 2016, those supporting Leave, like Nigel Farage, took the EU, which the public never really thought about, and linked it in the public’s mind to something they absolutely did: immigration.
“If Burnham is going to try to get the sort of energy he’ll need to see the process through, he’s going to need to do something similar, though what, I don’t know.”

noticias.titulo: Qatar and Germany deepen strategic ties during emir’s Berlin visit
noticias.resumen: German chancellor says Qatar pledged $16.5bn in new investments as the two countries deepen defence and technology ties.
noticias.texto:
Qatar and Germany deepen strategic ties during emir’s Berlin visit
German chancellor says Qatar pledged $16.5bn in new investments as the two countries deepen defence and technology ties.
Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani has held talks with German leaders in Berlin on expanding defence and diplomatic cooperation, broadening a relationship long focused on trade and investment.
At a joint news conference with the emir on Friday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Qatar had pledged an additional 15 billion euros ($16.5bn) in investment, while the two governments planned closer cooperation on security and technology.
Merz said the investment would strengthen cooperation in artificial intelligence (AI), computer chips and aviation. He also expressed Germany’s interest in developing defence industry partnerships with Qatar, while the two countries agreed to work together to improve protection against cyberattacks.
The discussions come as Qatar continues pushing for a diplomatic solution to end the US-Israel war on Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a major route for global oil and gas supplies.
Sheikh Tamim also held talks with German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, who proposed a regional security conference for the Middle East.
Their meeting on Friday covered efforts to end the Iran war and restore maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, according to a joint statement by both countries.
Steinmeier suggested bringing regional governments together to build trust and address security disputes.
The emir invited him to the Doha Forum, an international policy conference in Qatar on December 5–6, to discuss the proposal further with other countries.
At the emir’s news conference with Merz, the German leader acknowledged Qatar’s role in mediating between the US and Iran and called for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen permanently. He also urged Tehran to halt its military nuclear programme.
Sheikh Tamim stressed that “peace and sustainable peace and security can only be reached through a political agreement”, adding that dialogue is the only way forward. He also described Germany as an important partner.
Sheikha Alanoud bint Hamad Al Thani, a fellow at the Middle East Council for Global Affairs, a regional research institute, told Al Jazeera in Berlin that the relationship had previously been driven mainly by commerce.
“But now we’re seeing a strategic dialogue,” she said, pointing to increasingly similar security concerns, including drone attacks on Qatar and hybrid warfare threats facing European countries.
That shift builds on a 2023 agreement to establish formal strategic talks between the two countries. Sheikh Tamim told Steinmeier on Friday that Qatar wanted the first round to take place, according to Qatar’s state news agency, QNA.

noticias.titulo: US Senate passes bill to speed up energy project approvals
noticias.resumen: The legislation aims to lower energy bills by making energy project approvals faster and limiting court challenges.
noticias.texto:
US Senate passes bill to speed up energy project approvals
The legislation aims to lower energy bills by making energy project approvals faster and limiting court challenges.
The United States Senate has passed a bipartisan bill to speed up approvals for power plants, transmission lines and other energy projects as lawmakers face pressure to bring down electricity bills and meet growing demand fuelled by the growth of artificial intelligence.
The Senate voted 62-33 on Thursday as 15 Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, backed the bill and two Republicans voted against it.
President Donald Trump had urged senators to pass the measure and said he would sign the bill if it passes the House of Representatives.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would shorten timelines for federal reviews for energy projects and limit how approvals may be challenged in court.
It would change several environmental laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act, which requires federal agencies to weigh a project’s environmental effects and gives the public a chance to weigh in before a project is approved.
The four senators who coauthored the bill, two from each party, argued that Americans are tired of paying high utility bills while projects that could lower them are stuck in the planning phase.
“We are going to make it easier to build in America again and make life more affordable for American families,” Republican Senator Mike Lee of Utah said.
Lee negotiated the deal with fellow Republican Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Democratic Senators Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island.
The bill would also require large AI data centres to pay for more of the cost of upgrading power grids to serve their needs.
The vote came after rising electricity bills and opposition to data centres became major issues in the midterm elections this month. Democrats campaigned on promises to rein in the industry and swept to victory. They won control of both chambers of the new US Congress, which will convene on January 3. Until then, Republicans hold slim majorities in both chambers.
Industry groups representing both renewable energy developers and oil and gas companies backed the bill, saying current delays can stretch timelines by a decade or more.
Why did critics oppose it?
Environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and the National Wildlife Federation, warned that the bill would weaken protections for water and wildlife and make it harder for communities to challenge project approvals.
Other groups said it would lead to more fossil fuel development.
“Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centres, oil and gas pipelines and [liquefied natural gas] terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the US,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project.
She called it a “gift to some of the biggest polluters in America”, arguing that any gains in renewable energy would be outweighed by emissions and pollution from the fossil fuel industry.
Critics also took issue with how quickly the bill was moving, arguing that it was being rushed through Congress.
Democratic Senator Maria Cantwell from Washington state said after meeting with tribal leaders that it would undermine tribal nations’ sovereignty and weaken protections for their water, land and wildlife.
She called for more time to consider those concerns and amend the bill.
Some Democrats who opposed the bill also argued the party should wait until January to push through stronger legislation that limits fossil fuel development while doing more to expand wind and solar power.
The Senate passed the measure without adopting amendments pushed by Oregon’s two senators, including one that would ban data centres on public land and another that would prevent the Trump administration from cancelling energy grants and other Democratic initiatives for “purely political purposes”.

noticias.titulo: ‘Expel invaders’: The dangerous promises of Spain’s far-right Vox party
noticias.resumen: As Spain prepares to vote, Vox is campaigning on mass deportations and 'national priority'.
noticias.texto:
‘Expel invaders’: The dangerous promises of Spain’s far-right Vox party
Spain heads to a snap election on November 29 with Vox campaigning on mass deportations, ‘remigration’ and ‘national priority’.
Santiago Abascal, wearing a blue suit and tie, looks straight into the camera. His campaign poster makes three promises: giving Spanish nationals priority in access to benefits, cutting regulation and “remigration”.
“It’s common sense,” the poster of his far-right Vox party reads.
With little more than a week to go until Spain’s November 29 snap election, opinion polls put Vox in third place behind the conservative Popular Party (PP), which is leading the race, and the governing Socialist Party.
But with the Socialists’ potential allies fragmented and the PP projected to fall short of an outright majority, Vox could emerge as a kingmaker.
The party, which once struggled to win a single seat in parliament, could join a PP-led coalition or back a minority PP government from outside the cabinet.
What is Vox, and who founded it?
Abascal was a regional lawmaker for the PP in the Basque Country. He left the party in 2013, accusing then-Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy of being too soft on the issue of Catalan separatism. He went on to cofound Vox.
The new party positioned itself to the PP’s right, making Spanish unity its central cause. It called for an end to the country’s system of regional autonomy and championed the idea of the “true Spaniard”, who was Catholic, Castilian-speaking and loyal to the monarchy.
Over time, the party started to adopt themes and tactics from other European far-right parties.
“At the beginning, they were the ultra-conservatives of the right, but then they started to study the handbook of the populist radical right across Europe, and they became the Spanish version of it,” said Carles Ferreira, lecturer in politics at the University of Girona.
In January 2017, Abascal made his international debut at a gathering of Europe’s far right in the German city of Koblenz alongside France’s Marine Le Pen and Frauke Petry, then-leader of the Alternative for Germany. But Vox was still a minor force at home, having won 0.2 percent of the vote and no seats in the previous year’s general election.
How did Vox break through?
That October nine years ago, Catalonia held an independence referendum in defiance of Spain’s Constitutional Court. A few weeks later, the Parliament of Catalonia unilaterally declared independence, plunging the country into a constitutional crisis.
Vox, which had filed a legal complaint over the preparation for the vote, used the crisis to raise its national profile over its opposition to Catalan independence.
It worked. Just over a year later, the party made its electoral breakthrough, winning 12 seats in the regional parliament of Andalusia in southern Spain. Four months later, it entered the national parliament for the first time by winning 24 seats.
Vox had transformed from a fringe party with zero representation into a relevant political force.
What does Vox want?
The first bullet point in its manifesto calls for the “immediate expulsion of all invaders”.
Abascal has accused the Socialist government of Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of enabling what he calls “a migrant invasion” to “replace the Spanish people”.
“It may well be that the upcoming elections will be the last ones to be decided by the Spanish people,” Abascal said on Thursday on X.
He wants to ban the mass regularisation of undocumented immigrants and deport them.
His manifesto calls for “remigration”, a plan to facilitate the expulsion of people who the party says do not contribute or who rely on public benefits.
Throughout the eight-year tenure of the current government, the number of foreign-born residents in Spain rose from 6.3 million to 10.4 million, according to the National Statistics Institute.
Vox is also campaigning for “national priority”, a system that would create a two-tier society in which Spanish nationals would have better access to social benefits.
Its exclusionary discourse often focuses on Muslim migrants.
“With Catalan independence no longer dominating the political debate, Vox has shifted its focus to what it calls the ‘Islamisation of Spain’ and the threat of a ‘Spanish caliphate’,” said Steven Forti, professor of contemporary history at the Autonomous University of Barcelona. “By hammering away at the issue, the party has turned it into a rallying point for voters.”
Vox draws on the idea of Hispanidad, a shared Hispanic identity, to portray Latin American migrants as culturally closer to Spaniards.
Spain has long welcomed Spanish-speaking people from Latin America. They represent the largest group of undocumented and documented foreigners in Spain, according to the Spanish think tank Funcas.
Vox’s idea of an “Iberosphere”, Forti added, invokes traditional Catholic values and a shared language and culture rooted in Spain’s colonial past. In that telling, Latin American migrants are welcome because they are “the children of our colonisation”.
On social issues, the party is staunchly conservative. It opposes abortion. Its politicians have derided LGBTQ advocacy as the work of a “lobby”, and Vox rejects treating gender-based violence as a distinct legal category, arguing that domestic violence laws should apply regardless of the victim’s sex.
It was the only party to oppose renewing Spain’s cross-party pact against gender-based violence in 2025 and has called for suspending an agreement that specifically protects women from violence by current and former partners.
Yet this year’s party manifesto is less specific about what it wants to do, calling more broadly for replacing “gender ideology” laws and strengthening police and judicial protection for women facing violence.
Who votes for Vox and why?
Traditionally, its core electoral base has been young, white and male.
In the past three years, support for Vox has risen from 13 percent to about 20 percent. Its supporters remain predominantly male, but the party has gained ground among women and voters with secondary or vocational educations.
Support has grown particularly among people aged 35 to 44 and voters under 35, including some who were too young to vote in 2023. Vox has also drawn support from people who sat out the last election.
“This trend appears linked to the party’s ability to position itself as an antiestablishment force that channels institutional disaffection and social frustration,” said Paco Camas, head of public opinion in Spain for the polling firm Ipsos. “Its message has resonated particularly with younger men facing economic uncertainty and limited opportunities for social advancement.”
But it’s not just about the economy.
When asked about their main concerns, Vox supporters cite “the government and politicians” more often than any other issue and at more than twice the rate of voters overall, Camas said.
Immigration and concerns about border management and relations with Morocco also ranked high. Housing was among their main concerns although they cited it less often than voters overall. Economic issues and job quality also ranked lower among Vox supporters than among the wider electorate.
Vox is drawing voters away from the PP. Polls suggested 15 to 20 percent of people who voted for the PP in 2023 intend to back Vox this month due to its clearer and more uncompromising positions on immigration, national identity and security.
“Some voters on the right perceive the PP as more cautious, technocratic and closely aligned with the mainstream European consensus, making Vox a more attractive option for those seeking a sharper ideological alternative,” Camas said.
