noticias.titulo: Kansas hosts become guests as Algeria repays World Cup welcome
noticias.resumen: A bond between Kansas and Algeria has deepened since the city hosted the North Africans during the World Cup.
noticias.texto:
Kansas hosts become guests as Algeria repays World Cup welcome
A bond between the people of Kansas and Algerians has deepened since the city hosted the North Africans during the World Cup.
Algiers, Algeria – Tommee Sherwood never expected that Algeria would come to play such a big role in his life.
Until recently, the 70-year-old from Lawrence, Kansas – a retired university custodian, musician, and volunteer English teacher for refugees – had never been to North Africa before and knew Algeria mostly from the film The Battle of Algiers.
He was aware, though, that Algeria had given refuge to members of the Black Panther Party in the 1970s, including Pete O’Neal, chairman of the Kansas City chapter.
“That connection between Algerians and Kansas City goes way further than most people realise,” he told Al Jazeera.
Sherwood was among 38 residents of Lawrence who visited Algeria from November 9-15 at the government’s expense as a gesture of gratitude from President Abdelmadjid Tebboune for the way their small university city had welcomed the Algerian national team, which used Lawrence as their official base camp during the World Cup.
Five months on, the football was long over, but the genuine bond it had forged between two communities separated by 8,000km (5,000 miles) had only grown stronger.
On a boat in the Bay of Algiers on their first day in the country, a DJ was playing.
“He started playing some old jazz music,” Sherwood recalls in audio messages sent to Al Jazeera. “And he was playing some old timers – some old Kansas City guys that I used to know. It really touched me.”
He gave the DJ a small gift and took photographs. The next day, the same DJ was playing at a different event. He came over to Sherwood and handed him three vintage 45s – old recordings of Algerian singers.
“He told me one of them sang a song to the French. It’s called ‘We Stay, You Go’. I really loved that,” Sherwood said. “These records, if they were made of gold, they wouldn’t be any more valuable to me.”
Sherwood describes the encounters with the DJ as “an example” of the hospitality they were shown by everyone during their time in Algeria.
“I never imagined that the World Cup would open such possibilities for cultural exchange and communication and I’m kind of astounded by it,” Sherwood said.
Five months earlier, Lawrence had hosted Algeria’s national team and its fans with a warmth that touched Algerians. Storefronts on Massachusetts Street flew Algerian flags. The city screened every Algeria and United States match on large outdoor screens. The Kansas University (KU) band played the Algerian national anthem for the team before training.
Algeria was among the 50 countries whose visa applicants faced a $10,000 bond requirement for the tournament, which meant few people from Algeria could make the journey. But the Algerian community in the US, estimated at no more than 50,000 across the country, also came to Lawrence in large numbers.
Saajida Andalsi, an Algerian whose mother has lived in Kansas for more than 36 years, served as an informal bridge between the different communities during the World Cup.
Originally from Algeria, the 24-year-old had not been back for 15 years, but was part of the November delegation. Remembering how Lawrence transformed during the tournament, the 24-year-old said: “My mum kept saying: ‘I didn’t go to Algeria. Algeria came to me’. Lawrence was like a city in Algeria.”
In July, Tebboune ordered the establishment of a twinning agreement between the Algerian town of Tipaza and Kansas City and extended invitations to 100 visitors at the state’s expense.
For Ruth DuWitt, director of community engagement at Explore Lawrence, the city’s tourism bureau, the trip to Algeria deepened her knowledge about the country’s struggle for independence.
Standing in the Casbah of Algiers, she watched the KU band and an Algerian group take the stage together. The Algerian conductor raised his baton over the KU ensemble and directed them through The Star-Spangled Banner, before the KU director conducted Algeria’s national anthem.
“We are standing in that very place – the Casbah – about freedom and revolution and all that spirit,” DuWitt says. “I’m getting choked up just thinking about it.”
Andalsi watched the same scene.
“It showed that there wasn’t just connection behind soccer. It was also music. It was the similarities in us just as humans,” she said.
When both bands played together, the crowd was invited into the middle to dance. “It felt like a movie. Nobody could have imagined that happening.”
‘Everyone benefits’
Madjid Khettar, an Algerian who has lived in Kansas with his family for 13 years, did not make the November trip but has watched the after-effects of the World Cup reshape his daily life.
“Today, when I meet an American and tell him I’m Algerian, he immediately talks to me about the World Cup,” he says. “Even at the football pitch, if one of us is wearing the national team shirt, Americans come up and say they know we’re Algerian and they’re happy to meet us. That didn’t exist before.”
He describes how, when fires broke out in Algeria in August, Americans in Kansas asked how to send aid, and donated when collection links were shared. “That didn’t exist before either.”
Elizabeth Moore Aubin, who was US ambassador to Algeria from December 2021 until January 2026, was part of the Lawrence contingent during the tournament and joined the November delegation to Algiers. She visited more than 50 of Algeria’s 58 provinces or “wilayas” during her posting and built a significant online following.
“As two people groups, Americans and Algerians have more in common than they both realise,” she told Al Jazeera.
She added that it was “great to see subnational diplomacy at work”, but said bonds built through sport need institutional support to last.
“Academic, cultural and sports engagements can all help deepen our ties,” she said. “Those ties then mean more economic and cultural exchange. Everyone benefits.”
Sherwood is already planning to return to Algeria next spring with his wife, primarily to visit refugee camps near Tindouf in the disputed territory of Western Sahara, to help draw US attention to a crisis that is largely ignored in his country.
“It’s saddening that kindness has become such a big news story,” he said of the bond between Lawrencians and Algerians.
“I understand why that is, though, and hope there will be a day when that kindness and mutual respect between peoples is an everyday occurrence. I know we’re a long way from that.”

noticias.titulo: Poland condemns Russian ‘provocation’ after airspace violations
noticias.resumen: The incidents came as European troops were taking part in a Ukraine post-war military exercise.
noticias.texto:
Poland condemns Russian ‘provocation’ after airspace violations
The incidents came as European troops were taking part in a Ukraine post-war military exercise.
Poland has said Russia violated its airspace three times overnight, in what Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said was a “provocation” by Moscow.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told a news conference on Friday that investigations were under way at three locations – Nowy Lipowiec, roughly 60km (37 miles) from the Poland-Ukraine border, Molodycz, about 50km (31 miles) to the south, and Rudnik nad Sanem, about 50km to the west.
Kosiniak-Kamysz added that the three objects were probably two missiles and a drone.
The incursions were reported as Poland held military exercises involving the “Coalition of the Willing“, a group of European countries coordinating help and support for Ukraine.
The potential crash site near Nowy Lipowiec is about 76km (47 miles) from where European troops were taking part in military exercises to prepare for a potential post-war mission in Ukraine, aimed at helping to stabilise the country and rebuild its military once the war ends.
“These exercises, combined with the presence of defence ministers from France, the United Kingdom, and the Baltic states – along with eight chiefs of staff, including those from our key allies – suggest that the convergence of these events is no accident,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.
The defence minister said Poland would ask NATO for more support securing the alliance’s eastern flank.
Reaction to incursion
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said in a post on X that the incident was “clearly dangerous” and that NATO stood in solidarity with Poland.
Tusk said Rutte would visit Warsaw on Saturday. The Polish prime minister added that there was no doubt the objects that landed in Poland were Russian.
“It seems we are dealing with an intentional provocation,” he said. “Today, it is clearer than ever before that Poland must participate in decisions and discussions regarding the future of Ukraine and security in Europe.”
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham condemned Russia’s violation of Polish airspace, calling it “utterly unacceptable”.
“Europe will not be deterred from our support for Ukraine,” he said at an EU-UK summit news conference in Brussels. “We will not allow [Russian President Vladimir] Putin to divide our continent, and we recognise that the front line in Ukraine is the front line for freedom and democracy everywhere.”
Drones have repeatedly strayed into the airspace of countries on NATO’s eastern flank during Russia’s war in Ukraine, fuelling tension with the Western military alliance and stoking fears that the conflict could spread.
The incident in Poland came against the backdrop of Russian attacks in Ukraine that killed eight people, injured dozens more and damaged bridges and transport infrastructure.

noticias.titulo: Blood Gold: The Munduruku’s fight for survival in the Brazilian Amazon
noticias.resumen: Fault Lines investigates how illegal gold mining poisons and threatens Indigenous communities in the Brazilian Amazon.
noticias.texto:
Fault Lines
Blood Gold: The Munduruku’s fight for survival in the Brazilian Amazon
Fault Lines investigates how illegal gold mining poisons and threatens Indigenous communities in the Brazilian Amazon.
For the Munduruku people of the Brazilian Amazon, the fish they depend on for survival have become poisoned with mercury. As soaring gold prices drive illegal miners deeper into the rainforest, mercury used to extract the gold contaminates rivers and enters the food chain, putting entire communities at risk.
In Blood Gold, Fault Lines meets Indigenous families confronting the health consequences of illegal mining and fighting to protect their land. With rare access to an illegal mine, senior correspondent Josh Rushing witnesses how mercury is used to extract gold. He meets a researcher documenting the contamination of Indigenous communities and a federal prosecutor working to stop the mercury trade. The film examines why illegal mining persists despite government crackdowns and who pays the price for the world’s appetite for gold.

noticias.titulo: As the Coalition stares down One Nation in NSW, a new threat is rising: the teals
noticias.resumen: The opposition’s struggle is creating an opportunity for progressive independents who are boosted by shrewd political operator Chris Minns Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast The New South Wales Coalition is facing a renewed threat to its heartland seats on Sydney’s north shore. This time, the threat is from independent candidates – and they’re backed by the same community activists who put a swathe of teal independents into federal parliament. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The New South Wales Coalition is facing a renewed threat to its heartland seats on Sydney’s north shore.
This time, the threat is from independent candidates – and they’re backed by the same community activists who put a swathe of teal independents into federal parliament.
The challenge, which has so far remained under the radar, comes as the NSW Coalition tries to shore up its right flank against a surging One Nation before the March state election. This has resulted in the Coalition lurching to the right on issues ranging from gun control to law and order, and, in the case of the NSW Nationals, to abandon climate targets altogether.
As former opposition leader Mark Speakman resigned from the Liberals on Thursday – joining an exodus of MPs announcing they wouldn’t contest their seats in March – he warned his party against becoming “One Nation lite”.
But the move to the right has also created an opportunity for progressive independents running in urban seats usually held by Liberal moderates, with several candidates about to launch their campaigns.
This weekend, Amelia Loye, a management consultant who specialises in stakeholder and community engagement, will announce she is running in the seat of Willoughby, on Sydney’s north shore. She will attempt to oust Liberal MP Tim James, who holds the seat on a 2.6% margin.
Loye is backed by community group Willoughby Votes, which came close to securing an independent in the 2023 election with 47% of the two-party preferred vote.
“Willoughby has already shown it is ready for an independent,” she said. “Nearly half of voters backed one last time. I want to earn their support, and the support of those still deciding.”
She joins high-profile candidate Elouise Massa, a small business owner, who became a household name after campaigning for Northern Beaches hospital to return to public hands after her toddler’s death in emergency.
Massa will run in the Sydney seat of Manly against Liberal Adelaide Cuneo, who is seeking to replace the retiring MP, James Griffin.
The independent deputy mayor of Mosman, Michael Randall, announced last weekend he will run in North Shore as a community independent. Several of the people behind former independent federal MP Kylea Tink’s campaign are supporting him.
Monica Wulff, another independent, has announced a run in Davidson.
Voters on the northern beaches have already sent two independents to Macquarie street – and both have a good chance of being returned.
At the federal level, teal independents Sophie Scamps, Zali Steggall and Nicolette Boele hold McKellar, Warringah and Bradfield respectively. Tink held North Sydney for one term before the seat was abolished.
The NSW Liberal party is not giving up on the northern beaches and the north shore, despite the trend towards independents.
“We’ll keep making our case directly to voters, including why we oppose Labor’s gun buyback that targets law-abiding owners rather than criminals and terrorists,” a Liberal spokesperson said.
This time, however, the independents have a boost in the form of NSW Labor premier, Chris Minns.
During the final weeks of parliament before the NSW election, Minns joked that independent Jacqui Scruby, who won Pittwater at a byelection, should be known as “the member for Mona Vale road” for her tenacity in seeking an upgrade. It’s now being fast-tracked by the Minns government.
Minns has also appeared with Massa, and praised her for her advocacy.
But Minns, a shrewd political operator, has not fallen in love with independents – he’s just hedging his bets.
A year ago, with the Liberals languishing in the polls, Labor could have expected to increase its majority in 2027. But with One Nation storming to a primary vote as high as 30% in some polls, that prospect has dimmed.
In the current parliament, Labor has support of three independents – Greg Piper, Joe McGirr and Alex Greenwich – to ensure confidence and supply for its minority government. An expanded crossbench would give more options and provide a buffer for Labor losses to One Nation in western Sydney, the Hunter and possibly the Central Coast.
If all independents were successful – and that is a big if – almost the entire north shore region would go to state independents, except the seat of Wahroonga.
Most of the commentary about the 2027 election has focused on the likely Armageddon facing the Nationals, who could lose as many eight or nine of their 11 seats in the regions.
But a teal wave also remains a threat to the Liberal party, especially as the Coalition try to position themselves to fight off One Nation in the regions with policies that don’t sit well with urban voters.
One Nation could also prove helpful to independents if it makes good on its promise to run candidates in every seat. The party is more likely to shave votes from the Liberal primary vote, making it easier for the independents to overtake the Liberal on preferences from Labor and the Greens.
NSW’s optional preferential voting makes it hard to predict how strong flows will be – and it depends what parties advocate on how to votes. But in 2023 only 41% of One Nation voters nominated preferences, compared to 70% of Green voters and 49% of Labor voters.
The opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, has not ruled out either a preference deal or a post-election arrangement with One Nation, describing such options as “hypothetical”. But if they do end up preferencing One Nation, it may alienate moderate Liberals and ultimately work against them.
- Disclosure: Anne Davies worked as a media and policy adviser to the independent federal MP Sophie Scamps from October 2023 to October 2024.

noticias.titulo: Spain frees wealthy US-sought activist on bail as Irish police raid Dublin home
noticias.resumen: Pro-Palestinian donor James ‘Fergie’ Chambers released as court considers extradition request In a blur of events surrounding the Trump administration’s effort to extradite James “Fergie” Chambers, Spain released the wealthy US activist and donor on bail even as Irish police raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and his partner, Stella Schnabel, acting on a request from US authorities. Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal co
noticias.texto:
In a blur of events surrounding the Trump administration’s effort to extradite James “Fergie” Chambers, Spain released the wealthy US activist and donor on bail even as Irish police raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and his partner, Stella Schnabel, acting on a request from US authorities.
Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.
Speaking outside Madrid’s Aranjuez prison upon his release on Friday, Chambers called the charges against him “baseless”, adding that his release was “hopefully the first step in recognizing that internationally”.
Chambers also said: “Spain is a country that has stood on the right side of this most important issue of our time, that has stood on the right side of the genocide, and where this is some reason and some justice.”
An appeals court ordered the conditional release on Friday due to issues surrounding the legally required US translation of the extradition request’s core documents into Spanish, first reported on by the Guardian. He had been detained since 10 July, when Spanish authorities arrested him in Ibiza.
The order asserts that the translation issues cause “a diminishment, at least for the time being, in the solidity or foundation of the extradition request”.
Chambers’s release follows a separate decision on Thursday by the three-judge panel at the high court tasked with deciding on the extradition to pause the proceedings in order to evaluate the impact of the alterations the US made to the original, machine-made translation of the extradition request into Spanish.
The Guardian detailed four examples of the alterations on 7 November and the US admitted to tampering with the translation, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent” on 17 November – and citing the same four examples. Chambers’s defense team has asserted for weeks that there are as many as 30 such alterations.
The changes introduced prejudicial notions with specific legal implications that in turn wound up in the Spanish prosecutor’s report on the case, Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian earlier this week. The judges must consider the prosecutor’s report in deciding on the extradition request.
The high court was expected to rule on the extradition this week, following a 13 November hearing. But as of Thursday’s decision, the deadline has been extended indefinitely as the judges evaluate the translation, including a 345-page report submitted by the defense team that identifies 30 “incriminating changes” Trump administration officials made to a translation prepared by DeepL, “an AI-first translation platform”, according to its website.
The decision also gives the prosecutor an opportunity to address the issue in writing, after dismissing it in the 13 November hearing by referring to “supposed translation errors”.
Chambers’s views and donations to progressive and humanitarian projects have been extensively profiled in US media, including his controversial public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”
The heir to $250m from his family’s business, Cox Enterprises, is being sought in extradition because of such views, his defense team has asserted throughout the case.
Meanwhile, the Irish Garda Síochána, acting on a request from US authorities, raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and Schnabel on Wednesday, destroying the front door and removing electronic items and other possessions, according to their attorney in Ireland, Ciarán Mulholland.
Schnabel, who is five months pregnant, said: “It is difficult to see this raid as anything other than a desperate fishing expedition by the US authorities to find evidence to bolster their case against Fergie.”
The attorney told the Guardian that the raid was the result of a “mutual legal assistance” request from the US – and that such a request “wouldn’t give [the Garda Síochána] permission to kick in the doors of someone’s dwelling in Ireland”.
“It’s unusual for the Irish state to be acting in such a clandestine manner,” Mulholland said. He has asked authorities to produce a search warrant and an itemized list of what was taken. “My fear is that whatever was taken has been put on a plane and taken to the US,” he added.
“This [extradition case] shows the complete disregard for due process … that the Trump administration seems to have,” Mulholland said.

noticias.titulo: Misty-eyed Burnham gambles on closer ties with EU as he throws down gauntlet to Tories and Reform
noticias.resumen: PM challenges rivals to rebuff plan he says could add 0.5% annual growth to economy and offer young people hope Several sentences into a slightly convoluted answer about where UK-EU relations might go next, Andy Burnham abruptly changed tack. “The important point is that the Britain of today and the EU of today is not the one of 2016,” he said. “Life has moved on in so many ways.” This is undoubtedly true. But Burnham’s political gamble on closer ties with Brussels hinges on the assumption that most British voters feel this way as well. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Several sentences into a slightly convoluted answer about where UK-EU relations might go next, Andy Burnham abruptly changed tack. “The important point is that the Britain of today and the EU of today is not the one of 2016,” he said. “Life has moved on in so many ways.”
This is undoubtedly true. But Burnham’s political gamble on closer ties with Brussels hinges on the assumption that most British voters feel this way as well.
Seeking to push his deal on food checks, emissions trading and a new youth exchange scheme, Burnham was at first in full consumer politics mode, saying it would bring cheaper food – with a namecheck for Tesco, Asda and other supermarket chains – as well as lower electricity costs and a claimed 0.5% boost to overall growth.
But as the Brussels press conference went on, the prime minister became more misty-eyed, particularly in describing the youth exchange scheme as a gift to a generation stripped of choices by the 2016 referendum and then Covid. “Hope is a word,” he intoned. “And it starts now.”
For all that Burnham is a skilled political salesman, his oratory is backed up with some helpful political context, matched with cooperative allies.
To begin with, not only politics but polling results are now different. A new constituency-level survey released on Friday showed that of 394 constituencies estimated to have voted leave in 2016, voters in 274 of them would back rejoining the EU – including Burnham’s Makerfield seat.
Standing alongside the UK prime minister in the venue, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and António Costa, the European Council president, at times resembled proud parents, beaming at every positive phrase.
They, of course, began work when the EU reset was the personal project of one Keir Starmer. His name was not mentioned on Friday, and it is undeniable that Brussels finds life easier dealing with a UK leader who is both bold and popular.
Speaking to British reporters later in the day, Burnham openly challenged political opponents to rebuff a plan that, he said, could add 0.5% annual growth to the economy in the long term – more, he said, than any other single intervention.
“Why would anybody turn their back on that?” he said, with particular focus on Nigel Farage, who was, soon after Burnham spoke, hosting a retaliatory press conference of his own, 10 minutes’ walk from the EU building.
Even with the tight timing – Farage had to delay his event as the summit timetable slipped – the Reform UK leader drew a decent crowd of reporters. But there will be a sense in No 10 that beyond Farage, most of the formidable Brexit forces of 2016 have melted away.
Kemi Badenoch, who has been advised by her team to talk more about the economy and less about Brexit, spent the day on a visit in Essex. The Conservatives did send out a condemnatory press release about the EU deal, but it focused more on Burnham “reopening the divisions of the past” than the specifics.
More trenchant was a statement from Stay Out, the recently formed Brexit purity group, which floated its argument that rejoining the EU would cost the UK £750m a week.
For all that the dominance of vote leave alumni in Stay Out gives the campaign the slight air of a historic battle re-enactment society, Burnham cannot ignore them. A resonant sidenote of the summit was how he was happy to talk about the specifics of the deal, but not much beyond that.
While it was the PM himself who provoked a debate about a future in which the UK rejoined the EU, the brakes were firmly on in regard to any discussion of such ideas.
Pre-summit talk of possible closer future links with Brussels was replaced by much vaguer language about mutual “brainstorming” on what would come next, with UK officials saying any progress could be months in the making.
Another sign of the caution embedded within Burnham’s ambition was the lineup of UK cabinet ministers who watched as the prime minister, von der Leyen and Costa arrived on Friday morning.
Alongside those you might expect – Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, John Healey, the chancellor, and Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary – was Anneliese Midgley, a close ally of Burnham who has the job of chief whip, No 10’s liaison with Labour MPs.
She was there because a bill setting into UK law the new EU deal will be presented to parliament next week. Most Labour MPs agree with Burnham that the world has changed since 2016. But, as with the voters, he needs to bring them along with him.

noticias.titulo: Denmark to expel Russian diplomat over alleged Moscow link to attempted killing of rapper
noticias.resumen: Russian intelligence thought to be behind plan to kill US-Ukrainian musician Kyivstoner before concert in Denmark Denmark’s foreign minister has said Russia’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Moscow was suspected of being behind an attempted killing of a US-Ukrainian rapper. “We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark,”, Lars Løkke Rasmussen told a news conference. The expulsion will happen within seven days. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Denmark’s foreign minister has said Russia’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Moscow was suspected of being behind an attempted killing of a US-Ukrainian rapper.
“We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark,”, Lars Løkke Rasmussen told a news conference. The expulsion will happen within seven days.
“We are saying this very clearly: we have exposed you,” he added.
Danish police said they had averted an attempt by Russian intelligence services to kill the US-Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner in September before a planned performance in Denmark.
Rasmussen also said that Denmark was considering suspending Schengen visas to Russians.
“We have launched work at the European level to further tighten the rules governing access of Russian nationals to Europe,” he said. “We are now stepping up our efforts towards a halt to all non-essential visas.
“The strongest response Denmark can give is not to waver and to support Ukraine. And we fully intend to continue supporting Ukraine.”
Police thwarted the alleged plot when they arrested three men with links to the Danish criminal underworld shortly before Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Viktorovich Vasiliev, was due to perform at a concert on 25 September, which was then cancelled, officials said. Vasiliev holds US and Ukrainian nationality.
Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen, the head of Denmark’s national security and intelligence service, said: “It is our clear assessment that the assassination attempt was planned by the Russian intelligence services.”
According to prosecutors, the suspects were driving towards the concert venue north of Copenhagen with two loaded pistols and two knives when police arrested them at about 9.55pm, five minutes before the concert was due to begin. A fourth suspect was arrested later that evening, police said.
One of the suspects had bought a ticket to the concert, according to the charges.
The suspects are charged under Section 108 of Denmark’s criminal code, which covers assisting a foreign intelligence service, as well as attempted murder. They denied wrongdoing in court, the broadcaster DR reported.
Kieffer-Kristensen said: “A Russian assassination attempt is not something we’ve seen in Denmark before, and that gives me an impression of an increasingly aggressive and risk-taking Russia.
“We believe that the case is important for understanding the threat that Denmark faces from Russia.”

noticias.titulo: Burnham seals trade and youth mobility deals in biggest step towards EU since Brexit
noticias.resumen: Agreements reached on food and drink, emissions and to allow young people to move around continent, but may be derailed over student fees Andy Burnham has taken the biggest step towards deeper ties with the EU since Brexit, sealing deals to ease trade and create a mobility scheme for young people as he declared a “new world” of cooperation between the two sides. At a major summit in Brussels on Friday the EU and UK announced three deals, on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, which will allow 100,000 young Britons to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with recip
noticias.texto:
Andy Burnham has taken the biggest step towards deeper ties with the EU since Brexit, sealing deals to ease trade and create a mobility scheme for young people as he declared a “new world” of cooperation between the two sides.
At a major summit in Brussels on Friday the EU and UK announced three deals, on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, which will allow 100,000 young Britons to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with reciprocal access for Europeans in the UK.
But the trio of deals could be derailed in six months, as the EU threatened to block them unless the UK allows European students to pay domestic-level fees to study at British universities.
Burnham rejected suggestions there was any confusion over the deals coming into force: “The deal is done. It is there in black and white in front of you,” he said, adding that the legislation would enter parliament next week.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, played down the disagreement, saying she was “confident we are going to find a solution”.
Hailing the “historic” agreement Burnham said: “This is a good day for Britain and this is a good day for Europe,” as he argued that the agreements answer “the biggest challenges of our times and the biggest worries that people have”, citing the cost of living, lack of economic growth, illegal immigration and challenges facing young people.
The prime minister said he would “brainstorm” with the EU over future ties, while also reiterating that he would not get ahead of public opinion.
Speaking to reporters, Burnham stressed that nothing would happen in the current parliament that went much beyond this deal. The so-called brainstorming process was, he said, “just looking at options in a new world, and having an open discussion about what those might be. It will be to inform the next parliament.”
Burnham also challenged political opponents, notably Nigel Farage, who was in Brussels on Friday to hold a retaliatory press conference, to justify why they would reject a deal which, he said, would boost growth and lead to cheaper food and electricity. “Why would anybody turn their back on that?”
The prime minister said the deals, which were initiated by Keir Starmer, would add 0.5% to British GDP, a £17bn boost to the British economy.
Farage said Burnham had been naive and the EU had “used this moment to strongarm the British prime minister over tuition fee cuts for hundreds of thousands of EU students”.
EU leaders sought to play down differences over tuition fees. “We are heading in the same direction and that is what matters,” the European Council president, António Costa, said of the broad relationship. He described the UK as “our closest neighbour, a reliable ally and a natural partner”.
Von der Leyen said it was up to the UK to decide where the journey was going, adding: “We welcome this brainstorming, so count on us.”
In a sign of tension in the negotiations, the EU agreed a declaration that the three deals would not come into force without equal treatment on fees for EU students at British universities.
“The [EU] Council and [European] Commission consider that this agreement is to provide for equal treatment with nationals as regards tuition fees for all students,” stated the confidential statement seen by the Guardian. The EU would not adopt the three agreements before “the conclusions of the negotiations … providing for equal treatment on tuition fees”, it added.
Another potential flashpoint could be the UK’s status as a rule-taker. The food and drink and emissions trading deals require the UK to align with EU rules. British experts will be invited to relevant EU meetings, including dealing with potential animal health emergencies. But Britain will not have voting rights. Burnham rejected suggestions this was a fig leaf, saying it would be “quite a moment” to have British experts back in EU meeting rooms.
France was said to be instrumental in shaping Britain’s exclusion, although Paris argues its position was widely supported and reflects the reality that a non-member state cannot be a decision-maker.
Following the talks, Burnham was invited to a lunch of pea and mint soup, battered North Sea cod and chips, followed by Brussels waffle with fruit.
The summit began with a highly choreographed welcome ceremony in the Europa “space egg” European Council building, where a quintet played the British and EU anthems.
The UK hailed a joint decision to create a “partnership for economic resilience”, as an answer to its concerns over the EU’s Made in Europe plans. The EU is still finalising legislation that will give EU companies preference when public money is spent on the key technologies, such as renewables and electric cars. The UK has been arguing for Britain to be included in Made in Europe to ensure UK firms are not locked out of European supply chains.
In response, the two sides agreed to set up “a common prosperity and economic security space”, essentially an answer to shared concerns about artificially cheap Chinese goods that are depressing prices across Europe. But questions over whether the UK needs to align with EU trade defences remain open. Burnham said the two sides had reached an agreement “to work together where we have common threats”.
In an echo of the Brexit years, the final deal emerged after late-night talks went to the wire.
The German Social Democrat MEP Bernd Lange called on both sides to resolve the tuition fees issue to make studying affordable in a way that works for universities: “We can’t open the door to young people and then price them out of walking through it.”
The EU has welcomed Burnham’s breaking of taboos over rejoining, but also voiced frustration at British negotiating tactics. “The UK has a tendency to make even small questions so difficult,” an EU diplomat said. “A British prime minister talks about a change of approach … Then in negotiations it seems like British negotiators act the same way they always had.”

noticias.titulo: Indian man sentenced to 19 years in prison for conspiring to kill Sikh separatist in New York
noticias.resumen: Nikhil Gupta admitted to plotting with Indian government official to hire hitman to murder dual US-Canadian citizen An Indian ⁠man was sentenced to more ⁠than 19 ​years in US prison on Friday after admitting to orchestrating a failed Indian government-backed plot to kill a Sikh separatist in New York ⁠City , in connection with what US and Canadian authorities have called a broader effort to target Indian dissidents. Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy ⁠to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
An Indian man was sentenced to more than 19 years in US prison on Friday after admitting to orchestrating a failed Indian government-backed plot to kill a Sikh separatist in New York City, in connection with what US and Canadian authorities have called a broader effort to target Indian dissidents.
Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.
The US district judge Victor Marrero handed down the 235-month sentence at a hearing in a Manhattan federal court.
The discovery of alleged assassination plots against Sikh separatists in the US and Canada has tested relations with India, which has denied involvement in such plots.
Prosecutors accused Gupta of plotting with an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer at Sikhs for Justice in New York who has advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India.
Gupta and the Indian government official, Vikash Yadav, arranged to have $15,000 in cash delivered to a purported hitman who was actually an undercover US law enforcement officer, court papers show.
Yadav is also charged in the case but is not in US custody. It is unclear whether he has hired a defense lawyer.
India’s government has dissociated itself from any plot against Pannun, saying it was against government policy.
Prosecutors with the Manhattan US attorney’s office had recommended a sentence of about 24 years in prison.
“This case cuts to the very core of American values,” prosecutor Ashley Nicolas said in court. “We don’t condone the use of violence to silence voices in this country, ever.”
Addressing the court on Friday, Gupta said he regretted straying from the non-violent example set by the Indian independence leader Mahatma Gandhi.
“I’m sorry to Mr Pannun, I’m sorry to the communities I hurt, I’m sorry to my own family,” Gupta said.
Pannun told the court that he was grateful to the US for prosecuting Gupta and said he would keep advocating for Sikh sovereignty.
“Self-determination for my people and my homeland, Punjab, is my lifetime goal,” he said.

noticias.titulo: US reacts cautiously to Myanmar genocide ruling as EU praises ‘critical’ role of UN’s top court
noticias.resumen: Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach. Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims,
noticias.texto:
The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.
Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel.
The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.
But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.
“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue.”
Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.
Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson said on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.
“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”
The US state department said on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.
Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.
The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.
In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.
“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement.
“The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”
The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.
The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.
The ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.
Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.
The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.
The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited.
While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.
Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.
About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.
Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.
South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia. Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

noticias.titulo: JP Morgan boss says he will find ways to offset ‘unfair’ rise in UK tax on banks
noticias.resumen: Jamie Dimon says he is ‘setting an example’ in seeking to claw back Labour’s increase in surcharge, from 3% to 6% Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair. Speaking at an event in London on Thursday, Dimon said he would seek to claw back the increase and was “setting an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair.
Speaking at an event in London on Thursday, Dimon said he would seek to claw back the increase and was “setting an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”.
The bank surcharge is to rise from 3% to 6% in January as a temporary 15-month measure. It was unclear how JP Morgan, which employs 23,000 people in the UK, would make up for the extra cost.
In comments first reported by the Financial Times, citing people who attended the event, Dimon said he would set an example in making up for the added costs, and that the decision was “more in sorrow” than in anger.
Dimon has repeatedly lobbied Labour against raising taxes on banks, and suggested in May that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn tower in the Canary Wharf district of London that is expected to serve as JP Morgan’s UK headquarters.
Shortly after the chancellor, John Healey, announced the policy during his inaugural budget in October, a source familiar with the matter told the Guardian that plans for the 279,000 sq metre (3m sq ft) building were still going ahead. But the bank also said at the time that the policy “lacks principle” for singling the sector out, adding that it operated in a “highly competitive global marketplace”.
JP Morgan also has a sprawling campus in Bournemouth, where it employs more than 5,300 staff who process more than $1tn (£750bn) worth of global transactions each day. Earlier this month, the Guardian reported fears that the advance of artificial intelligence could put their jobs at risk.
Lenders in the UK pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, and the separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets, which is set for the temporary rise. JP Morgan, the biggest bank in the US, expected to pay £120m more in taxes because of the increase, the FT reported.
Bank share prices rallied after Healey’s October announcement because the increase was less than many people in the industry had expected. The chancellor said at the time that he was “looking to our banks to help fund breathing space for British families”.
JP Morgan declined to comment.

noticias.titulo: Police arrest teacher who missed sentencing after indecent assault conviction
noticias.resumen: Sally-Anne Bowen was found guilty of having sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the 1980s A chemistry teacher who had sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the late 1980s has been arrested by police in Hampshire after she failed to turn up to her sentencing hearing. Sally-Anne Bowen, 65, could not be found at her home by Metropolitan police officers on Friday morning after a warrant was issued for her arrest, a court heard. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
A chemistry teacher who had sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the late 1980s has been arrested by police in Hampshire after she failed to turn up to her sentencing hearing.
Sally-Anne Bowen, 65, could not be found at her home by Metropolitan police officers on Friday morning after a warrant was issued for her arrest, a court heard.
The former teacher, who was in her 20s when she had sex with one pupil up to 30 times and kissed a second boy when they were aged about 14 to 15, was convicted in August of seven counts of indecent assault and granted bail before her sentencing.
Her trial heard she wore short, tight skirts and flirted in class, with one former pupil comparing her behaviour to “a Sabrina Carpenter video”.
After her conviction she was granted bail and was due to be sentenced at Harrow crown court on Friday.
But Bowen, from Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, did not turn up to court in the morning, and the judge, Karim Ezzat, issued a warrant for her arrest, “not backed by bail”.
Neelam Gomersall, prosecuting, said Bowen’s partner of 36 years, Darren Scotchbrook, was at the address when officers arrived, but Bowen was not.
Gomersall had earlier told the court there was “no evidence” that Bowen could not attend the sentencing, and that information from Scotchbrook was “suggestive of refusal rather than inability” to attend.
Bowen’s barrister, Mark Kimsey, said: “Our instructing solicitor has tried to contact her and the phone rings but doesn’t answer.”
He had earlier said that Bowen was in contact with solicitors on Thursday and had engaged with a pre-sentence report, adding there had been “concerns as to her welfare due to the content of the messages” from her.
In an update on Friday afternoon, the Met said: “On Friday November 20, officers were made aware that a 65-year-old woman had failed to appear at Harrow crown court for sentencing.
“A warrant was issued for her arrest and officers promptly launched inquiries to locate her.
“At around 3pm, officers from a neighbouring force found the woman at a location in Hampshire and arrested her on suspicion of failing to appear at court.
“She has been taken into police custody. A new sentencing date will be set by the court in due course.”
Bowen’s trial heard that she was in her mid-20s when she taught at Christ’s College in Finchley, north London.
One victim had told jurors he had had sex with her “about 20 or 30 times” over several months, considered her his girlfriend and kept it secret. He said it had led to “the destruction of my education”.
The second victim described spending lunchtimes with Bowen in a cafe, where he was “goaded” into kissing her by other boys and recalled touching her breasts.
Bowen denied the allegations as “total fabrication” and claimed a medical condition made sex difficult and painful. She denied flirting, saying: “I didn’t flirt with students, I was just friendly.” Defending her clothes, she said she “wasn’t going to dress like Margaret Thatcher”.

noticias.titulo: Florida mechanic found guilty of murdering British woman who attorney says came to US to die
noticias.resumen: Dwain Hall was convicted of stabbing Sonia Exelby, a music teacher who prosecutors say suffered from mental illness A Florida mechanic has been found guilty of stabbing to death a British music teacher, whom he convinced to travel to the United States. Dwain Hall, an auto repair and tow truck driver, groomed 32-year-old Sonia Exelby from Portsmouth, England, on a fetish website before luring her to the US. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
A Florida mechanic has been found guilty of stabbing to death a British music teacher, whom he convinced to travel to the United States.
Dwain Hall, an auto repair and tow truck driver, groomed 32-year-old Sonia Exelby from Portsmouth, England, on a fetish website before luring her to the US.
Hall had pleaded not guilty to the charges of kidnap and first-degree murder.
At trial, jurors heard from several witnesses, most of them law enforcement officials, who detailed Hall’s email, phone records, social media accounts and other records to trace his movements after Exelby travelled from the UK to meet him.
Exelby’s disappearance from her home sparked an international investigation. Prosecutors this week described how she suffered from mental illness. Investigators said that Exelby had traveled to Florida after posting online about wanting someone to end her life.
Hall’s arrest affidavit said that Exelby had previously expressed suicidal thoughts and investigators alleged that Hall knew about her struggles and used that vulnerability to bring her to Florida, the Ocala Starbanner reported.
The authorities said Exelby boarded a flight to the US seemingly with an intention “to be possibly sexually abused, tortured and murdered by unknown individuals living in the United States”.
After Exelby traveled to the US in October 2025, authorities say Hall picked her up from the Gainesville airport in central Florida.
He drove her to an Airbnb rental, where investigators later found evidence they say connected him to her disappearance and death, including transactions on her bank cards and a video of Exelby on Hall’s cellphone.
According to the Times, Junior Barrett, Hall’s attorney, argued that Exelby took her own life. “She came here with the intention of dying, she thought she was worthless, useless, a burden on other people,” he said in his closing statement.
“This isn’t a question about what porn he likes. You can disagree with him about what he likes, but the case can’t be decided on you not liking his lifestyle. The fact he did not stop her from killing herself does not make it murder.”
Prosecutor Amy Beth Berndt said jurors should use their “common sense”. She added that Hall targeted Exelby for her mental illness and killed her for his sadistic pleasure.
Berndt said Exelby “was beautiful. She was kind and she was deeply loved by everyone who knew her. And she also suffered from mental illness for most of her life. She should be alive today.”
She added: “No one could save her from the defendant, the ‘Alpha Sadist’. He took advantage of a severely depressed, mentally ill woman who was incapable of making any rational decisions.”
After the verdict was read, Exelby’s brother Barry Wilton said: “This last year has been one of the hardest of our lives. Losing our dear sister Sonia has had a profound impact on me and my entire family. I’m not sure we will ever be the same again.”
Wilton then addressed Hall directly, adding: “You pretended to care for Sonia. You didn’t at all. You used her to fulfil your sick fantasies. You had her life in your hands. You had the opportunity to save her, but instead you preyed on her vulnerabilities and you took her from us.”

noticias.titulo: Two men killed after glider crashes into Loch Leven in Scotland
noticias.resumen: The pair had taken off from the Scottish Gliding Centre at nearby Portmoak on a training flight Two men have been killed after their glider crashed into Loch Leven, a large body of water in Perth and Kinross, on Friday morning. Police Scotland said their bodies were recovered from the loch by the emergency services after the alarm was raised at 11.05am on Friday. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Two men have been killed after their glider crashed into Loch Leven, a large body of water in Perth and Kinross, on Friday morning.
Police Scotland said their bodies were recovered from the loch by the emergency services after the alarm was raised at 11.05am on Friday.
The force said next of kin had been told and the incident was not being treated as suspicious. Two HM Coastguard helicopters and an air ambulance were sent to the scene, along with a fire service appliance and a specialist crew.
The pair had taken off from the Scottish Gliding Centre at Portmoak airfield near the loch’s eastern shore in a Perkoz two-person glider on a training flight.
A spokesperson for the gliding centre said: “The incident is currently under investigation by the Air Accident Investigation Branch [AAIB] of the Department for Transport and the police in conjunction with the British Gliding Association.
“Our club is cooperating fully with these organisations. At the present time, there is no indication as to the cause of the accident.”
An AAIB spokesperson said: “A multidisciplinary team including inspectors with expertise in aircraft operations, engineering and recorded data have been deployed to gather evidence and make inquiries.”
The police said airspace restrictions had been put in place after the crash was reported.

noticias.titulo: No one else in Reform is suitable to lead the party, Nigel Farage says
noticias.resumen: Farage issues warning to potential rivals and says he will fight next election as leader if ‘still here and fit and healthy’ Nigel Farage has said he does not see another person who could do his job as leader of Reform UK, in a warning shot to potential rivals who might seek to replace him. The Reform UK leader delivered a message that he was going nowhere despite his worries over his personal safety in the wake of the killing of the Reform politician Ann Widdecombe. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Nigel Farage has said he does not see another person who could do his job as leader of Reform UK, in a warning shot to potential rivals who might seek to replace him.
The Reform UK leader delivered a message that he was going nowhere despite his worries over his personal safety in the wake of the killing of the Reform politician Ann Widdecombe.
There has been speculation over Farage’s future in light of police and parliamentary investigations of Reform’s financial affairs. The Commons standards watchdog is due to report soon on whether he should have declared a £5m personal gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne before the last election. If he gets a substantial suspension from parliament, he could face a second byelection, contested by other main parties, in his Clacton constituency.
However, Farage sounded a note of defiance in an interview with the Sun, saying: “These are very thoughtful moments, but, you know what, if I’m not here doing this job right now, who else could? Who else would? I don’t see that person. So I’m gonna do it.”
A number of other Reform UK politicians are potential contenders to succeed him, including the party’s economics spokesperson and former Conservative, Robert Jenrick, the home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, and the former leader Richard Tice. Another possibility is the return of Rupert Lowe, who left Reform in acrimonious circumstances and founded his own party, Restore Britain, but who is popular on the online hard right.
The party is going through a difficult period after slipping from first place in the polls to second or third behind behind Labour and sometimes the Conservatives.
Asked by the Sun if he had “blown” his chances of reaching No 10, Farage said: “No, far from it.”
He admitted there had been “self-inflicted wounds” in the past year but said he still had a chance of becoming prime minister.
He told the newspaper that he would fight the next election as Reform leader if he was “still here and fit and healthy”.
He also batted away questions about the £5m, which he has insisted was to pay for his personal security despite the fact the party has been providing this.
“What’s it got to do with you? Drugs, sports cars, desert islands. It’s a gift,” he said, adding that although the party had had “ebbs and flows” and had made mistakes after growing “too far and too fast”, he was confident it was “more than through the worst of it”.
On the prospect of another battle over Europe as Andy Burnham weighs the case for rejoining the EU, the Reform leader said: “If you ask me, have I got the energy and the enthusiasm to do this again? I would say to you, hold my jacket. I’m ready for it.”
He also warned of people taking to the streets with “direct action” if Brexit is reversed.
In a separate interview with the Times while travelling to Brussels, where Burnham was attempting a reset deal, Farage said he believed the issue of Europe would dominate the years to come.
“It’s going to be absolutely huge. It’s going to be much bigger than anyone realises. The genie is out of the bottle; it literally can’t be stopped now,” he said.
He also ruled out joining a new campaign called Stay Out, led by former Tories, suggesting he would make his own case for keeping Brexit.

noticias.titulo: Home Alone sequel reportedly in development with Macaulay Culkin returning
noticias.resumen: Christmas comedy hit is set for a follow-up from the point of view of the father with Seth Rogen as writer and producer A Home Alone sequel is reportedly in development with original star Macaulay Culkin set to return. According to Puck’s Matthew Belloni , Culkin met with Disney executives earlier this year with a pitch for a follow-up and now the project has been met with a green light. The new Home Alone film will bring the 46-year-old back to the franchise as Kevin McCallister for a comedy that, according to Deadline , will be from the father’s point of view. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
A Home Alone sequel is reportedly in development with original star Macaulay Culkin set to return.
According to Puck’s Matthew Belloni, Culkin met with Disney executives earlier this year with a pitch for a follow-up and now the project has been met with a green light. The new Home Alone film will bring the 46-year-old back to the franchise as Kevin McCallister for a comedy that, according to Deadline, will be from the father’s point of view.
The film will also recruit Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg as writers and producers and they will work with Culkin to craft the script. Rogen and Goldberg recently worked with Disney on a Muppets TV special.
Home Alone was a major box office hit upon release in 1990, grossing $476m worldwide and becoming the year’s second-biggest movie. Culkin returned for the sequel Home Alone 2: Lost in New York, which made $359m two years later.
The franchise continued without the actor for three further movies and then in 2021, after Fox had been bought by Disney, there was a straight-to-streaming reboot.
Culkin later reprised the role in a 2018 commercial for Google and this year has once again returned as Kevin for a new McDonald’s advert.
Last year, he was asked about a sequel at an anniversary event.
“I kind of had this idea,” he said. “I’m either a widower or a divorcee. I’m raising a kid and all that stuff. I’m working really hard and I’m not really paying enough attention and the kid is kind of getting miffed at me and then I get locked out.”
In his pitch, the character’s son won’t let him in and would be the one setting the traps with the house as “some sort of metaphor for our relationship”.
The original film’s director, Chris Columbus, who later went on to direct the first two Harry Potter adventures, has spoken out about a possible sequel. “I think it’s a mistake to try to go back and recapture something we did 35 years ago,” he said. “I think it should be left alone.”

noticias.titulo: ‘Worth fighting for’: senators vow to restore financial watchdog agency after Guardian investigation
noticias.resumen: Democrats – including incoming banking chair and both majority leader candidates – said wealthy interests were prioritized over the needs of working Americans In response to a Guardian investigation , four US Senate Democrats say they will work to resurrect a financial watchdog agency that has abandoned dozens of enforcement actions under the second Trump administration . The Guardian found that after the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) dropped more than 20 lawsuits against banks and corporations accused of a range of financial misconduct, complaints against those firms rose by an
noticias.texto:
In response to a Guardian investigation, four US Senate Democrats say they will work to resurrect a financial watchdog agency that has abandoned dozens of enforcement actions under the second Trump administration.
The Guardian found that after the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) dropped more than 20 lawsuits against banks and corporations accused of a range of financial misconduct, complaints against those firms rose by an average of more than 75%. In many of these recent complaints, consumers described the same issues the CFPB’s suits had sought to address.
The Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren – who first proposed the CFPB’s creation after the 2008 financial crash, and is now poised to become chair of the Senate banking committee in January – promised to investigate the administration’s attempts to weaken the CFPB.
“Donald Trump has sidelined the financial cop on the beat that has returned more than $21bn directly to Americans who were cheated by big banks and giant corporations,” Warren said in a statement.
The Guardian’s reporting, she added, “shows what came next: Trump’s billionaire friends and Wall Street donors getting away with scamming Americans. The next Congress will defend the CFPB, investigate how the Trump administration has abandoned cheated Americans, and put forward legislation to protect consumers and bring down costs.”
Since Trump took office, the CFPB has dramatically scaled back public enforcement actions against companies – even while Americans submit record numbers of complaints to the agency. After filing an average of roughly 30 public enforcement actions each year for more than a decade, the bureau has initiated just one since then director Rohit Chopra, a Joe Biden appointee, was fired on 30 January 2025.
The leadership of the CFPB under the second Trump administration has claimed that the agency has long been harmful to companies and consumers alike. An agency spokesperson asserted in a statement to the Guardian that the CFPB had cost Americans hundreds of billions of dollars – “making the American Dream, like homeownership, more costly by the thousands for each borrower”.
“This Weaponized agency attacked political enemies and disfavored industries and used novel legal theories and secret justifications to ruin lives and businesses,” the statement added. “We are fixing that and bringing the agency back to operating within statute and away from breaking the law and helping all business and Americans who were victims of thuggery.”
The Guardian’s reporting on the agency comes in the wake of midterm elections in which the economy and cost of living concerns were at the top of most voters’ minds.
In response to the investigation, the Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, vowed to “make sure that the CFPB is operating at its full capacity” once Democrats gain control of Congress.
“The Trump administration has done everything in its power to bow down to special interests and billionaires at the expense of American families,” Schumer said. “The CFPB was created to make sure that everyday folks could be protected from predatory actors, but Republicans have undermined it at every turn.”
The Maryland senator Chris Van Hollen, who announced on 12 November that he would challenge Schumer for the role of Senate majority leader when the new Congress convenes, said the CFPB’s rollback demanded greater focus on working Americans.
“The CFPB returned billions of dollars to Americans who were conned and scammed by big corporations,” Van Hollen said in a statement. “Naturally, many billionaires didn’t like that, so they had Trump and his cronies use every tool they could to dismantle an agency whose job is to stand up for working families.”
Van Hollen’s fellow senator from Maryland, Angela Alsobrooks, also weighed in.
“The CFPB works for the American people,” she said. “The CFPB is worth fighting for.”

noticias.titulo: Lauren Boebert says Trump ‘did some things to hurt’ her constituents
noticias.resumen: Controversial Colorado Republican narrowly lost House seat in midterms but says ‘I’m not mad at the president’ Lauren Boebert says Donald Trump “did some things that hurt” her constituents before they voted the pugnacious Colorado Republican out of her US House seat during midterm elections, which saw her and the president’s party lose control of Congress. “This could be a referendum on President Trump,” Boebert said to the Associated Press in an interview published on Friday. “It could be the referendum on Congress or the Republican party. I think it’s all of it. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Lauren Boebert says Donald Trump “did some things that hurt” her constituents before they voted the pugnacious Colorado Republican out of her US House seat during midterm elections, which saw her and the president’s party lose control of Congress.
“This could be a referendum on President Trump,” Boebert said to the Associated Press in an interview published on Friday. “It could be the referendum on Congress or the Republican party. I think it’s all of it.
“I’m not mad at the president. [But] the president did some things that hurt my voters.”
Boebert expressed those thoughts during some of her first comments to the news media after Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher defeated her by less than a 1% margin in a race called 10 days after the polls closed.
The conservative firebrand who first joined Congress in 2021 had widely been favored to win a fourth consecutive term. But low approval ratings for Trump after he started the war in Iran, pursuing an aggressive mass deportation campaign and other unpopular initiatives created an environment in which Democrats flipped nine seats in the US Senate and about four dozen in the House – including Boebert’s.
In Friday’s interview, Boebert pinned some of the blame for that outcome on the agenda that Trump set for the first half of his second presidency. But she also said, “it’s all of the Republican party,” which had majorities in both congressional chambers dating back to the latter part of Joe Biden’s lone Oval Office term.
“I think it’s more all of us,” Boebert told the AP, alluding to high fuel prices after the Iran war, Republican infighting and unfulfilled promises. “We had solutions, and we didn’t take action.”
Boebert navigated various controversies throughout her time in Congress, which began with her supporting Trump’s lies that the 2020 election that he lost to Biden was unduly rigged by fraudsters.
A 2023 scandal saw her and a man with whom she was on a date get kicked out of a performance of the stage production Beetlejuice in Denver for inappropriate behavior, including vaping and groping each other. She later apologized for the conduct, which was recorded on surveillance video, saying: “I simply fell short of my values.”
Just weeks before her contest against Laubacher, an ethics complaint filed against her accused her of having sexual relationships with three staffers, including one who was paid to stay silent. She denied the allegations cited in the complaint, which she dismissed as “politically motivated”.
Boebert’s interview with the AP on Friday was not the first time she has spoken out against Trump. Notably, she was among the Congress members who most loudly called for the full disclosure of files related to the prosecution of Jeffrey Epstein, the late accused sex trafficker whose social circle encompassed the US and global elite – even after the Trump administration tried to convince her to drop her support for a measure that would compel such a release.
Trump responded to Boebert by calling her “dumb”. He also kicked off his second presidency by vetoing a Boebert-sponsored bill that would have funded a drinking water project in her district after the legislation unanimously cleared the House and Senate.
That prompted a critical statement from Boebert saying: “If this administration wants to make its legacy blocking projects that deliver water to rural Americans, that’s on them.”
Boebert struck a more conciliatory tone in Friday’s interview with the AP, remarking, “I respect President Trump, I still work with him, I want to continue to work with him. Not for him, with him.”
She only referred to her future plans in vague terms, telling the outlet: “Too many people come to Congress and get rich. I am not one of those. I’m gonna go make some money now.”

noticias.titulo: Princeton doctoral student reportedly detained by ICE on way back from conference
noticias.resumen: Eva Yi Xie was taken into custody at Washington DC airport after presenting research at neuroscience conference A Princeton University doctoral student has reportedly been taken into custody by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after traveling to Washington DC, for a neuroscience conference. Eva Yi Xie, a third-year PhD candidate at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute, was detained Thursday at a Washington-area airport, according to university officials and her colleagues. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
A Princeton University doctoral student has reportedly been taken into custody by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after traveling to Washington DC, for a neuroscience conference.
Eva Yi Xie, a third-year PhD candidate at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute, was detained Thursday at a Washington-area airport, according to university officials and her colleagues.
The Daily Princetonian, the university’s student newspaper, reported that Xie is believed to be held at an immigration detention facility in Chantilly, Virginia.
The Brody Lab, a Princeton neuroscience research group, identified Ronald Reagan National airport as the location of her detention in a post on X. According to the lab, Xie had been returning from the Society for Neuroscience conference, where she presented a research poster, when immigration authorities detained her.
Princeton has since secured legal representation for Xie, university spokesperson Michael Hotchkiss confirmed to the Daily Princetonian.
The detention also prompted a late-night message to graduate students from Rodney Priestley, dean of Princeton’s graduate school. Priestley sent the email to students at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute late Thursday night, acknowledging the situation and outlining the university’s response.
“We hope she is able to soon resume her studies at Princeton,” the email, obtained by the Daily Princetonian, read. “Please be assured that we will stay in close contact with the student’s family, her legal team, and her PNI colleagues as this situation is resolved.”
Xie’s current immigration status has not been publicly disclosed.
Xie moved to the US from China in 2016. She earned degrees in computer science and mathematics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2024, alongside a concentration in economics, according to her portfolio.
Her professional experience includes internships at Meta, Microsoft AI and IBM Research, among other organizations. At Princeton, her doctoral work focuses on the “neural basis of decision-making,” according to the Daily Princetonian.
The Guardian has reached out to ICE and Princeton for comment.
Xie’s detention comes amid an aggressive nationwide immigration enforcement campaign under Donald Trump, whose administration has made mass deportations a defining priority.
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) figures show that ICE deported 483,200 people and conducted more than 491,000 immigration arrests during fiscal year 2026, setting new annual records for the agency.
The Trump administration maintains that its enforcement efforts are intended to uphold immigration laws and remove dangerous offenders from the country. However, federal figures and independent reviews indicate that substantial numbers of people kept in ICE detention have no criminal convictions.
The enforcement campaign has affected international students and immigrants who originally entered the US legally. Xie’s detention now joins a string of prominent immigration cases that have drawn worldwide scrutiny and raised serious questions about the administration’s tactics.
Among those cases is Rümeysa Öztürk, a Tufts University student detained by immigration agents in Massachusetts last year. Videos of Öztürk’s arrest spread rapidly online, drawing widespread attention to the administration’s treatment of international students.
She was among numerous foreign students targeted over pro-Palestinian expression and protest during demonstrations against Israel’s military campaign in Gaza. Those protests have been particularly prominent on American university campuses.
Another high-profile case involved Mahmoud Khalil, a 30-year-old Palestinian permanent resident and Columbia University graduate student who emerged as a leading figure in campus protests last year.
