Khalil was arrested without due process in front of his pregnant wife and subsequently detained at an immigration facility. Authorities denied him permission to leave detention to attend the birth of his child.
The administration’s enforcement policies also came under intense scrutiny after the wrongful deportation of Kilmar Ábrego García, a Salvadoran immigrant who had been living in Maryland. Ábrego García was deported from the US to El Salvador in March 2025, despite the Trump administration’s admission that the removal was an error.

noticias.titulo: Latest botched execution prompts calls for US moratorium on lethal injections
noticias.resumen: Reinaldo Dennes screamed in pain and took over an hour to die – but Texas officials branded the execution a success A botched execution in Texas on Thursday night that lasted more than an hour and caused the prisoner to scream out, begging the Lord to end his suffering, has led to renewed calls for a nationwide moratorium that would pause all lethal injections. It took 63 minutes for Reinaldo Dennes , 70, to be proclaimed dead in the Huntsville penitentiary. The execution team had struggled to find a vein through which a lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital could be administered. Continue
noticias.texto:
A botched execution in Texas on Thursday night that lasted more than an hour and caused the prisoner to scream out, begging the Lord to end his suffering, has led to renewed calls for a nationwide moratorium that would pause all lethal injections.
It took 63 minutes for Reinaldo Dennes, 70, to be proclaimed dead in the Huntsville penitentiary. The execution team had struggled to find a vein through which a lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital could be administered.
Descriptions of the botched lethal injection bear chilling similarities to the recent failed execution in Tennessee of Christa Pike who in September became the only person ever to survive a full dose of execution drugs. Both Dennes and Pike were subjected to lethal injection protocols using pentobarbital, in both cases staff struggled to establish intravenous lines, and in both the prisoner expressed experiencing excruciating pain and burning sensations.
“The world saw what happened to Christa Pike, and now to Mr Dennes,” said Robin Maher, executive director of the authoritative Death Penalty Information Center. “The question now is, how many more of these botched executions will be tolerated by the American people?”
A harrowing eyewitness account of the night’s events was given by the prisoner’s spiritual adviser, the Rev Jeff Hood, who stood beside the gurney with his hand on Dennes’s shoulder. Hood describes how for up to five minutes Dennes fought against the pain.
“The pain!” Dennes shouted, according to Hood’s account.
“My leg, my leg, my leg,” he screamed, adding that his leg was “on fire”.
Hood writes in his account that Dennes “shifted on the gurney, back and forth, back and forth. He contorted. He grabbed hold of the leather straps and pulled against them until his body lifted. His shoulder drove up into my palm. Then it fell away. Then it drove up again. Twice he screamed, ‘It’s not working like it’s supposed to. Fuck. Fuck. Fuck. What is going on? Fuck. Fuck. Fuck.’”
Throughout the ordeal, Hood reports, the prisoner continued to pray, begging for an end to it.
“Take me home, Father. I don’t think this is normal. Take me, Father. Don’t let me suffer like this. C’mon.”
Dennes was convicted of capital murder in the 1996 death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer who was shot and killed in Houston.
Maya Foa, chief executive of the human rights group Reprieve, called for a moratorium on lethal injections. She said: “Lethal injection is torture – and Reinaldo Dennes was not sentenced to be tortured. Even the most ardent supporters of capital punishment must recognise that the dominant method of execution in the US is broken and cannot be allowed to continue.”
The Texas department of criminal justice insisted that the execution went fully according to plan. Its spokeswoman, Amanda Hernandez, told the New York Times that “as far as this agency is concerned, it is 100 percent not a botched execution. This was a successful execution, and we did follow all of the proper protocols to do it correctly.”
But such a blanket dismissal of any concerns failed to dampen a chorus of criticism. “Americans are now seeing the harsh reality of the death penalty, and I just don’t know how much longer state officials think they can double down on a story that is false,” Maher said.
Texas has been under the spotlight for many years for the way it obtains and stores its stocks of lethal execution drugs, a manoeuvre which it is careful to shroud in secrecy in an attempt to avoid public scrutiny. In the wake of an international boycott, the state’s prison service has taken to buying pentobarbital from compounding pharmacies that make up the chemicals to order.
Lawyers for condemned prisoners have long argued that the supplies can be of variable quality and are often held by the state beyond their expiration dates, running the risk of causing excruciating deaths.
The way that Texas conducts executions is likely to come under fresh review given the political upheaval that the state has experienced in the midterm elections. Not only did the governor’s mansion fall to the Democrat Gina Hinojosa, but Democrats flipped 20 state House seats as well as taking all seats up for election in the Texas supreme court and court of criminal appeals that have enormous power over capital cases.
Jonathan Groner, an expert on execution methods and emeritus professor of clinical surgery at Ohio State University, said that the Dennes execution illustrated why lethal injections were a “medical charade”. He said: “They imitate general anesthesia which is done in hospitals across the country thousands of times a day, by people with expertise, but when it is done in the death chamber without necessary equipment or skills, people suffer.”
Groner said that the location of the two IV lines placed in Dennes’s body – in a foot and in his shoulder – indicated that the execution team was struggling. “Placing IVs in the neck is very painful and difficult, and a last resort; and the foot is not a top choice because there is a long way to the heart for the medication to be circulated.”
He added: “It’s time for the medical profession to make a stand on executions. People are being tortured. We need to stop, and take a hard look at why we are still doing this.”

noticias.titulo: At COP31, conflict over climate science slows action on global warming
noticias.resumen: Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?
noticias.texto:
At COP31, conflict over climate science slows action on global warming
November 20, 2026
The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's plans to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.
But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.
"We are extremely concerned about the situation," said a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.
The IPCC's scientific assessments, published every six to seven years, provide the basis for major international climate agreements, including the 2015 Paris Agreement. The IPCC began evaluating the latest climate science in 1988 and its most recent report was published in 2023.
Researchers should have actually already started work on the next edition but the last plenary session was put on hold in October at the urging of Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Kenya.
"The IPCC finds itself in a difficult situation," a spokesperson from the German Environment Ministry told DW at COP. "We stand ready to help resolve this issue, so that the panel can continue its work. To that end, we are holding many discussions with various countries to explore possible solutions."
2028 climate report card risks delay
At the core of the dispute is the question of whether future UN climate talks base their negotiations on the latest scientific knowledge — or not.
That's especially relevant for the next "global stocktake," due in 2028, a report card on the world's climate efforts, which will shape action plans for countries around the world to lower planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.
The European Union, Brazil, the United Kingdom, small island states and several other countries especially at risk of the effects of climate change have called for the IPCC's seventh assessment report to be published in 2028, so it can be used to inform next steps for climate action. The report cover climate protection and impact.
"It's much more difficult without these scientific reports. Otherwise, we're just talking to ourselves or relying on information that's no longer current," said a delegation source.
But Russia, Iran, India and Saudi Arabia want the IPCC report postponed until 2029, after the global stocktake.
The official reason: the tight timeline would be detrimental to the quality of the research, and could hinder the participation of researchers and governments representing developing countries.
Disagreements over budget issues have also held up the IPCC's work. Among other expenses, the funds are used to pay the travel arrangements for the hundreds of volunteer scientists, especially those from poorer countries, to attend the IPCC sessions.
"No budget means no more IPCC," said a member from another delegation, also speaking on condition of anonymity.
It hasn't come to that point yet, but without planning certainty the whole process risks being delayed — along with the climate negotiations that depend on this knowledge.
Researchers with the IPCC, however, have said the timeline is attainable.
"We have no time to lose," said an open letter released in October signed by more than 100 researchers from 36 countries — including India and China. "We stand committed to continue working to deliver the [seventh assessment report] in a manner that is rigorous, timely and inclusive."
But while the dispute over the timeline won't alter the scientific findings themselves, it could delay their political impact.
EU stresses need to 'protect the integrity of climate science'
In its pre-COP communications, France accused the countries delaying the report's publication schedule of attempting to "obstruct science in order to lower the ambition of the global stocktake."
The IPCC isn't a stranger to attempts at political persuasion: At past climate conferences, delegates from many countries have regularly negotiated the exact phrasing of the summary reports intended for policymakers.
Speaking at COP31 on November 17, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said it was "fundamental to protect the integrity of climate science and the role of the IPCC as the source of best available science."
Although there is no vote on the IPCC at COP31, it's possible that its significance and a timeline for the next report will be included in the final declaration of the climate talks, expected this weekend.
Disinformation hindering climate action
The IPCC has been warning for years that disinformation is hindering global climate action. And the struggle for information and control over the narrative in Antalya hasn't just been limited to the IPCC.
DW was able to obtain a copy of a presentation which included misleading statements on the COP's electrification targets, one of the key goals at this year's talks. Turkey has proposed boosting global electrification to 35% by 2035, to reduce the world's reliance on planet-warming fossil fuels.
The contents of the presentation, said to have been leaked to some states in advance, was confirmed to DW by two countries. Its origin, however, could not be verified.
The presentation portrays electrification as a business venture undertaken by wealthy countries at the expense of poorer nations. The International Energy Agency, however, has calculated that developing countries could save around $100 billion (€90 billion) in fossil fuel imports by 2035 through electrification.
The presentation also gives the impression that all countries must meet fixed electrification targets. In fact, according to the UN, the 35% target represents a global goal, with individual countries free to determine their own national pathways.
This article was originally written in German.

noticias.titulo: Germany news: Kids take to streets over school, climate and costs
noticias.resumen: Thousands of young people turned in Germany demanding improvements in education, climate and affordability. Protesters say they aren't being taken seriously and will keep protesting until things change. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
Germany news: Kids take to streets over school, climate and costs
Published November 20, 2026last updated November 20, 2026
What you need to know
- Large rallies took place across Germany with young people protesting in Berlin, Cologne, Hamburg and elsewhere
- Young people feel politicians are not taking their concerns seriously
- Chancellor Merz announces Qatar to invest €15 billion more in German defense tech
- Lufthansa to reportedly slash 1,000 positions at Frankfurt and Munich hubs
Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines in Germany on Friday, November 20:
Police in Leipzig respond to fireworks attacks with water cannon
Police in the German state of Saxony say they deployed water cannons to Leipzig and used them on individuals who repeatedly shot fireworks at officers there after a large demonstration ended.
Police say roughly 2,500 people took part in a demonstration in Leipzig organized by the group Gen Z Takes Charge, far fewer than the estimated 7,000 who joined the first of these on October 31 (see entries below).
Across Germany, some 87,000 people joined in demonstrations, according to Gen Z Takes Charge.
Qatar to invest €15 billion more in German defense tech, says Merz
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday announced that Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani had pledged €15 billion ($16.5 billion) in new German defense and technology investments.
During a Berlin press conference with the emir, Merz said, "This strengthens both of us, particularly in future technologies such as artificial intelligence, semiconductors and aviation."
The Qatar-Germany collaboration is aimed at improving security and defense projects that also include defending against cyberattacks, with Merz saying, "We are particularly open to new partnerships in the defense industry."
That cooperation comes as both nations look to beef up defenses amid regional conflicts with global consequences.
The chancellor and the emir also stressed the fundamental importance of diplomacy in the resolution of conflict, with the two leaders' focused largely on Iran and the Middle East — and the need to get the flow of shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz closer to pre-war levels.
The emir called for deescalation, saying, "We are convinced that true political resolution is the only way to achieve lasting peace."
Merz added that the two agreed on the war in Ukraine, saying: "Russia must stop its time-wasting diplomatic games. Moscow has to finally sit down for real peace negotiations."
Merz was straightforward on Iran, saying Germany wants peace in the Middle East because it needs affordable energy.
He later called out Russian maritime marauding on the Black Sea, labeling it a threat to global food security.
Germany's Sky TV won't send staff to F1 race in Qatar
The German broadcaster Sky TV — not to be confused with the British-based Sky Sports F1 which is the largest English-language commercial F1 broadcaster — will not be sending any staff to the Formula 1 Qatar Grand Prix because of security concerns in connection with the conflict in Iran and the wider Middle East.
Sky TV announced the move on Friday, just a week before the contentious race weekend from November 27-29.
Sky will broadcast the entire race weekend as usual, but will use global feed images and will not send any of its own staff to Lusail International Circuit.
F1 races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia this spring were canceled as the US war with Iran was in its most active phase, with major disruptions to commercial flights.
The season-ending double header in Qatar and then the United Arab Emirates a week later has been in serious doubt ever since.
Nominally at least, both races are going ahead — and in all likelihood, teams will have already started dispatching equipment and personnel to the region to begin preparations by now.
Sky TV said it still planned to send a team to the season finale in Abu Dhabi, just across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, on December 6.
But it said it continued to "monitor developments and assess the situation on an ongoing basis."
Gen Z protesters rally around Germany
Organizers of the Gen Z Takes Charge protest group spoke out about why they took to the streets again.
Co-organizer Akram Selo called on Germany's leadership to meet the young people's demands.
"Talks won't make us stop demonstrating," he told RBB-Inforadio in comments aired on Friday.
"Essentially, our demands should be addressed, and we should be given assurances. That is what needs to happen, not empty promises," Selo added.
"So far, we feel that we aren't being taken seriously at all," he said. "The way we're being treated suggests that the aim is to sideline our demands and discriminate against us by focusing on other trivial matters."
Another group, the alliance "School strike against conscription" held its own protest to demand an immediate halt to surveys about potential availability for the German Armed Forces, or Bundeswehr, that are currently non-binding and only obligatory for teenage boys.
Merz urges Ukraine to push reforms in return for investment
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Ukraine must continue to push ahead swiftly with reforms, particularly on the rule of law and tackling corruption, if it hopes to receive a prerequisite for further financial aid and investment.
Merz made the comment at a business summit in Berlin that was organized by the German Chamber of Industry and Commerce.
"It is now essential to press ahead with these reforms swiftly and resolutely —particularly, and I say this openly, with regard to the rule of law and corruption," Merz told attendees.
The German chancellor said that sustained reform efforts by Kyiv were necessary to justify long-term Western support for Ukraine, adding that Germany would step up its backing in defense and humanitarian aid as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter.
"What we invest in Ukraine now, we will receive back many times over as dividends in the form of stability, export opportunities, joint projects, and growth," the German chancellor said.
In 2025, the two countries traded goods worth around €12 billion ($13 billion).
"Freedom and security are now unleashing forces of progress and resilience on a scale never seen before. This is precisely the stance we are now taking against the autocratic and imperialist actors of this world. We are the world of freedom," Merz added.
At home, Merz has faced increasing pressure to justify Germany's ongoing support for Ukraine. In recent regional elections, political parties opposing sending military aid have performed well.
Merz argued that Russia's war against Ukraine is an attack on democratic values everywhere.
Germany's electricity exports rise
Germany's electricity exports rose in the first three quarters of this year, according to official data released on Friday.
According to the energy association BDEW, Germany has been a net importer of electricity since 2023.
The neighbouring countries Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands, were the most important buyers of German electricity in the first nine months of 2026.
Together, they bought about half of all German electricity exports.
The volume of German electricity exported rose by 25.5% compared with the same period last year, to 48.8 terawatt-hours, while its value increased by 51.3% to €4.3 billion ($4.7 billion). 
Electricity imports into Germany fell by 13.3% in volume, but at 49.2 terawatt-hours they remained slightly above exports.
While imported electricity cost an average of €116 per megawatt-hour, 39% more than a year earlier, exported electricity from Germany averaged only €87 per megawatt-hour, some 20.6% more than a year earlier.
With a high share of renewable energy sources, wind and solar, Germany tends to offer electricity when supply is high and prices are low, but in times of shortage it has to pay higher prices for imported electricity.
German Finance Ministry launches dialogue on economic future
Finance Ministry officials said they are launching a dialogue process, dubbed "Germany 2035," to develop proposals for the future of the country's economy.
Officials want to study how Germany can secure growth and prosperity and what that could look like in terms of fiscal policy.
Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil will begin the dialogue process on December 2, when he welcomes economists from around the world to Berlin.
Additionally, think tanks, research organizations, universities and civil society groups have been asked to host workshops, which would take place in the first half of 2027.
Among 12 economic topics that the ministry seeks to explore are tax and fiscal policy, investment and domestic demand, industrial policy, energy and climate transition, foreign trade and sovereignty, and housing and local infrastructure.
The dialogue will culminate in a white paper, to be published in 2028, that can provide recommendations for Germany's economic future up to 2035.
Youth protests expected in German cities
A group called "Gen Z Takes Charge" (Gen Z regelt) has called for thousands of young people to demonstrate in many German cities.
The gathering comes almost three weeks after the first major youth protests hit Germany, inspired by the protests that took place in France in the last weeks.
Those protests, which took place on October 31, saw tens of thousands take to the streets across Germany, with crowds remaining largely peaceful, although rioting broke out in several cities, including Frankfurt, later in the evening.
Among the demands of the "Gen Z Takes Charge" group are increased funding for schools, addiction support and psychotherapy, affordable living, opposition to conscription and consistent action on climate change.
Another group, the Federal Pupils' Conference, has also organized its own demonstration at the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin, with police saying that some 5,000 people have already signed up.
The pupils' conference advocates for improvements in education policy in Germany, including school renovation, school social work, relief for teachers and the inclusion of climate action in curricula.
The demonstrations are set to begin in the morning and run until late afternoon.
President Steinmeier welcomes Emir of Qatar
President Frank-Walter Steinmeier welcomed the Emir of Qatar Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani in Berlin with military honors.
Steinmeier will also host a state banquet for the emir and his delegation in the evening. Al Thani is also expected to meet with Chancellor Friedrich Merz during the day.
The visit comes in the midst of tensions in the Middle East, with the war in Iran likely to be a critical topic in the talks between the two governments. Qatar is currently one of the mediators in the deadlocked conflict between the US and Iran.
Economic and bilateral relations are also expected to take center stage.
On Saturday, the emir will visit Germany's most populous state of North Rhine-Westphalia, where he will be greeted by its state premier Hendrik Wüst at the military section of Cologne/Bonn Konrad Adenauer Airport.
During the visit, Al Thani and North Rhine-Wesphalia leaders will hold an economic conference in the small city of Königswinter, near Bonn, where the Emir will also visit Drachenburg Castle.
Merz to visit German-Ukrainian business forum in Berlin
Following a political summit on Ukraine in Berlin yesterday, the German Chamber of Industry and Commerce (DIHK) said it would host a German-Ukrainian business forum.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz and German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche are expected to be in attendance, along with Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi, among others.
Christian Bruch, deputy chair of the Eastern Committee of the German Economy and chief executive of Siemens Energy, said German companies are committed to invest in Ukraine, despite Russia's ongoing war and were open to expand their business partnerships.
Bruch said bilateral trade was expected to rise to around €13 billion ($14.1 billion) in 2026.
Lufthansa to slash 1,000 jobs in Frankfurt, Munich — reports
German flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its airport hubs in Frankfurt and Munich, according to a company letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets.
The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa Airlines CEO Jens Ritter and four other managers.
The timeframe of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were apart of a previously announced downsizing.
In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization.
Lufthansa's parent company Lufthansa Group had 67,100 employees in Germany by the end of last year. In the letter seen by news agencies, Lufthansa said financial struggles were the reason behind the planned cuts.
"Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said, while pointing out that the company operated at a €180 million ($197 million) loss in the first nine months of this year.
In addition, Lufthansa Airlines is now in its third straight year of being unprofitable.
In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook.
WATCH: Leaked files raise questions over Deutsche Bank's Russia ties
Leaked documents raise new questions about Deutsche Bank's dealings in Russia up to Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, adding to scrutiny over the bank's risk controls and past controversies.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Tag and welcome to DW's daily coverage of Germany-related news on Friday.
Lufthansa is reportedly planning on cutting jobs as the German flag carrier faces financial difficulties.
Meanwhile, youth-protests are expected across Germany and Qatari's emir is visiting Berlin, where he is expected to meet with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Stay tuned for the latest on all this and more throughout the day from the heart of Europe.

noticias.titulo: Better educated than ever — yet Germany's Gen Z is being shut out of its own future
noticias.resumen: Never before have young people faced so many challenges. Young Germans are asking: Will I be better off than my parents later in life?
noticias.texto:
Gen Z in Germany: Better educated, bleaker future
November 20, 2026
It is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training. And finding an affordable place to live in a big city, and finally starting to live independently is becoming almost impossible.
Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on issues that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It, therefore, shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe once again took to the streets this Friday, which was World Children's Day too, to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 towns and cities.
What particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.
One example of such rhetoric was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.
It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran a headline that translated as: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today."
"Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," says Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests."
Gen Z is better educated but faces a bleaker future
The 18-year-old Sczygiol is almost an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW). This year's report, entitled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future," is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z.
UN researchers surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries for the report, some of whose findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them, with 78% of adolescents across the globe completing at least lower secondary education. But finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise.
This economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, people often do not achieve financial independence until they are in their mid-to-late 20s, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities before their early-to-mid 30s.
Young people are underrepresented in the German parliament
Nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30."
Young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," says Brod.
He is somewhat close to the political decision-making process as he has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an important step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.
Political participation often remains purely symbolic
Nevertheless, both Brod and Sczygiol have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.
"Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," says Brod.
Sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people."
The promise that 'our children will have a better life' no longer holds true
Medical student Amelie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva in May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.
Her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have said 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We young people need to be able to believe in our future again!"
This article was originally published in German.

noticias.titulo: Measles in America: Here's a constructive approach to beating the disease, based on Brazil's experience
noticias.resumen: The US is now officially a measles contagion zone. By mid-2026, there were more infections than in all of the previous year. But the country could beat measles again, just like Brazil did two years ago.
noticias.texto:
Brazil beat measles. The US can, too.
November 20, 2026
Health experts saw it coming — the fact that after 26 years, the US would lose its status as measles-free. Back in July 2026, DW reported how one epidemiologist had suggested an 'amnesia' about the measles risk was pushing a growth in US infections.
Four months later, it was official. On November 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) said the US had lost its measles elimination status, along with Mexico.
But it doesn't have to stay this way.
Look at Brazil, where in 2019, with more than 21,000 measles cases, the country also lost its measles-free status. But within five years — during the COVID-19 pandemic — it fought and won back its measles-free status. And since 2024, Brazil has stayed measles-free, even as the highly contagious disease spread across the rest of the Americas.
In 2026, with the data available up to the time of writing this article, Brazil had only had 70 measles cases. They were all linked to infections brought in from abroad, often from neighboring Peru.
Brazil has fewer people than the US, about 213 million compared to the US's nearly 350 million, but the two countries are similar in size. So the comparison is worth considering.
What Brazil does differently from the US
Brazil moves fast. The PAHO asks countries to respond within 72 hours of a suspected measles case. Here's Brazil's own rule:
- Report cases within 24 hours
- Investigate within 48 hours
- Vaccinate people close to the case within 72 hours
It has also made hunting for cases a national habit. In a program called "Dia S," health workers knock on doors and visit schools, daycare centers and churches to find people who may be sick but have not seen a doctor.
Brazil also holds mass vaccination days called "Dia D." There was one in November, in the area where Brazil borders Colombia and Peru.
If someone is diagnosed with measles, health workers try to track down every person the patient may have met ("contact persons") and vaccinate them and other people living nearby.
The country has so far provided more than 16 million doses of the measles vaccine in 2026 and has donated 500,000 doses to Peru.
Brazil isn't perfect, though. According to official estimates from the World Health Organization, only 76% of children got both required doses of the vaccine in 2025 — well short of the 95% target. Experts warn this leaves the country at risk because measles is so highly contagious. A country needs to be as close to 100% immunized as possible to protect people and stop the disease from spreading.
"Elimination is not a trophy that we win once and put on a shelf. It must be protected every day," says PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa.
Why the US lost its measle-free status
The US lost its measles-free status because the PAHO found that the same strain of the virus had been spreading in the country for 12 months or more. Mexico and Bolivia lost their status on the same day as the US.
The US has had more than 5,400 cases in 2026 (at time of writing), more than twice as many as in all of 2025, and about 19 times as many as in 2024. Nearly everyone who got sick with measles was unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status.
US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on new vaccination recommendations for children in August 2026. It came at a time, when, as we reported, experts said people had stopped getting vaccinated against measles because infection rates were low. But like PAHO's Barbosa said, neglecting vaccination when infection rates are low is a mistake.
To be fair, Trump's executive order listed the measles vaccine in a top category of vaccinations recommended for every child. But the administration's stance on vaccination in general is unclear.
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has often declared opposition to vaccination, including against measles, advising people to take vitamin A instead. In Texas, this led to children being hospitalized with toxic levels of the supplement, and left them with no protection against measles.
Before the COVID-19 pandemic, 95% of US kindergartners had their measles shots. Now, it's 92%, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Protection (CDC). That leaves about 280,000 kindergartners in the US unprotected.
In the Texas counties where a 2025 measles outbreak began, coverage was as low as 77% at the time.
US children usually need vaccines to start school, but most states let parents opt out for religious or personal reasons, with no doctor involved.
But vaccination rates have fallen elsewhere in the world as well, including in Europe. In Germany, where measles infections have also risen, experts blame anti-vaccination rhetoric that emerged during the COVID-19 pandemic.
The 95% measles vaccination rule explained
It all comes down to math.
A person sick with measles can infect up to18 other, unprotected people. With vaccination, it is possible to increase the number of protected people and lower the number of people the sick person can infect.
To prevent a measles outbreak, a community needs about 95% of people to be vaccinated and/or immune. The vaccination consists of two doses of the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) vaccine.
But even after the two doses, a person can expect to have only 97% protection against measles — 3% short of full protection — so, nearly everyone in the community has to be vaccinated to keep the average level of protect as close to 100% as possible.
"For some diseases like measles, even a small decrease in vaccination rates can lead to more outbreaks of disease [so] community immunity requires over 95% of susceptible individuals to be immunized," says Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics.
And the 95% has to hold everywhere. A good national average can be affected by, for example, a single school where only 70% of the children are vaccinated. And that is where the outbreak is likely to start.
The picture is mixed worldwide
Around the world, measles deaths have dropped by 88% since 2000, thanks to vaccines.
But progress has stalled. Only about three out of four children worldwide get both doses of the vaccine. The biggest outbreaks right now are in Bangladesh, Indonesia and Guatemala.
Data from Europe shows that things can get better. In the European Union, cases fell from more than 35,000 in 2024 to about 2,300 the following year, with no measles-related deaths.
Romania went from more than 30,000 cases in 2024 to about 4,200 in 2025.
In Hungary, where 99% of children are vaccinated, there have been no measles cases in the past year.
But in January, six European countries lost their measles-free status, including the UK, Spain and Austria. Across Europe, eight out of ten people who got measles in 2025 were unvaccinated.
The Americas are seeing a major surge in measles infections, with more than 58,000 cases in 2026, over four times as many as by November in 2025. Guatemala has been hit hardest, with almost 35,000 cases.
The deadliest outbreaks are in Africa. African Union countries have so far reported nearly 1,800 measles deaths in 2026, about 1,650 of them in Democratic Republic of Congo. Yet, Sudan, despite the war, raised first-dose measles coverage by 22 percentage points in 2025, which was the world's largest gain.
What you need to know about measles
Measles is extremely contagious. One person can infect up to 18 unprotected people, which makes it about 12 times more contagious than the flu.
The virus can linger in the air for up to two hours after a sick person has left the room. And people spread it before they know they are sick. Someone with measles is contagious for four days before the rash appears and four days after.
It's not just a rash. About one in five unvaccinated people who get measles in the US ends up in the hospital. Measles can weaken the immune system for years, making it harder to fight off other infections.
But it's preventable. Two doses of the MMR vaccine (which also protects against mumps and rubella) protect 97% of people for life.

noticias.titulo: Is Pakistan backing anti-Taliban groups in Afghanistan?
noticias.resumen: The Taliban rulers in Afghanistan have accused Pakistan of aiding and sheltering armed resistance groups. The allegations come amid heightened tensions and are likely to deepen the rift between the two neighbors.
noticias.texto:
Is Pakistan backing anti-Taliban groups in Afghanistan?
November 20, 2026
The Taliban authorities in Afghanistan claim that the Pakistani government is supporting armed Afghan groups that are opposed to their rule, an accusation Islamabaddenies.
Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi recently alleged that Pakistan had launched a "project to destabilize Afghanistan."
He claimed that "thousands of armed individuals have gathered along the Durand Line [Afghanistan-Pakistan border] to undermine the stability achieved in Afghanistan."
The accusations come after months of border clashes between Afghan Taliban and Pakistani forces.
In July, the Afghanistan Freedom Front (AFF), an anti-Taliban group, reportedly clashed with Taliban forces in the Zebak district of Badakhshan, a northeastern Afghan province. The group said it also carried out attacks in Nooristan and Kunar provinces in October.
Another "resistance group," the United Front of Afghanistan, claimed it attacked Taliban forces in Kandahar province along the border with Pakistan.
"The people who created insecurity in Badakhshan crossed from Chitral [in Pakistan] and later fled back to Chitral. They had been brought in. Even Pakistani military personnel were with them," alleged Zabihullah Mujahid, the Taliban's main spokesperson, in an interview with DW's Pashto-Dari service in September.
Pakistan's Ministry of Information swiftly dismissed the allegations as propaganda.
Groups that oppose Taliban rule in Afghanistan say they are not supported by any external force, and their resistance is purely indigenous.
Pakistan's 'leverage' amid tense ties
More than five years since returning to power in Kabul, the Taliban have consolidated their control over Afghanistan and largely suppressed both armed resistance groups and political dissidents.
Shinkai Karokhail, a former Afghan lawmaker, told DW it would be logistically difficult for anti-Taliban Afghan groups to cross the Pakistani border and enter Afghanistan without Islamabad's support, referring to clashes in Badakhshan and Nooristan provinces. "It is simply impossible," she said.
The Taliban themselves maintained close ties with Pakistan in the 1990s during their first stint in power. Some US officials have even claimed that Islamabad didn't relinquish its support to the Islamist group even after the 2001 September 11 terrorist attacks in the United States. Islamabad has always refuted these allegations.
Afrasiab Khattak, a Pakistani political analyst and former senator, believes that Pakistani support for anti-Taliban groups is "real."
"Taliban opponents come to Islamabad, hold meetings, and it is a part of Pakistan's policy toward Afghanistan," he told DW.
Qandil Abbas, an associate professor of politics and international relations at Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad, disagrees.
"Pakistan may provide political support [to Taliban opponents], but not military support," she told DW.
Ali Ahmad Jalali, a professor at the Near East South Asia Center for Strategic Studies at the National Defense University in Washington DC, said it is possible that Islamabad is backing opponents of the Taliban as "leverage."
"When such incidents take place along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border, and given Pakistan's history of support for Afghan groups, it would not be surprising if Pakistan is supporting these groups," Jalali said.
Islamabad accuses Taliban of similar tactics
Pakistani officials have repeatedly demanded that the Taliban take action against anti-Pakistan militant groups, particularly the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), a militant group responsible for attacking Pakistani civilians and soldiers, and the Baloch Liberation Army (BLA), an outlawed armed separatist group active in its western Balochistan province.
Islamabad alleges that these groups organize and launch attacks on Pakistan from Afghan territory with Taliban support.
"Meaningful progress requires Afghan authorities to address legitimate security concerns of neighboring countries, particularly the threat of terrorism," Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said this week at the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) summit in Islamabad.
The Pakistani government said on Friday that Afghanistan was not invited to participate in the ECO gathering as Pakistan does not recognize the Taliban regime in Kabul.
Jalali, who served as Afghanistan's interior minister from 2003 to 2005, argued that Islamabad is demanding something the Taliban may neither be willing nor able to provide.
"Pakistan wants the Taliban to cooperate in fighting against groups such as the TTP. But the TTP has long fought alongside the Afghan Taliban. There are ideological as well as friendly ties between the two. They seek a similar political system, and some Afghan Taliban members may even be among TTP fighters," the analyst added.
Experts also point to the Taliban's efforts to strengthen relations with India, Pakistan's long-standing regional rival, as a cause of concern for Islamabad.
Malek Sitez, an Afghan international relations researcher, argued that Pakistan was not keen on Kabul getting closer to New Delhi but added that Pakistan no longer had the kind of influence over Afghanistan that it had in the past.
Is Pakistan seeking to remove the Taliban from power?
Despite accusations and counteraccusations from both sides, Jalali did not believe that Pakistan was seeking regime change in Afghanistan.
"I do not think Pakistan can or wants to overthrow the Taliban and replace them with another group," he underlined. Instead, he stressed, Islamabad's objective is to pressure the Taliban into cooperating against the TTP.
Aziz Barez, a political analyst, was of the view that Afghan groups opposed to the Taliban could not fully trust Islamabad, adding that they may welcome alleged Pakistani support but are also aware that such backing could be temporary.
"It is possible that Pakistan and the Taliban will resolve their differences tomorrow and become close allies again," he told DW.
Ahmad Waheed Ahmady and Helay Asad contributed to this report.

noticias.titulo: Germany face belgium in Nations League quarterfinals — Klopp plays down favorites tag
noticias.resumen: Germany coach Jürgen Klopp is looking to "carry positive momentum forward" as his team draw neighboring Belgium in the quarterfinals of the UEFA Nations League.
noticias.texto:
Germany draw Belgium in Nations League quarterfinals
November 20, 2026
Germany, who finished top of Group A2 following their 5-0 win over the Netherlands in Berlin on Monday are to face Belgium in the Nations League quarterfinals—after they finished second in Group A1. The Belgians recently came up with a statement result of their own, beating Italy 4-1. The match-up between the neighboring countries promises to be closely contested, with Belgium sitting at No. 8 in the men's rankings, three places above Germany.
The head coach of Belgium is former Bayern Munich player Mark van Bommel, who took over from Rudi Garcia following the World Cup, where they were knocked out by eventual champions Spain in the quarterfinals.
Germany head into the knockout phase on a high note, not only because they won their group, but also the way they performed in their last two matches, against Serbia and the Netherlands in the group stage.
Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp followed the draw, held in Nyon on Friday, from the German FA's (DFB) Frankfurt offices. He played down the notion that Germany enter the tie as the favorites.
"I've practically never given it any thought. It's never interested me," he said.
"An awful lot can happen in that time. We're very happy with the final impression we left, yet we're also fully aware that we're only at the very beginning of a development process. We want to carry this positive momentum forward—there's still a great deal to be done."
Historical success for Germany against Belgium
The matches are slated for March 25 and March 30, 2027, and having won their group, Germany will have home-field advantage for the second leg.
Germany and Belgium have faced each other 26 times to date, with West Germany and Germany having the upper hand with 20 wins, five defeats and one draw.
Should Germany advance to the semifinals, they will go on to face the winner of England and Norway – a World Cup quarterfinals rematch.
In the other two semifinals matchups, the Netherlands drew Portugal, while the top pairing sees Spain face France in a rematch of one of last summer's World Cup semifinals.
The "Final Four" mini tournament is to be held from June 9 to 13 but the host venue won't be determined until the semifinal lineup has been completed.

noticias.titulo: EU and UK strike 'landmark deal' to strengthen ties after Brexit
noticias.resumen: The European Union and the United Kingdom have agreed on "landmark" deals on youth mobility and trade. Leaders on both sides praised the agreement as they seek to rebuild ties.
noticias.texto:
EU and UK strike 'landmark deal' to strengthen ties after Brexit
November 20, 2026
European Union top officials and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced deals on trade and youth mobility at Friday's Brussels summit.
This might be the first step to rebuild ties, a decade after Britain voted to leave the EU.
During the delegations' meeting, Burnham said the deal was a "landmark agreement," while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it a "turning point" in relations.
'A good day for Britain' and 'A good day for Europe'
"This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe," Burnham said.
Speaking at the joint press conference, European Council President Antonio Costa said the bloc respected the British decision to leave the EU and would respect its choice to strengthen ties in the post-Brexit era.
He said jokingly that the EU and UK "may drive on the opposite sides of the road, but what matters is they are heading for the same direction."
Burnham said that the deals were made with young people in mind, adding: "This deal is for you. This deal really is about lifting your life chances."
'Brexit took opportunities from young people'
He went further and said "Brexit took opportunities from young people," and that they have to "open up new opportunities" for young people.
Von der Leyen said the youth experience project would "open horizons and create friendships that will last a lifetime."
She said the trade agreement is a "two way street" and it means "more choice for the customers."
Von der Leyen also mentioned the agreement on the carbon market, saying that it would cut emissions and generate investments in cleaner industries.
She also said Britain will rejoin the Erasmus+ program, adding, "We miss them so much."
Burnham said the agreements reached Friday, however, represent the most the UK could achieve at the moment, "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it."
In September, Burnham said he would seek a political consensus on the country's future relationship with the EU, even suggesting he could campaign to take Britain back into the bloc at the next election.
"Britain and Europe share values, interests and a global neighborhood. In a more dangerous world, we are stronger together. A closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe," Burnham said as he arrived in Brussels.
What do the deals involve?
The three key agreements establish ways to:
- Simplify food exports by reducing red tape
- Link the UK and EU emissions-trading systems
- Establish a youth experience scheme
The "youth experience scheme" would allow 100,000 people under 30 from each side to reside for up to three years in each other's territory for work, study or travel without being subject to existing visa requirements.
No deal was reached on tuition fees for EU students studying in Britain, a deal-breaker for the bloc. The EU has pressed for the UK to reduce university tuition fees for EU students to the same level paid by British students
"There will be further discussions coming out of it on issues including on tuition fees," Burnham said.
Von der Leyen said she was confident negotiators would reach a solution on tuition fees, "We will be working on that in the next month and as we have a track record of finding solutions,."
On the food deal, the EU and UK have agreed to scrap certificates and border checks on food and animal products to ease post-Brexit trade. In return, Britain will align more closely with EU food safety and animal health rules.
They also agreed to link their emissions-trading systems, allowing them to recognize each other's carbon allowances and exempt traded goods from carbon border taxes.
According to the AFP news agency, London estimates the deal could boost the British economy by 3.8 billion pounds annually, and spare 6.5 billion pounds worth of steel, aluminum and other industrial exports from additional taxation.
Leaders said they will establish a "structured dialogue on migration." Their joint summit statement said this would include "engagement with third countries" and "returns to third countries," among other issues.
The two sides agreed to launch formal talks on economic security and strengthen cooperation on export controls and supply chains, among other areas.
How do Brits feel about Brexit now?
On Monday, Burnham said it was the "obvious truth" that Britain had lost more than it had gained from Brexit.
Polling firm YouGov runs a regular tracker on whether the UK was right or wrong to vote to quit.
Since mid-2022, a majority of people surveyed said Britain was wrong to leave.In September, the "Bregret" camp rose to 60% — the highest ever.

noticias.titulo: Turkey takes control of opposition broadcaster Sozcu TV
noticias.resumen: In the latest in a series of raids and arrests, another major pro-opposition Turkish broadcaster has been brought under state control. This is the third in a year.
noticias.texto:
Turkey takes control of opposition broadcaster Sozcu TV
November 20, 2026
Another important opposition media outlet in Turkey has been placed under state control. On Tuesday morning, authorities raided the offices of the television broadcaster Sozcu TV and the news portal Sozcu.com.tr, and arrested several executives.
A trustee has also been appointed: The state deposit protection fund, TMSF, which usually administers the assets of insolvent companies, has been put in charge. Sozcu was one of the last big media companies in Turkey to regularly report critically on the government of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
A large police contingent raided the broadcaster's headquarters in Istanbul, with counterterrorism officers searching the offices. According to Sozcu, its chairwoman, Funda Tuncer Sidali, and Asim Akgul, the former chief executive of the Sozcu group, were among those arrested.
The broadcaster did not initially announce the appointment of the trustee on its digital channels. It did call on its audience to follow it under a new account. The leader of the main opposition party, Ozgur Ozel, declared on X: "You will never be able to prevent this nation's voice from rising, its rebellion from being heard, its cry from echoing."
Accused of ties to the Gülen movement
The Istanbul public prosecutor's office has confirmed the arrangements. It justified the investigation with claims of a suspected connection between the owner of Sozcu, Burak Akhay, and the Gülen movement. The Turkish government blames this movement, which was once allied to Erdogan, for the attempted coup in 2016, and has designated it a terrorist organization.
According to the investigators, Akbay is said to have used foreign bank accounts to finance two companies involved in media activities on behalf of the Gülen movement. They claim there is strong suspicion that he was able, in this way, to hold a leadership position in the organization.
A familiar pattern in Turkey
It is not new for the Turkish state to take over media organizations by appointing trustees. Many media companies accused of being close to the Gülen movement were brought under state control in this way after the attempted coup in 2016. What is new is that for about a year now this is also happening to media seen as pro-opposition.
Sozcu is not the first opposition broadcaster to be targeted by the authorities. The TELEI TV channel was searched on October 24, 2025. Its editor-in-chief, Merdan Yanardag, was arrested on charges of espionage and remains in custody. The offices of Halk TV were raided on October 14 this year. There, too, a trustee was put in charge.
In the space of just over a year, three of the most important opposition television channels have been brought under state control. Observers see this as another step toward an increasingly authoritarian and politically isolated system.
The opposition is being silenced
Berk Esen, a political scientist with Sabanci University in Istanbul, sees these measures as a significant weakening of the opposition in the public domain.
Esen told DW that the government may first have acted behind the scenes and tried to bring Sozcu to heel politically. When this didn't succeed, it invoked the judiciary. Esen says Turkey is increasingly moving toward an authoritarian system. The attempt to prevent opposition organizations and media from gaining strength and influence is part of this.
Esen describes the opposition's success in local government elections in March 2024 as a political turning point. Since then, he says, the government has seen its chances of winning political competitions at the ballot box receding. "It's become harder for the AKP to win elections," says Esen. "That's why it's attacking the opposition and the free media both at once."
Several opposition mayors have also been arrested in recent months and replaced by trustees. They include the mayor of Istanbul and presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu, who has been in detention since his arrest in March last year. He is regarded as one of Erdogan's most promising challengers.
'Black winter for press freedom'
The Turkish Journalists' Association (TGC) spoke of a "black winter for press freedom," and announced its solidarity with all those affected. It described the recent developments as a serious attack on press freedom. The fact that a trustee had been appointed, first at Halk TV and now at Sozcu, showed how the media climate in Turkey has deteriorated, it said.
"These days, too, shall pass," the TGC declared. "When that day comes, those journalists who seek the truth today will be remembered, as will the decisions that prevent the public from hearing that truth."
This article has been translated from German.

noticias.titulo: Africa at COP31: Will climate cash finally flow?
noticias.resumen: As the curtains draw to a close on COP31 in Antalya, one question looms large for African countries: Will climate promises finally translate into the funding African communities need to cope with a warming world?
noticias.texto:
Africa at COP31: Will climate cash finally flow?
November 20, 2026
For millions across the continent, climate change is no longer an abstract environmental concern debated in conference halls. It is already reshaping daily life, livelihoods and even decisions about where people can live.
In Zimbabwe, Harare resident Tsitsi Moyo says the effects are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore: "The extreme heat wave we have been experiencing I think also has issues to do with rainfall patterns."
Jane Okello has witnessed similar changes in Uganda, describing increasingly erratic weather, including periods of unusually heavy rainfall associated with El Nino.
Their experiences reflect a wider trend across the continent. Communities that depend on predictable seasons for agriculture, water supplies and income are finding it harder to plan for the future as weather patterns become more extreme and less reliable.
For some, the consequences go beyond disrupted harvests or shrinking water supplies. Climate pressures are also influencing migration patterns. According to Professor Alfred Ngomanda, permanent secretary of the Gabon Climate Council, environmental stress can push people to leave their homes in search of more favorable conditions and more secure livelihoods.
Climate change is rarely the sole reason people migrate. However, droughts, floods, declining agricultural output and other environmental strains often intensify existing economic and social challenges, making displacement more likely.
As African countries prepare to make their case at the climate negotiations, Ngomanda stressed that the continent must emphasize the global importance of its natural resources.
"We will go to Ethiopia [the host of COP32 in November 2027] to assert that the Congo Basin is a stabilizing element for the global climate, and not just for Africans," Ngomanda said.
Why climate finance matters
At the heart of the discussions at COP31 is climate finance, the funding used to help countries reduce greenhouse gas emissions and adapt to the impacts of climate change.
COP, or the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, brings together governments from around the world to negotiate action on global warming. The talks build on the Paris Agreement, adopted at COP21 in 2015, which aims to keep global temperature rise well below 2 degrees Celsius while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 degrees.
For African countries, the challenge is not simply making climate commitments, but securing the resources needed to turn those commitments into reality.
Opening the conference, United Nations (UN) Secretary-General Antonio Guterres highlighted what he described as a fundamental injustice in the global response to climate change.
"Developing countries face a double injustice: They bear the brunt of climate change but struggle to access the finance they urgently need," Guterres said.
The scale of the financing gap remains stark. According to the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa, the continent received about $52 billion (€44.5 billion) in climate finance in 2022, far short of its estimated annual requirement of $190 billion. Much of that funding also comes as loans, adding pressure to already strained public finances.
The shortfall is especially significant given that Africa contributes only about 4% of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet remains one of the regions most vulnerable to climate change.
African governments are therefore calling for funding that is more predictable, accessible and affordable, particularly for programs intended to help communities adapt to extreme weather, strengthen resilience and protect livelihoods.
From commitments to action
African negotiators say the focus now must be on making sure that climate commitments produce tangible results on the ground. Speaking at a press conference on November 19, Veronica Nonhlanhla Jakarasi, lead negotiator for the African Group of Negotiators, argued that the continent needs a dedicated mechanism to translate climate proposals into funded projects.
"What we need is a mitigation implementation facility that moves Africa's proposals into actual financing and projects on the ground."
She said such a facility would help direct more resources to the continent while supporting economic growth, green industrialization and the development of Africa's critical minerals sector without driving up emissions.
Mitigation focuses on reducing greenhouse gas emissions, while adaptation involves preparing for and responding to climate impacts. African countries insist both are essential if the continent is to pursue development while coping with increasingly severe weather events.
Negotiations remain difficult. A revised COP31 draft circulated on November 19, removed references to phasing out fossil fuels and dropped a proposed annual adaptation-finance target of $120 billion. While talks are ongoing and the text does not represent a final agreement, the changes underscore the political and financial battles that still shape international climate action.
For women like Moyo and Okello, however, the significance of COP31 will ultimately be measured far from the conference venue. Climate finance can support drought-resistant farming, improved water management systems, early-warning networks and infrastructure intended to withstand floods and extreme heat. But pledges alone will not deliver those outcomes. Countries must be able to access the money, implement projects effectively and ensure support reaches the communities that need it most.
Gerauds Wilfried Obangome contributed to this article

noticias.titulo: Myanmar genocide ruling: Rohingya say struggle for justice not over
noticias.resumen: The ICJ has held Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya and ordered restitution and reparations. Community members have hailed the ruling, but caution that achieving real change will be long and hard.
noticias.texto:
Myanmar genocide ruling: Rohingya say struggle for justice not over
November 20, 2026
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the country's Rohingya community a decade ago, in a historic judgment hailed by the long-persecuted minority and rights groups.
The United Nations' top court also ordered the Myanmar government to prevent a repeat of the crimes, undertake legal reforms to protect the Rohingya and provide the victims with reparations or, where it cannot, compensate them.
The judgment came seven years after The Gambia filed the case with the court, accusing Buddhist-majority Myanmar of a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder against the country's predominantly Muslim Rohingya community in 2016 and 2017.
It is the ICJ's first finding of genocide against a state, and the first ruling in any of the cases filed against Myanmar or its leaders in multiple courts around the world.
How do Rohingya see the ruling?
Lucky Karim was 14 when she and her mother and brothers were forced to flee their village in Rakhine State to escape the Myanmar military's advance in August 2017.
She joined the roughly 700,000 other Rohingya who crossed the border into Bangladesh at the time.
Now a prominent Rohingya activist, Karim heard the court's judgment in person in The Hague.
"For me … it's a very personal day, a personal moment, as someone who survived and escaped genocide in 2017. It took nearly a decade for the world to finally hear our voice," she said.
"For generations the [Myanmar] military stripped away our identity, our citizenship, tried to erase us from our homeland, told the world that what they did to us in 2017 was merely clearance operations, or worse, that we didn't even exist," said Wai Wai Nu, another Rohingya activist and former political prisoner.
Today, she said, their decades of persecution "is actually validated, and the truth has come out."
Tun Khin, a Rohingya activist and plaintiff in a universal jurisdiction case against Myanmar in Argentina, called the judgment "a historic moment" and "a big day for the Rohingya."
The press bureau of the Myanmar president's office did not respond to DW's requests for comment. The government's main mouthpiece, the state-run New Light of Myanmar newspaper, made no mention of the ruling online.
'Far in excess of what was justified'
Throughout the trial, Myanmar claimed that its actions in Rakhine State were strictly part of legitimate counterinsurgency operations against the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, an armed group in the area that had been attacking police and military posts.
The ICJ flatly rejected the argument. "The court views casualties and damage far in excess of what was justified by military necessity," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said, reading from the 15-judge panel's 9-6 ruling in The Hague.
"The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations," he added.
A UN-backed fact-finding mission concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the pogroms. By some estimates, about 1 in 5 of them were children.
Michael Becker, an associate professor of international human rights law at Trinity College Dublin in Ireland, said the court's ruling was both historic and "monumental" not only because it found a state responsible for genocide, but also because "it demonstrates that establishing genocidal intent is not impossible."
He noted that the panel took pains to show that The Gambia's case passed the court's established "only reasonable inference" test for genocidal intent. The ruling also "helpfully affirms" that forced transfer, targeting children and sexual violence could be relevant factors, he added.
'Not conditions amenable to … relief'
Amid elation among the Rohingya and rights groups, the focus quickly turned to making the court's prescribed remedies real.
The ICJ said Myanmar was now obliged to allow the "safe, voluntary and dignified" return of those who fled, investigate the crimes, and prosecute those found responsible. It also told Myanmar to return or replace all stolen property or, within two years, show the court it was compensating victims for what it could not.
But those behind the genocide, including former military chief and current president, Min Aung Hlaing, have remained in power since toppling Myanmar's democratically elected government in 2021.
Much of the country, including Rakhine State, is still in the midst of a brutal civil war between the military and an array of armed resistance groups. And the group that now controls most of Rakhine, the Arakan Army, is widely accused of persecuting the Rohingya as well.
"These are not conditions amenable to realizing the relief ordered by the ICJ anytime soon," said Becker.
Enforcing the court's orders ultimately falls to the UN Security Council. But China and Russia, which both back the Myanmar government and keep it well armed, would "almost certainly" veto any proposed Council resolution that aims to punish Myanmar, said Richard Horsey, senior Asia adviser at the International Crisis Group.
"Whatever pressure there is will come from governments and the General Assembly, not the Council," he said.
Immediately after Thursday's ICJ judgment, the UK said it was expelling Myanmar's defense attache in London and would call for a UN Security Council session to discuss the court's decision.
'This is just the beginning'
A number of Western governments have already buried Myanmar under round after round of sanctions over the past decade, but with little to no apparent effect.
Myanmar is even taking tentative steps to shake off its global pariah status and restore regular relations with the rest of the world. Min Aung Hlaing has been warmly hosted by eight Asian and Eastern European countries since arranging his transition from army general to president earlier this year following rigged elections.
Horsey said the ICJ judgment would slow those efforts but not reverse them.
"Most governments in the region will keep engaging, but those with Muslim-majority publics, especially Malaysia and Indonesia, will find it harder to justify at home," he said.
Japan and South Korea, which maintain extensive business ties with Myanmar, are likely to remain cautious, he added, while the United States, which has reportedly had recent meetings with senior government officials, would keep up a transactional relationship.
"For [Myanmar], the real cost is that every government that deals with it will now have to explain why it is engaging a state found responsible for genocide," Horsey said.
'They want to return home'
The Rohingya, meanwhile, expect a long and difficult fight for real change.
"A judgment in The Hague will not on its own stop the bombs or feed starving families or stop the atrocities in Rakhine State," said Wai Wai Nu. "It is imperative that the international community take action to enforce the ruling," she added.
Karim said other countries should use the ICJ judgment "as a tool to open every possible door to help us and protect the people on the ground."
The Gambia's lead counsel in the case, Arsalan Suleman, said the genocide ruling could be used to help hold the perpetrators to account in other courts. The International Criminal Court, for one, is weighing an arrest warrant request for Min Aung Hlaing for alleged crimes against humanity, also against the Rohingya.
Tun Khin said the wish of most Rohingya is simple, if still hard to foresee. "They want to return home, to their houses and own villages," he said, but this time with full citizenship rights and legal protection.
"It will take time," he acknowledged. "This is just the beginning."

noticias.titulo: FIFA presidential election 2027: Infantino facing Diallo and Tashima — could an alliance change everything?
noticias.resumen: Two challengers to Gianni Infantino have registered for next year's FIFA presidential election. What do Philippe Diallo and Kozo Tashima stand for – and do they stand a chance against the incumbent?
noticias.texto:
FIFA election 2027: Can Diallo or Tashima defeat Infantino?
November 20, 2026
Three men are vying for one of the most powerful positions in sports when delegates from more than 200 member nations of FIFA, soccer's global governing body, cast their ballots at the FIFA presidential election, to be held in Rabat on March 18, 2027. DW looks at the field of candidates.
Gianni Infantino – the powerful incumbent
Gianni Infantino was first elected FIFA president in February 2016, promising greater transparency and a fresh start in the wake of the corruption scandals that marked the Sepp Blatter era. Under Infantino's leadership, FIFA's revenues have continued to grow, the Club World Cup has been revamped, and the men's World Cup has been expanded to include 48 teams.
During his decade in office, the 56-year-old Swiss has built a global network of support. Infantino enjoys significant backing in Africa, South America, and large parts of Asia — a result of multi-billion-dollar development programs and financial grants provided to national associations. Many smaller member associations view him as a president who takes their interests more seriously than his predecessors did.
At the same time, critics accuse Infantino of consolidating power within the organization around himself. During his tenure, oversight and control bodies have been restructured multiple times, and key positions have been filled with his own loyalists.
Infantino's ostentatious closeness to political leaders has also sparked debate — whether exemplified by his conduct during the World Cup in Qatar, his tight ties to Saudi Arabia or his public appearances alongside US President Donald Trump (though that relationship is said to have cooled significantly after the 2026 World Cup). Detractors accuse him of seeking proximity to authoritarian rulers and intermingling political interests too closely with football.
A failed initiative to grant private investors a larger stake in lucrative FIFA competitions (FIFA Forward Enterprise) has also placed Infantino under considerable pressure. As the FIFA election approaches, he faces the prospect of legal challenges; European football's governing body UEFA is aiming to take action over the investment plan, while other critics are calling for an investigation by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).
However, his time in office has brought many of FIFA's 211 member associations additional development funding and other revenue. This makes him the man to beat in the March vote.
Philippe Diallo — Europe's principled alternative
Philippe Diallo is Europe's candidate. The 63-year-old, who was elected president of the French Football Federation in 2023, is seen as an experienced sports administrator with a pragmatic and measured leadership style.
He has the backing of UEFA, as well as many of its 55 member associations, including the German Football Association (DEB).
"Philippe Diallo stands for a version of football that embraces responsibility and tackles future challenges with determination," DFB President Bernd Neuendorf said in a statement announcing the German FA's position.
"We want a FIFA that serves the sport in the interest of all its member associations. That is why we support Philippe Diallo with great conviction."
Diallo is positioning himself as a clear alternative to Infantino. His supporters see him as a candidate who stands for sound leadership, transparency, and a stronger dialogue with member associations. Unlike the incumbent, however, he lacks a global network of allies.
Kozo Tashima — an underdog as a possible king maker?
