The third man in the race is Kozo Tashima. The 68-year-old was president of the Japan Football Association (JFA) from 2016 to 2024 and has been one of the most influential officials in Asia for decades.
During a press conference in the Japanese capital Tokyo on Friday, Tashima mentioned the words "integrity, fairness, trust and transparency" several times in explaining his decision to run.
"I just don't only want to be the FIFA president, my intention is to make FIFA better," he said.
"Being the president is the shortcut to making that happen. I just want to clean up the federation and make it a fair organization. I want to help rebuild the whole organization."
Tashima also acknowledged that failing to have won the endorsement of any of the regional confederations — the Asian Football Confederation is supporting Infantino — makes him a longshot to win the election.
But he could still play a key role in the outcome. At a press conference on Tuesday, Diallo said he intended to reach out to Tashima to "unite forces" to defeat Infantino. Tashima hasn't ruled out the notion.
"We do share some moral or ethical positions, so he's a great person to team up with," he said.
"Diallo is also very strict in governance and he does have a lot of experience in management," he added.
However, Tashima also noted that he hadn't had any thoughts of withdrawing from the race.
If Infantino's challengers do manage to join forces in some way, they might just stand a chance of upsetting the highly favored incumbent.

noticias.titulo: Putin proposes second humanitarian ceasefire — is it a trap?
noticias.resumen: Russian President Putin has suggested evacuating civilians from the embattled Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka. But experts warn this could serve military, not humanitarian, aims. What should Kyiv do?
noticias.texto:
Putin proposes second humanitarian ceasefire — is it a trap?
November 19, 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a humanitarian mission in the city of Kostiantynivka similar to a recent operation in Oleshky. According to Putin, Russia has control of the city in the Donbas; the remaining civilian population, he says, could be evacuated. It would take five days to clear the access roads. The Russian leader has suggested that human rights organizations from Ukraine and Russia and delegates from the foreign press be incorporated into the mission.
Putin's proposal comes after discussions between the Russian government and US representatives, who have been negotiating to try to bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. Experts say that while Russia is indicating a readiness to make agreements, at the same time it is propagating its own depiction of the situation on the front line.
In July, Russia announced that it had taken Kostiantynivka but did not provide any proof. Ukraine says the fighting there is still ongoing. Experts from the Ukrainian open-source interactive map of military operations project DeepState say that the city is still controlled by the Ukrainian army, but that the situation there is "extremely difficult."
Responding to the proposal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists: "Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city." He emphasized that Ukraine had always given the civilian population in Kostiantynivka opportunities to leave, and said that Russia had used the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky to bring military equipment and weapons into the city.
What is the situation for civilians?
Kostiantynivka is the southernmost city in the so-called Donetsk "fortress belt," which also includes Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. Taking Kostiantynivka would open the way for Russian troops to advance to Druzhkivka, and on to the conurbation of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military expert at the Dmytro Tymchuk Center for Security Studies, a Ukrainian think tank, said Kostiantynivka's role is similar to that of Bakhmut, Avdiivka or Chasiv Yar — towns whose defensive installations were able to hold back Russian enemy forces for years.
Local authorities say the humanitarian situation in the city, whose population before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion was around 70,000, is catastrophic and that some 340 civilians remain. They add thatKostiantynivkahas no central water, electricity or gas supplies, there is no public transport, and since the spring of 2026 people have only been able to evacuate on foot.
"Those who stayed in Kostiantynivka need to be evacuated, they need a chance of a better life," military analyst Denys Popovych told DW. However, he added that an evacuation was virtually impossible without a ceasefire, as Russian troops had occupied the road between the town and Druzhkivka and drones were being deployed throughout the region. Ukraine, therefore, could not carry out such an operation unilaterally. "It still takes two to tango — to evacuate the people, that is," he said.
Humanitarian proposals as leverage
Kovalenko believes that Moscow is simply using the humanitarian issue for purposes of manipulation and to strengthen its negotiating position. The Russian army, he said, wants to gain time in order to reinforce units fighting in the vicinity.
Yevhen Zakharov, the director of the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group, has similar concerns. "I'm afraid that this proposal by the Russians has very different objectives to those they claim to pursue," he told DW. He described Putin's initiative as suspect, and said the Ukrainian side should treat it with the utmost caution.
Kyiv is in a difficult position, as the idea of a mission for Kostiantynivka is also being pushed by US intermediaries. "If we reject it, they'll say to us: 'You're rejecting peace proposals, you're not taking care of your own citizens, why should we keep talking to you, Zelenskyy wants to continue the war.' This is precisely the calculation behind it all," said Popovych.
Ceasefire as military tactic
After the end of the ceasefire in Oleshky, which was in place from October 27 to November 1, the Ukrainian General Staff announced that, in that time, the Russians had rotated their troops, entrenched their positions, reinforced measures to repel drones and brought in ammunition.
Kovalenko is convinced that the reason Russia is proposing a ceasefire is because its army is gradually losing ground in Kostiantynivka. From Moscow's perspective, the Russian troops that are meant to be storming the city are in urgent need of reinforcements, which they can't get because of the fighting on the ground.
"If a so-called humanitarian mission were to take place in Kostiantynivka, it would be a disaster for Kyiv, because Russia would use that time to consolidate forces that would enable it to take the city," he warned.
How should Kyiv respond to Moscow's proposal?
Popovych, however, does not think Ukraine should reject the Russian proposal. In his view, Kyiv should base its tactics on experiences with previous ceasefires and insist on very clear conditions in advance. "If there is a ceasefire, soldiers currently at their posts should stay there and not move," he suggested.
Oleksandr Pavlichenko from the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union believes Ukraine should submit a counter-proposal, which envisages the withdrawal of Russian troops from the Ukrainian city and the unimpeded departure of the civilian population.
The human rights activist said that, for a genuine humanitarian mission to be put in place, a strong, neutral third party should be brought in to supervise and ensure safe passage. In his view, the only party with such a mandate is the International Committee of the Red Cross. "If a proposal comes from only one side, and from a side such as Russia, it doesn't inspire confidence," he said.
This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

noticias.titulo: A second judge blocks Trump's arch, saying it's unlikely to succeed in court
noticias.resumen: A federal judge in Virginia said she will issue a preliminary injunction against Trump's arch, going a step further than the D.C. federal judge who temporarily blocked construction earlier this week.
noticias.texto:
A second judge blocks Trump's arch, saying it's unlikely to succeed in court
A federal judge in Virginia plans to issue a preliminary injunction blocking President Trump's triumphal arch indefinitely.
District Judge Leonie Brinkema said during a Friday hearing that she would grant the request of the county board of Arlington, Va., which sued over the arch in October. Democracy Forward, the nonprofit representing the plaintiffs, confirmed the ruling in a statement shared with NPR.
"We are pleased that the court has recognized the irreparable harm that will come to people who live and work in Arlington and stopped the massive vanity project while our case is heard and considered by the court," said senior counsel Kate Talmor.
Justice Department spokesperson Matthew Nies told NPR it will appeal the decision immediately.
The 250-foot arch would be built in Memorial Circle, which is part of D.C. but sits on the Virginia side of the Potomac River, a short distance from both Arlington National Cemetery and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, both in Arlington.
Arlington County has argued that the arch would "cause significant harm" to its residents in multiple ways, including increasing noise and air pollution and "clogging thoroughfares needed for emergency transport services." And it said an arch that doubles as a military complex — as Trump has suggested — would pose public safety risks and require additional county resources to manage.
Arlington also argues the arch would disrupt historic sightlines between Arlington National Cemetery and D.C.'s National Mall, and pose logistical challenges for the roughly 24 to 27 funerals the cemetery holds every weekday. The county also has concerns about air and road traffic, saying construction-related delays could cause more accidents and disrupt emergency vehicles far beyond the traffic circle.
"In the last 60 days, Arlington police, fire, and emergency units have responded to approximately 200 incidents in the area surrounding the Circle, including traffic stops and assisting with unconscious persons within Arlington National Cemetery," they wrote. "And the visitors the Arch is intended to attract will increase demand for those same emergency services."
The plaintiffs, like many critics of the arch, accused the Trump administration of rushing through federally mandated environmental reviews and failing to consider alternatives. The National Park Service has defended the federal review process — which ended in approval earlier this month — and said building the arch somewhere else would defeat its purpose.
"The County brings this lawsuit to halt the agency's feverish pace toward construction of the Arch and to ensure that the 'hard look' mandated by [the National Environmental Preservation Act] is completed before the agency commences disruptive and harmful ground-disturbing activities," the plaintiffs wrote last month.
NPR has reached out to the White House for comment. Spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR earlier this week that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."
Brinkema, an appointee of President Clinton, is the second judge to rule against the arch this week.
On Wednesday, D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended a restraining order that prevents the Trump administration from breaking ground through Dec. 3 while she considers the underlying legal arguments.
That case was brought earlier this year by a group that includes Vietnam War veterans and was joined by the governments of D.C. and Virginia last month. Nine Kennedy family members moved to get involved last week.
Friday's ruling goes even further, preventing construction while Arlington's legal challenge plays out.
And Brinkema suggested that Arlington is likely to prevail. The judge said in court that she didn't see "any way" the government could win the case on the merits.
She reiterated that the project lacks congressional approval, which the Trump administration has not sought. It argues that the arch is covered by a 1925 law authorizing a pair of much shorter columns at that same location, which were never built. Both judges have frowned upon that argument.
"It hurts your credibility with the court by focusing on that," Brinkema told lawyers Friday, according to Reuters.
Brinkema also called it a "rushed job," and seemed to find the government's analysis of the structure's environmental and economic impact inadequate, particularly concerning the impact of construction cranes — which the government has said would be taller than the arch itself — on airspace.
The Federal Aviation Administration has said the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft as long as it is lit a certain way, including with a controversial eternal flame on top. But aviation safety experts are concerned that the structure would add an additional layer of risk to an already notoriously complicated airspace. They say that's especially true if it has any military capabilities, which were not included in the FAA's analysis.

noticias.titulo: Trump initially accepted the midterm results, but most GOP voters doubt they were fair
noticias.resumen: Less than half of Republicans nationwide considered the midterm elections "free and fair," according to new polling.
noticias.texto:
Trump initially accepted the midterm results, but most GOP voters doubt they were fair
President Trump may have initially accepted the results of his party's midterm losses, but data released Friday shows there is still broad distrust in the elections process among Republicans.
Less than half of Republican voters nationwide considered the midterm elections "free and fair," according to new polling by the University of California San Diego. Just 52% of Republicans said they trusted votes were counted accurately.
Loading...
In comparison, after the 2024 election that Trump won, more than 80% of Republicans said they had confidence in the vote-counting process.
While trust in elections often dips for voters of the losing party, the GOP has seen bigger swings in confidence in recent years, as Trump has falsely claimed that U.S. elections are corrupt.
"There are still a lot of people who remain unconvinced that they can trust elections," said Thad Kousser, a co-director of UC San Diego's Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections. "And they're predominantly located in one [political] party."
Overall, a wide majority — 66% — of Americans said they think the midterms were fair. That represents an improvement from before the election, when less than half of U.S. adults said they expected free and fair contests.
But that post-election increase in trust was buoyed by Democrats and independents — many of whom worried before Election Day about potential federal interference at the polls that didn't come to pass.
"It would be a mistake to [look at the 66%] and think, 'Oh, everyone has a pretty good view of the election,'" said Lauren Prather, also a co-director of UC San Diego's election center. "It really buries the lede a little bit about the partisan gap."
The widespread doubt among Republicans may be a reality check for those wondering whether Trump's brand of election denial has run its course in American politics.
On the one hand, there will be fewer politicians who deny or question election results in office next year. And the vast majority of election-denying candidates running for positions involved in overseeing statewide elections lost their races this year, according to tracking by the advocacy group States United Action.
Election experts have also celebrated as Trump and high-profile losing candidates on the ballot this year conceded their losses.
"Sure, I'll accept [the results]," Trump told Fox News' Bret Baier on election night, as it became clear Democrats would retake the House and Senate. "Why wouldn't I?"
But just a few days later, he began conspiracy theorizing about those same results.
"Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest," Trump posted online.
The new polling from UC San Diego shows that among Republicans, there still may be a receptive audience to such claims. When asked if politicians are discussing voter fraud too much, too little or about the right amount, just 15% of Republicans answered "too much."
"There is both demand among the Republican base for continued focus on this issue, and as we saw even after the election, politicians are continuing to supply it," Kousser said. "As long as those two dynamics are there, there's still going to be a market for these concerns."
To be clear, in most elections — domestically and internationally — supporters of the losing party usually see a dip in trust.
"It's sort of like asking people after an overtime basketball game, do you trust the referees?" Kousser said.
But in an ideal world, he said that oscillation would be more like 10 percentage points in either direction. Not the 30-point swing seen among Republicans between 2024 and 2026.
The numbers do still represent an improvement from 2020, however. At that time, leading up to the Jan. 6 riot at the U.S. Capitol in 2021, just 22% of Republicans said they had confidence in the nationwide vote count, according to similar polling done by MIT's Election Data and Science Lab.

noticias.titulo: How Orchestra Noir turned classical music into a cultural movement
noticias.resumen: Orchestra Noir is back on tour, selling out stages across the country and proving classical music can be anything you want it to be.
noticias.texto:
How Orchestra Noir turned classical music into a cultural movement
Ashley Branch, Orchestra Noir's operations manager, hurriedly completes her final tasks before curtain call at the Warner Theater in Washington, D.C. It is two hours before the ensemble's Saturday night concert and her main goal is simple: plan to deal with whatever she didn't plan for.
The D.C. show comes partway through the ensemble's 20-city The Culture 2000s tour, which has taken the group to cities like Jacksonville and Philadelphia.
Founded in 2016 by music director Jason Ikeem Rodgers, the all-Black Atlanta-based orchestra performs classic hits spanning the genres of jazz, blues and R&B. Branch has been with Orchestra Noir for about two years, hired to bring relief to Keisha Rodgers, the orchestra's original operations manager, who now serves as president of operations. On show nights, it's Branch who is directing the final details on show prep.
In its early days, the Orchestra Noir team was small — just Keisha and Jason handling everything. While Jason was responsible for all music-related details, Keisha handled other tasks, such as creating the logo and website.
"I wore every single hat there was to wear," Keisha told NPR. "It was just very day-to-day. I mean, every little thing you could think of operationally was me."
But over the last decade, Orchestra Noir has expanded to 23 musicians and a leadership staff of four people. The orchestra averages about 20 shows per tour.
Saxophonist Taj Davis and violinist Nicole Wright have been with the ensemble for three tours. They say the size of the production has grown considerably since they joined.
"Every go round is a new element," Davis said.
The latest season added several new details to their performances — including a full display screen cycling through visuals from previous performances, fog machines and lighting and choreography threaded throughout the show.
"Every time I come back, I'm excited," Wright said, "because not only am I experiencing something different, but the audience is too." The theme for each tour, Rodgers explained, comes from whatever is igniting his creativity at the moment. For their most recent The Culture 2000s tour, Rodgers said they really wanted the "Bad Gal Rihanna energy."
"I chose the theme based on basically what inspired me at the time. And that's kind of where I want to go. I want to go deep into the 2000's," he said.
When it comes to picking which songs to perform and how they will be arranged, Rodgers compares it to developing a secret sauce he's been trying perfect "for a long time."
"We developed the formula where we can orchestrate and we can arrange," Rogers said. "We can orchestrate for those songs and arrange those songs in a way that is still so authentic, like how we're playing the melody, which instruments should have the bass line or the the harmony." "So it's really about seeing the orchestration in each song," Rogers continued. "Now when I hear a hip-hop song or a R&B song — I don't even hear the words anymore. I just hear instruments."
The journey to the stage
Preparation for an Orchestra Noir show starts long before the curtain rises. Wright logs two hours of individual practice daily. She writes out compositions by hand and thinks through fingerings and lyrics before bed. She says the show's music is often top of her mind as she moves through the day, even when her violin isn't in her hands. Wright says that her intense focus on the details of the show's music ahead of the show allows her to "just let loose and become one with the audience" once showtime arrives.
Davis takes a similar full-body approach. He listens to the repertoire while driving, catching details such as notes he may have missed in previous runs. He also exercises four to five times a week — including weightlifting workouts and walking.
Focusing on his endurance on stage is vital — since each Orchestra Noir performance demands a high level of stamina due to the ensemble's musicians performing choreography while also playing their instruments.
"Taking care of myself physically helps me when it's time to perform. It also gives me a chance to clear my mind and stay disciplined," Davis said.
On performance days, pre-show rituals also keep the musicians grounded. Davis plays long tones on his saxophone — sustaining single notes to center his breath and tone. Wright practices specific musical cues, calls her mother and will try on dresses until she finds the perfect one to wear on stage. And both of them remember to pray.
"Me and God are walking the entire time together," Wright said with a laugh.
A night to remember
By the time the lights go down, the audience inside Warner Theatre is already buzzing with excitement.
Orchestra Noir takes the stage in custom black-and-red letterman jackets that feature red-and-black sleeves with the letters "ATL" stitched on the right.
They open with Usher's 2004 hit "Yeah!" — with musicians rushing in from both ends of the stage and smoke sprouting up from the stage floor.
When an electric guitar joins the orchestra for Jagged Edge's "Where the Party at," the room shifts even higher. Then comes Ciara's "Like a Boy" — which features a violin solo from Wright that she plays so intensely that her bow snaps mid-solo.
Orchestra Noir closes the night with Lil Boosie's "Wipe Me Down." By this point, nearly the whole crowd is standing, with several audience members already making their way towards the stage.
As a part of their post-show ritual, the musicians come to the end of the stage to meet the people who came out to hear them perform. It is a cherished tradition that makes them feel even closer to the multigenerational audience supporting them from city to city.
"[During the 2025 season] out in California, someone in the audience came and cried," Davis recalled. "They just moved to Cali and haven't had anything for them — and then seeing us made that huge difference for them. So, it's a great thing. It's a blessing."
"We're being seen. We have something to say," he added. "Younger folk, older folk — they can say, okay, we see Black people playing in orchestras. Which is a serious thing."
For Wright, who grew up in Brownsville, Brooklyn, the ensemble has built a musical bridge she always wished existed.
"When I stepped outside, I was hearing Beyoncé or Brandy," she said. "But when I was practicing in the house, I was practicing Vivaldi." "We come to the edge of the stage, we can meet as many audience members as we can and we talk to them," Wright said. "Some of their children are playing the violin or the viola, and they'll ask us to take a picture or they'll ask us to make a video to inspire their daughter. Because sometimes when their daughter is practicing, they don't get to see the end result. Because practicing can take quite a bit of time. So they want us to show their daughters and send these videos to them to help inspire them."
"My goal is making sure [audience members] leave feeling something awesome or something great," Wright added. "And that's what we're doing. We treat every show as if it's our last."

noticias.titulo: Trump touts meeting with Xi and Putin but offers little results
noticias.resumen: At a White House press conference Friday, Trump offered little in actual results of the meetings, beyond a joint statement on unity over some issues.
noticias.texto:
Trump touts meeting with Xi and Putin but offers little results
President Trump touted his recent trip to Asia where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin during a White House press conference Friday, saying the U.S. took the stage from a position of strength.
"The United States entered this trip from a position of unmatched economic and diplomatic strength," he said, though the historic summit between the three countries yielded few tangible results.
But Trump offered little in actual results of the meetings, beyond a joint statement on unity over some issues, such as continuing to discuss reducing nuclear risks.
Trump, flanked by Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, gave a wide-ranging opening statement that veered from recounting his trip and who he met with to asides about Iran, the U.S. Federal Reserve, his quest for a Nobel Peace Prize and domestic manufacturing.
Trump also said he and Chinese President Xi were agreeing to "joint guardrails" amid the race to develop artificial intelligence, a notable acknowledgement about the risks involved.
Trump, who said Xi also likes his term "super intelligence" rather than artificial, said, "Problem is, it may be too super. So, President Xi and I agree that we're going to do some joint guardrails, the two of us."
Trump added that he would continue to push for the construction of data centers in the U.S.
"Make them pay your community, but take advantage. Don't shut them off. And there's always somebody else in this country. But if it's not this country, there's somebody else outside. And we're not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We're not going to allow that to happen," Trump said.
Trump said he only wants "older chips" from the U.S. to be sold to China, in the wake of the Nvidia scandal. "We want only older chips, and we don't mind if none go, but only older. You have to understand, China makes chips too, and if we're not going to sell them, they'll make them themselves," he said.
Vance and Rubio both spoke before the president took questions, with the vice president saying he missed the president and Rubio, who was on the trip with Trump, also recounting the highlights from overseas.
Historic meetings in Asia
Trump did not formally take questions while in China at the end of his trip, though it's typically expected on presidential foreign trips. Putin did hold a press conference before leaving the country.
Ahead of the press conference, Trump said he will be discussing the historic meetings in China as well as trade agreements reached during the earlier part of the trip in the Philippines, where he arrived for the tail end of a summit with South Asian leaders.
Trump, Xi and Putin, who command the world's largest nuclear arsenals, gathered at a lakeside resort in Shenzhen, China, where they sat around a large round wooden table to discuss nuclear proliferation, Iran and global relations.
While the displays of power were prominent, the talks offered few signs that either Xi or Putin was prepared to make significant concessions to Trump.
"The trip enabled the president to bask in the glow of great power amity after a really bruising election outcome here at home," Suzanne Maloney, vice president and director of the foreign policy program at the Brookings Institution, said of Trump. "He wanted the optics of this direct engagement with Presidents Xi and Putin as a sort of validation of his own standing as a historical figure. And I think the photo op provided that."

noticias.titulo: Texas execution took over an hour as staff struggled to find vein; Reinaldo Dennes moaned about pain
noticias.resumen: The same day Dennes was given lethal injection, Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year.
noticias.texto:
Texas execution took over an hour as staff struggled to find vein; Reinaldo Dennes moaned about pain
HUNTSVILLE, Texas — Texas executed Reinaldo Dennes on Thursday in a procedure that took over an hour, as prison staffers struggled to find a suitable vein for the two intravenous needles carrying the lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital.
And once it began, he moaned repeatedly about pain, groaned several times and asked God to take him away from the pain. A prison spokesperson said all procedures were followed appropriately and suggested that Dennes might have exaggerated or faked the pain.
The execution followed renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the U.S. in the aftermath of Tennessee's failed execution in September of Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital that her lawyers say probably did not enter her bloodstream correctly and instead pooled in her arms, leaving them burned and blistered.
Dennes, who was found guilty of capital murder in the death of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer found shot multiple times in his Houston office in January 1996, was the second person put to death in the country on the day, after Florida carried out a record-breaking 20th execution of the year, of Thomas Mitchell Overton.
Dennes gave a brief statement in which he said he wanted his loved ones to know he was blessed the past 30 years "knowing the love of the father." Then he told the warden: "Go, warden!"
Almost immediately he exclaimed: "The pain! Go! Go!" He uttered an expletive and implored "the father" to "take this pain." "Let me go, father," he said again and again. "Let me go. … I'm here. I've been your son all these years."
Then he shouted: "My right leg is killing me!" and described it as a cramp. After another profanity, he grunted, then said, "I don't think this is normal. Take me, father. Don't let me suffer like this. C'mon."
After three loud groans, Dennes began snoring sounds — eight of them — that progressively got quieter before a final loud snore. Then he began breathing quietly, about a dozen breaths, also getting progressively less pronounced.
The procedure was completed at 7:07 p.m., 63 minutes after he was strapped to the gurney. A minute later, after being examined by a physician, Dennes was pronounced dead at 7:08 p.m. at the penitentiary in Huntsville.
Prison officials said all procedures were followed appropriately. Spokesperson Amanda Hernandez acknowledged a number of unsuccessful attempts to find a suitable vein before the execution team managed to insert the needles in Dennes' left foot and on the left side of his neck.
She did not know how many attempts were unsuccessful but said the sites ultimately used were in accordance with the state's procedures.
Hernandez also suggested that Dennes may have been exaggerating the pain, saying he began complaining before the drugs began to flow and also of pain in places where there was no IV.
Asked if he was faking, she replied, "I think, yeah, there were allegations. ... There was nothing abnormal on our part."
"This isn't the first time we had to insert IVs into other locations. It's also not the first time we've had an inmate make allegations of pain immediately," Hernandez said.
Witness Janice Copeland's husband, David, was a security guard shot during the robbery. He survived his wounds and died five years ago.
"David always felt Reinaldo would outlive him. Unfortunately he was right," she said Thursday. "Finally after 30 years, justice has been served."
Earlier in the day Florida carried out its execution of Overton, 71, who was convicted of murdering a pregnant woman and her husband, Susan and Michael MacIvor, during a home invasion.
Overton was pronounced dead at 6:19 p.m. following a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison. In a final statement, he denied ever breaking into the couple's home and attacking them, saying, "I never killed anyone."
Florida has now carried out more than half the nation's 39 executions to date this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors.
DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said he wanted justice for families who wait decades for death sentences to be carried out. He signed the death warrants that led to a record of 19 executions in 2025, then the most in a single year in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Florida still plans two more executions, in December.
Texas set a record for executions there when 40 people were put to death in 2000.
The executions of two men in their 70s cast a renewed spotlight on the aging of the U.S. death row population.

noticias.titulo: Dems aim to block Iran war funding. And, Army delays lead azide detonation in Iowa
noticias.resumen: Congress needs to pass a funding measure to avoid a shutdown next month, providing Dems an opportunity to leverage power. And, the Army says waiting to detonate lead azide could become dangerous.
noticias.texto:
Dems aim to block Iran war funding. And, Army delays lead azide detonation in Iowa
Government Funding Pressure On Iran War, National Security & Tech, Iowa Detonation
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories
Democrats who won this month's election are looking to use their influence to block funding for the war in Iran before officially taking charge of Congress. President Trump launched attacks last winter without congressional approval, breaking from the tradition of seeking bipartisan support for wars.
- 🎧 Congress must pass a funding measure to avoid a shutdown by Dec. 11. NPR's Claudia Grisales tells Up First that Democrats hold leverage, since their votes are essential for the Republican-controlled Senate to meet the 60-vote threshold. Senate Democrats argue they should use their authority to end what they call an illegal war. Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine aims to include a provision to end war funding in the stopgap bill. Republicans counter that cutting war funding jeopardizes service members in the region. N.C. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis tells Grisales his party may need to explore alternatives if Democrats push for a shutdown. That could include using reconciliation to pass legislation without Democratic votes.
Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping met for the third time this year, underscoring a dilemma for Americans who see China as a business opportunity and a national security risk. Nvidia's former CEO, Jensen Huang, convinced Trump to approve several chip sales before his departure. The House Foreign Affairs Committee yesterday, in a highly unusual step, released a list of requests this year from Nvidia and AMD to sell chips directly to Chinese companies.
- 🎧 The Trump administration approved the sale of nearly 900,000 advanced chips to Chinese companies as of May 2026. Some of those approvals included well-known firms such as Alibaba and Tencent, which the Pentagon lists as having ties to China's military, NPR's Greg Myre says. During his second term, Trump shifted his stance on China, partly influenced by his relationship with Jinping. The two may meet again next month in Miami.
The U.S. Army has rescheduled the detonation of around 9,500 pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown to Monday, Nov. 23. This decision comes after Iowa lawmakers and two environmental groups pushed for a delay. The plant, which manufactures various types of ammunition, has stored lead azide in a water-ethanol solution in underground tanks for 20 years. Recent inspections found that the tanks were too dry, leading to crystallization and instability. To prevent an accidental explosion, the Army wants to detonate the lead azide under controlled conditions.
- 🎧 Many Iowans were unaware of the situation until earlier this week, prompting the delay, says Eliza Billingham of NPR network station Iowa Public Radio. Acting Army Secretary Adam R. Telle said on social media that he directed Army Materiel Command to postpone the blasts until the "latest possible moment" before a forecasted drop in temperatures. Army spokesperson Justine Barati previously said that cold weather could make the situation more dangerous. Last month, the Army hosted an informational open house for Middletown residents and shared maps predicting the movement of lead dust. Those maps will need to be revised based on the new forecast, Billingham says. If the detonation proceeds, the Army, EPA and the University of Iowa will monitor air quality.
Picture show
Iraqi environmentalist Jassim al-Asadi has dedicated his life to protecting Iraq's ancient marshlands. He even helped reflood areas that Saddam Hussein drained and set fire to decades ago to flush out resistance fighters. In February 2023, an Iran-backed militia kidnapped and tortured Asadi for two weeks on false charges that he was an Israeli spy who had ignited anti-government protests. He endured the trauma by reciting poetry until his Bani Asad tribe mobilized armed tribal fighters to secure his release. Once freed, he refused European asylum so he could continue his work. Today, despite drought and other hardships on the land, Asadi continues to monitor recovering water levels as wildlife slowly starts to return to the marshes.
Weekend picks
Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:
🍿 Movies: Being Heumann chronicles Judy Heumann, the "mother of the disability rights movement," and her coalition as they embark on a historic 1970s sit-in to advocate for disability rights legislation.
📺 TV: In the new British comedy-fantasy Small Prophets, a man summons magical spirits in an attempt to locate his long-missing girlfriend.
📚 Books: Longtime host of Reading Rainbow LeVar Burton shares his journey in his new memoir, Take My Word for It. He reflects on his life, both in and out of his iconic roles, and the unexpected twists he's encountered.
🎵 Music: On Graceland Way, singer-songwriter and harpist Mikaela Davis blends psychedelic and alternative country, showcasing her boundary-pushing harp play.
🎮 Gaming: After years of waiting, fans can now revel in the Bonnie-and-Clyde love story in Grand Theft Auto VI. The game is poised to steal the crown as the biggest entertainment launch ever with up to $5 billion in projected first-week sales, according to estimates.
❓ Quiz: What a week! A new James Bond was named, SpaceX made history and the Alaska Senate race was called. Think you were paying attention? Let's find out.
3 things to know before you go
- A new Pew Research Center report shows that by 2035, Muslims will become the largest religious group globally, surpassing Christians.
- The Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden announced that Fiona, the famous 9-year-old hippo, has died after failing to pass a hat she ingested more than a week ago. (via WVXU)
- Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed a bill yesterday banning New York City's 160-year-old horse-drawn carriage industry. Animal rights activists have fought for decades to end the practice. (via Gothamist)

noticias.titulo: Just how vulnerable are we to cyberattacks?
noticias.resumen: In a week of outages, we're thinking about the rising threat of AI-powered cyberattacks. But sometimes, it's not the most sophisticated attack that's concerning, but the easy targets buried in old software.
noticias.texto:
Just how vulnerable are we to cyberattacks?
You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.
There is a certain thrill in spotting a dollar bill on the ground. It's free money! Well one lucky person found a Georgia O'Keeffe painting in her aunt's closet, under a pile of fur coats. The Smithsonian magazine reported the painting, "Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I," is part of a three-part series based on Keeffe's time in northern New Mexico. O'Keeffe has described her time there as particularly impactful.
The woman's aunt received the painting as a graduation gift from her parents way back when. They bought it for $3,800. That's the equivalent of $42,000 in today's dollars. This week, it sold at Christie's for $4,878,000 million. Double check your closet, people.
Coming up: 
- Why old software is so risky
- Why Steam is pulling in less revenue from NEW games
- What cohost Adrian Ma is reading this week
News We're Watching
This has been a long and strange week of outages from United Airlines to Apple Pay to the F.A.A. It's got many people thinking about this seemingly omnipresent threat of cyberattack. The agencies and companies experiencing the outages insist they're unrelated to cyberattacks. But there is a lot of concern right now about how vulnerable the U.S. is to these digital threats with the combination of fast-growing AI and decidedly fragile infrastructure.
Case in point, earlier this month, Europe faced ANOTHER hack on its supermarket refrigeration. Grocery stores and butcher shops across seven countries saw their fridges and freezers turned up to more than 100 degrees Fahrenheit.
It wasn't some complicated, sophisticated attack. It was hackers that found a vulnerability in old software. A vulnerability that had existed for a long time.
"That's where attackers see a big opportunity," said Aaron Mitchell, CEO of HeroDevs. "That's an easy way for me to get access and start to do some real damage."
After all, there is a lot of old software out there. Ones that touch utilities, hospitals, and critical infrastructure - or airlines. In some cases, companies didn't feel much urgency to address security gaps.
HeroDevs is a cybersecurity firm that does the addressing FOR companies. They help maintain support for a certain kind of software called open-source. When a software reaches end-of-life, and a company has moved on to new ideas, they might pay HeroDevs to maintain it and (importantly!!) patch vulnerabilities.
That could be more important than ever because AI is helping find a record number of these vulnerabilities. Last week, VulnCheck, a cybersecurity consulting firm, posted that more than 100,000 vulnerabilities have been found and disclosed so far this year, more than double than 2025. Hackers are exploiting vulnerabilities 33% faster compared to 2025.
In other words, vulnerabilities in outdated software are a prime target for hackers.
"About half of all exploits that happen, known exploits of a vulnerability, are happening on versions that are no longer supported by the maintainer," said Mitchell. "That number is rapidly growing."
This is a problem because countless websites, companies, and governments have outdated software somewhere.
Just last month, AI discovered two flaws in a programming language known as PHP that's built more than two-thirds of websites. The flaws could give a bad guy total access and even remote control of a web server without a password. An alert went out with a patch for every software to download.
"It was a huge deal, and for the whole week the whole internet was kind of on fire trying to get this thing patched," said Mitchell.
Still, in some cases, Mitchell said there were documented cases of websites that DID get exploited.
This is one example of how a small entrance for bad guys can be so dangerous. But these little doorways keep popping up. On Tuesday, an AI company revealed a critical vulnerability in Java known as Java4Shell prompting websites and companies to quickly take actions to patch against it.
As we can see and perhaps even feel, hackers are taking advantage. The most common cyberattack on utilities involves outdated software. Early this month, a cyberattack hit French blood banks, looking to increase temperatures using a similar tactic to the refrigeration hacks, although French authorities caught the attack in time and stopped it.
Richard Horne, the head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre said that "vulnerabilities that have been tolerated for far too long." In 2028, the UK predicts AI cyberattacks on critical infrastructure.
For now, Aaron Mitchell says, exploitation of vulnerabilities isn't taking off as much as it could be, "but every day that goes by, we get that much closer to the edge."
Just yesterday, Axios reported President Trump's National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross will be leaving his role. He did not want to serve an additional two-year term, leaving an important role to be filled.
Today's Indicator
We got this economics podcast before GTA VI
If you HAVEN'T listened: This is the week of Grand Theft Auto VI. The wildly hyped game has already collected more than $1.5 billion in pre-sales. But the game itself is almost like a cover charge for an entire digital world, and, importantly, economy.
"Take-Two Interactive learned from GTA V that selling a product at retail is great, but better yet, what if you could continue to sell expansions and in-game events and items over a longer term?" said Joost van Dreunen, a professor at the NYU Stern School of Business.
GTA VI isn't launching its story mode with micro-transactions. That will likely come with the online mode of the game, expected to be released next year. The story mode can hook players into the world, and the online mode can keep them there. THEN you might start wanting to buy a few things. In the current GTA Online, based in the previous game's world, you can buy a digital yacht for $100 real US dollars.
If you HAVE listened: Overall, Steam is doing just fine, but in 2024, new releases accounted for just 29% of Steam revenue. In 2025, 27%. This year, it's down to 21%, according to the Alinea Insight substack.
To reporter Ricky Mulvey, this means people might not want new games and GTA VI is an exception to the rule.
"What is the purpose of playing a game? Not just the coolest, most advanced graphics," Ricky said. "I want to talk to my friends"
Other reasons back catalogue items are doing well: they're a fraction of the price. Plus, who can keep up with the latest and greatest console?
Rest of the Week
- How three archetypes determine the way influencers make their money
- How a $5B tribal settlement could shake up Western water markets
- Is manufacturing ever coming back to the US in a big way?
Listener Mailbag
Listener Chris Browett sent in a question from Virginia Beach, VA
Question: Longtime fan, and I really enjoyed the episode on the death of the sitcoms. I've been rewatching old shows lately and just finished White Collar. It made me realize how much I miss full length seasons. They give you something to look forward to week after week. Eight episode seasons are over before they even start. The new economics make sense for most shows, but what about the big franchises like Star Wars, where Disney earns money from licensing and merchandise anyway? More episodes would mean more material to sell around, so why not lean into longer seasons? As streaming bills creep toward a regular cable bill, do you think that math changes?
Reporter Ricky Mulvey's Response
Hi Chris! Glad you enjoyed the episode and thanks for writing in. You're kind of describing an economic concept called "marginal utility". Or how much enjoyment do you get from your tenth episode of a binge watch versus the eighth? I imagine that this is the concept that the streaming execs are looking at too.
How much more likely are you to buy a Star Wars shirt after five episodes or ten? Does it matter?
Add into this the incredible cost of some streaming shows. Disney's Andor cost more than $20 million per episode. I think these higher production costs are a key reason why you see shorter seasons too.
And I think that as streaming bills creep toward cable bills the move is to live events. Streamers are looking to give you a reason to watch live and not cancel. You've seen this with Netflix adding the WWE and the Women's World Cup in 2027, Apple adding Formula 1, and Amazon with Thursday Night Football.
Cheers,
Ricky
In Our Spare Time
Co-host Adrian Ma read The Hot Young Widows Club
Recently, I read a book that deeply resonated with me called The Hot Young Widows Club.(Okay, actually, I listened to the audiobook. But I've been assured by various totally unbiased friends that listening to audiobooks counts as reading.) This memoir by Nora McInerny, written after she lost, in quick succession, a pregnancy, her husband, and her father, is one of the sharpest articulations of grief that I've ever read (or listened to).
And somehow, amazingly, it is also funny. This book made me cry. And laugh. And very often, cry and laugh at the same time. She manages to vividly capture the soul-wrenching pain and messiness of grief, while telling it to you in a comforting, conversational style, like you're commiserating with a best-friend over bottomless cups of diner coffee. If you've lost a partner, or are wondering how to support someone who has, I think you'll find this book helpful.

noticias.titulo: GOP Sen. Johnson rejects tying government funding to an end to the Iran war
noticias.resumen: "We're not going to shut down the war," Sen. Ron Johnson said as Republicans and Democrats struggle to reach a government funding deal.
noticias.texto:
GOP Sen. Johnson rejects tying government funding to an end to the Iran war
Sen. Ron Johnson on efforts to avert government shutdown during lame duck session
Republican Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, who has defended President Trump's war with Iran, said Friday that he opposes tying government funding to an end to the conflict as Congress struggles to avert a shutdown before Christmas.
"We're not going to shut down the war. That is President Trump's power. He's exercising his constitutional authority," Johnson, who chairs the Senate Budget Committee, told Morning Edition.
Congress faces a Dec. 11 deadline to keep federal agencies operating, giving Democrats leverage in the Republican-controlled Senate, where most legislation requires 60 votes to advance. But both parties face divisions. Democrats disagree over whether to use the funding deadline to force an end to the war, while Republicans are weighing bipartisan negotiations against a party-line approach to securing additional military spending.
Johnson said Republicans would prefer to negotiate a spending agreement with Democrats rather than use budget reconciliation, a procedure that could allow them to approve defense funding without Democratic support.
"I think we'll give them one more chance," he said, referring to negotiations before the Thanksgiving recess.
Johnson, who previously supported military aid to Ukraine but later opposed additional funding, warned that temporary spending measures would hinder military modernization and weapons procurement. He pointed to the changing nature of warfare in Ukraine as an example.
A shutdown could furlough hundreds of thousands of federal workers or delay their pay just weeks before Christmas. Johnson said he hoped to avoid one but warned that Republicans would need Democratic support.
The war launched by the U.S. and Israel against Iran has killed thousands of people, threatened U.S. military bases across the region and become a point of contention in the American midterm elections. Asked what he wanted to see happen in Iran, Johnson said he hoped Iranians would rise up against their government and that Iran would never acquire a nuclear weapon.
"I want to see the Ayatollahs on the dustbin of history," he said.

noticias.titulo: Trump accuses Iran of dishonesty while defending Putin ties
noticias.resumen: Speaking at a White House press conference on Friday, Trump defended his ties with Xi and Putin, called for a "real deal" with Iran and claimed the Russian leader wanted to end the war in Ukraine through diplomacy.
noticias.texto:
Speaking at a White House press conference on Friday, Trump defended his ties with Xi and Putin, called for a "real deal" with Iran and claimed the Russian leader wanted to end the war in Ukraine through diplomacy.
US President Donald Trump praised his recent trip to Asia during a White House press conference on Friday, highlighting his meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, as well as trade discussions during the visit.
Trump described the historic trilateral meeting as a success, praising his relationship with both leaders.
"We have a very great relationship. That's a positive, by the way," Trump told reporters. He also called critics of his relationships with Putin and Xi "stupid", responding to backlash over his description of Putin as his "friend".
Turning to Iran, Trump said Tehran wanted an agreement with Washington but had yet to offer terms he considered acceptable. He insisted the US was seeking a "real deal" rather than a "fake" agreement.
“We want to make a real deal, not a fake deal,” adding that Iranian government has been “bull-----ing people for 51 years.”
On Ukraine, Trump said Putin had expressed a desire to end the war "by diplomatic means", but blamed tensions between the Russian leader and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for complicating peace efforts.
"The problem is President Zelenskyy and President Putin have tremendous hatred, and that's never easy," he told reporters.
Trump also addressed artificial intelligence, warning that US companies building data centres overseas could face heavy taxes, arguing that the facilities should remain in the United States.

noticias.titulo: Thousands protest across Europe demanding better wages and services
noticias.resumen: Demonstrations began Friday in over 25 European countries and are expected to continue through the weekend as part of a coordinated international protest movement.
noticias.texto:
Demonstrations began Friday in over 25 European countries and are expected to continue through the weekend as part of a coordinated international protest movement.
Workers and students took to the streets across Europe on Friday, demanding higher wages, better living conditions and greater investment in public services.
The demonstrations follow weeks of protests over rising housing costs, worsening education conditions and increased military spending, with many calling for peace and more funding for healthcare and welfare.
Italy: Protesters demand higher wages and better public services
In Italy, a 24-hour strike called by the Italian General Confederation of Labour (CGIL) trade union sparked demonstrations in more than 100 locations.
Protesters criticised stagnant wages, rising living costs and what organisers described as the government's failure to improve public services and protect workers' rights.
The protests also drew opposition leaders, who joined demonstrations and criticised Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government over wages and social spending.
The strike, which coincided with the International Day of Student Mobilisation, affected both public and private sectors, disrupting public transport in several cities, as well as schools and some health facilities.
Planned strikes by air transport workers were cancelled for Friday, although separate walkouts involving airport staff remain scheduled for Sunday at Milan and Venice airports.
Authorities deployed additional police in several Italian cities where multiple demonstrations took place.
Croatia, Austria and Germany: Students call for education over military spending
In Croatia, students boycotted classes and protested in around a dozen cities, demanding more investment in education, housing and public services rather than military spending.
In Austria, several hundred people gathered outside the University of Vienna for a youth-led protest calling for more education funding and less spending on weapons. Police dispersed the demonstration following reported disturbances, using pepper spray and making several arrests.
In Germany, demonstrators called for greater investment in education and opposed a possible return to compulsory military service. The rallies followed protests on 31 October that drew thousands of people into the streets, with violence reported in some cities.

noticias.titulo: What do we know about Rwanda return hubs and how effective will they be?
noticias.resumen: Five EU countries have announced a controversial plan to set up a centre in Rwanda for migrants with no legal right to stay in Europe. While supporters say it will help governments to deter illegal immigration, critics are concerned about potential human rights violations and a lack of oversight.
noticias.texto:
Five EU countries have announced a controversial plan to set up a centre in Rwanda for migrants with no legal right to stay in Europe. While supporters say it will help governments to deter illegal immigration, critics are concerned about potential human rights violations and a lack of oversight.
Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands have announced plans to set up a return hub in Rwanda, which they say will allow the EU to secure control of its borders.
The group of five want to start deporting rejected asylum seekers — and those who have exhausted all appeal options against their removal — to Rwanda in 2027. Today's Euronews Verify episode takes a closer look at the measure.
The details of the return hubs are still being ironed out, but the first is expected to accommodate around 100 people with no legal right to stay in the EU at a time, in a pilot run of the model.
Those moved to Rwanda will be free to live and work there or return to their home countries.
Announcing the plan on 16 November, Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said that the move will serve as a strong deterrent for anyone looking to enter the EU illegally.
"The signal that we are sending, that you can no longer enter the European Union illegally and think that you can just stay around ... will prevent a lot and ensure that thousands of people will think it through before starting their journey into Europe," she said.
Rwanda has also hailed the plan as a way to "protect the right to asylum while treating migrants with dignity at every stage".
What don't we know and what are the concerns?
There's still a lot we don't know, however, and critics are concerned about the lack of detail given in the announcement of the Rwanda plan.
"We don't know how much it will cost; we don't know what Rwanda has been offered in exchange; we don't know what guarantees exist for people; we don't know how the courts will intervene; we don't know what protections will be in place; and we don't know who's legally responsible if something goes wrong," Olivia Sundberg, EU advocate on migration and asylum at Amnesty International, told Euronews Verify.
While both the EU countries in question and Rwanda itself assure that the hubs will comply with EU, international and human rights law, critics and experts are less convinced.
They've also raised concerns about the hubs' ability to even deter illegal immigrants, as such measures, they say, only force people to take more dangerous trips to Europe rather than giving up the plan entirely.
Can nuclear play a part in Europe's energy transition?
Also on today's episode of Euronews Verify is a look at whether Europe is heading for a nuclear revival.
As the COP climate summit in Turkey wraps up, nuclear energy has been a particularly big elephant in the room, complete with nuclear-related events on the sidelines.
From calls to triple capacity by 2050 to countries reconsidering their phase-outs, there is a growing push to bring nuclear back to the table as a low-carbon source.
Soaring energy bills in Europe are also presenting the industry with an opportunity to turn political momentum into climate legitimacy.
"If you want to have cheap energy, it's going to be very, very difficult to do it without nuclear power," Damien Erst, electromechanics professor at the University of Liège, told Euronews Verify.
"Especially in a context where gas is becoming extremely expensive, and in a context where foreign powers also use our dependency on energy imports to threaten and weaken the EU."
Several countries are already weighing up their options, with Italy giving the strongest indication that it's time for change: the government just passed new legislation this year to pave the way for a return to nuclear energy after decades without it.
Spain and Belgium, meanwhile, have postponed reactor shutdowns; the Netherlands is planning new units; and Poland and Estonia are laying the groundwork for their first nuclear plants.

Join Euronews Verify live on TV, Euronews' website, and on digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram) every weekday at 6:40 pm Brussels time. In just under 11 minutes, our new format goes beyond the headlines to make sense of what's happening, fact-checking and untangling the day's most pressing issues to explain why they matter to you.

noticias.titulo: Europe Tonight: EU and UK strike post-Brexit reset deal as Russian missiles hit Poland
noticias.resumen: The EU and UK have struck a major post-Brexit reset deal in Brussels. In tonight’s edition of Europe Tonight, we bring you a live interview from the summit, assess security alarms after Russian missiles hit Poland, and examine the final-day standoff at COP31.
noticias.texto:
The EU and UK have struck a major post-Brexit reset deal in Brussels. In tonight’s edition of Europe Tonight, we bring you a live interview from the summit, assess security alarms after Russian missiles hit Poland, and examine the final-day standoff at COP31.
EU and UK sign Brussels summit deal
At today’s summit in Brussels, EU and UK leaders agreed to ease barriers on food exports, link carbon emissions systems, and launch a youth mobility scheme. Both sides also pledged to debate their future relationship, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham signalling a potentially closer arrangement after the next election.
Russian missiles hit Poland amid reports of US peace trade-off
Two Russian missiles crashed in southeastern Poland during deadly strikes on Ukraine overnight an incident Warsaw condemned as an intentional provocation. The attacks came hours after Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin jointly vowed to pursue global peace, and amid reports that Washington is considering NATO membership for Ukraine in exchange for Kyiv ceding the Donbas region. We bring you full analysis on what this means for European security.
COP31 runs into weekend overtime over four sticking points
Finally, negotiators at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya are pushing talks into the weekend after failing to reach a deal on its final scheduled day. Talks remain deadlocked over four key issues: a concrete roadmap to phase out fossil fuels, ensuring the 35% by 2035 electrification goal relies on clean energy, delivering climate finance, and guaranteeing a just transition that leaves no one behind.
When and where to watch Europe Tonight?
You can join Euronews’ Mared Gwyn live on TV and Euronews' website as well as digital platforms (YouTube, Facebook, X, and Instagram), every weekday at 6 pm, 7 pm and 8 pm Brussels time.
In just 28 minutes, our new format brings the day's top stories through a European lens, with live analysis and debate with MEPs and leaders.
