noticias.titulo: Researchers find that cats tailor their communication to get human attention
noticias.resumen: A plaintive meow, a gentle purr or an innocent wide-eyed look: cats clearly know how to get their humans' attention. Scientific studies show that they use surprisingly sophisticated communication strategies.
noticias.texto:
A plaintive meow, a gentle purr or an innocent wide-eyed look: cats clearly know how to get their humans' attention. Scientific studies show that they use surprisingly sophisticated communication strategies.
Researchers have found that cats are remarkably good at getting our attention and adapting the way they communicate with us. They use a combination of vocalisations, eye contact and body language. And we humans seem more than happy to play along.
A purr with a hidden message
One particularly interesting study, published in 2009 by researchers at the University of Sussex, examined how cats use purring when they want food.
Led by researcher Karen McComb, the team identified a distinctive type of purring known as "solicitation purring". This special purr contains a high-pitched sound that resembles a human baby's cry, making it particularly difficult for people to ignore.
It is a clever acoustic trick that seems to work remarkably well on their human housemates.
This insistent purr combines the familiar deep rumble with a high-pitched sound resembling a baby's cry. People who listened to recordings of this type of purring rated it as more urgent and less pleasant than ordinary purring. It seems we are particularly sensitive to sounds that remind us of a baby crying for attention.
A friendly blink: body language is part of the repertoire, too
Cats don't just use their voices to get their way. Their eyes also play an important role in how they communicate.
A 2020 study published in the journal Scientific Reports explored what is known as slow blinking. This is when cats gently narrow their eyes before closing them briefly.
The researchers found that cats responded to slow blinking from their owners, often blinking back. They were also more likely to approach people who had given them this friendly signal.
Slow blinking is therefore considered a form of positive communication between cats and humans. Anyone wanting to tell their feline companion "I like you" can try a gentle, slow blink. Who knows – you might even get one in return.
Cats don't just miaow at random – they deliberately communicate with their humans
Just how skilfully cats use their voices is illustrated by a new study from the University of São Paulo in Brazil. For the experiment, researchers observed 38 pet cats sitting in front of a closed plastic box containing their favourite food. The cats could smell the food but were unable to open the box themselves. Each cat was observed for one minute, first with an attentive person present and then alone.
The results were striking: when a person was in the room, the researchers recorded a total of 86 miaows. When the cats were alone, that number dropped to just 20. While miaowing, the animals also frequently sought eye contact, alternating their gaze between their human companion and the food box.
The researchers suggest that cats direct their vocalisations specifically at people they hope will help them. However, whether the animals consciously follow a particular strategy remains an open question.
A cat may therefore know exactly when it is worth appealing to a human – and when it is better not to bother.
They even know their own names
Anyone who thinks their cat only responds when food is involved may be underestimating these little furry companions.
A study published in 2019 in the journal Scientific Reports found that domestic cats can recognise their own names, distinguishing them from other words and even from the names of other cats.
The cats responded differently to hearing their own names than to hearing similar words. That does not mean, however, that every cat comes running when called. Unlike dogs, which often trot over eagerly at the sound of their name, cats seem to prefer to acknowledge the information first and then decide, entirely on their own terms, whether responding is worth the effort.
Humans don't always understand cats
As skilfully as cats communicate, understanding one another is not always straightforward.
A study published in 2024 in Applied Animal Behaviour Science examined how well people can interpret cats' signals.
For the study, 630 people were shown videos of cats in different situations. The researchers assessed how accurately participants could identify the animals' emotional states based on their vocalisations, body language or a combination of the two.
The results were striking: when people could both see a cat's body language and hear its vocalisations, they correctly identified its emotional state in 91.8 per cent of cases. When relying on sounds alone, the figure dropped to 72.2 per cent.
Participants found it particularly difficult to recognise when cats were feeling uncomfortable or unhappy.
A miaow alone does not necessarily reveal what is going on inside a cat's head. Anyone hoping to understand their feline companion should also pay attention to its ears, tail, eyes and overall posture.
Manipulation or simply very good communication?
Over generations of living alongside humans, cats seem to have developed ways of communicating that are particularly effective with us. Whether they consciously manipulate their owners is difficult to establish scientifically. What the studies do show, however, is that cats are remarkably good at picking up on human attention and adapting their signals accordingly.
An insistent purr, a gentle blink or a well-timed miaow can sometimes achieve more than even the most convincing argument.
Perhaps cats have simply figured out how humans work.

noticias.titulo: Morocco commits €366 million to build a national defence industry by 2035
noticias.resumen: The royal cabinet said the plan aims to meet 40% of the armed forces’ and security services’ equipment needs through domestic production by 2035 and to generate more than 65% of industry revenues from exports, supported by a new strategic agency, a holding company, and two new industrial zones.
noticias.texto:
The royal cabinet said the plan aims to meet 40% of the armed forces’ and security services’ equipment needs through domestic production by 2035 and to generate more than 65% of industry revenues from exports, supported by a new strategic agency, a holding company, and two new industrial zones.
King Mohammed VI has allocated 4 billion dirhams (€366 million) from the Hassan II Fund for Economic and Social Development to launch a national defence industry roadmap, the Moroccan Royal Cabinet announced on Wednesday.
The plan sets 2035 as its target date, with three main goals: creating around 50,000 direct and indirect jobs, meeting 40% of the Royal Armed Forces' and security services' equipment needs through domestic production, and generating more than 65% of defence industry revenues from exports.
The roadmap will be backed by a new strategic agency responsible for implementing national defence industry policy and supporting investors, alongside an industrial holding company to organise the production ecosystem and mobilise public and private capital.
Two new industrial zones dedicated to defence manufacturing will be created in Ben Guerir and Benslimane, adding to existing defence zones in Nouaceur and Sidi Yahya.
Morocco is seeking to leverage its existing expertise in automotive, aviation and electronics manufacturing to develop a domestic defence sector.
Priority areas include drones and autonomous systems, land and naval systems, defence electronics, cybersecurity and artificial intelligence. The strategy also covers dual-use technologies with both civilian and military applications.
According to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, Morocco ranks among Africa's leading importers of major weapon systems.
International partnerships
Morocco has begun forming partnerships with foreign defence companies. The Indian group Tata Advanced Systems is cooperating with Morocco to manufacture WhAP 8×8 armoured vehicles in Berrechid, aiming to progressively increase the share of locally produced components.
Moroccan company MMI manufactures military turrets and remotely controlled weapon systems, forming an initial base for broader domestic production.
The Emirati defence group EDGE signed two agreements with Morocco's National Defence Administration at the Marrakech Air Show in October.
The first is a memorandum of understanding to explore manufacturing small arms and aircraft engines in Morocco through local partnerships.
The second covers supplying Desert Sting 16 and Thunder P-31 guided munitions to the Royal Moroccan Air Force for integration into its fleet of unmanned combat aircraft.
The king also instructed authorities to establish a specialised academy offering advanced training programmes in partnership with industrial companies, drawing on Moroccan civilian and military expertise, including professionals based abroad.
A programme to channel young talent into the sector and adapt vocational training to defence industry needs — particularly in engineering, electronics and digital fields — was also ordered.

noticias.titulo: Spain requires data centres to draw 80% of their electricity from renewables
noticias.resumen: Spain tightens regulation of data centres with new requirements on renewable energy, efficiency and digital sovereignty to limit their impact on the power grid and attract sustainable investment.
noticias.texto:
Spain tightens regulation of data centres with new requirements on renewable energy, efficiency and digital sovereignty to limit their impact on the power grid and attract sustainable investment.
The Spanish government has approved new rules for data centres that set renewable energy consumption requirements, water and energy efficiency standards and digital sovereignty obligations, with the aim of aligning the growth of these infrastructures with the capacity of the electricity system and the country’s environmental commitments.
The Royal Decree, approved on Friday by the Council of Ministers, requires data centres to prove that 80% of their electricity consumption comes from renewable sources, with hourly matching between generation and consumption and additionality criteria to drive new clean production capacity.
The regulation provides for long-term power supply contracts, self-consumption and energy storage. It also establishes a voluntary transitional regime for operators that agree to the possibility of being disconnected with priority when this is necessary to safeguard the stability of the electricity grid.
Stricter energy and environmental requirements
The rules introduce provisional limits on water and electricity use in data centres: they will have to use water more efficiently and cut the energy needed for their operation, while European criteria are finalised. The text also incorporates into national law other transparency and water and energy efficiency requirements laid down by European regulation, adapting them to Spain’s specific circumstances.
The regulation introduces sustainability reporting obligations for the largest facilities and sets specific data protection and digital sovereignty requirements for high-category information systems under the National Security Framework.
In these cases, the most sensitive data must remain within the European Economic Area and controls will be tightened on access from third countries to administration, maintenance and support tasks.
Failure to comply with certain obligations may lead to financial compensation and sanctions, including suspension of grid access and connection rights for up to three years. Projects that are already being processed will generally have six months to adapt to the new conditions.
35 GW between permitted capacity and projects in the queue
The decision comes at a time of strong growth in demand for digital infrastructure in Spain. Third Vice-President and Minister for Ecological Transition, Sara Aagesen, said that data centres currently have 15 gigawatts (GW) of granted access capacity to the electricity grid, while a further 20 GW remain on the waiting list.
The minister warned that, without control measures, the expansion of these facilities could generate an additional cost of up to 5,000 million euros per year in the electricity system, according to government estimates: 4,000 million from the impact on wholesale prices and another 1,000 million from capacity mechanisms.
"In the absence of this Royal Decree, we would see an impact of 5,000 million euros on our bills," said Energy Transition Minister Sara Aagesen. "We have different scenarios, but it would lead, for example, to industrial consumers having to pay 25% more for the electricity they use," she added. These figures are government forecasts for a hypothetical scenario, not costs already incurred or savings guaranteed by the new rules.
17,142 million euros of investment in the electricity grid
At the same time, the government has approved new electricity grid planning up to 2030, providing for investments of 17.142 million euros to expand and reinforce infrastructure and meet rising demand. The plan includes capacity for new forms of consumption, including data centres, although it is not specifically dedicated to these facilities.
Spain is seeking to consolidate its position as a destination for international investment in data centres, drawing on its renewable resources, connectivity and strategic location in Europe.
The new regulation is designed to tie that growth to greater energy and environmental efficiency, in a context where the availability of electricity, water and connection capacity has become one of the key factors in the development of these projects. The impact on ongoing projects and future investment will depend on how the new obligations are applied and on the deadlines set out in the final text.

noticias.titulo: France investigates suspected confidential leaks to Le Pen's far-right party
noticias.resumen: A former senior Interior Ministry official is suspected of sharing details of investigations into National Rally's election campaign finances, according a French newspaper.
noticias.texto:
A former senior Interior Ministry official is suspected of sharing details of investigations into National Rally's election campaign finances, according a French newspaper.
French authorities are investigating whether a former senior Interior Ministry official leaked confidential information about judicial investigations to Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party, months before the presidential election.
According to Le Monde newspaper, Hugues Moutouh, now prefect of the Centre-Val de Loire region, is suspected of sharing information about investigations into the financing of the party's 2022 and 2024 election campaigns.
Judicial investigation
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez confirmed on Friday that an investigation had been opened and that he had summoned Moutouh for a meeting.
The Paris prosecutor's office told The Associated Press news agency it was investigating possible breaches of professional confidentiality and investigative secrecy, as well as the handling of information obtained through these offences.
No one has been formally charged, prosecutors said, adding that investigators searched the National Rally's headquarters on 9 November.
Le Pen has not commented on the case.
"If the facts are confirmed, they are obviously very serious," Nuñez told BFM TV.
Further controversies ahead of the election
The investigation adds to a series of controversies involving Le Pen's party less than six months before France's presidential election.
In September, Jordan Bardella, Le Pen's choice for prime minister if elected, was accused of making antisemitic remarks as a young party member. Bardella, 31, strongly denied writing the comments reported by investigative website Mediapart.
Le Pen, 58 is also facing legal challenges after being sentenced in July to a year of home detention with electronic monitoring following an embezzlement conviction. She has appealed to France's highest court and believes she will not have to wear the device.
Despite her legal troubles, Le Pen leads opinion polls ahead of next year's presidential election to succeed Emmanuel Macron.

noticias.titulo: Deepening EU–Canada ties: From critical minerals and defence to erasmus+
noticias.resumen: ‘We are determined to drive the renewed political momentum between the EU and Canada forward,’ write four Members of the European People’s Party (EPP) Group in the European Parliament in an op-ed for Euronews, published on the occasion of a visit by an EPP delegation to Canada on 19–21 November.
noticias.texto:
‘We are determined to drive the renewed political momentum between the EU and Canada forward,’ write four Members of the European People’s Party (EPP) Group in the European Parliament in an op-ed for Euronews, published on the occasion of a visit by an EPP delegation to Canada on 19–21 November.
Europe and Canada have always been natural allies, through both good times and bad, and are growing even closer. It´s not only politics, trade and security, but culture, sports and way of life that joins us. Next year will mark a historic milestone when Canada will compete at the Eurovision Song Contest for the first time. May the best song win!
Canada is a trusted democratic partner
For Europe, Canada is a trusted democratic partner. As Canada´s Prime Minister Mark Carney said when addressing the European Parliament: “Our commitment to the rule of law, and our unyielding defence of human dignity, individual freedom, and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication”. And those shared values are translating into concrete cooperation.
Trade is obvious area where the partnership has delivered tangible results. Since the provisional application of Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), bilateral trade in goods and services has grown by around 80%, rising from €72.1 billion in 2016 to €130 billion in 2025.
More opportunities lie ahead: critical raw materials and defence
And more opportunities lie ahead. For example, Europe is seeking to reduce its dependence on China, particularly in the supply of critical raw materials. Fortunately, Canada is one of the few democratic partners with the resources and capacity to supply the EU with minerals essential to batteries, semiconductors, defence, aerospace, renewable energy and telecommunications.
Canada is also a major producer of uranium, cobalt, nickel and zinc, as well as the world's leading producer of potash.
During this time of Russian aggression, defence and security are of the utmost importance. Europe must build a circle of trusted friends around our continent and, here, Canada plays a vital role. Canada has stood firmly with Ukraine and contributes directly to European security through its leadership of NATO operations in Latvia.
Canada’s defence spending reached 2.0% of GDP this year, and its new federal budget sets out a path towards more than 4% by the end of the decade. This is an ambitious commitment, bringing Canada closer to the level of investment pursued by frontline allies like Poland.
Earlier this year, Canada also became the first non-European country to join the €150 billion defence procurement instrument, SAFE, though more remains to be done to better integrate Canada into European defence markets and defence industry development.
Education and research offer other chances for mutual benefits
Education offers another chance for mutual benefits. Canada consistently performs well in international education, remaining among the strongest OECD countries. According to PISA 2025, it outperforms most EU Member States in science and reading.
We can deepen this relationship by welcoming Canada into the Erasmus+ exchange scheme, one of the most tangible benefits of European integration for young people. Following the launch of formal negotiations at the recent Canada-EU Summit in Montréal, Canada is poised to become the first non-European country associated with the programme, which funds people and organisations to study and train abroad.
Research cooperation is also moving forward. In 2024, Canada became associated with Pillar II of Horizon Europe, which supports collaborative research across a wide scientific and technological fields. Although this is an important milestone, there is still room to strengthen Canada’s participation. Negotiations on deeper participation have now begun and we fully support Canada’s closer integration into Horizon Europe.
Europe and Canada have every reason to stand together
Generations of Europeans have made Canada their home, contributing to Canadian society while maintaining ties with their countries of origin. These communities help sustain cultural links, connect businesses and create opportunities for younger generations to study and work on both sides of the Atlantic.
The case for a stronger EU–Canada partnership is clear. From critical minerals and trade to defence, education and research, there is considerable scope to work closer together. Great partnerships, like great oaks, do not grow overnight. But with the right foundations, they can weather even the roughest political storms. We must make full use of the opportunities available under our existing treaties and agreements. Whether we describe this relationship as an alliance or an association matters less than what we achieve together.
As the strongest political force in the EU political system with majorities in the main institutions, the Commission, the Council and the Parliament, the EPP is an effective broker. We are determined to drive the renewed political momentum between the EU and Canada forward. In an increasingly uncertain world, Europe and Canada have every reason to stand together, whatever the political weather. The timing of our visit couldn’t be better.
Andrzej Halicki, MEP, Vice-president, EPP Group
Zeljana Zovko, Vice-president, EPP Group
Łukasz Kohut, Vice-President, Subcommittee of the Human Rights
Loucas Fourlas, Chair, Delegation to the EU-Serbia Stabilisation and Association Parliamentary Committee

noticias.titulo: Turkey: Activists chant 'shame' as COP31 negotiations falter
noticias.resumen: Climate activists denounced the proposed outcome of COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday 20 November 2026, accusing governments of failing to deliver meaningful progress on tackling climate change. They chanted "shame" as negotiations approached their deadline.
noticias.texto:
Chants of "shame, shame, shame" echoed through a packed press conference as climate campaigners fiercely rejected the draft negotiating text on the scheduled final day of the two-week United Nations climate summit. Organised by Climate Action Network (CAN) International, the briefing saw delegates and activists applaud speakers who accused governments of failing to tackle fossil fuel dependence, spanning coal, oil and gas, or build on pledges made at last year’s summit in Belém, Brazil.
CAN executive director Tasneem Essop urged nations, particularly across the Global South, to walk away from the current text, while the network’s acting head of global political strategy, Anabella Rosemberg, warned: "We will fight back, and we say thank you for nothing." Questioning how COP31 could be judged a success without tangible progress over the past 12 months, Power Shift Africa director Mohamed Adow echoed wider anger that the talks had sidelined the priorities of climate-vulnerable states.
With the United States, one of the world’s top greenhouse gas emitters, absent for a second consecutive year, nearly 200 participating countries remained deadlocked over a final declaration whose commitments largely stay voluntary and non-binding, raising the prospect that negotiations could spill well past Friday’s official closing deadline.

noticias.titulo: Italy: Workers and students stage nationwide strike over living costs
noticias.resumen: Workers and students marched through Rome, on Friday 20 November 2026, joining a nationwide strike over stagnant wages, rising living costs and government spending priorities. Protesters also demanded more funding for education and criticised military spending.
noticias.texto:
From the shadow of Rome’s Colosseum to major squares in Milan, Turin, Naples and Palermo, tens of thousands of workers and students took to the streets across more than 100 Italian cities as a 24-hour general strike disrupted schools, hospitals and public transport. Called by Italy’s largest trade union, CGIL, alongside grassroots unions such as Cobas, the mobilisation coincided with an international student protest day in over 45 cities and a wider European day of action over living costs, military spending and the climate crisis.
Carrying banners declaring "Education builds, war destroys" and "Funds for schools, not for war" through Rome’s historic centre, demonstrators demanded higher wages, stronger social protections and public investment instead of defence outlays. Protester Giorgia Giordani faulted the government’s handling of surging energy bills and everyday household expenses, while a student outside La Sapienza University said crowds wanted answers, and that some were demanding the government’s resignation, echoing CGIL Secretary-General Maurizio Landini’s call for sweeping reform of Italy’s social and economic model.

noticias.titulo: UAE's Lana Nusseibeh pledges ‘relentless diplomacy’ in bid to lead the UN
noticias.resumen: Lana Nusseibeh, the Emirati star diplomat running to succeed António Guterres, told Euronews the UN must return to its core purpose of peace, development, and prosperity. She has pledged relentless diplomacy, a leaner UN judged on results, and early action on wars from Ukraine to Gaza if chosen.
noticias.texto:
Lana Nusseibeh, the Emirati star diplomat running to succeed António Guterres, told Euronews the UN must return to its core purpose of peace, development, and prosperity. She has pledged relentless diplomacy, a leaner UN judged on results, and early action on wars from Ukraine to Gaza if chosen.
As the race to elect the next UN Secretary-General enters its final phase, UAE Minister of State Lana Nusseibeh, who is running to succeed António Guterres, has pledged to serve as the UN's chief mediator and take political risks for peace if chosen for the organisation's top post.
Speaking in a wide-ranging interview with Euronews, Nusseibeh, who served as the UAE's ambassador to the UN for more than a decade, said the organisation must get back to its core purpose of bringing governments and people together for peace, development and prosperity to restore its credibility.
"I think it's a turning point moment for the United Nations," she said.
"I am a relentless diplomat and I intend to offer a candidacy that is about relentless diplomacy," Nusseibeh told Euronews.
Nusseibeh said the UN was too often seen as absent from the 65 active conflicts she said exist worldwide, and that the next secretary-general should act as mediator in chief, pursuing humanitarian truces and aid access first, then a political strategy to make them last.
"It's not about political theatre, it's about political risk-taking," she said.
With official development assistance down 23%, Nusseibeh said the UN would have to narrow its scope, partner with others where they are better placed, and publish a scorecard of results for member states and donors.
"It's not around organograms or design structures of the system, but it's about impact and cost of impact and delivery," she said.
In her first 100 days, she said she would agree on a shared vision with member states and civil society, cut duplication across the thousands of mandates given to the secretariat and move the UN's focus from headquarters to the field.
First woman to lead the UN?
If chosen, Nusseibeh would become the first woman to lead the UN since its establishment in 1945, the first of Palestinian descent, and the second secretary-general from the Arabic-speaking world after Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali.
"But I'm not running because I'm a woman. I'm running because of over two decades of experience and judgment in international diplomacy," Nusseibeh said.
Asked about critics who have questioned her independence, Nusseibeh pointed to the UN Charter. She has taken leave from her post as UAE minister of state to campaign.
"Article 100 of the UN Charter stipulates the independence of a secretary-general," she said.
"So the allegiance of a secretary-general is to the UN Charter and to international law and that is what I would pledge in that role," she said.
"I welcome the criticism, I welcome feedback, I will always welcome the feedback if I am in this role as well," she added.
Nusseibeh said the next secretary-general must combine public advocacy for peace with discreet diplomacy.
"Sometimes quiet diplomacy is needed, keeping channels open to all parties when the doors are closed," she said.
She said she would set up a mediation board of outside experts and UN officials, draw on local community leaders and make women's networks the first point of contact for her mediation team. Nusseibeh would also create a focal point in her own office for the protection of aid workers, 300 of whom she said had been killed in the past year.
"I would continue to try relentlessly until there is an outcome that serves the people on the ground better," she said.
Approaching conflict 'with a lot of humility'
On Ukraine, she said any settlement must rest on the UN Charter's principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity.
"I would offer my good offices immediately," she said. "Where that is welcomed, I would come with options, practical options for how to move from first agreements to a political strategy."
Nusseibeh said 38% of the Security Council's agenda concerned the Middle East, a region she said had seen generations of war.
A fluent Hebrew speaker and a highly regarded diplomat who grew up between Abu Dhabi and the UK in a family of well-known Palestinian political figures, Nusseibeh previously served as the UAE ambassador to the UN and is credited with elevating the UAE's profile during that time.
"One of my driving purposes in seeking this role is to try and pass on a region that is more stable, more prosperous for my own children," she said.
On Gaza, Nusseibeh cited Security Council Resolution 2720, which she negotiated in December 2023 after taking council ambassadors to the Rafah crossing. She said Resolution 2803, which endorsed a 20-point plan for Gaza, had stalled.
"As Secretary General, I would want to see that through in terms of implementation," she said.
Nusseibeh, who is of Palestinian heritage with family roots in Jerusalem, said the issue was both professional and personal for her.
"I come to every conflict with a lot of humility that what we have done in all of these situations has not been nearly enough for the people who've needed it the most," she said.
The Security Council has held repeated informal straw polls, with no candidate yet clearing opposition from all five permanent members, and Guterres's term is due to end on 31 December.
Race remains tight
In the closely watched UN race, former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan still holds a challenging lead as Argentina’s International Atomic Energy Agency Director-General Rafael Grossi and UAE Minister of State Lana Nusseibeh actively campaign to emerge as winners.
The growing excitement around the race is also fueled by the prospect of a female UN secretary-general, something that has never happened in the UN's more than 80-year history.
Campaigning alongside Grynspan, Nusseibeh and Rossi are Guyana’s former Foreign Minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, former Ecuadorian Foreign Minister Maria Fernanda Espinosa, former Senegalese President Macky Sall, former UN Under-Secretary-General Olara Otunnu of Uganda, and Ecuadorian diplomat Ivonne A-Baki.
Costa Rica's former Vice President Rebeca Grynspan, 70, was born to Jewish parents who fled Poland before World War II. She lost her grandparents in the Holocaust after they decided to remain in Poland.
In a May interview with Euronews, Grynspan said, “I know exactly what wars take away from you and what peace allows you to do.”
“I am a generation that have lived in peace. I have never experienced war directly. But millions of people in the world today live in war zones, in conflict. And that is why I am running, because I know the difference, what peace and opportunity can do for you and your family,” Grynspan told Euronews at the time.

noticias.titulo: From Tashkent to Amman: Books and Universities Bring Uzbekistan and Jordan Closer Together
noticias.resumen: Uzbekistan and Jordan deepen ties through book launches, academic conferences and university partnerships, highlighting reforms and shared cultural heritage.
noticias.texto:
A series of international events took place in Amman aimed at strengthening cultural, humanitarian, scientific and educational ties between Uzbekistan and Jordan. The Jordanian public was introduced to works by the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan, Shavkat Mirziyoyev, studies of contemporary Uzbekistan by international authors, and illustrated publications devoted to the country’s historical and cultural heritage. The programme also included international conferences, book presentations and meetings with representatives of Jordan’s academic community.
The events continued a dialogue that had received fresh impetus from the leaders of the two countries during their meetings in Samarkand and Astana.
On 26 August 2025, during King Abdullah II of Jordan’s state visit to Uzbekistan, the two sides discussed prospects for expanding bilateral cooperation, including in the cultural and humanitarian spheres. On 6 November 2026, on the sidelines of a meeting held as part of the Aqaba Process in Astana, the President of Uzbekistan and the King of Jordan reviewed progress in implementing their earlier agreements and discussed the further development of bilateral relations.
New Uzbekistan in Arabic
On 18 November 2026, as part of the Uzbek delegation’s visit to Jordan, an international conference and presentation was held to mark the tenth anniversary of the “New Uzbekistan” phenomenon.
The central event in the programme of book presentations was the launch of the Arabic edition of The Contemporary World and New Uzbekistan by President Shavkat Mirziyoyev. The book examines the main directions of the reforms being implemented in the country, the state’s strategic development objectives and approaches to addressing pressing global challenges. Particular attention is paid to protecting the interests of the people, safeguarding citizens’ rights and freedoms, and improving their well-being.
Alongside the President’s book, nine additional Arabic-language publications and photo albums were presented, introducing readers to Uzbekistan’s history, cultural heritage and contemporary transformations.
Among them were the photo albums Shavkat Mirziyoyev: A Statesman and Political Figure of Global Stature, New Uzbekistan: A Country of Peace, Humanism and Tolerance and Chronicle of the Victories of Independence, as well as the book Uzbekistan: The Third Renaissance — A Concept for Development.
An important part of the programme was the book exhibition Uzbekistan: Civilisations, Personalities, Discoveries. The publications on display were donated to libraries in Jordan. In addition, with the support of Jordanian research centres and higher education institutions, plans have been made to establish dedicated “New Uzbekistan” book sections in the country’s libraries and educational institutions.
Amman also hosted the international academic conference Mawarannahr: The Light of Islamic Civilisation Through the Ages and an international presentation of the Center for Islamic Civilization in Uzbekistan.
The events were attended by representatives of Jordanian government and public institutions, parliamentarians, scholars, researchers, religious organisations and the media. The total number of participants exceeded 1,500.
Universities as a Platform for Cooperation
The scientific and educational dimension of bilateral cooperation was further developed through meetings with representatives of Jordanian universities.
On 18 November, Al al-Bayt University hosted an academic symposium devoted to President Mirziyoyev’s book The Contemporary World and New Uzbekistan. Participants discussed the book’s main ideas, the nature of the transformations taking place in the country and prospects for further developing academic and scientific ties between the two countries.
At the same time, the first Forum of Rectors of Higher Education Institutions of Uzbekistan and Jordan took place in Tashkent on 17–18 November. The Jordanian delegation was led by Azmi Mahafza, Jordan’s Minister of Education and Human Resources Development. The forum brought together rectors from 16 Jordanian universities and representatives of 19 leading higher education institutions in Uzbekistan.
The forum was held at the National Research University “Tashkent Institute of Irrigation and Agricultural Mechanization Engineers”. Participants considered prospects for expanding inter-university ties, implementing joint educational programmes, conducting scientific research and developing academic exchanges.
Priority areas of cooperation included artificial intelligence and digital technologies, engineering education, renewable energy, efficient water resource management, medical education and pharmaceuticals.
Cooperation between the two countries thus extends beyond the cultural and spiritual spheres to practical areas of professional training, scientific development and the exchange of academic experience.
A Cultural Bridge Between the Two Countries
Another important event complementing the mutual exchange of books was the presentation in Tashkent of King Abdullah II of Jordan’s book Our Last Best Chance: The Pursuit of Peace in a Time of Peril.
The event took place on 13 November 2026 at the University of World Economy and Diplomacy. The book introduces readers to the Jordanian King’s reflections on international relations, regional security, diplomacy and the search for peaceful solutions to contemporary challenges.
The exchange of books has thus become reciprocal: works by the President of Uzbekistan were presented in Jordan, while King Abdullah II’s book was presented in Tashkent. This has broadened opportunities for the public and academic communities of both countries to learn about each other’s political views, history and development priorities.
Books and university initiatives are becoming important tools for strengthening Uzbek-Jordanian relations. They lay the groundwork for further cooperation in education, science, the preservation of historical heritage and the development of intercultural dialogue.

noticias.titulo: EU Commission partially clears Hungary’s €10bn recovery fund payment after rule of law reforms
noticias.resumen: The European Commission says Budapest has met all but one of the conditions for the full €10bn payment. The financial penalty for the missing milestone is expected to be “minimal”, sources told Euronews.
noticias.texto:
The European Commission says Budapest has met all but one of the conditions for the full €10bn payment. The financial penalty for the missing milestone is expected to be “minimal”, sources told Euronews.
The European Commission has given partial approval to Hungary’s request for €10 billion in funding under the EU’s Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), clearing the way for the country to receive almost the entire amount.
The Commission found that Hungary had fulfilled 126 of the 127 required milestones, with one taxation-related condition only partially met.
It remains unclear how much funding Hungary could lose as a result. However, a Commission official, speaking to Euronews on condition of unanimity, said the “financial consequences of the non-fulfilment will be minimal”.
The decision marks a major step towards unlocking EU funds withheld over concerns about the rule of law and corruption, and represents a significant victory for Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s government.
Magyar, who swept to power in a landslide election victory in April, campaigned on a promise to secure the release of EU funding frozen during Viktor Orbán’s 16 years in office.
In May, Magyar and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen agreed on a roadmap to unlock €16.4 billion withheld over concerns about the previous government’s record on the rule of law and corruption.
Of that amount, €10 billion comes from the EU’s post-pandemic recovery fund, which is due to expire later this year. The payment must be authorised by the end of November to ensure the money can be disbursed before the end of the year.
Hungary announced in late August that it had met the EU’s requirements for the payment, following substantial delays under Orbán. The Commission subsequently launched a verification process.
The country was required to meet 27 so-called “super milestones” alongside more than 127 additional targets. Parliament amended more than 100 laws over the summer to meet the requirements, most of them relating to judicial independence and anti-corruption measures.
Hungary’s revised National Recovery Plan also includes investments to modernise the country’s energy grid and railway network, as well as its rental housing stock.
Following the Commission’s positive assessment, EU member states must also approve the payment before the funds can be released. Euronews understands that their decision is expected to be positive.
In September, the Commission approved the release of €4.2 billion in frozen cohesion funds after Magyar’s government introduced reforms on the rule of law and anti-corruption.
However, a further €2.2 billion remains blocked over concerns relating to academic freedom and LGBTI+ rights. Budapest has yet to provide evidence that the relevant reforms have been implemented.

noticias.titulo: Ukraine: Rescue teams search wreckage after deadly Russian strike on Kyiv
noticias.resumen: A Russian overnight attack on Kyiv, Ukraine, killed eight people on Friday 20 November 2026, according to Associated Press, leaving buildings and warehouses damaged across the capital. Firefighters battled blazes as emergency crews searched the wreckage and police collected evidence.
noticias.texto:
Smoke billowed over Kyiv and flames tore through apartment blocks and offices after Russia unleashed more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles across Ukraine overnight, killing at least eight people, six of them in the capital, and injuring 15, according to Ukrainian authorities and emergency services.
Alongside residential and commercial buildings, strikes hit hospitals, essential infrastructure and three bridges spanning the Dnipro River, leaving streets littered with shattered masonry, twisted metal and wrecked cars.
Across the battered capital, firefighters battled blazes while rescue teams searched ruined structures for survivors, police combed the debris for forensic evidence and utility crews worked to restore vital services. Some fires had been brought under control, but responders continued working to extinguish remaining blazes, clear rubble and assess damage across the capital.
The devastating barrage, coming just a day after an earlier wave of attacks damaged diplomatic premises in Kyiv, made good on Russian President Vladimir Putin’s warning of a "painful" retaliation for Ukraine’s strike on the Crimean Bridge earlier in the week.

noticias.titulo: Candidate or kingmaker: could ECB President Lagarde influence France's presidential race?
noticias.resumen: Lagarde remains bound to political neutrality until her tenure as ECB president ends in February 2027, just two months ahead of the first election round of France's presidential elections.
noticias.texto:
Lagarde remains bound to political neutrality until her tenure as ECB president ends in February 2027, just two months ahead of the first election round of France's presidential elections.
Christine Lagarde's decision last month to bring forward her departure as president of the European Central Bank's (ECB) has reignited major speculation around whether she could run to become France's first female President — or play a role in the country's election race.
Interest in Lagarde's next move is growing as the former minister, who has no clear political affiliation, could be seen as a potential unifying figure for France's fragmented centrist camp. This comes amid a deeply polarised political climate, just five months ahead of the presidential election.
However, analysts caution that Lagarde's support remains largely confined to an educated, elite electorate, and that her strength reflects the French right's lack of direction rather than genuine enthusiasm for her potential presidential candidacy.
Although Lagarde has not announced that she is running, a survey published by Politico on 11 November predicted that she could perform just as well as the center-right former prime minister Édouard Philippe. When the pair were tested separately against other presidential candidates, they respectively garnered 13.5% and 14% of voting intentions.
Current polls point to Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally and Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the hard-left France Unbowed leading the race, highlighting the deep divisions shaping the country’s political landscape.
They are respectively polling around 32-34% and 17-19.5%, according to a survey conducted on 18 November by Ifop-Fiducial. Between them, candidates on the left, right and centre, are struggling to make headway.
Lagarde: 'I don't think I can remain neutral'
Before presiding over the ECB, Lagarde headed the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and served as France's Economy Minister from 2007-2011 under former conservative President Nicolas Sarkozy.
Upon announcing her decision to step down from the ECB on 29 October, she declared that she wished to have the freedom to "engage in matters that are not monetary policy."
“I don’t think that I can remain neutral,” she said, adding that she was interested in the truth, which is "very often damaged, contradicted by misrepresentation."
She remains bound to political neutrality until her tenure as ECB president ends in February 2027, just two months ahead of the first round of France's elections.
Asked about a possible bid, she told Euronews in July “I’m not a candidate for anything, but I’m very keen that Europe is protected, that Europe is the framework within which member states operate, including France."
In August, Swiss newspaper Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ) reported that Lagarde had been referred to as a "putative candidate" to lead the World Economic Forum during a board meeting near Geneva earlier this week.
Citing unnamed sources, Lagarde, who is on the WEF's Board of Trustees, reportedly thanked fellow board members for their confidence in her and said she is "ready to serve", the outlet reported.
The following month, she told French newspaper La Croix that running "would not be a good idea," stating "there's the question of vitality, energy, and strength. There's also an unavoidable sense of sacrifice in this type of commitment. And I'm 70 years old."
France's centrists and right searching for direction
According to Bruno Cautrès, a researcher at the Cevipof institute and lecturer at Sciences Po Paris, Lagarde's polling scores reflect a "loss of direction for France's right, rather than a deep adherence to the idea of Christine Lagarde becoming President."
She could resonate with centrist and conservative voters, "who are financially secure, educated and worried about public debt", while another portion of voters "have likely not followed her career and don't really know who she is."
Lagarde's extensive experience at the IMF and ECB could bolster her credentials with certain voters, but for others it could reinforce perceptions of her as an out-of-touch "technocrat" — a criticism that has also dogged French President Emmanuel Macron.
Her public standing within international institutions could possibly act as a double-edged sword, given that "she will be perceived as part of the elite, which the public believes is responsible for the current economic situation", said Cautrès.
"She's been living abroad for fifteen years, working in prestigious international institutions, where she's earned a very good living. There is a question mark around her ability to understand French voters and the population," he added.
'She would not take votes from Mélenchon or Le Pen'
Ultimately, a Lagarde candidacy would not "take any votes away from Mélenchon or Le Pen", Bernard Dolez, professor of political science at the Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne university told Euronews.
She is likely to seduce voters inclined to support centrist Gabriel Attal and conservative Édouard Philippe, both of whom served as prime ministers under Emmanuel Macron.
"The challenge for any candidate at this stage in the central and conservative bloc is to expand beyond their existing base. This is a significant challenge, as current candidates, including Glucksmann, Philippe Attal, Retailleau, and even established figures, are struggling to do so", commented Dolez.
Over the past decade, the country's political landscape has been reshaped, precipitated by the election of centrist Emmanuel Macron in 2017, who fractured the traditional left and right with the party he created.
As France's central and conservative blocs struggle to gain ground, they remain divided over the prospect of holding a primary to select a single candidate. Disputes have also centred around including politicians on the right of the political spectrum in a possible primary.
Public debt remains a major campaign flashpoint
Given that she is not an official candidate, nor the author of a programme, Lagarde's positions remain unknown, beyond her pro-European stance, along with her support for fiscal discipline and structural reform.
Nevertheless, France's public debt and fiscal crisis have emerged as a major campaign flashpoint, as the government seeks to push its 2027 budget through a divided parliament. Its proposed austerity measures have sparked a backlash among opposition parties and trade unions, amid major social unrest.
This comes as protests which started out in secondary schools have broadened into a wider movement, fuelled by the cost of living crisis and rising energy prices, exacerbated by the Iran war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
Bernard Dolez underlined that "economic decision-makers domestically and abroad are counting on the arrival of a charismatic figure who could emerge as a saviour for them."
In September, Lagarde criticised Mélenchon's proposal to cancel a proportion of French debt held by the ECB, warning that such a move would violate EU treaty rules and undermine confidence among financial markets.
A possible Le Pen victory has unsettled markets, who fear that her economic policies could complicate efforts to reduce France's public debt, push up borrowing costs and create further uncertainty across the eurozone.

noticias.titulo: Burnham drew a line under Brexit at the EU-UK summit. But where does Britain go next?
noticias.resumen: The EU-UK summit delivered landmark agreements at their Brussels summit, but also exposed the limits of negotiating one deal at a time. As Brussels signals its willingness to explore closer ties, Andy Burnham faces a bigger question: how far does Britain want to go?
noticias.texto:
The EU-UK summit delivered landmark agreements at their Brussels summit, but also exposed the limits of negotiating one deal at a time. As Brussels signals its willingness to explore closer ties, Andy Burnham faces a bigger question: how far does Britain want to go?
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has secured the biggest breakthrough in relations with the European Union since Brexit. But after a landmark summit in Brussels on Friday, a more fundamental question remains: what kind of relationship does Britain ultimately want with its nearest neighbours?
The second EU-UK summit since Brexit delivered a series of agreements covering food and agricultural standards, carbon markets and youth mobility. Yet for all the diplomatic fanfare, it also exposed the limits of rebuilding ties one deal at a time.
"Today, we do draw a line on a decade of drift and division by reconnecting with old friends, by building a much more constructive relationship with our nearest neighbours and our largest market," Burnham told reporters.
"This is a good day for Britain, and this is a good day for Europe."
But is this as good as it gets?
The case for closer cooperation has rarely been stronger. Donald Trump's unpredictable foreign policy, Russia's war in Ukraine and China's increasingly assertive trade agenda have given Britain and the EU powerful reasons to work together.
London has taken a leading role in the Coalition of the Willing, which is preparing security guarantees for Ukraine in the event of a peace agreement with Russia. Britain is also part of the European negotiating team endorsed by EU leaders last week to ensure Europe's interests are represented in the peace talks.
On security, the two sides are increasingly acting as partners. On trade and economic relations, however, the old Brexit arguments have proved harder to escape.
The price of closer ties
EU governments remain determined that Britain should not enjoy the benefits of membership without accepting the corresponding obligations. That principle has shaped every stage of the negotiations, even as both sides acknowledge the need for closer ties.
“Difficult geopolitical circumstances call for keeping like-minded countries close,” an EU diplomat told Euronews. "But this does not mean compromising our interests."
Indeed, some of Friday's agreements could still run into trouble over an unresolved dispute about university tuition fees. Brussels wants EU students to pay the same fees as their British counterparts, while London is offering a more limited reduction.
British participation in the EU electricity market has also been left for further negotiations, with several member states demanding a UK contribution to the bloc's cohesion funds, which support poorer regions.
Not everyone in Europe believes such a hard line is helpful.
“We need to get out of the mindset that Britain needs to be punished. Let’s not concentrate on the past and revisit old arguments. Let’s focus on the future,” Finnish President Alexander Stubb said at the EU Enlargement Forum on Monday.
The disputes underline a wider problem: negotiating individual agreements may deliver practical improvements, but each new deal risks reopening arguments over money, sovereignty and the balance of rights and obligations.
Beyond the piecemeal approach
Since moving into Downing Street from Greater Manchester's mayoral office in July, Burnham has been unusually forthright about Brexit's shortcomings.
He has argued that leaving the EU failed to deliver its promised benefits, declared the existing relationship inadequate and even raised the possibility of Britain eventually rejoining the bloc.
But while Burnham has been clear about what he wants to move away from, he has been less specific about what should replace it.
Friday's summit appeared to mark a turning point. The Prime Minister himself acknowledged that the sector-by-sector approach was approaching its limits and said Britain would begin exploring more ambitious options for its long-term relationship with the EU.
His government is preparing a ten-year plan for Britain, due to be published next month, setting out ambitions for economic growth, reindustrialisation and greater opportunities for young people. Burnham believes those goals cannot be separated from the country's relationship with Europe.
He also proposed an informal brainstorming exercise with EU leaders over the coming year, ahead of the next summit, to examine what a more comprehensive settlement might look like.
"What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it," he said.
"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."
Crucially, Burnham has stopped short of committing himself to any particular destination. He insists the British public will ultimately decide how far the country should go.
An open door, but on Brussels' terms
The EU's response has been cautiously encouraging.
European Council President António Costa made clear that Brussels would respect whatever course Britain chose, just as it had respected the 2016 referendum result.
"We will equally respect whatever decision the United Kingdom takes about the future of its long-term relationship with the European Union," he said. "Of course, we follow with great interest the debate you have relaunched about our common future."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen was similarly receptive, welcoming Burnham's willingness to consider the bigger picture and declaring Brussels open to brainstorming.
But neither offered any indication that the EU would relax its fundamental principles, particularly the indivisibility of the single market's four freedoms and the balance between rights and obligations.
The contrast with the treatment reserved for Canada is striking.
Ottawa's proposal to become the bloc's first "associate member" was greeted with cheers and applause in the European Parliament in September. Despite German reservations about the terminology, Brussels moved quickly to offer Canada closer consultations at both political and technical levels.
Britain, by contrast, had to fight for a much narrower concession: a so-called "decision-shaping" arrangement allowing British officials to participate in certain EU technical discussions where the UK is closely integrated with European rules, but without a vote.
Burnham defended the arrangement on Friday, arguing that getting British experts back into the room was a significant step forward.
London also welcomed language in the summit declaration on reciprocal market openness, which could help British manufacturers avoid being excluded from the EU's proposed "Made in Europe" preferences for public procurement.
The fact that Friday's summit took place at all was itself a diplomatic achievement. Its prospects had been uncertain after Burnham replaced Keir Starmer in July.
"Today's summit is the continuation of last year's summit and the work that we've been doing for the past year," an EU official said. "The idea today is very much to have concrete deliverables for the relationship and, of course, for our citizens."
The next big decision
The immediate priority for both sides will be implementing Friday's agreements and settling the outstanding disputes over tuition fees and electricity market access.
But the more consequential debate will unfold over the coming year, as Burnham sets out the options for Britain's longer-term future in Europe.
For Brussels, the question is whether London is finally ready to define the relationship it wants, rather than continuing to negotiate its individual components.
For Burnham, the challenge is greater still: turning growing public dissatisfaction with Brexit into a coherent political proposition without reopening all the divisions of the past decade.
Friday's summit may have drawn a line under the acrimony of Brexit. But it has left the biggest question of all for another day: how close does Britain really want to get?

noticias.titulo: Russia stalls UN bid to regulate AI 'killer robots' as talks near deadline
noticias.resumen: Campaigners warn the world is approaching an "Oppenheimer moment" over weapons that can choose and attack targets with no human involved.
noticias.texto:
Campaigners warn the world is approaching an "Oppenheimer moment" over weapons that can choose and attack targets with no human involved.
Diplomats in Geneva, Switzerland, were racing against the clock on Friday after Russia in particular held up five days of gruelling talks over whether to start negotiating rules for lethal autonomous weapons.
The talks, at the United Nations' Review Conference of the Convention on Conventional Weapons (CCW), were due to end on Friday evening. By mid-afternoon, states had still not found a way past the deadlock.
Armies are trying to use artificial intelligence (AI) to identify and strike targets faster and more accurately.
Once activated, lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS) can select and attack targets without any human intervention. Stop Killer Robots, a global coalition of more than 300 organisations, says such systems have already been tested or deployed, including in the war in Ukraine.
Critics say the weapons raise the risk of indiscriminate strikes, make it unclear who is accountable, and may not be used in line with the rules of war.
A divided room
The 128 states party to the CCW spent the week deciding whether to open negotiations, and if so on what terms and over what timeline. Any decision needs full consensus.
Most countries favour a legally binding agreement. But countries that have the technology, including the United States and Russia, are reluctant to have their hands tied.
They also disagree on timing. The International Committee of the Red Cross and various non-governmental organisations (NGOs) want negotiations to take one year, while Washington has proposed five years.
France is among those pushing a hybrid of legally binding and non-binding measures.
"On the final day of talks, a minority of states continue to block progress," said Anna Hehir, head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute.
Russia in the spotlight
When the conference opened on Monday, Russia triggered a procedural standoff by objecting to observers taking part in the debate, including the European Union and civil society organisations. That forced states to continue their discussions in an informal format.
On Thursday, Russia repeatedly demanded changes to the draft final report, including to passages unrelated to the core issues.
Even so, one diplomat told AFP, speaking anonymously, that the week had brought the camps closer together.
"We're very close to consensus on the need to negotiate something. There is only one delegation that is actively opposing a process that is focused on negotiations."
Oppenheimer moment
Magnus Lovold, of the Lex International philanthropic fund, said autonomous weapons were reaching an "Oppenheimer moment", a nod to Robert Oppenheimer, the physicist who brought the world into the nuclear age.
"We’re really at the brink now where it may be very much more difficult in the future to actually get these rules that we need," Lovold said on the sidelines of the talks.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told the conference on Monday to "take action to prevent the use and spread of these merciless weapons".
"We must never stop shielding civilians from the carnage and devastation of armed conflict," Guterres said.

noticias.titulo: Estonia to shut border with Russia over GRU-linked sabotage attack
noticias.resumen: The five checkpoints will close from 1 December, with a possible review in six months, after an attempted arson at a defence facility near Tallinn that Estonian authorities say Russian military intelligence ordered. Rail services will remain unaffected.
noticias.texto:
The five checkpoints will close from 1 December, with a possible review in six months, after an attempted arson at a defence facility near Tallinn that Estonian authorities say Russian military intelligence ordered. Rail services will remain unaffected.
Estonia formally approved the closure of all road crossings on its border with Russia from 1 December, in response to a sabotage attack on a defence company that Tallinn attributed to Russian military intelligence.
All five checkpoints — Narva-1, Narva-2, Koidula, Luhamaa and Saatse — will be closed. The government said it may review the decision in six months. Rail services will not be affected.
The government described the move as "a response to Russia's ongoing hostile actions against Estonia and other European countries." Prime Minister Kristen Michal said Estonia would "not allow Russia to use our openness against us."
The closure follows an attempted arson at the Threod Systems defence facility in Viimsi, near Tallinn, on the night of 14 November. Production and products were undamaged.
Authorities detained eight people from Latvia in connection with the incident.
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna announced last Sunday that Estonia was considering closing the border, citing evidence that the GRU, Russia's military intelligence agency, had ordered the attack.
Estonian defence companies have been targeted twice this year. The Estonian Internal Security Service said Russian security services authorised both operations.
Earlier this week, President Ülle Madise urged the cabinet not to act "under the influence of emotions," while acknowledging that keeping the borders open meant extra work for Estonia's security agency Kapo.
Estonia is not the first EU country on Russia's border to take such a step. Finland closed its land border with Russia in December 2023, and Latvia, Lithuania and Poland have significantly curtailed crossings at their eastern borders in recent years.
In practice, only three of the five checkpoints — at Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula — were in active use before the decision. Russia suspended road traffic at Narva in February 2024, though pedestrian crossings remained open.
Moscow denied involvement in the sabotage attacks, and the Foreign Ministry slammed the decision as "Russophobia".
