noticias.titulo: Norway signs carbon credit deals with Indonesia and Morocco to help fund renewable energy
noticias.resumen: Norway’s carbon credit purchases will help finance projects that might otherwise go unbuilt, while allowing it to count emissions cuts towards its own targets.
noticias.texto:
Norway’s carbon credit purchases will help finance projects that might otherwise go unbuilt, while allowing it to count emissions cuts towards its own targets.
Norway has agreed to buy carbon credits from Indonesia and Morocco to help finance new renewable energy projects in the two countries.
The agreements cover up to 12 million tonnes of emissions reductions in Indonesia and 8.78 million tonnes in Morocco, over a 10-year period for each programme, Norway’s climate ministry said on Monday (16 November).
Both deals were signed at the COP31 UN climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye. The Indonesian agreement was signed on 11 November, followed by Morocco’s the next day.
Under the arrangements, Norway would pay for emissions avoided by generating electricity from renewable sources. The income from selling carbon credits is intended to help fund projects that would not otherwise be built.
Norway will only pay once the emissions cuts have been achieved, independently verified and the credits transferred. The reductions must go beyond what would have happened without the programmes.
The Indonesian agreement was signed by PLN, the country’s state-owned electricity company, and the Global Green Growth Institute (GGGI), acting on Norway’s behalf. Indonesia relies heavily on coal for electricity and is seeking to expand renewable generation.
The programme will initially focus on floating solar farms, where panels are installed on water. It will prioritise projects paired with batteries so electricity can be stored and supplied during the evening and periods of high demand, GGGI said.
Payments for carbon credits would supplement income from electricity sales, helping projects cover their costs. GGGI described the agreement as Indonesia’s first carbon credit purchase contract under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement.
Indonesia’s environment ministry said on Monday that technical arrangements were still being completed, including rules for approving and recording the transfer of credits.
New solar and wind projects in Morocco
Morocco’s programme will support new solar and wind farms, including projects with battery storage. It aims to help develop around two gigawatts of additional renewable power capacity, according to GGGI.
The agreement covers emissions reductions generated between 2027 and 2036, although the first cuts are expected from 2028. The partners are still finalising operating rules and monitoring arrangements before launching a pilot phase, GGGI said.
Both agreements fall under Article 6.2 of the Paris Agreement, which allows countries to trade emissions reductions. Norway could use the credits towards its own climate targets, but the same cuts cannot also be counted towards the selling country’s targets.
Norway says it plans to achieve most of its required emissions reductions through action at home and cooperation with the European Union. Credits bought from other countries could help cover any remaining shortfall.

noticias.titulo: Chevron to begin offshore oil and gas exploration in Greece
noticias.resumen: Chevron and HELLENiQ ENERGY are set to begin seismic surveys for oil and gas in Greece’s southern Ionian Sea. The results could help determine whether to drill in a country that relies on imported gas.
noticias.texto:
Chevron and HELLENiQ ENERGY are set to begin seismic surveys for oil and gas in Greece’s southern Ionian Sea. The results could help determine whether to drill in a country that relies on imported gas.
Chevron and HELLENiQ ENERGY are set to begin seismic surveys for oil and gas in the southern Ionian Sea in the coming days, Greece's Environment and Energy Minister Stavros Papastavrou said. Energy data company TGS will carry out the surveys.
The TGS survey vessel Ramform Tethys has already arrived in the area after a request to issue a maritime notice, known as a NAVTEX, was approved. It will survey the areas where the consortium holds exploration rights. The surveys are expected to be completed by the end of January 2027.
Greece relies on imported gas, and a commercially viable discovery could give it a domestic source of supply. The survey data will help Chevron and HELLENiQ ENERGY decide whether there are promising sites for exploratory drilling.
In a separate tender, three leading companies in the sector, SLB, Viridien and BGP, have submitted bids to collect and process non-exclusive seismic data off western and southern Greece. The international tender is run by the Hellenic Hydrocarbons and Energy Resources Management Company (HEREMA).
HEREMA's evaluation committee met on Thursday 19 November to open the three bids. The committee will now assess them and aims to select one or more bidders to carry out the work.
Greece's plans for its domestic energy resources
Papastavrou said the arrival of the TGS vessel in the southern Ionian Sea and the participation of SLB, Viridien and BGP in the HEREMA tender showed strong international interest in Greece's energy potential.
He said four of the world's largest seismic survey companies had now shown interest in Greece, following moves by Chevron and ExxonMobil.
Papastavrou said developing domestic energy resources was a priority for the government. He said the surveys would follow international law, including the law of the sea, and meet strict safety and environmental requirements.
He also said the government had a responsibility to establish what oil and gas resources Greece might have.
He said that if the surveys confirmed commercially viable deposits, developing them could strengthen Greece's energy security, help supply Europe with energy and improve living standards in Greece.
The surveys and the interest from international companies mark another step in Greece's efforts to play a bigger role in the region's energy sector. The results will help determine what economic and geopolitical benefits Greece could gain.

noticias.titulo: Euronews Culture's Film of the Week: 'You Can See Everything' - Is this Elizabeth Holmes doc 2026's best film?
noticias.resumen: Finally arriving to Europe with a staggered theatrical release, this documentary is every bit as strange and fascinating as you've heard.
noticias.texto:
Finally arriving to Europe with a staggered theatrical release, this documentary is every bit as strange and fascinating as you've heard.
NB: This is a spoiler-free review.
In 2015, Forbes named biomedical entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes the youngest and wealthiest self-made female billionaire in the US, based on a $9-billion valuation of her company, Theranos.
It all came crashing down when the company's revolutionary method of conducting blood tests through a single drop of blood was revealed to have been a scam. Holmes was found guilty of misleading everyone, convicted of defrauding investors, and sentenced to more than 11 years in prison in 2022.
The spectacular rise and fall of the disgraced entrepreneur became a Silicon Valley cautionary tale - one which has been adapted into numerous podcasts and books, as well as an HBO documentary by Alex Gibney titled The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley and the miniseries The Dropout, for which Amanda Seyfried won an Emmy for playing Holmes.
Having exhausted her multiple appeals, You Can See Everything starts 34 days before the infamous fraudster reports to federal prison in May 2023.
The Theranos founder and her husband Billy Evans invite a film crew to document her life... Co-directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim enter their rented home with the offer of “radical transparency”.
For those of you unfamiliar with those names, Oppenheim's work has blended nonfiction storytelling with cinematic formalism, with documentaries including Some Kind Of Heaven and Spermworld, and is perhaps best known for his narrative directorial debut Primetime.
As for Fielder, he has made a name for himself as the creator and host of the satirical docu-reality series Nathan For You, in which he plays a fictional version of himself. His follow-up series, The Rehearsal, is another docu-comedy show which blends awkward comedy and irony in a bid to satirically explore the blurring ideas of reality, artifice and performance.
Three words which make him and Oppenheim the perfect co-helmers of a film about Elizabeth Holmes. The pair have crafted a fascinating film that resists easy summary or explanation. It's simply one that needs to be experienced and will spark endless discussion and debate.
Still, here goes – with no spoilers ahead.
For the first part of You Can See Everything, Fielder lurks in the rented beach house, observing Holmes and Evans' quotidian, and asks blunt questions about Theranos and life after the conviction. Holmes obfuscates, stares at a skeptical Fielder with her unblinking bugeyes, and unwaveringly asserts that "the world believes a reality about me that isn't true".
The convicted scammer is adamant that she hasn’t committed a crime – so much so that she comes off as more than a pathological liar. Holmes seems to believe in her version of events and has bypassed the reality of her manipulation. Either she's a master storyteller, like Oppenheim and Fielder, or she lives in some sort of alternate reality of her own making. Or both.
Throughout, Fielder says the quiet things out loud, and even calls out Evans, asking him: "Why are you being so weird and cryptic with your words?"
The footage is revealing, tense, at times shocking, and often dryly hilarious.
Halfway through the film, Holmes goes to prison. Two years pass. The claustrophobic huis clos ends and perspectives shift (and not for the last time), as Evans assumes his wife's place as the documentary's secondary and unnerving subject.
He was already a troubling presence in the beach house, evidently just as manipulative as Holmes and with no compunction about being filmed in the shower, with a full-frontal shot which no one asked for.
Plus, seriously: What kind of sociopath brushes his teeth while showering?
Like his saucer-eyed wife, Evans never seems to blink, and we witness him trying to control the narrative of the documentary. Concurrently, he announces that he can speak for Holmes and has turned her incarceration into a business model of sorts, believing Theranos 2.0 is on its way.
What follows – like the film as a whole, in fact – deserves to go unspoiled and is best seen with no foreknowledge whatsoever.
What is fascinating about You Can See Everything is its ever-deepening layers and the way it subverts itself and the audience's perceptions through its very deliberate motions.
It starts off about two people gaslighting themselves and others. There's a sizeable amount of schadenfreude that decries from this, as seeing the imminent final act of snake oil saleswoman feels like just retribution.
However, it feels like tense game of "Who's playing who?", with the folie à deux shared by Holmes and Evans quickly becoming a folie à trois with Fielder. It then becomes an unnerving folie à plenty with the viewers, as witnessing the footage is akin to plunging into another person's parallel reality in which their delusion has taken hold and threatens to spread.
It then morphs from a manipulator who has convinced herself that she wasn't manipulating anyone to a woman seemingly being manipulated by a partner who attempts to manipulate others via manipulating the documentary and its filmmakers, who see through the manipulation and lead the audience back to the question: Who's manipulating who?
Still with us?
Good. And just when you think you've got You Can See Everything figured out, a surprise guest star or a new thematic strand is introduced, leading to more meditations in what can only be described as an ever-multiplying matryoshka doll.
As the riveting mise en abyme touches upon deception, so too does it explore the limits of performance, language and communication. From the text message sent by Holmes to Fielder - "You can totally see everything" (with the word 'can' doing a lot of heavy lifting) - to that standout scene in which Fielder shows the couple the famous Abbott and Costello routine "Who's on First?", a single word or a supposed misunderstanding can be used as a loophole. Or worse, can be twisted to alter perception.
In this respect, You Can See Everything becomes a damning portrait of our modern times, in which Fielder and Oppenheim expose how we are exploited by grifters who have drunk their own Kool Aid and expect us to follow suit. Elon Musk is mentioned several times during the documentary, and that's no fluke. Whether it's the X founder attempting to impose and manipulate under the guise of progress and his version of free speech; the Sam Altmans of this world encouraging us to surrender the very act of critical thought to machines; the Zuckerbergs who cloak their insidiousness in so-called innovation... The fact is we are constantly allowing ourselves to be fooled by charlatans in the age of the con artist. Why?
Is it because they've understood that the stories and lies we tell ourselves can be exploited? That language and intent have become elusive and malleable concepts? Can it be because truth isn't just the first casualty of war; it's also the first thing to go when we willingly give up our ability to think critically?
Not that You Can See Everything topples into nihilism, asserts that no truths can be known, or ignores the crucial matter of accountability. It just dares to question and go further. In its final moments, it unexpectedly reveals a blink-and-you'll-miss-it moment pertaining to the arbitrary labels of fiction and nonfiction, confronting the nature of objectivity within documentary filmmaking, and questioning how our judgements are shaped.
It sounds like a lot. And it is a head trip when you replay the film in your mind or discuss it with a fellow moviegoer. As Feilder says in the film's closing moments: "It's very complicated". But as thought-provoking, confounding and heady as You Can See Everything can be, it is also simply an absurdist and fascinating watch from start to finish.
No matter how deep you choose to go down the rabbit hole, you can file it alongside the likes of Cameraperson, Grizzly Man, Citizenfour, The Act Of Killing, The Imposter and No Other Land as a defining piece of modern documentary filmmaking. You can also hope that history will be made when Academy nominations come a knockin'... No documentary has ever been nominated for Best Picture at the Oscars. Maybe that can change with one of the strangest and most mesmerising films of the year.
You Can See Everything is out now in the UK, Ireland and Norway. Its staggered release in European cinemas continues this year, with theatrical release dates in Italy (27 November), Germany (3 December), Spain (25 December) and France, Belgium and Luxembourg (30 December).

noticias.titulo: Slovenia’s Ljubljana and Majorca’s Calvià named the 2027 European Capitals of Tourism
noticias.resumen: The Slovenian capital city was recognised for its resident-focused approach and year-round tourism, while the Majorcan municipality was praised for moving away from mass tourism towards a more sustainable model.
noticias.texto:
The Slovenian capital city was recognised for its resident-focused approach and year-round tourism, while the Majorcan municipality was praised for moving away from mass tourism towards a more sustainable model.
Ljubljana and Calvià have been announced as the 2027 European Capitals of Tourism by the European Commission.
The Slovenian capital city and the Majorcan municipality were recognised for their achievements in advancing smart and sustainable tourism.
Ljubljana took the title in the category for cities with more than 100,000 inhabitants, while Calvià won it for destinations with between 25,000 and 100,000 inhabitants.
The winners were selected by a European Jury following presentations by the shortlisted destinations in Brussels on 18 and 19 November.
In total, 83 destinations across 24 countries applied to be considered for the designation, with a total of 16 spots shortlisted.
On the shortlist for the larger destinations were Aalborg in Denmark, Braga in Portugal, Genoa in Italy, Konya in Türkiye, Lviv in Ukraine, Salzburg in Austria and Sofia in Bulgaria.
Calais in France, Geestland in Germany, Ibiza in Spain, Nova Gorica in Slovenia, Sandanski in Bulgaria, Selçuk in Türkiye and Zadar in Croatia made up the shortlist of the smaller destination entries.
According to the European Commission, the jury chose Ljubljana due to its “commitment to knowledge sharing, continuous learning and resident-focused initiatives”. It was also praised for its strong performance across accessible, sustainable, digital and cultural tourism criteria, as well as an ambitious programme of activities planned for 2027.
Ljubljana was hailed, too, for its approach to visitor data management – which demonstrates how destinations can use knowledge, data and innovation to continuously learn and grow responsibly – as well as its development of more creative and sustainable tourism solutions and promoting year-round travel.
Meanwhile, the jury applauded Calvià for its decision to move away from high-volume mass tourism towards a more sustainable and year-round approach.
It also took into account Calvià’s efforts to rethink how tourism can contribute to long-term economic, environmental and social well-being, while creating a more “balanced relationship between visitors, residents and the local environment”.
Inspiring other tourism destinations
By awarding it the honour, the jury hopes this transformation will inspire other established destinations to make their tourism models more sustainable.
Congratulating Ljubljana and Calvià on being named the 2027 European Capitals of Tourism, European Commissioner for Sustainable Transport and Tourism Apostolos Tzitzikostas said: “This honour recognises their leadership in sustainable, innovative tourism that delivers for businesses, visitors and local communities. Their example will inspire destinations across Europe."
Throughout 2027, Ljubljana and Calvià will showcase their sustainable tourism initiatives and share best practices with other European destinations. Both will receive promotional support – as well as a specially designed award sculpture to be put on display – and join a network encouraging collaboration on smarter, greener and more sustainable tourism.

noticias.titulo: Denmark expels Russian defence attaché over alleged assassination plot
noticias.resumen: Two men linked to one of Denmark's most notorious criminal gangs have been charged over a plot to kill a Ukrainian rapper, prompting a nationwide crackdown on the outlawed group.
noticias.texto:
Two men linked to one of Denmark's most notorious criminal gangs have been charged over a plot to kill a Ukrainian rapper, prompting a nationwide crackdown on the outlawed group.
Denmark will expel Russia's defence attaché over an alleged Russian-backed plot to assassinate a Ukrainian rapper on Danish soil, Denmark's foreign minister said at a press conference on Friday.
Two Danish men have been charged and remanded in custody in connection with the attempted assassination.
The plot was planned and initiated by Russian intelligence services, according to Denmark's Security and Intelligence Service (PET).
The two men have links to one of Denmark's most notorious criminal gangs, Loyal to Familia (LTF), a statement by Danish police said.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the case would have diplomatic consequences for Moscow.
"He must leave Denmark within seven days," Rasmussen said, referring to the Russian defence attaché.
The alleged plot appears to have been thwarted when the men were arrested shortly before the rapper's scheduled concert on 25 September, according to Danish public broadcaster DR.
The two men have been held in pre-trial detention since September after they were found with weapons in their car in Hellerup, an affluent residential area north of Copenhagen.
Both men have reportedly pleaded not guilty.
Kyivstoner's Danish concert, part of a European tour, was subsequently cancelled.
The rapper said in an Instagram post, which is now unavailable, that Danish intelligence officials had warned him of a threat to his life and prevented him from performing in Denmark, according to local media.
Kyivstoner was also reportedly the target of an assassination plot in Poland earlier this year.
Denmark steps up crackdown on outlawed gang
Danish police announced intensified nationwide operations against Loyal to Familia on Friday, targeting both its violent activities and sources of income.
"Police will now further intensify their overall efforts in response to this particular case," Lasse Boje, national police commissioner of Danish police, said in the statement.
The operation will also target key figures within the gang, including those based abroad, in an effort to weaken the organisation.
The gang has been involved in several violent conflicts with rival criminal groups and remains active despite being permanently banned by Denmark's Supreme Court in 2021.
Over the past five years, Danish police have brought more than 5,000 criminal charges against members of the gang, involving offences including violent crime, drug trafficking, weapons offences, fraud and money laundering, according to the statement.
Police estimate that around a third of the gang's members are currently behind bars.

noticias.titulo: TikTok rolls out deepfake detection tool for public figures to fight back against disinformation
noticias.resumen: The social media company’s ‘Likeness detection’ feature is aimed at politicians dealing with the deluge of disinformation online.
noticias.texto:
The social media company’s ‘Likeness detection’ feature is aimed at politicians dealing with the deluge of disinformation online.
TikTok announced on Friday that it had begun rolling out an opt-in feature called 'Likeness Detection' to help creators find and flag AI-generated content that uses their likeness on the platform, as the company tries to fight back against AI-generated disinformation.
The tool is aimed at helping public figures, including members of government, politicians and political party accounts, to spot and report AI-generated content that uses their image without consent.
It comes at a time when Europe is already facing a wave of AI-driven disinformation and deepfake campaigns disrupting its election processes, and with nine more European countries heading to the polls in the next 12 months, it could prove decisive.
Eligible users can sign up by verifying their ID with a trusted third-party partner. They are then notified when content and accounts on TikTok may be using their likeness and can review them within the tool.
Users can then report content directly to TikTok’s safety teams for review and action.
The EU began rolling out artificial intelligence transparency rules on 2 August under the AI Act, including a requirement for deepfakes and other AI-generated content to be labelled.
TikTok has made efforts to curb deepfakes in recent years, such as requiring content creators to label realistic AI-generated images, audio and video as stipulated in the AI Act as well.
Identify AI-Generated Content
The company also launched a new transparency tool for users to check whether content is made or edited with the social media platform’s creation features.
The ‘Identify AI-Generated Content’ tool is free to use by anyone, said TikTok, even those without an account.
The platform allows users to upload an image or video to check if it was generated or edited with TikTok’s own AI tools including parent company ByteDance’s CapCut, Dreamina, Hypic and Pippit apps.
It supports a wide range of formats including popular ones like JPEG, PNG, and MP4, with a file size limit of 20 megabytes per image or 100 megabytes for each video or audio.
The tool checks for two signs that the content was AI-generated: metadata credentials added by TikTok and ByteDance apps and invisible watermarks embedded directly into the content that are harder to remove.
The company has said that the tool deletes all content as soon as it has been uploaded and checked, and it is never used to train AI models.
TikTok warn users that it only detects whether AI edited or created content using its own or ByteDance app tools, so it’s not a foolproof way to spot AI content.

noticias.titulo: ‘Dream Trips of Europe’: Stunning holiday destinations to visit in 2027
noticias.resumen: Lonely Planet’s latest guide highlights journeys spanning ancient history, dramatic natural landscapes, scenic rail routes and some of Europe’s most distinctive food and wine destinations.
noticias.texto:
Lonely Planet’s latest guide highlights journeys spanning ancient history, dramatic natural landscapes, scenic rail routes and some of Europe’s most distinctive food and wine destinations.
Fancy exploring fairy-tale castles, crossing wild landscapes or sipping wine in the country where it was first made?
In its new book, “Dream Trips of Europe”, Lonely Planet has picked out some of the continent’s most memorable places and experiences.
Showcasing 100 inspiring journeys, they range from exploring Germany’s castles and taking scenic rail trips through the Baltics to discovering Iceland’s wild landscapes, Georgia’s wine heritage and Sicily’s ancient history.
These are some of the spots to add to your 2027 travel wish list.
King Ludwig’s fairy tale castles, Germany
Ludwig II, also called the Swan King or the Fairy Tale King, was King of Bavaria from 1864 until his death in 1886.
In that time, he was obsessed with medieval legends, Wagnerian opera and romantic fantasy and, as such, commissioned several extravagant castles as private retreats.
Thanks to his obsessions, Bavaria is now the place to see the very best fairy tale castles.
Neuschwanstein Castle is world-famous, but the magnificent island palace of Herrenchiemsee, inspired by Versailles, is less known, and the theatrical gardens and grottoes of Schloss Linderhof are well worth a visit.
For a smaller – but no less magical – spot, head to the mountains to see Königshaus am Schachen, an apparently unassuming Alpine retreat which conceals a spectacular, Moorish-inspired hall.
Time travel through Orkney, Scotland
Many people visit Scotland and see Edinburgh and the Highlands and then leave. They’re missing more than 5,000 years of rich history to be found on the Orkney Islands off the north of the mainland.
A visit offers the chance to see one of Europe's most remarkable prehistoric landscapes, including the UNESCO-listed Heart of Neolithic Orkney, a collection of four ancient monuments.
These include the well-preserved settlement of Skara Brae, the mysterious Ring of Brodgar and the Standing Stones of Stenness.
If you’re into Viking history, be sure to venture underground into the ancient Maeshowe chambered tomb, where the historical visitors left their mark in centuries-old runic graffiti.
Journey to the ‘centre of the Earth’ in Iceland
Inspired by Jules Verne’s “Journey to the Centre of the Earth”, Lonely Planet suggests a road trip which takes in Iceland’s Snæfellsnes Peninsula, where volcanic peaks, vast lava fields, underground caves and black-sand beaches give the landscape an almost otherworldly feel.
The route includes a visit to Búðakirkja, the striking black wooden church standing alone against the surrounding scenery, as well as guided explorations of the Vatnshellir lava tubes.
Other must-sees include the distinctive Kirkjufell mountain, one of Iceland’s most photographed landmarks, and the colourful harbour town of Stykkishólmur.
Trek the Juliana Trail to Lake Bled, Slovenia
Arguably one of Europe’s most beautiful outdoor destinations, Slovenia’s 168-mile Juliana Trail loops around the Julian Alps, taking walkers through mountain valleys, forests and traditional villages, with views of turquoise rivers, waterfalls and dramatic peaks along the way.
One of its best-known stops is Lake Bled, where an island church sits in emerald-green water beneath a medieval castle perched on the cliffs. Visitors can swim, walk around the lakeshore or explore by traditional wooden rowing boat or paddleboard.
Experience a Baltic Rail odyssey – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania
Slow rail travel is set to be as popular as ever in 2027, and a journey between the three Baltic states is a perfect way to embrace the trend.
Starting in the medieval streets of Estonia’s capital, Tallinn, head to Tartu, the second-largest city, widely known as the nation's cradle of culture.
From there, a scenic train ride filled with views of birch forests and peaceful lakes takes passengers to Riga in Latvia, with its striking Art Nouveau architecture and vibrant Central Market.
The last stop is Lithuania’s historic capital, Vilnius, known for its beautiful rooftops, panoramic viewpoints, UNESCO Old Town, lively arts and café culture.
Explore the birthplace of wine, Georgia
Think of wine, and you’ll probably think of France or Italy, but the beverage was actually first made in Georgia, some 8,000 years ago.
Against the spectacular backdrop of the Caucasus Mountains in the Kakheti wine region, family-run vineyards encourage visitors to discover the ancient Qvevri winemaking tradition.
When you’ve had your fill of wine, don’t miss the atmospheric capital of Tbilisi, known for its historic bathhouses, ancient churches and colourful streets, as well as its unique food offerings, built around fresh herbs, walnuts, cheeses, and slow-cooked stews.
See all of Europe’s tiny principality, Liechtenstein
For travellers who’ve ticked off most of the Alpine countries, Liechtenstein is a good bet.
What’s even better is that the 47-mile Liechtenstein Trail offers the opportunity to explore the entire, tiny country on foot.
The route stretches from the Swiss border in the south to Austria in the north, and takes hikers through vineyards, forests, meadows and traditional villages, with stunning mountain and Rhine Valley views.
Highlights along the way include the Walser heritage of Triesenberg – settled around 1280 by Germanic migrants from the Swiss Valais region and maintaining a distinct cultural identity – and the capital of Vaduz, famous for its 12th-century hilltop castle overlooking the town.
Discover the rich history of Sicily, Italy
There are seemingly endless things to discover on the Italian island of Sicily and, if you haven’t been, 2027 is the time to go.
Lonely Planet recommends a trip to the southeast of the island, starting with a visit to the Greek ruins and atmospheric waterfront streets of Syracuse and Ortygia.
Next up on the list are the striking baroque towns of Noto, Modica and Ragusa, the ideal places to indulge in the island's celebrated food and wine scene.
No trip to Sicily is complete without seeing the towering slopes of iconic Mount Etna, where you can explore volcanic craters, dramatic valleys and lava caves.

noticias.titulo: Himalaya-sized ancient 'supermountains' found beneath Antarctica's ice sheet
noticias.resumen: The discovery offers a window into the continent's geological past and of how life on Earth has evolved.
noticias.texto:
The discovery offers a window into the continent's geological past and of how life on Earth has evolved.
A previously unknown system of ancient mountain ranges, comparable in size to the Himalayas and known as 'supermountains', has had its roots identified beneath Antarctica's ice sheet by an international team of scientists.
The discovery by experts from the Australian National University (ANU) and Germany's GFZ Research Centre for Geosciences, published in the journal Earth and Planetary Science Letters, not only rewrites the continent's geological past but also offers a new explanation for the evolution of life on Earth.
The researchers identified the remnants of vast ancient mountain chains that formed during the assembly of the Gondwana supercontinent between 650 and 450 million years ago.
According to the scientists, these ranges were created when Antarctica collided with India and Africa, a process they describe as the largest mountain-building event to have affected the continent.
How were the mountains discovered?
Since more than 99.5 per cent of Antarctica is covered by a thick ice sheet, the team did not study the rocks directly. Instead they analysed sediments obtained from ocean drilling along the continental margin.
The experts examined 1,712 tiny mineral grains, zircon crystals. Thanks to their geochemical composition, these crystals preserve information about the pressure conditions and the time when they formed.
From the samples, the scientists were able to determine the age and chemical composition of the rocks they came from, and to infer the geological processes by which they were created, revealing the deeply buried, eroded roots of the former giant mountain ranges.
What do we know about the ancient mountain ranges?
Ian Campbell, emeritus professor at ANU and co-author of the study, says the rapid erosion of the mountains played a key role in the development of life on Earth. The weathering rocks delivered huge quantities of nutrients to the oceans, lowered the level of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere and increased oxygen concentrations.
This created the conditions for the appearance of the first organisms with hard skeletons, 539 million years ago, and for a sudden increase in animal diversity known as the Cambrian explosion.
How does zircon crystal dating work?
Zircon crystal dating, known in technical terms as uranium-lead radiometric dating, is one of the most reliable methods for studying the Earth's oldest rocks. The technique is based on the fact that crystallising zircon traps radioactive uranium but excludes lead, so any lead later measured in the crystal comes from the decay of uranium.
Zircon (ZrSiO₄) is an extremely resistant mineral that can preserve its original structure for billions of years despite geological processes such as erosion, high temperatures and pressure.
When magma cools and zircon crystals form, the crystal lattice readily incorporates uranium atoms, which are similar in size and charge to zirconium, but excludes lead atoms. This means that a newly formed crystal begins from a 'lead-free' starting point.
The crystal lattice is so stable that the decay products created within it stay trapped unless it is exposed to extreme heat.
The radioactive 'hourglass'
Two different uranium isotopes are present in zircon, each decaying at a different rate into stable lead isotopes. This allows two independent measurements to be made in the same crystal.
Because the half-lives are precisely known, the ratio of uranium to lead can be used to calculate how much time has passed since the crystal solidified. If the two different decay chains indicate the same age, a state known as concordance, the result is extremely reliable.
This method was used, for example, to determine the age of zircon crystals from Jack Hills in Western Australia, which are 4.4 billion years old and are the oldest known mineral remnants on Earth.
Another major breakthrough earlier this year
Using a new high-resolution satellite and ice-flow-based map, scientists also identified thousands of previously unknown smaller subglacial ridges and landforms beneath Antarctica.
The new map, published in January 2026 in the Science journal, reveals the bedrock beneath Antarctica's multi-kilometre-thick ice sheet in greater detail than ever before, identifying nearly 72,000 previously unknown hills, jagged alpine mountain ranges and vast ancient river channels under the continent.
Using a technique called ice-flow perturbation analysis (IFPA), which combines high-resolution satellite images of the surface with physical equations describing glacier movement, the researchers were able to make visible landforms between 2 and 30 kilometres in size.
The map identified exactly 71,997 subglacial hills, more than twice the number shown in previous models. Earlier, blurrier radar surveys had suggested a relatively smooth bed beneath the ice, but the new map reveals dramatic landscapes of sharp ridges and deeply incised valleys.
In the Maud Subglacial Basin, the team also discovered a steep-sided channel almost 400 kilometres long, six kilometres wide and 50 metres deep. These ancient waterways carved their beds before the continent became glaciated.
Why are this year's Antarctic discoveries important?
The roughness of the landscape beneath the ice directly determines how fast the ice sheet slides towards the ocean, a key factor in forecasting global sea-level rise.
Closely spaced hills and jagged peaks increase friction at the base of the ice, slowing the movement of glaciers. In contrast, deep valleys sloping towards the ocean act like motorways, channelling ice into the sea and accelerating ice loss.

noticias.titulo: UK anthem returns to the EU stage in symbolic post-Brexit moment
noticias.resumen: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham was welcomed by EU leaders in Brussels for a summit aimed at strengthening post-Brexit relations. God Save the King rang out for the first time since Brexit at the UK–EU summit.
noticias.texto:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham was welcomed to Brussels on 20 November 2026 to the strains of God Save the King, the first time the UK national anthem has been played at an EU institution since Britain’s 2020 exit.
European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen welcomed the British leader before the trio posed for cameras, listened to Beethoven’s Ode to Joy and greeted their negotiating teams.
The ceremonial warmth underscored a broader diplomatic push to mend fences between London and Brussels while respecting the UK’s exit from the bloc. With economic relations and youth mobility topping the agenda, both sides are poised to announce deals aimed at cutting trade red tape and making it easier for young Britons and Europeans to live, work and travel across borders.

noticias.titulo: Furious Farage accuses Burnham of betraying Brexit as EU-UK summit gets underway
noticias.resumen: Speaking exclusively to Euronews, the Reform UK leader admitted Brexit had failed to deliver on immigration, but accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of betraying voters by bringing Britain closer to the EU.
noticias.texto:
Speaking exclusively to Euronews, the Reform UK leader admitted Brexit had failed to deliver on immigration, but accused Prime Minister Andy Burnham of betraying voters by bringing Britain closer to the EU.
Nigel Farage has accused British Prime Minister Andy Burnham of betraying Brexit voters by bringing Britain back into parts of the EU single market, as the two sides prepared to seal a series of agreements at a summit in Brussels on Friday.
Speaking to Euronews' Europe Today as Burnham arrived for his first EU summit since taking office in July, the Reform UK leader and longtime Brexit campaigner said he was "pretty angry" at having to fight the Brexit battle all over again.
"What is happening this morning in Brussels is Andy Burnham is bringing us back into the single market in the areas of foodstuffs and farming," Farage said.
He argued that Britain would have to accept EU regulations without having a vote on them, describing the move as a betrayal of Labour's promise not to rejoin the single market.
But Farage struggled to offer a convincing rebuttal to Burnham's argument that Brexit had damaged Britain's economy and international standing.
He claimed Britain's global influence had actually increased since leaving the EU, citing its support for Ukraine and the AUKUS nuclear submarine agreement with Australia.
"There's no question we stand taller," he insisted.
On the economic damage, however, Farage argued that the Covid pandemic made it difficult to assess Brexit's impact. He claimed Britain had prospered in sectors such as artificial intelligence and financial services, while dismissing the EU single market as a "failing, backward model".
Farage was more candid about immigration, acknowledging that Brexit had failed to deliver one of its central promises.
"It was the biggest," he said when asked whether the failure to control immigration was Brexit's greatest disappointment.
He blamed successive Conservative governments for allowing record immigration despite regaining control of Britain's borders.
Farage also acknowledged that many Britons felt Brexit had failed to deliver, but insisted this did not mean they wanted to reverse it.
He warned that reopening the question of EU membership would divide the country and demanded another referendum if Burnham sought to rejoin.
"If Labour, if Burnham, fights the next election on a ticket of rejoining the EU, he'd have to have a referendum," Farage said.
EU would welcome Britain back, says MEP
German Socialist MEP Tobias Cremer offered a sharply different assessment, telling Europe Today that Brexit had imposed enormous economic costs on Britain and that a majority of voters now favoured rejoining.
"£260 billion a year, £10,000 per household," he said. "And immigration as well. Yes, EU immigration went down by 100,000 or 150,000, but overall non-EU immigration has gone up by three million since then."
Cremer said the geopolitical landscape had transformed since 2016, citing Russia's war in Ukraine, China's growing assertiveness and an increasingly unpredictable United States.
"It's in both the British and European interest to stick together," he said, arguing that closer cooperation on security, defence and trade would benefit both sides.
Asked whether Britain could be back in the EU within five years, Cremer replied: "That would be my wish."

noticias.titulo: This vaccine can prevent cervical cancer. Which Europeans actually get it?
noticias.resumen: HPV vaccination rates vary by country and gender, EU health data shows.
noticias.texto:
HPV vaccination rates vary by country and gender, EU health data shows.
A vaccine against a common virus can prevent several cancers — but whether teenagers get it depends largely on where they live, European health data shows.
Teenage girls in the Nordics, Spain and Portugal are more likely to be vaccinated against HPV, or human papillomavirus, than anywhere else, while boys in Central and Eastern Europe are least likely to get the jab, according to data from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC).
HPV is a group of common viruses, some of which spread through sex. Most infections clear up on their own, but certain types can linger and cause cancer years later. That includes cervical cancer — which kills about 280,000 women worldwide each year — and rarer cancers in both women and men.
HPV vaccines have been authorised in the European Union since 2006, and most countries recommend that all girls and boys are vaccinated by the time they are 15. Older people who have not been vaccinated can get catch-up jabs.
Health authorities have long recommended two doses, but dozens of countries have switched to a single-dose schedule. Research indicates that even one jab may be enough to protect against infection with the HPV strains most likely to cause cancer.
Countries that adopted the vaccine early on, such as Sweden and Scotland, have reported far lower rates of cervical cancer in the years since. But there are wide gaps in who actually gets the HPV vaccine, ECDC data shows.
In Portugal, 95% of girls get all doses of the HPV vaccine by age 15, compared with just 4% in Bulgaria. The rates are generally lower among boys, who have only been offered HPV vaccination in more recent years. It ranges from 94% of boys in Portugal to 1% in Romania.
On average, 64% of girls and 51% of boys had gotten all doses of the HPV vaccine by age 15, below the European Union’s 90% target for girls.
Several countries have taken steps to boost immunisations. In 2021, Sweden began offering catch-up jabs for women who were not vaccinated when they were younger, as part of its campaign to become the first country to eliminate cervical cancer. By 2025, Sweden also had one of the smallest gender gaps in HPV vaccination: 91% of girls and 87% of boys had gotten the jab by age 15, according to ECDC data.
Meanwhile, France launched a school-based HPV vaccination programme in 2023; in the first year, vaccination rates climbed from 31% to 48% among 12-year-olds. And Bulgaria began offering free HPV vaccination to boys in 2025.
Yet HPV vaccination rates have also fallen in some countries, largely due to social media misinformation around the jab, according to a set of reviews carried out last year by Cochrane, an influential nonprofit research group.
In Romania, Bulgaria and Croatia, rumours that the HPV vaccine could harm children or cause side effects, coupled with a lack of trust in health authorities, help explain why vaccine uptake has remained low, another study in the BMJ Public Health journal found.
There is no evidence that the HPV vaccine causes commonly reported side effects, according to Cochrane, which analysed both clinical trials and real-world studies involving more than 132 million people.
Teenage girls who were vaccinated against HPV were 80% less likely to develop cervical cancer than unvaccinated girls, the Cochrane review found.
The researchers said the HPV vaccine is most effective when people get it before they are exposed to the virus or become sexually active.

noticias.titulo: In the billionaires club: Ashton Kutcher gets mega rich after Anthropic's Wall Street debut
noticias.resumen: Some actors, artists and sports stars are big fans of AI. Actor Ashton Kutcher, Black Eyed Peas singer will.i.am and former NBA player Tristan Thompson are among those reported to have made a fortune from backing Anthropic, the US company behind the Claude AI chatbot.
noticias.texto:
Some actors, artists and sports stars are big fans of AI. Actor Ashton Kutcher, Black Eyed Peas singer will.i.am and former NBA player Tristan Thompson are among those reported to have made a fortune from backing Anthropic, the US company behind the Claude AI chatbot.
From Hollywood to basketball courts, several celebrities are estimated to have made millions after investing in artificial intelligence's company Anthropic following its record-breaking stock market debut.
The US technology company, which develops Claude, a chatbot competing with OpenAI's ChatGPT, has attracted high-profile investors from the entertainment and sports industries, including actor Ashton Kutcher, Black Eyed Peas frontman will.i.am and former NBA basketball player Tristan Thompson.
Anthropic made its Wall Street debut on Thursday, 19 November, in one of the biggest stock market listings in history. The company raised $81.3 billion by selling shares at $83 each.
Actor Ashton Kutcher invested through Sound Ventures, the venture capital firm he co-founded with music industry executive Guy Oseary, Madonna's former manager. The firm reportedly sunk around $435 million in Anthropic across several funding rounds.
Will.i.am, the Black Eyed Peas frontman, whose real name is William Adams, is also among the reported investors. The musician and entrepreneur backed the company through a private investment group, although the size of his individual investment has not been disclosed.
Former NBA player Tristan Thompson has also publicly confirmed investing in Anthropic. He said he became interested in the company after meeting technology investors at dinners in San Francisco.
Tech industry investors
Beyond the entertainment industry, Anthropic attracted early backing from prominent figures in the technology world. Former Google chief executive Eric Schmidt invested tens of millions of dollars in the company's first funding round. He reportedly owns around 1% of Anthropic, potentially positioning him for one of the largest individual gains from its stock market debut. Jaan Tallinn, the Estonian computer programmer and co-founder of Skype, was another early backer. He led Anthropic's first $124 million funding round in 2021 and invested again the following year. The size of his current stake has not been disclosed.
What is Anthropic?
Anthropic was founded in January 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees, including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei.
The company develops artificial intelligence systems, including Claude, which can assist with writing, research, data analysis and computer programming.
Its historic Wall Street debut marks a major milestone in the global AI race.

noticias.titulo: Unrest around French cost-of-living protests could cost insurers €207mn
noticias.resumen: Damage from the unrest around France's October cost-of-living protests could cost insurers €207 million. France Assureurs says the estimate is "particularly high for events concentrated into 24 hours". Over 95% of the estimated cost relates to damage to business property.
noticias.texto:
Damage from the unrest around France's October cost-of-living protests could cost insurers €207 million. France Assureurs says the estimate is "particularly high for events concentrated into 24 hours". Over 95% of the estimated cost relates to damage to business property.
The total amount of insured damage from unrest and looting around cost-of-living protests in France on 17 and 18 October could reach €207 million across 5,280 claims, according to an initial assessment by France Assureurs, the French insurance industry body, based on data available as of 12 November.
More than 95% of the estimated total cost, or €198mn, relates to damage to business property, across 4,050 claims. Damage to individuals' property could reach €3.5mn across 370 claims, while damage to vehicles could reach €6mn across 860 claims.
France Assureurs president Florence Lustman said, "The cost of the urban violence on 17 and 18 October is particularly high in view of the brevity of the events".
The statement added that the 2005 riots cost insurers €209mn over four weeks, while the 2018-2019 Yellow Vests movement cost €256mn over several months.
Government sets out grants for small businesses
The government published the rules on Friday in the Official Journal (source in French) for grants to eligible businesses with fewer than 50 employees that suffered damage during the urban violence in October and November.
To receive a grant of €1,000 to €10,000, eligible businesses must apply via the Démarche numérique platform "no later than six weeks after the date of signature" of the decree.
The decree says the grants are aimed at the small businesses worst affected by damage during unrest around demonstrations held between 17 October and 19 November 2026, when the decree was signed.
In each region, a committee chaired by the regional prefect or their representative will review applications from local businesses.
The committee will decide on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the scale of the operating losses, the nature and extent of the damage, and eligibility for other national or local support schemes.
Emergency funds have also been released by local authorities in the worst-affected areas, while an interest-free loan from Bpifrance allows affected shopkeepers to borrow up to €50,000, including to replenish stock ahead of Christmas.

noticias.titulo: European Commission staff criticise lack of communication over cyberattack
noticias.resumen: The main civil servants’ union has criticized senior management for letting staff learn of the breach from the press, as employees fear their personal data is at risk.
noticias.texto:
The main civil servants’ union has criticized senior management for letting staff learn of the breach from the press, as employees fear their personal data is at risk.
European Commission staff have voiced frustration over the lack of communication surrounding a large-scale cyberattack that struck the institution in October.
Renouveau & Démocratie (R&D), the main trade union representing EU civil servants, criticised the Commission's handling of the incident, saying staff were not notified when the cyberattack was detected on 22 October and that the institution only acknowledged it after it was reported in the media.
“This failure of internal communication is unacceptable,” R&D chair Cristiano Sebastiani said in a statement on Thursday. Staff should not “have to learn from a newspaper headline” that their personal data could be at risk, he added.
For several days, officials have been unable to access Sysper, the internal HR platform where they check salary information, request holidays and sick leave, submit timesheets and sign up for training.
According to R&D, civil servants have been contacting the union to express their concern and anger.
“Discovering this from the press is absurd. Transparency would have been a better choice,” a Commission official told Euronews on condition of anonymity.
The Commission eventually notified staff in an internal note on Friday, a day after the news was first reported by the media. “The Commission has recently been targeted by a series of cyberattacks, including through the use of AI,” it reads. The note says the breaches affected a limited number of systems and that there is no evidence of a data breach affecting staff as a whole.
In a further statement to Euronews, Sebastiani described the note as “absolutely inadequate given the gravity of the failure” and called on senior management to issue a formal apology.
Most civil servants have experienced only minor disruption to their daily work, but the incident has raised concerns. “The mere possibility of my data being leaked scares me, particularly given all the phishing emails I get every day,” another official told Euronews.
A Commission spokesperson said on Thursday that the attack relied on a publicly available AI tool, without saying whether it was still ongoing or attributing it to a specific actor. The tool, called ARTEX, identifies software vulnerabilities, which can then be patched or, in the hands of malicious actors, exploited.
This is not the first time the Commission has been targeted by a cyberattack.
In March, hackers compromised the cloud infrastructure hosting its Europa.eu websites, stealing around 91.7 GB of data. Earlier, in January, an attack on the Commission's central mobile-device infrastructure potentially exposed staff members' names and phone numbers.

noticias.titulo: Bending Spoons to buy Mailchimp from Intuit in €3.35bn deal
noticias.resumen: The Italian tech company behind WeTransfer and Vimeo has agreed to buy email marketing platform Mailchimp. Intuit is selling it for less than a third of what it paid in 2021.
noticias.texto:
The Italian tech company behind WeTransfer and Vimeo has agreed to buy email marketing platform Mailchimp. Intuit is selling it for less than a third of what it paid in 2021.
The Italian company Bending Spoons agreed on Thursday to buy Mailchimp, the US email marketing platform, from Intuit for $3.68 billion (€3.35bn).
Intuit bought Mailchimp in 2021 for around $12bn (€10.9bn at the 19 November exchange rate).
Under the agreement, Intuit will reinvest $368 million (€335mn) of its proceeds in new Bending Spoons shares, according to the Italian company.
Mailchimp's quarterly revenue fell 1% to $313mn (€285mn), Intuit said. The US company said the sale would help it focus on AI-powered tools for businesses.
The company’s co-founder and chief executive Luca Ferrari described Mailchimp as "a prestigious brand which in more than twenty years has revolutionised the email marketing sector, redefining the way companies grow their audiences".
He said Bending Spoons planned to invest heavily in the business and build on the tools its customers already use.
Intuit's board approved the deal, which still needs regulatory approval and is expected to close in early 2027.
Under the agreement, Bending Spoons will buy all of The Rocket Science Group LLC, the company behind Mailchimp, along with other Mailchimp assets and liabilities.
How Bending Spoons grew through acquisitions
Founded in 2013 in Copenhagen and now based in Milan, Bending Spoons has grown by acquiring other companies in the web services sector, then improving and relaunching their products. It has been listed on Nasdaq since 1 July 2026, with an IPO price of $29 a share.
The company started out designing, developing and maintaining software. It has since made more than 50 acquisitions, including WeTransfer in 2024, Vimeo in 2025 and Eventbrite and Airtable in 2026. It often buys products it sees as underperforming and invests in improving them.
The company has also been described as a "unicorn", a term generally used for a privately held start-up valued at more than $1bn (€910mn). In a 2024 LinkedIn post, Roma Startup president Gianmarco Carnovale argued that the label did not fit Bending Spoons because of how it started.
In Italy, the firm is also known for developing the Immuni app, which the Italian government promoted during the Covid-19 pandemic and which struggled to gain traction. Immuni and Live Quiz are examples of apps Bending Spoons developed from scratch.

noticias.titulo: Lufthansa plans 1,000 job cuts in Frankfurt and Munich as Iran war slows turnaround
noticias.resumen: Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 full-time jobs in Frankfurt and Munich as strikes and soaring fuel costs linked to the Iran war slow its turnaround. Its flagship airline lost €20 million a month on average from January to September, according to a letter to staff.
noticias.texto:
Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 full-time jobs in Frankfurt and Munich as strikes and soaring fuel costs linked to the Iran war slow its turnaround. Its flagship airline lost €20 million a month on average from January to September, according to a letter to staff.
German airline Lufthansa plans to axe 1,000 full-time jobs at its hubs in Frankfurt and Munich, after its core carrier lost €20 million a month on average between January and September, according to a letter to employees seen by AFP on Friday.
Strikes by pilots and cabin crew, and a surge in jet fuel prices since the Iran war began, have slowed its turnaround.
Launched in 2024, the turnaround plan includes more than 700 measures meant to lift earnings by €2.5 billion by 2028, but those announced to date are "no longer sufficient", the letter warned.
"The year 2026 has set us back: the war in the Middle East, the still very high fuel costs, nine days of strike action and our already very high cost base have intensified the situation," the letter said.
It is unclear whether the 1,000 posts, about 2.5% of the airline's roughly 40,000 staff, are part of the 4,000 mostly administrative jobs Lufthansa Group said last year it would cut by 2030.
Mixed group results
The wider group, which also owns Swiss, Austrian Airlines and Brussels Airlines and is buying up to 49.9% of TAP Air Portugal in a €1.2 billion deal, has fared better.
Its operating profit, which excludes one-off items, rose 6% to €1.4bn in the third quarter, beating analysts' expectations on strong demand for premium long-haul seats.
Net profit, which includes one-off items, jumped 30% to €1.26bn, partly thanks to valuation gains and a tax charge that had weighed on the year-earlier figure.
Nine-month net profit was still down 35%, and on 3 November the group trimmed its full-year operating profit forecast to between €1.7bn and €2bn, from up to €2.2bn.
The core airline's third-quarter operating profit fell by a third to €300mn, and CEO Carsten Spohr said that "we must now accelerate the financial turnaround of our core brand".
Lufthansa expects to spend €9.3bn on fuel this year, about €2bn more than in 2025, despite scrapping 20,000 short-haul flights through to October to cut fuel use.

noticias.titulo: Vatican: Giant Christmas tree lifted into place beside St Peter's Basilica
noticias.resumen: A towering 25-metre Christmas tree was lifted into place in St Peter's Square, Vatican City, on Friday 20 November 2026, as preparations began for this year's Christmas celebrations. The silver fir, donated by a community in southern Italy, will be unveiled on 7 December.
noticias.texto:
With ropes taut and chainsaws humming to trim its base, a giant silver fir was carefully hoisted by crane into St Peter's Square, rising against the facade of St Peter's Basilica as visitors and a photograph-snapping nun looked on. Felled in Pollino National Park in southern Italy's Basilicata region, the tree will be dressed in lights and ornaments ahead of its formal unveiling on 7 December.
The gift is the fruit of 10 years of planning by residents of Terranova di Pollino, working in partnership with the Basilicata regional government and park authorities, said Giuseppe Ciancia of the town's mayor's office. Crews are simultaneously assembling a traditional nativity scene nearby as the Vatican gears up for the holidays.
Standing beside the basilica for the duration of the festive season, the fir and nativity display transform the square each winter into a focal point for pilgrims and visitors converging on the centre of the Catholic world.

noticias.titulo: Moving my religion: Vatican Museums explore a century of Popemobiles
noticias.resumen: From Pius XI's Mercedes to John Paul II's Popemobile: eight historic cars show how Popes' vehicles have changed. The Vatican Museums exhibition retraces a century of history, between technology, curiosities and safety.
noticias.texto:
From Pius XI's Mercedes to John Paul II's Popemobile: eight historic cars show how Popes' vehicles have changed. The Vatican Museums exhibition retraces a century of history, between technology, curiosities and safety.
There once was a pope who could tell his driver when to accelerate, when to slow down and even when to return to the Vatican, simply by pressing a button. Another, by contrast, had a car turned into an open-top vehicle so that he could be seen more clearly by the crowd. And then there was John Paul II, who had a barber's chair adapted as a papal seat, so that he could greet the faithful.
The cars of popes tell a story that goes far beyond engines, bodywork and comfort. They reveal the character of the pontiffs, the way they choose to be among people and, above all, how communication of the papacy has changed - from the solemnity of limousines to the search for direct contact with the faithful, and the growing need to protect those who travel under the spotlight.
This is the journey traced by the exhibition "A century of Popemobiles", that's now on at the Vatican Museums (source in Italian). Eight historic Mercedes-Benz cars retrace almost 100 years of papal mobility. They are accompanied by a Benz Patent-Motorwagen from 1886, considered the first car in history, and a new Mercedes-Benz S-Class, broadening the view of how the automobile has evolved.
Sandro Barbagallo, curator of the Vatican Museums historical collections says each vehicle has its own story: "The message is very simple: papal mobility exists so that the pope can draw close to everyone, all over the world. The use of cars is not just about moving the Pontiff around within Vatican City".
A story in which each pontiff has, in one way or another, left his mark, including by choosing how he wished to be transported.
Pius XI, the Pope who fell in love with his car
The relationship between Mercedes-Benz and the Vatican officially begins in 1930, when Pius XI receives a Nürburg 460 (W 08), a large limousine donated by the German car manufacturer. It is the first Mercedes regularly used by a pope.
Achille Ratti, elected in 1922, was a man of culture, a scholar and lover of the mountains, with a past as a mountaineer and explorer. A Pontiff accustomed to looking far ahead, who did not shun the innovations of his time. The car also became a tool for leaving the Vatican, after the long period of the so-called imprisonment of the popes, which began with the end of the Papal States in 1870.
The Nürburg 460 is far from a standard official car: the interior is customised with a single seat for the pope, upholstered in fine silk brocade, selected woods, metallic detailing and a decorated ceiling. A kind of travelling sitting room, designed to underline the prestige of the papal figure.
But it is not just a question of luxury. Some papal cars from that era had a 'backseat driver' function panel, allowing the pope to instruct the chauffeur using buttons labelled "Forward", "Slow", "Right" and "Return to the Vatican". A sort of remote control before its time.
John XXIII, the "good Pope" who opens the windows
The pope's public presence also changed with John XXIII. Angelo Roncalli, a.ka. the "good Pope", had an informal style, a cheerful manner and a natural ability to relate to people. His pontificate, shaped by the Second Vatican Council, led the Church into a period of greater dialogue and openness.
The cars began to follow this transformation as well. In 1960, the Mercedes 300 d Landaulet (W 189) arrived, with rear windows that can be completely removed to allow the pope to be seen more easily and better greet people during public outings.
The features are already those of a vehicle built around the needs of the most important passenger: an electrically adjustable central seat, controls for the air conditioning and communications within easy reach, automatic steps to make it easier to get in and out of the vehicle.
Mercedes seems to have understood that the pope's car must not only take him to his destination: it must also allow him to meet people along the way.
Paul VI, the travelling Pope who invents the papamobile
If there is one pontiff who turned travel into a fundamental part of papal communication, it is Paul VI. Giovanni Battista Montini is the first modern pope to travel by plane and to make a series of international apostolic journeys, reaching places never before visited by a pontiff.
In 1964 he flew to the Holy Land, then to India in 1965, and in the following years to other continents. His mission was to reach the faithful in Rome and beyond by going to their countries to meet people and let them see him up close.
His Mercedes 600 Pullman Landaulet (W 100) from 1965 has a roof that opens at the rear specifically so that the pontiff can greet the crowds.
In 1967, a Mercedes 300 SEL Pullman (W 109) also arrives, another of the cars that mark the evolution of papal automobiles.
But the birth of the modern papamobile is above all linked to a practical need. As Barbagallo explains, "up until Paul VI, and then also with John Paul I, who as we all know had a very brief pontificate, the Pope went to audiences and even entered the Paul VI Audience Hall on a sedia gestatoria".
That first vehicle was still a production car made available to the Pontiff. But it marked a decisive change: the Pope no longer simply had to be transported, he could now cross the square and be seen by all the pilgrims.
To grasp the difference between the traditional papal saloons and the papamobiles, Barbagallo retraces the evolution of these vehicles: "The way they have developed has constantly highlighted, on the one hand, the Pope's comfort, on the other his security, and on yet another the fact that the Pope can be seen. In saloons, that is the black cars, the Pope is only seen by those on his side of the vehicle, whereas in a papamobile he can be seen equally from the right, the left, the front or the back. That, of course, is what creates the difference between the two means of transport".
John Paul II, the Pope of the crowds and the barber's chair
With John Paul II, the popemobile became an icon. Karol Wojtyła was a pope with a strong physical presence, used to direct contact, long international journeys and vast crowds. Before becoming Pope he was an actor, poet, sports enthusiast and lover of the mountains. It is no surprise that he was not especially drawn to the idea of remaining seated in a closed limousine.
From the beginning he refused to use the traditional sedia gestatoria, the ceremonial chair on which popes were carried during ceremonies. He preferred a motor vehicle that allowed him to move around and greet people freely.
This is where one of the most curious episodes in the history of popemobiles comes in: for some of the first open vehicles a swivelling barber's chair was adapted, mounted on a metal base. A decidedly unusual seat for the head of the Catholic Church, but practical in allowing him to turn and greet the crowd from every side.
The Mercedes that fixed the image of the modern popemobile in the public imagination arrived in 1980, for John Paul II's trip to Germany. It is a 230 G (W 460), based on the G-Class, with a raised seat and a large transparent dome at the rear. The Pope can be seen from every side while remaining protected from the weather.
On 13 May 1981, however, the attempted assassination in St Peter's Square changed everything. From that moment the pope's safety became a central concern and the popemobiles were gradually fitted with bullet-proof protection.
As Barbagallo recalls, "that first popemobile was, of course, a standard production car given for the Pope's use; it had no comforts and no particular safety features. But from then on there was an evolution that, sadly, is also closely linked to the attack in St Peter's Square on John Paul II, after which heavily armoured popemobiles began to be used, as they still are today".
The G-Class became one of the most recognisable models of his pontificate. In 1997, a long-wheelbase Mercedes S 500 Landaulet (series 140) also joined the fleet, with a hydraulically operated rear soft top and a large seat for the pope.
In 2002 the Mercedes ML 430 "Popemobile" (W 163) was added to the history of papal vehicles, another off-roader adapted to the pontiff's needs.
Benedict XVI, technology and the search for protection
With Benedict XVI the style changes again. Joseph Ratzinger, a theologian and intellectual, has a more reserved approach than his predecessor's stage presence, but maintains the tradition of close encounters with the faithful.
In 2012, the Mercedes ML 500 "Popemobile" (W 166) arrives, with larger glass surfaces to improve visibility and reduce the sense of separation between the pope and the people.
It is a popemobile that attempts to reconcile two needs that have become inseparable: protection and proximity. The pontiff must be visible, but must also be able to travel in safety.
A car that is more than just a car
Today, the popemobile is far more than a means of transport. As Leo XIV made clear at the inauguration of the exhibition, it has become a means of bringing the pontiff closer to people.
And there is a curious detail that illustrates how special the relationship with these vehicles is: the Pope's seat is unlike any other. Designed for him alone, every detail, from the position of the seat to the heated support bar, is suited to his needs.
Een the way a pope chooses to travel can say a great deal about how he chooses to be in the world.
The exhibition at the Vatican Museums, set up in the glass pavilion of the Giardino Quadrato, will remain open until 28 January 2027.
The papal vehicles on display
· Mercedes-Benz Nürburg 460 (W 08), 1930
· Mercedes-Benz 300 d Landaulet (W 189), 1960
· Mercedes-Benz 600 Pullman Landaulet (W 100), 1965
· Mercedes-Benz 300 SEL Pullman (W 109), 1967
· Mercedes-Benz 230 G (W 460), 1980
· Mercedes-Benz S 500 long-wheelbase Landaulet (series 140), 1997
· Mercedes-Benz ML 430 "Papamobile" (W 163), 2002
· Mercedes-Benz ML 500 "Papamobile" (W 166), 2012
Two other vehicles broaden the historical perspective of the exhibition: a Benz Patent-Motorwagen from 1886 and a new Mercedes-Benz S-Class.

noticias.titulo: World is being ‘held hostage by oil mafia’: How one tiny country is putting its foot down at COP31
noticias.resumen: On the final day of COP31, one country says it will “not lend its name” to “complacent or ineffective language” in the final pact, which requires consensus.
noticias.texto:
On the final day of COP31, one country says it will “not lend its name” to “complacent or ineffective language” in the final pact, which requires consensus.
It’s crunch time as COP31 enters its final day of discussions, following a lacklustre draft deal that sparked heavy backlash.
The annual UN climate summit, which is being held in Antalya, Türkiye, may overrun into the weekend amid growing divisions.
Yesterday (19 November), co-host Australia unveiled a slimmed-down draft deal that removed all mentions of fossil fuels – the leading driver of climate change – despite growing momentum to publish an exit strategy.
It signals a repeat of the COP30 summit in Belém last year, where the transition away from fossil fuels (TAFF) was erased from the final deal following resistance from fossil-fuel exporting countries.
Panama threatens to block final COP31 deal
COP agreements require consensus from all parties – that’s almost 200 nations – which means progress is often slow and incremental.
However, Panama appears to be putting its foot down, threatening to block any final deal that doesn’t deliver on a cap of oil production alongside a strident defence of science.
In a letter to COP31 hosts, Panama’s environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro said his country would “not join any consensus, and will formally object in the closing plenaries, to the adoption of any decision that does not lead to an outcome satisfactory” to its principles and values.
Navarro added that Panama would “not lend its name” to “complacent or ineffective language” in the final pact.
Earlier this week, the politician argued that the world is being “held hostage by the petroleum mafia” and that nations are “in love with its kidnappers”.
“They torture us for our own good, they destroy our planet for our own good. They destroy nature to help us, and they demand our unrequited, endless, unlimited, boundless love. And we are so stupid that we fall for it.”
TAFF roadmaps gain appeal outside of the UN remit
Nations agreed at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 to transition away from fossil fuels, but language around energy sources is highly contested at the yearly talks.
However, following the first TAFF conference in Santa Marta, Colombia, which took place in April, several countries have established their own exit strategy – with Europe leading the way.
Before COP31, France, Germany and the Netherlands published national roadmaps to get away from coal, oil and gas.
On 11 November, two days into the talks, Finland affirmed its commitment to TAFF.
Almost a week later (17 November), Denmark, Portugal, Luxembourg and Spain announced their own national plans.
While “you can always wish and fight” for TAFF to be anchored in the cover decision, “this is not for us the ultimate benchmark for success,” German Environment Ministry State Secretary Heike Henn told reporters on Monday (16 November), ahead of the draft’s publication. “The success is in doing, in a growing coalition,” she said.
What will COP31 actually decide?
Experts have criticised the erasure of fossil fuels from the latest draft deal, warning that the talks risk becoming a “ghost COP”.
"The summit will have nothing to show for what happened here,” Mohamed Adow, founder and director of climate think tank Power Shift Africa said on Thursday, 19 November.
“After the progress made in 2023 at COP28 in Dubai where fossil fuels were mentioned for the first time, there is now no mention of the f-word at all.
“COP31 has been muzzled on the most important threat causing the climate crisis.”
Inga Fritzen Buan from environmental group WWF told news agency AFP that some major fossil energy producers are attempting to “undermine” everything related to emissions cuts and the energy transition.
“With this draft, they’re succeeding,” Buan added. “This is not a mere disagreement over the placement of a comma.”
Electrification takes centre stage
The latest text included a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35 per cent by 2035 – a key initiative of Türkiye.
However, concern remains that the draft deal does not explicitly require that extra electricity be powered by clean energy rather than coal or gas.
“We are going to fight for clean electrification” met by renewables and nuclear energy, French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut told reporters.
Some countries rejected calls to ramp up carbon capture, utilisation and storage technology, which critics see as an expensive distraction from cutting pollution.
The draft also proposes further discussions toward “tripling” finance for climate adaptation measures by 2035, but drops a $120 billion (approximately €109 billion) goal being sought by developing nations.
Rich nations have long resisted calls to increase support for countries struggling to adapt to climate change, citing budget constraints and insisting that big emerging economies such as China also contribute.
The draft deal also contains a recognition of the “best-available science” and a reference to the work of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), a key battleground at COP31.
