noticias.titulo: Portugal national public sector strike over pay disrupts key services
noticias.resumen: Public administration workers are holding a national strike this Friday, demanding better pay and working conditions. Health, education and justice are among the hardest hit sectors, with many public services likely to face disruption.
noticias.texto:
Public administration workers are holding a national strike this Friday, demanding better pay and working conditions. Health, education and justice are among the hardest hit sectors, with many public services likely to face disruption.
Public administration workers are staging a nationwide strike this Friday.
In Lisbon, the coordinator of the Frente Comum said this morning that the protest has been seeing strong participation since overnight and that the first effects can already be felt in areas such as health, education and rubbish collection.
In some of these services, such as hospitals, only minimum services are being provided. On the figures for education, Sebastião Santana said, quoted by the Lusa news agency, that "data are still being collected" but "many schools are closed across the country".
Also in the morning, the secretary general of FENPROF, José Feliciano Costa, said there was a "significant number of schools on strike", particularly in Greater Lisbon. "Today teachers will join the public sector strike also because they see their careers being devalued," the union leader told Lusa.
In health, more specifically in hospitals, Joana Bordalo e Sá, vice president of the National Federation of Doctors (FNAM), said that "minimum services are being rigorously complied with", with the greatest constraints affecting consultations and scheduled surgeries.
"This is a strike for patients and for the National Health Service. Ana Paula Martins [health minister] knows the chaos that is going on in healthcare and does nothing to solve it," she told reporters this morning.
The protest was called by the Frente Comum, affiliated to the CGTP, to demand better wages to keep up with inflation and cope with the cost of living. The union front is calling for a pay rise of no less than 15%, with a minimum increase of 150 euros for everyone, and is also advocating raising the basic pay in the public administration to 1,150 euros, with effect from 1 January.
Unions want to influence budget debate
In an interview with RTP, the coordinator of the Frente Comum accused the government of having no real will to negotiate.
"We are at the fourth round of negotiations and the government insists on not moving from its starting point," said Sebastião Santana, who cited the executive's proposal to increase the meal allowance as an example.
"The government proposed an increase of 15 cents compared with the first proposal it presented for the meal allowance, which is ridiculous." The union organisation is demanding a 13 euro increase in this area, stressing that the government's proposal would raise the current amount to 6.45%, falling far short of workers' demands who, according to Sebastião Santa, have some of the lowest wages in Europe and have been losing purchasing power "for more than a decade and a half".
The union leader also explained that the choice of date for the protest is intended to influence the budget debate.
"The strike is on the 20th and not on the 25th in order to influence the discussion of the State Budget," he said.

noticias.titulo: Former French PM de Villepin launches presidential bid, as centrists and conservatives slide in polls
noticias.resumen: Dominique de Villepin's presidential bid comes as France's centrists and conservatives have been struggling to gain ground.
noticias.texto:
Dominique de Villepin's presidential bid comes as France's centrists and conservatives have been struggling to gain ground.
Former conservative French Prime Minister Dominique de Villepin announced his presidential bid on Friday, as he decried the country's "decaying" political and social climate.
Under former conservative President Jacques Chirac, de Villepin served as foreign affairs minister (2002–2004), interior minister (2004–2005) and prime minister (2005–2007).
In an apparent reference to the hard-left France Unbowed and far-right National Rally party, he called out the rise of "radical forces", while accusing French President Emmanuel Macron of "paving the way" to their ascension.
The race is currently dominated by the National Rally and the France Unbowed party, with their respective candidates Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, polling around 32–36% and 17-19.5%, according to an Ifop-Fiducial survey published on 18 November.
The 73-year old is the third candidate to announce his presidential bid in November alone, after former French judoka heavyweight Teddy Riner and hard-right leader of the Reconquêtes Eric Zemmour.
His candidacy comes as France's centrists and conservatives — including centrist Gabriel Attal, alongside conservatives Édouard Philippe and Bruno Retailleau — have been struggling to gain ground in the latest polls.
This is also a result of a fractured political landscape, given that the traditional left and right have faced difficulties in reasserting themselves ever since Macron's election in 2017, which he won on a centrist platform with his party En Marche.
Outlining his policies, De Villepin stressed the vital need to address France's economic situation, as it grapples with one of the highest levels of public debt in the eurozone. He pledged to bring this debt below 3% of GDP, while backing increased taxes on the ultra-wealthy.
On Europe, he decried the bloc's lack of clout on the international scene, while stating that France also struggles to make its voice heard. De Villepin said he supported the creation of a European security council for the bloc's major powers — France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and Poland.
As the central and conservative political bloc struggles to unite, the prospect of a possible primary to select a joint candidate has become a hotly contested issue, with candidates such as Édouard Philippe refusing to take part.
De Villepin has also ruled out participating, declaring that he is not tied to "Macron's political legacy." Many of the possible centrist and conservative candidates, who would likely be his rivals in a primary, have formerly served in Macron's successive governments.
Disagreements have also centred over how broad the possible primary should be in terms of including candidates on the right, given that the objective is to rally as many possible votes from conservatives — but also centrists.
Dominique de Villepin must secure the 500 endorsements from elected officials in order to be eligible to run for office. His team recently claimed to have received just over 300 promises of support. This is a first hurdle that he failed to overcome during his attempted candidacy in 2012.

noticias.titulo: Brussels puts military fuel needs at heart of new oil security strategy
noticias.resumen: Brussels is incorporating military fuel needs into the planning and assessment of national emergency oil stocks, according to a document seen by Euronews.
noticias.texto:
Brussels is incorporating military fuel needs into the planning and assessment of national emergency oil stocks, according to a document seen by Euronews.
The European Commission wants EU governments to look beyond emergency oil stockpiles to secure enough diesel, jet fuel and other oil products to keep essential services and military operations running during a prolonged crisis, according to a draft document seen by Euronews.
More than half of EU countries (61.54%) reported trouble ensuring sufficient fuel access when armed forces move across the continent in a 2025 Commission impact assessment, posing a major hurdle for the bloc's plans for military readiness by 2030.
With Russia's war against Ukraine at its border and a series of hybrid attacks sweeping the continent over the past weeks, Defence Commissioner Andrius Kubilius recently warned that the EU needs to prepare for a substantial increase in military fuel consumption during a conflict.
He noted that in the event of a war outbreak, NATO could need to move and sustain 100,000 troops during the first ten days of a crisis, stressing the importance of diesel and jet fuel for military operations.
The EU's new approach to energy security deems it crucial to place oil supplies within the EU's wider defence and strategy preparedness agenda to "prevent or minimise risks" on a range of measures.
According to the draft document, which lays out an overhaul of the Commission's oil security rules, national governments would need to assess how much emergency fuel they hold and whether their refineries, ports, pipelines and distribution networks could withstand major disruptions.
"Inadequacy between the evolution of consumption, including military demand, and the evolution of the fuel supply chain, including along military mobility corridors," reads the paper, referring to assessments expected by EU governments.
Under the draft rules, EU countries would have to factor military demand into their national risk assessments, including the possibility of sudden increases in fuel requirements and simultaneous pressure from civilian and military consumers.
A recent NATO energy security study found that the EU's ability to fuel its armed forces could be undermined by a shrinking refinery industry, growing dependence on foreign suppliers and insufficient jet fuel reserves.
"Jet fuel is precisely the product on which NATO Europe is structurally short. It is also the fuel most likely to retain (or even grow) its demand to 2050, and the product with the least amount of stock cover at 49 days," reads the study.
NATO's study noted that Europe imports between 27% and 30% of its jet fuel from outside the region, leaving it exposed to foreign suppliers.
Dependence is also highly concentrated — 36% of external imports come from one supplier, while three countries account for 65% of all external supplies.
Assessing refinery's capacity
While EU governments are pursuing industrial decarbonisation, strategically important refining capacity is disappearing, raising the question of whether the bloc's refinery industry is becoming a national security liability.
Despite the efforts to accelerate the energy transition, the new energy security framework puts considerable attention on refineries — an industry sector in decline across Europe over the past nearly two decades.
"We need to counter this trend and ensure that we have adequate and flexible refining capacity in Europe. Today and for the future. This is not just a matter of economic competitiveness. It is also a matter of security," the Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen said after a dialogue on refineries alongside Defense Commissioner Kubilius.
Even if EU countries have access to crude oil alone, they need sufficient capacity to turn it into the diesel, gasoline and jet fuel required by transport, industry and defence.
According to the draft document, national authorities would have to identify their refineries, assess their production capacity and report major closures, expansions and planned investments.
Brussels also expects capitals to examine the consequences of losing critical infrastructure and becoming overly dependent on a limited number of foreign suppliers.
The document suggests the Commission is asking governments to consider whether allowing domestic refining capacity to disappear could create a strategic vulnerability that can't easily be repaired if a crisis hits.
The draft would also require EU capitals to map their dependence on individual suppliers, including the countries from which they import crude oil, diesel, gasoline and jet fuel.
The goal is to assess how these dependencies could evolve over the next five years and what would happen if a major supplier suddenly stopped deliveries.
EU countries could face greater scrutiny over their emergency preparedness.
The draft document suggests that capitals would need to prepare national risk assessments and preparedness and response plans covering physical attacks, cyber threats, extreme weather, ownership of critical infrastructure and prolonged disruptions affecting several supply routes.
Collision course with clean transition
Environmental campaigners have argued that reviving refineries across the EU could slow down the bloc's goal to cut CO2 emissions at a time when a series of climate policies are being diluted.
The softening of the EU's carbon market and the CO2 emissions car rules, alongside the delay in implementing methane rules, raises questions over whether Brussels will reach its 2040 climate target to ultimately become carbon neutral by 2050.
Despite seeking to boost electrification and reduce oil consumption, Brussels recognises that armed forces will continue to need reliable supplies of diesel and jet fuel, including during sudden increases in military demand.
The Commission is expected to unveil its proposal to revise oil security supply rules on 2 December.

noticias.titulo: Moment Dominique de Villepin announces his 2027 French presidential bid
noticias.resumen: Former French Prime Minister Dominique de Villepin has officially announced his candidacy for the 2027 presidential election. The 73-year-old, internationally known for opposing the US-led invasion of Iraq at the United Nations in 2003, will run with his political movement, La France humaniste.
noticias.texto:
Former French Prime Minister Dominique de Villepin has announced he will run for president in 2027, returning to the political frontline with a warning about what he describes as the country's decline.
"This decay of France, this instinct for defeat, this spirit of death that is taking hold of us, these are all reasons that lead me to stand before you today and say: I am a candidate in the 2027 presidential election," he said at a press conference in Paris on Friday.
The 73-year-old former prime minister and foreign minister is best known internationally for his passionate 2003 speech at the United Nations Security Council, when he opposed the US-led invasion of Iraq.
De Villepin served as prime minister under former president Jacques Chirac between 2005 and 2007. He is now running with his political movement, La France humaniste.

noticias.titulo: The biggest winners and losers of the EU-UK summit deals
noticias.resumen: We take stock of who’s up and who’s down after London and Brussels sign three new deals.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — U.K. and EU leaders on Friday hailed a “win-win” as they announced long-awaited deals on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme. The reality is more complicated. A summit press conference failed to resolve questions over whether the much-lauded food and drink rules, emissions trading and youth visas deals are contingent on a tuition fees agreement set to be negotiated over the next six months. U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham insisted that the deals are “done” and tuition fees are still to be negotiated — despite EU claims to the contrary earlier on Friday. If all the agreements take effect, there will be winners and losers on both sides of the English Channel and beyond. We take stock of who’s up and who’s down. Winners Students British and EU students are among the biggest winners from today’s announcements, benefiting from both a youth experience scheme and the planned tuition fee deal. Under the new scheme, 100,000 young people will be able to spend up to three years working or studying in Britain or the EU respectively — a significant improvement on current visa requirements. Under a deal yet to be thrashed out, students could also benefit from lower tuition fees when studying abroad. Two EU diplomats, granted anonymity to discuss the plans, said London had so far offered fees of £12,000. The EU would drop its fees too. If agreed, this would be a significant win for Brussels, with EU students currently subject to international student rates of up to £38,000 per year in the U.K. British supermarkets U.K. supermarkets — many of whom import from and export to the EU — were among the first to praise the agrifood deal, with major brands like Tesco and M&S saying the deal would make it easier and cheaper to trade with Europe. The deal will see Britain align with EU food and agriculture rules by 2028, removing the need for costly certification requirements and checks in a move the U.K. government claims could add up to £5.1 billion a year to the British economy. “Getting our spaghetti bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet’s signature and even the Latin name of a cow,” said M&S managing director Alex Freudmann. “When this deal comes into force, it will remove this bureaucracy.” That said, there are questions over whether retailers will be in a position to pass on any savings to the customer amid spiraling energy costs. Renewables providers British renewable energy producers have double reason to celebrate. The decision to link the U.K. and EU emissions trading schemes from 2028 means clean energy exported to the continent will no longer be subject to the EU’s carbon border tax — making British clean energy exports more competitive. Perhaps even more significant is a plan for the U.K. to join the EU internal electricity market, which they hope to finalize next year. If that comes off, it will make it much easier for British electricity generators to sell power to EU customers. “That would be a major prize for consumers and the renewable energy industry,” RenewableUK chief executive Tara Singh said in a statement Friday, adding it would allow “electricity to be traded more efficiently across our interconnectors and enabling Britain and Europe to make better use of the cheapest clean power available at any given time.” EU renewables groups have made the same point. The tech industry The plan to launch an EU-U.K. Digital Partnership early next year is a win for the tech industry on both sides of the channel. The statement’s wording is loose and doesn’t provide a ton of detail for industry types to sink their teeth into, but it spans a wide range of potential areas that “could cover” secure connectivity, quantum, online safety, as well as AI and its safety — areas that have seen considerable divergence since Brexit. The statement also includes digital wallets and credentials, which are of interest to U.K. businesses, especially since Andy Burnham ditched the British government’s plans for digital ID. Of the more political parts of the agreement, the Youth Experience Scheme element is a big win for smaller U.K. tech companies who want to welcome keen young Europeans and entrepreneurs to the British tech scene. The City While there was nothing of great direct benefit to the City of London in today’s deal, the mood music matters for the U.K.’s financial services industry. The City has been shut out of EU markets since Brexit, with only London’s clearinghouses, a key part of the plumbing of the financial system, maintaining the ability to directly serve European clients. Brussels for years refused to even talk to Britain about financial services until issues on the Northern Ireland border were resolved. Now, as Burnham pushes for better, financial services could yet benefit. While the City is in no great rush to give up the new U.K. regulatory regime developed since Brexit, there is hope of more collaboration in areas like investment, particularly for defense and start-ups, where both sides face a lack of cash and fears over economic resilience Losers British universities With so much potentially hinging on a tuition fee deal, the U.K. government is under increasing pressure to get this agreement over the line. But it’s also under a lot of domestic pressure from universities, which have warned the move could cost them £500 million a year — money that they say would otherwise be used to help fund research, teaching and jobs. Currently, tuition fees for EU nationals studying in the U.K. can reach up to £38,000 per year, in line with other international students, while British students pay a maximum of £9,790 a year in England. Hollie Chandler, director of strategic policy at the Russell Group of research-intensive universities, said any reduction in EU student fees would “put pressure on U.K. student places and take more money out of U.K. higher education, without necessarily achieving the ambition of growing opportunities for EU students to study in the U.K.” Chinese carmakers It could have been worse for Chinese carmakers, but they aren’t in the clear just yet. The EU wanted the U.K. to agree to a commitment binding it to the EU’s tariff regime on Chinese cars and other imports. The U.K. successfully pushed back, instead saying it would “ensure outcomes consistent with the relevant EU measures in order to ensure that the supply chain in question is protected in a consistent way” across the two markets and “guard against potential risks of circumvention.” But as talks over British access to the EU’s Made in Europe industrial scheme continue over the coming months, that phrasing leaves the door open to raising tariffs in the future. China experts Gregor Williams and Noah Barkin had previously warned that “acting before the terms of Made in Europe access are settled would weaken London’s negotiating leverage.” “The UK has an incentive to signal a willingness to align with the EU while stopping short of imposing immediate restrictions on Chinese imports, not least given Beijing’s threats of retaliation,” Williams and Barkin added. They expect “some form of UK trade action on Chinese vehicles will come in the next 12 months.” Food manufacturers A major selling point of the SPS deal is the idea that it will bring down food prices for British consumers — one that government ministers have pounced on during the cost-of-living crisis fueled by the Iran war. But U.K. food firms have taken issue with this framing , pointing out that alignment with EU rules will mean costly changes for manufacturers as they align with EU requirements on issues like food safety, packaging, labeling and pesticides. In guidance published alongside the summit statement, the U.K. government sets out a series of transitional arrangements aimed at helping firms adapt to the new changes. While she welcomed the prospect of closer trade ties with the EU in the longterm, Karen Betts, chief executive of the Food and Drink Federation, warned that “the timing remains tight.” She urged the U.K. government to pass the relevant legislation and publish detailed business guidance “as quickly as possible” to give firms time to make necessary changes. British steelmakers The deal might be a win for steelmakers in the long-run, but the sector will have to wait some time to feel the benefits. While the emissions trading scheme deal will ultimately spare Britain’s steel producers from the EU’s carbon border tax regime, it won’t take effect until 2028, leaving British producers exposed for at least another year. Brussels and London are also still in talks to forge a steel alliance that would see the two sides harmonize new quota and tariff regimes imposed in July after they slashed market access for each other. But they couldn’t get things wrapped up in time for the summit and talks are proving challenging. Defense firms Although the two sides committed to immediately setting up a new Dialogue on Economic Security to tackle shared economic dependencies, they said little about defense sector collaboration. Reviving talks for Britain to get access to the EU’s €150 billion SAFE fund for joint defense procurement loans “isn’t part of the summit negotiation,” Britain’s Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said Friday. But if the EU “wanted to return to it, I’d certainly suggest we’d be willing to do so,” he told Sky News. Potentially significant language in the joint statement includes plans to “enhance exchanges on defence industrial issues,” including the prospect of British involvement in the EU’s “Capability Coalitions” — groups of member states which pool resources and coordinate investment in making new defense capabilities.

noticias.titulo: Andy Burnham discovers nothing in Brussels is ever easy
noticias.resumen: Britain’s prime minister is banking on a ‘brainstorm’ to decide Britain’s future with the EU. He just has to get through the spin wars first.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — Hours before Andy Burnham arrived at a long-planned U.K.-EU summit Friday, it seemed like it’d be a humdrum victory lap. Talks ran late Thursday but that always happens; Britain seemed to believe everything was wrapping up as planned; Burnham even brought a super-delegation of seven Cabinet colleagues. “Deal done,” texted one U.K. official at 14 minutes to midnight. The spin war only came Friday morning — and not for the first time in Britain’s long Brexit saga, it arrived in a dry technical briefing in the European Council’s Europa building HQ. A joint statement by the Council and the European Commission, circulated by EU diplomats, said three long-planned deals on carbon emissions trading, food standards and a youth experience scheme would not be formally adopted until both sides had concluded talks on a pact “providing for equal treatment on tuition fees.” This derailed Downing Street’s media strategy on summit day after months of pitch-rolling. Negotiators had spent months tying together deals to align food standards and emissions trading, and finalized a cap on the youth experience scheme — allowing 100,000 EU citizens under 32 each year to move to the U.K. for up to three years, and vice versa. They also agreed, as expected, to delay the resolution of two issues by six months — Britain would work on a pledge to cut university tuition fees for EU students, in exchange for assurances that its industries would be protected from the EU’s Made in Europe scheme. David Henig, the U.K. government’s former assistant director on trade policy, said that different things could be true at the same time — that the three deals announced Friday were contingent on a tuition fees breakthrough, but also that “in reality, there will be a deal on tuition fees” no matter what. Henig, who now leads the U.K. Trade Policy Project at European Centre for International Political Economy, said the situation was “entirely normal” in the trade world but that handling of the communications had still been a “complete mess.” “The U.K. wanted to get something on Made in Europe, so that meant tuition fees being delayed as well. Somehow this has turned into a great defeat for the U.K. government because everything would be at the mercy of tuition fees,” he said. “That was what the U.K. government actually wanted.” Opposition politicians seized on the row, with Reform UK Leader Nigel Farage calling Burnham “naive.” Oliver Lewis, the former Conservative Brexit aide who has founded a new anti-EU campaign called Stay Out, said he had “been played like a fiddle by Brussels.” Brussels waffle If intended to seize the narrative, the statement worked. Other EU officials tried to downplay its significance as the morning unfolded — the key phrase “equal treatment” was, in fact, not in the final summit text — but the issue still dominated questions at a joint press conference by Burnham, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa. U.K. officials sprang up an unplanned briefing to counter-spin while Downing Street aides texted journalists with lines from a government spokesperson saying the deal was done. Burnham himself told the press conference: “I don’t think there’s any confusion at all. The deal is done. It’s there in black and white.” A senior U.K. official insisted to POLITICO that the three deals on food standards, emissions and youth experience were not contingent on a pact on tuition fees. Yet EU diplomats continued to suggest they were part of a “package,” a concept neither Costa nor von der Leyen tried very hard to shoot down. (Von der Leyen told journalists merely that the tuition fees deal was “on a different sheet of paper,” before Burnham was treated to a battered fish lunch with a dessert of fruit with actual Brussels waffle.) Later Friday, Britain’s European Relations Minister Hamish Falconer told POLITICO he was “confident” that a tuition fees deal would be reached over the next six months. But the risk is not negligible. The six-month deadline to ink an agreement includes a French presidential election; if the far-right politician Marine Le Pen wins it could have unpredictable results for the EU’s legislative agenda, including Made in Europe. And negotiations on the EU’s Industrial Accelerator Act (the legislation behind Made in Europe) are behind schedule, with talks between the Council and European Parliament yet to begin and disagreements over the automotive package adding to the complexity. Lower tuition fees, please The Commission and Council statement Friday morning seized the headlines for two reasons. The first was that it indicated the three deals tied up on Thursday night would not go ahead if Britain broke its promise to cut tuition fees. EU officials insisted they were not holding Britain “hostage,” but it was difficult to interpret the statement otherwise. The second was the phrase “equal treatment” — which appeared to suggest the whole deal was contingent on something Britain was not even willing to offer. Britain has signaled it will cut the international fees charged by U.K. universities — often well over £30,000 per year — to a lower level for students coming from the EU. But crucially, the U.K. has resisted European demands to match EU students’ fees with the £9,790-a-year “home fees” paid by U.K. students. Instead both sides have talked about a figure somewhere in the middle; negotiators have discussed a possible figure of £12,000 in private, according to two people with knowledge of the talks, who like others cited in this story were granted anonymity to share candid details. This is a deeply personal issue for many European politicians and diplomats, who either spent their youths at Britain’s famed elite universities — think Oxford, Cambridge or the London School of Economics — or now have children attending them, or hoping to, at least. There were immediate suspicions on the U.K. side that the EU’s statement was a piece of spin in the midst of a negotiation. The U.K. is holding its cards close on tuition fees to keep leverage over Made in Europe. A resolution on both issues was delayed because Made in Europe, designed to protect the bloc’s industries from a flood of cheap imports, remains in its early stages. The summit text agreed by the U.K. and EU contained no direct reference to the scheme, merely a pledge to “limit negative effects on one another in their measures impacting specific supply chains.” Despite this, there was a view in the British contingent that the U.K. pushed the EU successfully for assurances on Made in Europe — meaning the EU had to flex its muscles somewhere else. “It was a pretty complicated discussion, and the British took a very hard line,” said one EU diplomat. This person added: “The discussion on tuition fees fell out because of the issue related to equal treatment… Ultimately, it’s not the statement we would have wanted, but with a partner like this, it’s important to maintain dialogue.” ‘Dear Andy’ Both sides put on smiles at the press conference, with Burnham calling the deals a “good day for Britain and a good day for Europe.” Von der Leyen heaped praise on the man she referred to from the podium as “dear Andy.” Ultimately, the most important question about Friday’s row will be whether the deals Burnham announced are at any genuine risk of falling apart. “Six months seems a bit short to me” to sort out the tuition fees issue, said the EU diplomat quoted earlier in this story. British officials insist there is no issue. To make matters more complicated, Brussels is also pressing London to raise tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, potentially tying this to Made in Europe provisions. The U.K. has yet to decide, though there is a widespread expectation among Labour MPs and some ministers that Britain will end up raising tariffs on Chinese EVs. If Friday’s deals do go ahead, the spin battle will be filed alongside countless other technocratic spats of the Brexit wars that fade into background noise. But even so, the deals are not expected to see the light of day until at least 2028 — undercutting Burnham’s pitch to the British public that they will cut food costs and ease business red tape. (The prime minister highlighted Treasury analysis that showed Friday’s deals could add 0.5% or £17 billion to U.K. GDP.) Implementation of the agrifood deal is not planned until March 2028, while a deal to link the U.K. and EU Emissions Trading Systems is only expected in the same year — meaning British firms will see no immediate relief from EU carbon border taxes, a further blow to the struggling steel industry. With the youth experience scheme not expected to be up and running until 2030, there are also questions over whether the program will survive the next election, which must happen before August 2029. There will be other challenges in selling the deal too. The U.K. claimed a late breakthrough on Thursday night in securing a role in shaping EU food standards rules — but hours later, Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds suggested Britain’s role would be limited. “We’d have experts in the room. We’d have the ability to put our point of view into that process. We’re not getting a vote because we’re not a member of the EU,” Reynolds told the BBC. Farage seized on this Friday, saying Britain would be forced to follow European rules on agricultural technology and pesticides rather than forging its own path. ‘Informal brainstorm’ Perhaps most importantly, Friday’s spin war is a reminder that nothing in Brussels is ever easy. It is a collision between Burnham’s big-picture way of doing politics and the EU’s hard, rules-based world. This will matter for a prime minister who plans to stake much of his campaign at the next election on a battle for hearts and minds over Europe. That ballot isn’t due until July 2029, but Farage predicted on Friday that the election would come as soon as May 2027, about a year after Burnham’s ascent from the Greater Manchester mayoralty to Westminster. As POLITICO reported this week , the personally pro-rejoin Burnham has not decided exactly what to promise the British public — and is caught between his aspirational rhetoric and the reality of a divided Cabinet. Now he can throw in the difficulty of dealing with the EU too. Costa reflected this neatly in the press conference, telling Burnham he was “always welcome in the EU” — but almost in the next breath, reminding him that the EU’s principles, including the “indivisibility” of free movement from access to the single market, would “guide our engagement with the United Kingdom.” Burnham plans to set out the options he believes are available for the future relationship next month, tied in with his promised “10-year plan” for Britain. It will kick-start a conversation that will likely culminate in a Europe-shaped offer to the public in Labour’s election manifesto. But he also indicated Friday that he would not seek more policy-by-policy deals with the EU ahead of the next election, instead favoring a broader conversation. Even Starmer promised “iterative” deals once per year. The U.K. prime minister also continued to be vague about how that process would unfold. He spoke of “informal brainstorming” with the EU ahead of another summit next year. “We are open for brainstorming,” Von der Leyen replied. Sebastian Starcevic, Sam Francis and Sam Blewett contributed reporting.

noticias.titulo: France and Germany complete political deal for ECB leadership
noticias.resumen: Paris’ new market-operations portfolio at the European Central Bank could become pivotal in a French debt crisis.
noticias.texto: FRANKFURT — France and Germany on Friday submitted their candidates to fill two looming vacancies on the European Central Bank’s Executive Board, completing a political package that’ll decide the institution’s leadership for years to come. Berlin presented Markus Brunnermeier, a professor at Princeton University, as the ECB’s next chief economist, after the Irish incumbent Philip Lane concludes his eight-year term on May 31. Paris put forward Laurence Boone — a former minister of Europe and political ally of President Emmanuel Macron — who is now head of corporate and investment banking at Santander, to take over the ECB’s markets portfolio. That post will become available on Jan. 4, when Isabel Schnabel leaves the ECB for a job at the International Monetary Fund. The new set-up paves the way for Spain’s former central bank governor, Pablo Hernández de Cos, to become ECB President once Christine Lagarde steps down on Feb. 7. The Netherlands had hoped to secure the top job. But having Dutch and German monetary hawks in what are typically the ECB’s two most influential posts would have been unacceptable to the dovish south, analysts said. If approved, Boone will step into a pivotal position at the Bank if strains in French and other European debt markets continue to worsen — a clear risk in the European Commission’s new forecasts that show many eurozone members’ budget deficits widening next year. In an October interview with POLITICO, former ECB Chief Economist Peter Praet said the markets role matters most when market tensions increase pressure on the ECB to intervene in bond markets. “I think this would be a very strong board, combining deep economic expertise, extensive policymaking experience and strong international networks,” EFG Chief Economist Stefan Gerlach said. “These are all important qualities, particularly at a time when the ECB faces considerable economic and political uncertainty.” Fewer politicians A board stacked with economic expertise would mark a break from the previous lineup, when former politicians, Lagarde and Luis de Guindos, held both the presidency and vice-presidency. De Cos and Vice-President Boris Vujčić are seasoned central bankers, as is Piero Cipollone, who heads the payments department. Before becoming a politician, Boone had been chief economist at the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. While the reshuffle will leave the six-strong board looking more apolitical, the game of ECB musical chairs has been anything but, according to ING’s head of macro, Carsten Brzeski. “It looks like another masterpiece of French diplomacy and strategic personnel policy,” he said. “With the move to opt for the markets operation, France gave the impression of passing the more important job of chief economist to Germany.” “However, with a Spanish president and France holding the markets operation, the risk of a more dovish ECB has clearly increased,” Brzeski said.

noticias.titulo: Latvian leader calls for closure of EU borders to all Russians
noticias.resumen: Andris Kulbergs warned that Europe cannot screen hundreds of thousands of Russian tourists as Moscow escalates its hybrid attacks.
noticias.texto: Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs called for the EU to close its borders to all Russian citizens, warning that the bloc cannot vet the hundreds of thousands of Russian tourists it still lets in. “Letting so many people into the EU is currently too dangerous. We must not give in to Russia, we must not show weakness,” Kulbergs told WELT , which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network. “Nobody can screen that many people.” He also ruled out a return to normal ties with Moscow after any ceasefire in Ukraine. “Some believe that after a ceasefire there can be a return to normal relations with Russia. There cannot. It is a new era,” he said. Latvia was among the 11 countries that signed a Swedish-led letter in June urging Brussels to restrict visas for Russians. Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner suggested to POLITICO in October that the European Commission could present a proposal next year. Kulbergs warned that Russia’s hybrid attacks on NATO’s eastern flank were intensifying. “The situation is escalating,” he said, adding that Latvian and Estonian special forces had arrested eight people on Estonian soil last weekend who had “concrete instructions to attack a production facility in Estonia that supports Ukraine.” Russia, he said, “is behind this.” He called the coming months “a winter of truth,” arguing that Russia was striking Ukraine’s water, heating and power supplies because it was making little progress at the front, while also trying to sway public opinion in Germany and elsewhere. “Putin wants the Germans to be frightened and to demand that their government stop supporting Ukraine,” he said. Kulbergs dismissed fears that Thursday’s summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen amounted to a new Yalta as “an exaggeration,” arguing that the Russian leader had been humiliated. The Yalta summit in February 1945, where U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin shaped Europe’s postwar order, is widely seen as having left much of Central and Eastern Europe under Soviet domination. Kulbergs urged larger countries, especially Germany, not to give in to war fatigue. “It is entirely possible to be pro-European, to support Ukraine vigorously, to stand up to the aggressor — and still win an election by a large margin,” he said. The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, The Telegraph, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.

noticias.titulo: EU warns against COP31 becoming a ‘fossil fuel summit’
noticias.resumen: The current draft decision text discussed in Antalya would represent "a substantive step backwards" on climate action, European Union leaders said.
noticias.texto: ANTALYA, Turkey — This year’s U.N. climate conference risks turning into a “fossil fuel summit,” EU leaders warned in a strongly worded letter seen by POLITICO. “The EU must be clear that it cannot join consensus on a package that would represent a substantive step backwards for global climate action,” Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra and Irish Climate minister Darragh O’Brien wrote on behalf of the EU’s 27 member states. They insisted the current COP31 draft decision text , which does not mention fossil fuels, the main driver of climate change, would be “perceived as a retreat from previous commitments, and as disproportionately accommodating the interests of continued fossil fuel production and consumption.” The draft document calls on countries to scale up carbon storage and capture technologies (CCUS) to meet a specific target, and includes a pledge to raise the share of electricity in global energy use to 35% by 2035 — including power generated using fossil fuels. France, the bloc’s second-largest economy, has heavily criticized the inclusion of CCUS targets. “When it comes to carbon capture, we’re completely opposed — and this is a real red line — to any figures, any targets, or any quantified objectives,” French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut told reporters on Friday. Dated Nov. 19, the letter asks Australia and Turkey, who are jointly presiding over this year’s global climate talks, to address these demands. “The EU always prefers an ambitious negotiated outcome but cannot accept agreement at any cost,” the letter warned.

noticias.titulo: Tusk: Russian cruise missile incursion into Poland seems ‘intentional’
noticias.resumen: “This doesn’t look like an accident,” the Polish prime minister warned.
noticias.texto: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Friday that Russian projectiles entering his country’s territory appeared to be part of an “intentional provocation” from Moscow, hours after U.S. President Donald Trump characterized earlier Russian incursions as happening by “mistake.” One object exploded, but no one was hurt and there was no damage, Tusk said at a press conference. The incursion occurred as Russia launched a massive missile and drone assault on Ukraine , killing at least five people and damaging three major bridges in Kyiv. “This doesn’t look like an accident,” Tusk said, adding that he was choosing his words carefully because the matter was serious. Speaking to Fox News on Thursday , Trump said that “Putin has been landing drones in Poland and a couple of little missiles, by mistake,” referring to previous incidents. “To put it mildly, I don’t always agree with the American side’s assessment and interpretation of these incidents,” Tusk said in the press conference. He added that U.S. officials have access to the wreckage from Friday’s incursion. “I think that in this particular case, no one will try to pretend anymore that this was just an innocent accident,” Tusk said. Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said the objects fell at three locations in southeastern Poland: Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik nad Sanem and Mołodycz. The object found at Nowy Lipowiec was a Russian Ch-101 cruise missile, he said. A second object was also believed to be a missile, Kosiniak-Kamysz added, while the third was probably a jet-powered drone. Tusk pointed to a possible connection to military exercises by the “coalition of the willing” in nearby Nowa Dęba. Led by France and Britain, the drills involve 11 countries preparing to deploy a multinational force to support Ukraine after a ceasefire. “We can’t rule out the possibility — and this is a hypothesis — that the provocation was also connected to the exercises taking place in Poland,” he said . Kosiniak-Kamysz added later in the day : “This attack was no accident. It was closely coordinated with today’s demonstration of the Coalition of the Willing’s capabilities. It was directed against our citizens, intended to undermine society’s resilience and destroy cooperation within NATO, the European Union and the Coalition of the Willing,” he said. “We cannot give in to this. Our presence here shows that we cannot be frightened or intimidated. Nor can we be stopped in our efforts to ensure security and peace, protect our citizens and our territory, and support Ukraine.” He added that Russia’s intention was “to destroy the unity of Western countries … undermine that cooperation, weaken relations and ties and sow uncertainty among our citizens” and said he wanted to see “stronger involvement from our NATO partners.” Tusk said he was discussing a response with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, who is due in Warsaw on Saturday, and had also spoken with European leaders. “This incident is clearly dangerous — a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. I condemn Russia’s attacks as well as its ongoing war,” Rutte said on social media . This article has been updated.

noticias.titulo: German defense minister apologizes for calling US criticism of Ukraine strikes ‘stupid’
noticias.resumen: Boris Pistorius walked back his choice of words but stood by his support for Ukrainian strikes inside Russia.
noticias.texto: BERLIN — German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has personally apologized for his earlier remarks lambasting a senior Pentagon official’s criticism of Ukrainian strikes inside Russia as “quite a stupid thing.” “I apologized for my choice of words,” Pistorius said in a Friday phone interview with POLITICO. He said that he had spoken by phone Wednesday evening with Elbridge Colby, the Pentagon’s top policy official. However, Pistorius underlined that he has not changed his support for the Ukrainian strikes themselves. “But I also made clear — and he sees it the same way — that we simply have different views on this.” The two sides “agree to disagree,” Pistorius said. The apology follows a public clash at Tuesday’s meeting of Ukraine’s military backers in Brussels. Colby questioned the effectiveness of Ukrainian long-range strikes on Russian oil infrastructure and other targets, arguing they had done little to end the war or halt Russian advances. In a joint news conference following the meeting, Pistorius said: “Criticizing strikes like that in Russia to destroy strategic military … targets is quite a stupid thing.” The minister on Friday acknowledged that his language had been inappropriate, explaining that he had reached for the wrong expression while responding to a question in English. “I shouldn’t have done that,” he said. During Tuesday’s conference, U.K. Defense Secretary Wes Streeting also backed Ukraine, but used less colorful language to show his disagreement with Colby, saying: “It’s not for us to tell Ukraine how to fight their war.” The exchange highlighted differences between Washington and Berlin over Ukraine’s military strategy at a time when Germany is helping finance the development and production of Ukrainian long-range weapons and is Kyiv’s largest financial backer. The clash with Colby isn’t the only sign of a disagreement between the U.S. and Europe on Ukraine. After Thursday’s meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, U.S. President Donald Trump called European allies to complain about what he characterized as the waste of billions to support Ukraine in a conflict that is killing so many people, three European officials told POLITICO. Pistorius insisted that the disagreement with Colby would not damage bilateral defense cooperation, which both countries are seeking to deepen through joint weapons production. The U.S. is also a supplier of key weapons like Patriot air defense systems and F-35 jet fighters. “We are allies, we are partners. But that doesn’t mean we have to agree on everything,” he said, adding that his remarks would not strain relations. He called Colby an important interlocutor and praised the close exchanges with him and U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Wider stakes On Ukraine, Pistorius distinguished between helping Kyiv build long-range weapons and deciding how they are used. “Those are decisions for the Ukrainians to make,” he said. “We support them in developing and producing weapons systems that make this possible, but not only this.” He described Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russia as “targeted and strategic” and “not directed against the civilian population,” contrasting them with Moscow’s attacks on Ukraine’s energy, electricity and water infrastructure. The disagreement comes as the Trump administration pushes European allies to take greater responsibility for their own defense — what the U.S. calls NATO 3.0 — while Germany seeks to preserve American military support and expand industrial cooperation. “NATO’s European allies need the American armed forces,” Pistorius said. “But conversely, the United States also needs close ties with its European allies and needs its bases in Europe, including in Germany.” Pistorius backed continued talks under the U.S.-championed Bergen format, an informal smaller group of NATO allies discussing how Europe can shoulder more of the continent’s defense. Asked whether Germany could host future meetings of that format or seek to take over NATO’s top military command — traditionally an American job — Pistorius said: “That will become clear in the coming weeks.” He added: “What matters is that they continue to make clear that we see NATO 3.0 as a shared mission for the future.” Pistorius also addressed a U.S. proposal for Ukraine to give up territory in the Donbas in exchange for NATO membership as part of negotiations to end Russia’s war. “So far, I only know the proposals from media reports,” he said, adding that such options should not be discussed publicly but “with Ukraine and all other parties involved, including the Europeans.” “You cannot negotiate this over other people’s heads,” Pistorius said. “Every idea deserves to be examined, but not every idea is equally good. As for this particular one, I don’t know which applies,” he added. “We will have to see in the upcoming talks.”

noticias.titulo: Marine Le Pen’s party faces scrutiny over alleged leaks from interior ministry
noticias.resumen: A senior civil servant is under investigation for reportedly passing on confidential judicial information to the National Rally.
noticias.texto: PARIS — French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez on Friday summoned a senior civil servant who is under judicial investigation for allegedly leaking confidential information to the far-right National Rally. Hugues Moutouh, the senior state representative in the Centre-Val de Loire region, is under investigation by prosecutors in Paris for reportedly passing on information about judicial investigations into Marine Le Pen’s party, according to multiple French outlets including Le Monde, which first reported on the allegations . The investigation was opened in July and Moutouh has not been formally charged, Le Monde reported. Civil servants are bound by professional confidentiality, and sharing information on a judicial investigation is also an offense under French law. On Friday, Nuñez confirmed that Moutouh was being investigated but said he was not informed of the details of the inquiry. “If the allegations are verified, they are obviously very serious,” Nuñez told BFMTV. The interior minister also said he would see Moutouh on Friday morning. Moutouh could not be directly reached for comment. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Police reportedly carried out raids at the headquarters of the National Rally and at the interior ministry, Le Monde reported. Investigators looking into allegations of misuse of EU funds found documents which raised suspicions that the National Rally had received confidential judicial information. “The National Rally will not comment this ongoing investigation and stresses the confidentiality of judicial inquiries,” Bruno Bilde, a National Rally official, said in a statement.

noticias.titulo: Rwanda return hubs may violate EU human rights law, MEPs warn ahead of 2027 deportations
noticias.resumen: EU member states are aiming to deport rejected asylum seekers as early as 2027. But many MEPs believe that sending them to Rwanda is illegal as well as wrong.
noticias.texto: Plans by five member states and Rwanda to establish a migrant return hub, as confirmed on Monday (16 November), could be in violation of EU human rights obligations – and liberal and leftwing MEPs are asking the European commission to review its legality. On Monday (23 November), at least 40 MEPs from the Greens/EFA, the Left, Socialists and Democrats, and liberal Renew, will write to the EU Commission to express concerns Rwanda may be unable to fulfil key conditions under Europe’s return regulation. They are worried about international human rights standards being applied toward any people who might end up being hosted in Rwandan return hubs. In 2023, the UK’s Supreme Court blocked migrant transfers to the east African nation on the basis of human rights concerns and the principle of non-refoulement. Despite no agreement having yet being signed with Kigali, leaders and ministers from Denmark, Austria, Germany, Greece, the Netherlands announced in Vienna last Monday that a “partnership” had been agreed. Rwanda’s interior minister, Vincent Biruta, joined them in Austria to say human rights concerns were founded on “cliches.” Read more Five EU countries tout Rwanda deportation partnership, but no formal deal as key details remain secret The group met amid outstanding technical issues, with deportations to mainland Africa’s most densely populated country expected to start in 2027. Migrants from as far afield as Afghanistan could end up in Rwanda, a country most of them would have no connection to, if their asylum applications were rejected in the EU and they do not voluntarily comply with a return order. Right-wing and far-right groups in the European Parliament rammed through the return regulation, which broadly mandates deportations, in June. A letter by 22 EU leaders in August also urged the acceleration of the process after the mass arrival of migrants in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in north Africa in July. Guardian of the treaties Inscribed as a political footnote, the caveat on human rights monitoring in the return regulation is still to be seen working in practice, but MEPs still aim to hold the commission to its obligations as guardian of European treaties, in which it monitors the implementation of EU laws. noticias.titulo: ‘Fight for our future, not their wars’: youth protests sweep across Europe
noticias.resumen: Youth movements took to the streets of Europe's cities on Friday. Organised across the continent, they demand more government spending on education, welfare and action in curbing high housing costs.
noticias.texto: Europe’s young people from more than 20 countries across the continent took to the streets on Friday (20 November), joining forces in an International Youth Strike demanding a future built around education, housing and welfare rather than militarisation and war. Under the slogan “ Fight for our future, not their wars “ , more than 50 separate youth organisations joined the initiative, creating the biggest coordinated European youth protest in recent years. “We need a better education, we need housing, we need measures to deal with the rising cost of living,” Alessandro Di Miceli, an Italian organiser, told EUobserver. The movement demands that money currently being spent on militarisation and rearmament be redirected towards education and welfare. The strike is the result of months of organising. According to Di Miceli, organisations from around ten countries began coordinating in June, before the recent wave of youth demonstrations and labour unrest across Europe that spread across the continent over the summer. Read more Europe’s youth take to the streets as the post‑war promise of a better life breaks down The forms of protest on Friday differ across countries, with some organising demonstrations and marches, while others will hold actual strikes. “The different modalities are due also to the fact that country by country, the political context is different. Also, mobilisation tactics that are used are also historically different,” said Di Miceli. This article continues, but the full version is available only to EUobserver.com subscribers. noticias.titulo: Russian cruise missiles land in Poland, drones explode over EU diplomats in Kyiv (Ukraine Battlefield update, Day 1,730)
noticias.resumen: With bridges shattered, power cut and ships burning off EU coasts, this latest Russian barrage also turns Ukraine’s struggle into a direct test of safety for millions of Europeans and the trade routes they rely on.
noticias.texto: Russian aggression has once again crossed Nato’s borders. Russian missiles damaged three Kyiv bridges, power outages hit several areas, people died at a railway station in Lviv, and a drone exploded above the Slovak EU ambassador to Ukraine. There is nowhere to hide, the Russians are attacking everywhere, a Slovak diplomat wrote from Lviv. Russians are sinking ships off the Romanian and Bulgarian coasts. The railway section of the Crimean Bridge was hit where the arch joins the pier. Ukrainian pressure towards Velyka Novosilka continues. The Ukrainian army has halted the formation of new brigades. Maps of the day — Velyka Novosilka Videos of the day — Russian weapons in Poland; a Russian drone over central Kyiv; the Russian air force receives another Su-57, while a Ukrainian pilot suggests it is not a new aircraft; HIMARS in action; a Ka-52 helicopter repelling an attack on the Crimean Bridge. Russian aggression has once again crossed Nato’s borders. Polish prime minister Donald Tusk convened a state security council after Russian weapons entered Polish territory during a massive Russian air raid on western Ukraine. According to the latest information, these were two Kh-101 cruise missiles and one drone. “We know for certain that we are dealing with Russian devices. It appears to be a deliberate provocation,” Tusk said . “It is difficult to regard it as a coincidence that the time and place of the violation of Polish airspace coincided with an exercise by the coalition of the willing in Nowa Dęba,” deputy prime minister and defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote . “This is a dangerous incident — it is a consequence of Russia’s continuing war against Ukraine,” Nato secretary general Mark Rutte added . The drones landed in the east of the country, in Molodych and Rudnik nad Sanem in the Podkarpackie region, as well as in Nowy Lipowiec in the Lublin voivodeship. This was not a minor airspace violation that could simply be brushed aside. Rudnik nad Sanem is 80 km from the Ukrainian border as the crow flies. noticias.titulo: Burnham hails UK-EU reset on food, carbon markets and youth mobility, after Brexit ‘decade of drift’
noticias.resumen: There was plenty of warmth on display at an EU-UK summit in Brussels on Friday. The agreements on carbon emissions, food and youth mobility could form the foundation for a decade of closer EU-UK integration.
noticias.texto: The ‘reset’ deal between the EU and UK ends “a decade of drift and division”, UK prime minister Andy Burnham told reporters on Friday (20 November), after concluding a series of pacts with the EU at a summit in Brussels. “It is in tune with public opinion,” said Burnham, referencing recent opinion polls suggesting that 75 percent of Britons favour closer ties with the EU and “want a better deal than the hard Brexit they were given.” At the heart of the new agreements are food, youth mobility and carbon markets. The Youth Experience Scheme (YES) will allow 100,000 young people from the EU to live in the UK for up to three years, and vice versa. This comes in addition to the UK’s participation in Erasmus+ from 2027, agreed at the first Brexit reset summit in May 2025. “Brexit did take opportunity away from young people,” said Burnham, noting that they had been the biggest single losers from the UK’s EU exit. “We missed [British Erasmus students in the EU] so much,” said EU commission president Ursula von der Leyen. “The spirit of our cooperation is win-win”. Agreements on carbon emissions trading and food and agriculture, meanwhile, align EU and UK laws. Harmonising rules on emissions trading will also give the EU and UK mutual exemptions from their carbon border taxes. noticias.titulo: Estonia’s border closure makes Russia pay a price for alleged arson, as sabotage attacks spread across the EU
noticias.resumen: After eight Latvians were caught allegedly trying to burn down an Estonian drone maker, Tallinn’s swiftly decided to close its border with Russia.
noticias.texto: Estonia decided on Friday (20 November) to close all land border crossings with Russia from 1 December, in response to ongoing acts of sabotage across Europe. “Russia’s hostile actions have consequences. This is not a response to a single incident, but to Russia’s continued aggression, sabotage and hybrid operations targeting Estonia and Europe,” said the foreign affairs minister Margus Tsahkna. “We are protecting not only Estonia’s security, but also that of the European Union and the Schengen area,” he added. The move was announced earlier this month, following an attempted arson attack on a drone manufacturing plant on 14 November. Prime minister Kristen Michal said that the recent break-in at a facility north of the capital Tallinn was part of what he called Russia’s “wider hybrid war against Europe”. According to Estonia’s security service, Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, ordered the attack. On Monday, Moscow described the accusation as “unsubstantiated” and accused the Estonian government of “building a wall” between neighbouring countries. This was the second attempted attack on an Estonian defence company in the space of several months that Estonia has attributed to Russia. What happened over the weekend, and why is Estonia responding to Russian attacks differently from most European countries? A coordinated operation Early last Saturday, several people smashed windows at the premises of Threod Systems, a company in the town of Viimsi that manufactures long-range strike and reconnaissance drones. Its website lists Ukraine and Nato member states among its customers. The attackers then poured flammable liquids into the building. However, a security guard spotted them and immediately called the police. As the investigation is being conducted in secrecy, little is yet known about the planned attack. Estonian media reported that this was not a chance discovery but a coordinated operation by Latvian and Estonian security services. Agents from Latvia’s State Security Service (VDD) had obtained advance information about the planned sabotage and passed it to Estonia’s internal security service, KAPO. Thanks to cooperation between the two services, Estonian police detained all eight suspects that same night. All are Latvian nationals. Margo Palloson, head of Estonia’s internal security service, said that Russia was behind the attempted attack and that Russia’s military intelligence agency, the GRU, had coordinated the entire operation. “This was another attempt by Russia to carry out sabotage in Estonia,” he added, saying that had it gone exactly as the attackers planned, it “would have caused the company very serious damage”. Palloson also said that no one was injured in the incident, the company was not damaged in any way, and its production and supply capacities were not disrupted. Although police detained eight people, only five were remanded in custody. “Estonia has long sought to be as transparent as possible in informing the public about Russia’s hostile activities,” Estonian security expert Henrik Praks of the International Centre for Defence and Security (CDS) in Tallinn told Euobserver. According to him, this includes prosecuting people who cooperate with Russian intelligence services, as well as publicly attributing specific attacks to Russia where there is sufficient evidence. Although the attack took place on Saturday morning, Estonian authorities and politicians attributed it to Russia as early as the following day. “This approach is based on the belief that decisive action against such activities and publicly exposing them can help deter further aggressive acts. Estonia proceeds from the assumption that Russia sees restraint and leniency as a sign of weakness that it can exploit to exert further pressure,” Praks explained. Estonia’s response will be exactly the opposite Responding to the attempted sabotage, Michal announced that the country would close all its land border crossings with Russia. He said the move was necessary to reduce the risk of further attacks and to send a “clear signal that attacks on Estonia’s defence industry and defence capabilities are unacceptable”. noticias.titulo: Feijóo promete la creación de "un mando único en inmigración" para coordinar la respuesta al problema migratorio
noticias.texto:
Feijóo promete la creación de "un mando único en inmigración" para coordinar la respuesta al problema migratorio
- Cerca de 10.000 migrantes han llegado a El Hierro en cayuco solo en noviembre
- Promete medidas para luchar contras las mafias y más protección en las fronteras
El líder del PP y candidato a la Presidencia del Gobierno, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, ha anunciado este viernes la creación de un "mando único en inmigración" si llega a la Moncloa para dar una respuesta coordinada al problema migratorio y no haya, como en la actualidad, siete ministros con competencias "echándose la pelota de uno a otro".
"El Gobierno tiene que ser responsable de sus competencias, y su competencia es la seguridad de las fronteras. [...] Voy a hacer un mando único en inmigración en el próximo Gobierno de España", ha asegurado en su visita al puerto de La Restinga, en El Hierro.
Un día después del cara a cara con Pedro Sánchez, Feijóo ha viajado a El Hierro, para conocer la situación migratoria en la isla, a donde han llegado más de 10.000 inmigrantes en cayucos en lo que va de mes de noviembre. De hecho, recibe 9 de cada 10 embarcaciones que llegan a Canarias, aunque en las últimas 72 horas, la Ruta Canaria ha dado un respiro y no ha llegado ningún cayuco a la isla. "Mi obligación es estar donde hay problemas. Aquí hay una situación critica porque han entrado tantas personas como las que viven", ha justificado su presencia en la isla.
En su viaje a El Hierro, el aspirante a La Moncloa ha visitado el puerto de La Restinga, punto al que han estado llegando centenares de cayucos en las últimas semanas, y la Confradía de Pescadores.
Responsabiliza a Sánchez de una política migratoria de "efecto llamada"
Feijóo ha responsabilizado al Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez de que en los últimos ochos años "más de 400.000 inmigrantes han entrado de manera irregular" y "sin contar los 100.000 que invadieron Ceuta" y ha culpado de ello al "efecto llamada" que hace la política migratoria del Ejecutivo. "Cuando alguien llega de manera irregular no puede tener derechos", ha defendido. Y ha recordado que el Ejecutivo es responsable de la seguridad fronteriza
Como ya ha dicho en otras ocasiones durante esta campaña electoral, el candidato 'popular' ha abogado por una inmigración "regular" y "ordenada", vinculada a un contrato de trabajo y de los que "vienen a aportar". "El que entre en España tiene que entrar de forma regular y el que no será retornado a sus países", ha advertido.
Para ello, ha planteado varias medidas, entre las que ha destacado el cambiar el Código Penal para luchar contra las mafias que "trafican con seres humanos": "Se equivocan las mafias si piensan que España es un lugar para hacer negocio", ha avisado. Además, ha prometido que va a "garantizar las fronteras de las islas" y que él pedirá la "colaboración de Frontex y Europol", no como ha hecho Sánchez, al que ha acusado de actuar de manera "soberbia" y "frívola", pues, según él, "no ha querido la ayuda" de Europa.
También ha defendido la necesidad de mantener una política "diplomática" con los países en origen para solo dar fondos a los que "cooperen con la migración regular": "Los que no cooperen, no tendrán fondos", ha avisado. Otra de sus propuestas es la modificación de la ley del menor para hacer retornar con sus familias a los menores que han entrado irregularmente.
Y ha afirmado asimismo que dotará con "más medios" materiales y más agentes a las fuerzas y cuerpos de Seguridad del Estado para "proteger" las fronteras. "Lo que ha ocurrido en Ceuta no puede ocurrir en El Hierro, ni en Canarias", ha incidido.
Por la tarde, el líder del PP ha continuado su campaña con un mitin en Santa Cruz de Tenerife, en el Auditorio Adán Martín, donde ha recordado algunas de sus medidas en materia migratoria: "Hay que averiguar la identidad de quien llega en un máximo de siete días, y la verdadera edad en un máximo de 72 horas; y hay que desplegar a las Fuerzas Armadas cada vez que lo exija la seguridad nacional", ha señalado.
Promete no dejar a Canarias "sola" si es presidente del Gobierno
Feijóo, que ha estado acompañado en Tenerife del presidente del PP canario, Manuel Domínguez, y el candidato número uno al Congreso por esta provincia, Gustavo González de Vega, se ha comprometido a no dejar a Canarias "sola" si llega a la Moncloa y ha acusado al Ejecutivo de Sánchez de "abandono". "Si soy presidente, mi Gobierno jamás dejará a Canarias sola. A Canarias ni a ninguna parte de nuestro país", ha clamado.
Además, ha asegurado que trabajará "mano a mano" con el Gobierno autonómico canario para que el archipiélogo crezca: "Canarias necesita más vivienda, y las construiremos; más obras hidráulicas, y las ejecutaremos; necesita blindar los descuentos al transporte de los residentes, y los blindaremos", ha prometido.
Durante su intervención en Tenerife ha vuelto a repasar las medidas que ha anunciado en materia migratoria por la mañana en El Hierro. "Canarias necesita apoyo y necesita un Gobierno que ponga fin al descontrol migratorio. Vengo a comprometerme con El Hierro y Canarias", ha subrayado.
Feijóo afirma haber ganado el debate pero advierte: "Tenemos que ganar las elecciones"
Por otro lado, Feijóo se ha referido al cara a cara y se ha mostrado convencido de su victoria en el debate, aunque ha apelado igualmente a pelear "voto a voto" hasta llegar a la victoria el 29-N, porque "aún queda una semana de campaña": "Hemos ganado un debate, pero tenemos que ganar las elecciones", ha incidido.
Según Feijóo, en el debate puso a Sánchez "ante el espejo de su corrupción" y ofreció "una España mejor". "Ayer hice lo mismo que llevo haciendo estos tres años de legislatura: un relato de los hechos y de lo q ha sufrido España durante este tiempo y ofrecí la alternativa la alternativa que llevo cuatro años construyendo para hacer que nuestro país funcione", ha afirmado.
También ha señalado que "España no está condenada a la degradación del 'sanchismo', sino preparada para el cambio necesario" y ha vuelto a llamar a concentrar el voto en el PP tanto los que votaron "siempre" al partido, como a los que "dejaron de hacerlo", así como a los votantes del PSOE "desencantados" y a los que "piensan abstenerse".
